title: China's securities regulator will investigate suspected manipulation of the stock market, state news agency Xinhua reports.

title: Researchers have described new fossils belonging to an extinct crocodile-like creature that had a set of serrated teeth like those of a T. rex.
text_ai: The animal was a top predator in Madagascar 170 million years ago, around the time dinosaurs roamed Earth. "We're looking at a predator that was built for power, not speed. Its skull alone was over a metre long, and the jaw muscles were enormous." Instead, it belonged to a largely overlooked group of prehistoric reptiles, the Notosuchians, which are distant cousins of modern crocodiles and alligators. Most notosuchians were small, land-based, and often herbivorous or omnivorous, making *Razana* an outlier in both size and dietary specialisation. The serrated teeth — strikingly similar to those of a tyrannosaur — are the clearest evidence of its bone-crushing lifestyle. "T. rex used its 'banana-sized' serrated teeth to bite through solid bone," explained co-author Dr. Patrick O'Connor of Ohio University. "*Razana* had the same adaptation, but it evolved completely independently. That's a stunning example of convergent evolution." "This tells us that these animals were experimenting with hypercarnivory much earlier than we thought," Dr. Wysocki added. The discovery also sheds light on the ecosystems of Jurassic Madagascar. At the time, the island was part of the supercontinent Gondwana and hosted a mix of dinosaurs, early mammals, and giant amphibians. *Razana* would have been the largest terrestrial predator in its environment, capable of tackling prey far larger than itself. "We've only scratched the surface of Madagascar's Jurassic deposits," Dr. O'Connor noted. "This find suggests there may be many more surprises waiting in the rocks." For now, *Razana* stands as a testament to the extraordinary diversity of one of evolution's most successful lineages — the crocodile-like reptiles that once ruled the land as well as the water.

title: One of the 1974 Birmingham pub bombing victims' families has had a legal aid request granted, days before inquest proceedings are due to begin.

title: A Liberal Democrat councillor and parliamentary candidate has apologised for a Facebook post made in the wake of the Manchester attack.

title: A Devon town council acted unlawfully by allowing prayers to be said at meetings, the High Court has ruled.
text_ai: Action was brought against Bideford Town Council by the National Secular Society (NSS) after atheist councillor Clive Bone complained. Mr Justice Ouseley ruled the prayers were not lawful under section 111 of the Local Government Act 1972. However, he said prayers could be said as long as councillors were not formally summoned to attend. The ruling, delivered at the High Court in London, marks the first time a court has considered the legality of prayers as part of formal council proceedings. Mr Justice Ouseley's judgment drew a sharp distinction between prayers said as part of the official agenda and those held informally before or after the meeting. Speaking after the hearing, Mr Bone, a former mayor of Bideford, said he was "delighted" with the outcome. "This is a victory for democracy and for the principle that all citizens, regardless of their beliefs or lack of them, should be treated equally by their local council," he said. "I have nothing against people praying in private or in their places of worship, but a council chamber is a secular place where the business of the town is conducted. It is not a church." Terry Sanderson, the society's president, said: "This ruling confirms what we have long argued—that councillors cannot be compelled to participate in prayers as part of their official duties. The Local Government Act is clear: councils have no power to include prayers in their formal meetings. We hope that this will now put an end to the practice in hundreds of town and parish councils." Bideford Town Council, which had defended its tradition of opening meetings with a prayer led by a local clergyman, said it was "disappointed" but would study the judgment carefully before deciding whether to appeal. The council's solicitor, Mark Luxton, said: "We have always believed that our practice was lawful and in keeping with the long-standing traditions of local government. However, we respect the court's decision. The council will now consider how best to proceed, including the possibility of holding prayers separately from the formal meeting." The ruling does not ban prayers entirely. Mr Justice Ouseley made clear that councils could still hold prayers "outside the formal meeting"—for example, as a preliminary event that councillors could attend voluntarily without being summoned under standing orders. But crucially, he said, any attempt to include prayers as an item on the official agenda would be ultra vires—beyond the council's legal powers. Professor Richard Rawlings, a public law specialist at University College London, said: "The judge has drawn a neat line between the formal and the informal. Councils cannot use statutory powers to require attendance at prayers, but they can allow councillors to pray if they choose to, provided it does not interfere with the council's lawful business." The case has reignited debate about the role of religion in public life. The Church of England, which has a long history of involvement in local governance—from parish councils to the House of Lords—said it was "disappointed" that the court had not recognised the "important place" of prayer in civic life. A spokesman said: "Prayers have been a feature of local government meetings for centuries. They provide a moment of reflection and remind councillors of their duty to serve the community. We hope that councils will continue to find ways to include prayer voluntarily." But secularist groups welcomed the ruling as a step towards a more inclusive public square. Andrew Copson, chief executive of the British Humanist Association, said: "This is a clear signal that public institutions must be neutral on matters of belief. Councils exist to serve all residents, regardless of their religion or non-religion. Prayers as part of formal meetings exclude non-believers and those of minority faiths." The judgment is likely to have implications beyond Bideford. According to the National Association of Local Councils, around half of England's 9,000 parish and town councils have some form of prayer at meetings, though the practice varies widely. Some councils, such as those in neighbouring Torridge District, have already removed prayers from their formal agendas in response to the legal challenge. In Bideford itself, the ruling has divided opinion. Town councillor David Green, who supported the prayer tradition, said: "I'm very disappointed. We're a community with a strong Christian heritage, and many people feel that prayer has a place in our proceedings. It was never compulsory—councillors could step out if they wished. Now we're losing a bit of our identity." But local resident John Harris, a retired teacher, said the council should focus on "potholes and parking, not prayer". He added: "We live in a diverse society. It's time for these old traditions to go. The council's job is to run the town, not to lead worship." The Ministry of Justice, which was asked to intervene in the case, said it was considering the implications of the ruling. A spokesperson said: "The government respects the decision of the court. We will review the judgment carefully and consider whether any changes to the law are needed to give clarity to local authorities." For now, Bideford Town Council must decide how to adapt. Its next full meeting is scheduled for 5 March. Whether prayers will be said before or after—or not at all—remains to be seen. But the legal landscape has been irrevocably altered. As Mr Justice Ouseley concluded in his judgment: "The inclusion of prayers in the formal agenda of a local authority meeting is not lawful. That does not mean that prayers may not be said. It means only that they cannot be part of the official business of the council."

title: "Collecting fresh faecal samples is not as easy as it may sound," says researcher Sanjeeta Sharma Pokharel.
text_ai: But her efforts have helped scientists in India devise a unique, non-invasive way to monitor the physiological health of wild elephants. The key has been freeze-drying dung in the field to preserve the elephant's hormones. As a result, scientists found stress levels in females were more conspicuous than in male elephants. The research, led by Pokharel and her colleagues at the Indian Institute of Science in Bangalore, is a breakthrough in wildlife management. By analysing hormones in elephant dung, they can gauge stress, reproductive health and even social dynamics without disturbing the animals. "We wanted to understand what's happening to these elephants in the wild without having to dart them or take blood samples," Pokharel explains. "Dung is a window into their physiology." The freeze-drying technique is crucial. Hormones degrade quickly in the tropical heat, so preservatives are usually added – but those can skew results. Instead, the team used portable freeze-dryers to sublimate water from the faecal samples in the field, locking in the hormones exactly as they were at the moment of defecation. The process is demanding. Fresh dung must be collected within a few hours, ideally within two. "You have to follow the elephants, wait for them to defecate, then quickly bag the sample and get it into the freeze-dryer," says Pokharel. "It's a race against time and temperature." Once dried, the samples can be stored for months without degradation. Back in the lab, they are ground into a fine powder and analysed using immunoassay techniques to measure concentrations of glucocorticoid metabolites – stress hormones – and reproductive hormones like progesterone and testosterone. The results have been striking. Across several elephant populations in southern India, female elephants showed significantly higher and more variable stress levels than males. The pattern held across seasons and habitats, suggesting a chronic underlying pressure. "We expected to see stress peaks during droughts or when food is scarce," says Pokharel. "But what surprised us was the consistent baseline elevation in females. It points to something more persistent – likely the demands of raising calves in fragmented, human-dominated landscapes." Indian elephants live in matriarchal family groups. Females carry and rear calves for up to two years, and the loss of traditional migration routes, coupled with increasing encounters with humans, appears to take a heavy toll. In contrast, males are more solitary and mobile, able to avoid conflict zones. The findings have practical conservation implications. By tracking stress hormones across time and space, managers can identify 'hotspots' where elephants are most vulnerable. They can then prioritise habitat restoration, create safe corridors, or adjust the timing of human activities – such as crop harvesting or infrastructure projects – to reduce conflict. "This tool gives us a non-invasive, real-time health check for entire populations," says Dr K. V. R. Rao, a co-author and wildlife veterinarian. "It's like a blood test for the forest." The method is already being trialled in two other Indian states, and the team plans to extend it to African savanna elephants. "If we can monitor stress remotely, we can act before populations decline," Pokharel adds. "That's the ultimate goal – to prevent crisis, not just react to it." text_ai: Linda Norgrove, 36, from Lewis in the Western Isles of Scotland, was employed by US aid group DAI. She was seized with three local staff on 26 September. Their two-car convoy was ambushed in the eastern province of Kunar. Ms Norgrove was killed by her captors on Friday during a rescue mission by US forces. The three local staff members were released unharmed shortly after the abduction, but Ms Norgrove remained in captivity. The Foreign Office said the rescue operation was launched after intelligence indicated that the aid worker was in imminent danger of being moved to a more hostile location or potentially killed. US forces, acting with the consent of the Afghan government, attempted to free her at around midnight local time on Friday. Prime Minister David Cameron said he was "deeply saddened" by the news and paid tribute to Ms Norgrove's "bravery and dedication". In a statement, he said: "This is a terrible and tragic event. I want to express my deepest condolences to Linda's family and friends. The UK government did everything in its power to secure her safe return, and I am grateful to the US forces who undertook this rescue mission in such difficult circumstances. We will conduct a full investigation into the circumstances of this incident." Foreign Secretary William Hague said he was "devastated" by the death and that the government had been working "around the clock" to secure Ms Norgrove's release. "We had been in constant contact with the Afghan authorities and our US allies. The decision to attempt a rescue was taken because we believed Linda's life was at immediate risk. It is a tragedy that despite the best efforts of all involved, she was not brought home safely." Ms Norgrove's family, speaking through the Foreign Office, described her as a "caring, talented and wonderful person" who had devoted her life to helping others. "Linda was working in Afghanistan because she wanted to make a difference. She loved the country and its people. We are heartbroken beyond words. Our thanks go to everyone who worked so hard to try to save her, especially the US forces who risked their lives. We now ask that our privacy be respected as we grieve." The aid worker, who held a degree in agricultural economics, had been working for DAI, an American development consultancy, on a project aimed at creating jobs and improving livelihoods in rural areas. Her work involved helping farmers, something she had described as "the most rewarding thing I have ever done". She had been in Afghanistan for about a year and had previously worked on similar projects in Uganda and Laos. Kunar province, where the kidnapping took place, is a volatile region near the border with Pakistan. It is a known stronghold of the Taliban and other insurgent groups, and has been the scene of numerous attacks against Afghan and coalition forces. Aid workers have increasingly become targets, with militants seeking ransom payments or using hostages for propaganda purposes. The kidnapping occurred when Ms Norgrove's convoy was ambushed on the road between the provincial capital, Asadabad, and the rural district of Chawkay, where she was overseeing a meeting with local community leaders. The attackers, who are believed to have been linked to the Haqqani network, stopped the vehicles and forced the occupants out at gunpoint. The three Afghan colleagues were released within hours, but Ms Norgrove was taken to a remote location. The rescue mission was carried out by US special forces, who were alerted to her location through a combination of human intelligence and electronic surveillance. Commandos stormed the compound where she was being held, but during the firefight, Ms Norgrove was killed by one of her captors. It is understood that no US or Afghan troops were injured. Taliban sources later claimed that the rescue attempt had actually killed Ms Norgrove, but US and UK officials have stated that she was killed by her kidnappers. The incident has raised questions about the risks faced by aid workers in Afghanistan, where the security situation has deteriorated in recent years. More than 30 foreign civilians have been kidnapped in the country in the past 12 months, and several have been killed. The British government has repeatedly warned of the dangers for anyone working in the region. Opposition leader Ed Miliband said: "This is a terrible loss. Linda Norgrove was an inspiring person who gave her time and skill to help some of the most vulnerable people in the world. Our thoughts are with her family and friends." As the sun set over the rugged mountains of Kunar, tributes began to pour in from around the world. DAI said in a statement that the company was "profoundly saddened" and that Ms Norgrove had been "a valued colleague and a tireless advocate for the people of Afghanistan". The Afghan Ministry of Rural Rehabilitation and Development expressed its condolences, calling her death "a great loss to all Afghans who are trying to build a better future". Investigations into the precise circumstances of her death are now under way, with both the US and UK governments promising to provide full briefings to the family. A teacher who taught her recalled: "She was always determined to make a difference, and she did. We are all immensely proud of her." Linda Norgrove will be remembered not as a victim, but as a woman who gave her life for the people she served. Her death, in the chaos of a rescue attempt, underscores the fragile and dangerous nature of the humanitarian mission in Afghanistan—one that continues to exact a terrible price.

title: Rescuers are to review when to continue the search for two climbers missing on Ben Nevis for a week amid "increasingly hazardous weather".
text_ai: Rachel Slater, 24, and Tim Newton, 27, from Bradford, failed to return from an outing on the mountain last weekend. The decision to suspend the search came after days of relentless snowfall, high winds, and near-zero visibility on Britain's highest peak. Temperatures have plummeted to -12C, with drifting snow and ice making conditions treacherous for even the most experienced mountaineers. "We've been facing whiteout conditions, with winds gusting up to 60mph on the summits," said John Stevenson, leader of Lochaber Mountain Rescue Team. "Our team members are highly trained, but we have to balance the imperative to search with the safety of our own volunteers. The weather window hasn't allowed us to make any progress since Friday." The two male climbers who were rescued on Saturday were found in the area of the Carn Mor Dearg arête, a notoriously dangerous ridge. They had become benighted after underestimating the difficulty of the route, suffering from early signs of hypothermia and exhaustion. They were guided down by team members and are said to be recovering. Rachel Slater, an experienced hillwalker, and Tim Newton, an engineering graduate, were last seen on Sunday 12 February. Their families have made emotional appeals, with Rachel's mother describing her as "a bright and daring soul" who loved the outdoors. Police have said they are keeping an open mind about the circumstances, but foul play is not suspected. Ben Nevis claims an average of three to four lives a year, with many more rescues. The mountain's unpredictable weather can change within minutes, catching even seasoned climbers off guard. The missing pair were believed to have been tackling the Tower Ridge route, a classic Grade 3 scramble that demands technical skill and good conditions. "We are in constant communication with the families, who are understandably devastated," added Mr Stevenson. "Our thoughts are with them, but we must now assess the risk versus reward of continuing. Any further deployment would have to be based on a genuine chance of survival, and after a week in such conditions, the realism is stark." Police Scotland has urged anyone with information, or who may have seen the pair on the mountain that day, to come forward. The review on Monday will involve mountain rescue teams, police, and the Met Office, which forecasts further deterioration with another weather front expected midweek. "We will do everything we can, within the bounds of safety," Mr Stevenson concluded. "But we are preparing the families for the worst."

title: Dame Helen Mirren has said it would be "wonderful" if it became more fashionable not to wear make-up.
text_ai: The actress recently appeared without heavy make-up alongside actresses including Nicole Kidman and Lupita Nyong'o for the 2017 Pirelli Calendar. "I don't think it's about being anti-make-up," Dame Helen explained. "Make-up can be a wonderful form of self-expression. Her remarks come at a time of growing debate over the pressure on women – particularly those in the public eye – to maintain a flawless appearance. The #nomakeup movement has gained traction on social media, with celebrities such as Alicia Keys and Cameron Diaz publicly declaring they would go bare-faced on red carpets. However, Dame Helen cautioned against turning the trend into another rigid expectation. "The danger is always that we replace one set of rules with another," she said. "If a woman wants to wear lipstick every single day, that’s her business. What I’m talking about is the possibility of a culture where not wearing make-up is just as acceptable – and perhaps even admired – as wearing it." The Pirelli Calendar, long associated with glamorous, often provocative images of women, surprised many by choosing a natural, unretouched aesthetic for its 2017 edition. Photographer Peter Lindbergh captured the actresses without heavy make-up or digital enhancement, a deliberate departure from the calendar’s usual glossy style. Dame Helen praised the decision, saying it sent a powerful message to the industry. "It was a very conscious choice by Peter," she told the BBC. "He wanted to show us as we are, not as a fantasy. And I think that’s a brave and beautiful thing to do, especially in an era where so much of what we see is manipulated." Sales of "no-makeup makeup" products – tinted moisturisers, light concealers, and natural-finish powders – have soared, while heavy contouring kits and dramatic false lashes have seen a decline. According to market research firm Mintel, the "clean beauty" trend, prioritising skincare over coverage, is reshaping the industry. Dr. Alice Roberts, a cultural historian at the University of Birmingham, said Dame Helen’s comments reflect a broader cultural reassessment. "We’ve seen a generation raised on the impossible perfection of Instagram filters," she said. "Now, there’s a growing appetite for authenticity, for real faces. Celebrities like Helen Mirren are important because they show that ageing doesn’t have to be hidden – it can be celebrated." The actress, who turns 73 in July, has long been an advocate for women's visibility in later life. She has spoken previously about the "invisibility" that women over 50 can experience in Hollywood and welcomed the recent trend towards casting older actresses in leading roles. "I’m not saying we should all go make-up free forever," she concluded. "But I’d love to see a world where a woman’s face – with all its lines, its wrinkles, its history – is simply accepted as beautiful. That would be wonderful." The 2017 Pirelli Calendar is due to be released in November.

title: A US university has bowed to pressure to sack its head basketball coach over footage of him physically abusing players and screaming homophobic slurs.
text_ai: The dismissal of Mike Rice from Rutgers University in New Jersey was effective immediately, a college spokesman said. title: A 38-year-old former soldier from Antrim who murdered his father's partner has been jailed for nine years.
text_ai: Pauline Carmichael, 61, was found dead on the shores of Lough Neagh in February 2015. The mother of seven had died from drowning. He carried her a short distance to a nearby bridge over the Mill Burn river, which flows into Lough Neagh. He added that Foster had shown "a complete disregard for human life". Defence counsel Michael Boyd KC said his client had expressed genuine remorse and had pleaded guilty at the first opportunity. "This was not an act of spontaneous violence, but one which required forethought and deliberate action," the judge said. "You carried a vulnerable woman, in her nightclothes, through the streets, and you threw her from a bridge into a river, knowing she would drown." He described the case as "deeply tragic" and acknowledged the "profound loss" suffered by Ms Carmichael’s family – who are now left to mourn a mother, grandmother and sister. Speaking after the sentencing, Detective Chief Inspector Neil McGuinness of the Police Service of Northern Ireland said: "Alan Foster has shown himself to be a violent and dangerous individual. I welcome the sentence today and hope it brings some small measure of closure to Pauline’s family, who have endured unimaginable pain." He added: "This was a senseless killing. title: Rachel Priest's brilliant unbeaten century led Western Storm to a 10-wicket victory over Yorkshire Diamonds in the women's Super League.
text_ai: The New Zealand wicket-keeper hit 106 off 65 balls, including 14 fours and three sixes, as the visitors chased down their target of 161 in 17 overs. title: A Mumbai cinema has reversed its decision to stop screening an iconic Bollywood movie after a 20-year run following an outcry from fans.

title: Cornwall may not have been poor enough to justify receiving £1bn of European Union funding, it has emerged.
text_ai: In recent years the county has several times been listed at the bottom of the poverty table in England and Wales. title: Plans for new Holyrood powers fall short of recommendations made by the cross-party backed Smith Commission, a report by MSPs has said.

title: A Chinese province is debating the introduction of a law to force people to help others in obvious distress.

title: There are times, still, when James Fowler feels awkward when he is called "gaffer".

Sir David, who is 90, said he was "thrilled" by the honour, but admitted he felt "a little bit sorry" for the supporters of the winning nickname. **A vessel built for extremes** The £200m ship is designed to be one of the most advanced polar research vessels in the world. It will be capable of spending up to 60 days at sea, carrying a crew of 30 and up to 60 scientists. Its hull is reinforced with steel to smash through ice up to a metre thick, and it will be able to operate in temperatures as low as -50C. The RRS Sir David Attenborough will be equipped with a state-of-the-art laboratory, a helipad, and a moon pool – an opening in the hull that allows equipment to be lowered directly into the water without the ship needing to dock. It will also be fitted with a remotely operated vehicle (ROV) that can explore the ocean floor at depths of up to 6,000m. The ship will replace two ageing vessels – the RRS James Clark Ross and the RRS Ernest Shackleton – which have been in service since the 1990s. It will be used to study the effects of climate change on the polar regions, including the melting of ice sheets, changes in sea ice, and the impact on marine life. Scientists will also use it to investigate the geology of the seabed, and to drill into ancient ice cores to understand the Earth's climate history. The ship will be deployed in both the Arctic and the Antarctic, and its first mission is expected to be a trip to the Weddell Sea to study the Thwaites Glacier, a vast ice stream that is melting rapidly and contributing to sea level rise. **A local boost** The construction of the ship at Cammell Laird in Birkenhead is a significant boost to the UK's shipbuilding industry, which has suffered decades of decline. The yard, which once built the great ocean liners of the 20th century, has been revitalised by the contract, which has created 400 jobs directly and many more in the supply chain. The work will also safeguard the skills of a generation of shipbuilders, many of whom had feared the yard would close. The keel-laying ceremony was attended by local MPs, including Frank Field and Angela Eagle, who described the project as a "vote of confidence" in the region. The ship is being built in more than 100 separate steel sections, which will be assembled on the slipway over the next two years. The first piece – the keel section that was lowered on Monday – weighs about 90 tonnes. It was lifted by a giant crane and carefully positioned on blocks, in a tradition that dates back to the age of wooden ships. The ship's name was inscribed on a small plaque, which was attached to the keel by a welder. The team at Cammell Laird will now begin fitting out the interior, installing the engines, and testing the systems. The ship is due to be launched in 2018, and will be handed over to Nerc in 2019, after sea trials. **A symbol of British science** The RRS Sir David Attenborough is one of the most important investments in UK polar science for a generation. The ship will be operated by the British Antarctic Survey, which has been conducting research in the region for more than 60 years. Its director, Professor Dame Jane Francis, said the vessel would "transform our ability to understand the polar oceans". She added: "The ship will allow us to explore the most remote and hostile environments on Earth, and to gather vital data that will help us predict future changes in the climate." The naming of the ship after Sir David Attenborough, who is a former trustee of the British Antarctic Survey, was seen as a fitting tribute to a man who has dedicated his life to communicating the wonders of the natural world. The broadcaster said he was "proud" to have his name on the vessel, and hoped it would inspire a new generation of scientists. "The oceans are the last great unexplored frontier on our planet," he said. "This ship will help us to understand them, and to protect them for the future." **Boaty McBoatface lives on** The submersible that bears the name Boaty McBoatface is being built by the same company, and will operate from the mothership. It is a yellow, torpedo-shaped robot that can dive to depths of 6,000m and travel for hundreds of kilometres under the ice. It will be used to map the ocean floor and to collect samples from hydrothermal vents and cold seeps. The name Boaty McBoatface has already become something of a cult phenomenon, and the robot has its own Twitter account, which has more than 80,000 followers. The team behind the submersible said they were "delighted" to have inherited the name, and promised to make it a fitting ambassador for polar science. The controversy over the naming of the ship has not entirely faded, but Nerc insists that the public vote was never meant to be a binding decision. A spokesman said the exercise was intended to engage the public in science, and that it had been "overwhelmingly successful" in doing so. The story of Boaty McBoatface has been covered by media around the world, and has become one of the most talked-about episodes in British polar science. Whether the ship itself will achieve the same level of fame remains to be seen, but for now, the RRS Sir David Attenborough is firmly on track to become a vital tool in the fight against climate change.

title: A chronology of key events:
text_ai: 1917 - Britain conquers Palestine from Ottomans. Gives support to "national home for the Jewish people" in Palestine through the Balfour Declaration, along with an insistence that "nothing shall be done which may prejudice the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities". 1920 - The San Remo conference awards Britain the mandate for Palestine. The terms incorporate the Balfour Declaration, prompting Arab protests. 1921 - Arab riots in Jaffa leave dozens dead. Britain imposes restrictions on Jewish immigration in response. 1922 - The League of Nations formally approves the British Mandate for Palestine, which includes the obligation to facilitate a Jewish national home. 1929 - Violent clashes erupt over Jewish access to the Western Wall in Jerusalem. The Hebron massacre leaves 67 Jews dead; the British evacuate the surviving Jewish community. 1930 - The Passfield White Paper recommends curtailing Jewish immigration and land purchases, but is withdrawn after Zionist pressure. 1936 - A widespread Arab revolt begins, demanding an end to Jewish immigration and a halt to land sales. Britain deploys 20,000 troops. 1937 - The Peel Commission proposes partition of Palestine into Jewish and Arab states. Arab leaders reject it; Zionist leaders accept it in principle. 1939 - Britain issues the White Paper, limiting Jewish immigration to 75,000 over five years and restricting land sales. Arab leaders reject it, while Zionists see it as a betrayal. 1940-1945 - The Holocaust kills six million Jews in Europe. Survivors seek refuge in Palestine, many arriving illegally despite British naval blockades. 1946 - The Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry recommends immediate admission of 100,000 Jewish refugees. Britain rejects the plan. Zionist militias, including the Irgun and Lehi, intensify attacks against British targets. 1947 - The UN Special Committee on Palestine (UNSCOP) recommends partition. In November, the UN General Assembly votes to partition Palestine into Jewish and Arab states, with Jerusalem under international control. Arab states and Palestinian Arabs reject the plan; Zionist leaders accept it. 1948 - Britain withdraws from Palestine on 14 May. David Ben-Gurion declares the establishment of the State of Israel. Immediate war erupts as Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Lebanon, and Iraq invade. By the end of 1948, Israel controls more territory than the UN partition plan allocated. About 700,000 Palestinians flee or are expelled. No agreement is reached on their return. 1949 - Israel signs armistice agreements with Egypt, Lebanon, Jordan, and Syria. The West Bank is annexed by Jordan; the Gaza Strip comes under Egyptian administration. Jerusalem is divided: Israel controls the west, Jordan the east. 1950 - Israel moves its capital to Jerusalem (west). The US and most countries maintain their embassies in Tel Aviv. 1956 - The Suez Crisis: Israel, along with Britain and France, invades Egypt after the nationalisation of the Suez Canal. International pressure forces their withdrawal. The UN Emergency Force is deployed to the Sinai. 1964 - The Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) is founded in Cairo, with the aim of liberating Palestine through armed struggle. Yasser Arafat becomes its leader in 1969. 1967 - The Six-Day War: Israel launches pre-emptive strikes against Egypt, Syria, and Jordan. It captures the Sinai Peninsula, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights. The UN Security Council adopts Resolution 242, calling for the “withdrawal of Israeli armed forces from territories occupied” in exchange for peace and recognition. 1968 - The Palestinian Fatah faction takes control of the PLO. Armed raids into Israel increase. 1970 - The War of Attrition between Israel and Egypt ends without territorial change. Palestinian groups operate from Jordan until the Black September conflict, when Jordan’s King Hussein expels them. 1972 - Palestinian militants kill 11 Israeli athletes at the Munich Olympics. Israel responds with targeted assassinations. 1973 - The Yom Kippur War: Egypt and Syria launch a surprise attack on Israel on Yom Kippur. Israel recovers after initial losses. Oil-exporting Arab states impose an embargo, causing a global economic shock. UN Resolution 338 calls for immediate ceasefire and implementation of Resolution 242. 1974 - The PLO is recognised by the Arab League as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people. Arafat addresses the UN General Assembly. 1975 - The UN establishes the Committee on the Exercise of the Inalienable Rights of the Palestinian People. 1977 - Menachem Begin of Likud becomes Israeli prime minister. Egyptian President Anwar Sadat makes a historic visit to Jerusalem, offering peace. 1978 - The Camp David Accords are signed, leading to a peace treaty between Israel and Egypt in 1979. Israel agrees to return the Sinai to Egypt. The question of Palestinian self-government is deferred. 1979 - The Islamic Revolution in Iran brings a new ideological challenge to Israel. 1981 - Israel bombs Iraq’s Osirak nuclear reactor, claiming self-defence. The UN condemns the attack. 1982 - Israel invades Lebanon to expel Palestinian fighters. The PLO evacuates from Beirut under international supervision. The Sabra and Shatila massacres of Palestinian civilians by Lebanese Christian militias occur amid Israeli control. A multinational force is deployed. 1985 - Israel withdraws from most of Lebanon, maintaining a security zone in the south until 2000. 1987 - The First Intifada (uprising) erupts in Gaza and the West Bank, involving mass protests, strikes, and stone-throwing by Palestinians against Israeli occupation. The PLO gains renewed international attention. 1988 - Jordan renounces its claim to the West Bank. PLO leader Yasser Arafat declares an independent State of Palestine, recognising Israel’s right to exist and renouncing terrorism. The US opens a dialogue with the PLO. 1990 - Iraq invades Kuwait. The Gulf War of 1991 sees a US-led coalition, including Arab states, expel Iraqi forces. Israel is hit by Scud missiles but does not retaliate at US request. 1991 - The Madrid Conference convenes with Israel, Palestinians (as part of a joint Jordanian delegation), and Arab states. It marks the start of direct negotiations. 1993 - The Oslo Accords are signed: Israel and the PLO recognise each other. The Palestinian Authority (PA) is established, with limited self-rule in parts of the West Bank and Gaza. The accord sets a five-year interim period. 1994 - The Israel-Jordan peace treaty is signed. The PA takes control of Gaza and Jericho. Yasser Arafat returns to Gaza. 1995 - An Israeli settler, Yigal Amir, assassinates Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin at a peace rally. Shimon Peres becomes prime minister. 1996 - Benjamin Netanyahu is elected prime minister on a platform critical of the Oslo process. The peace process stalls. 1997 - The Wye River Memorandum between Israel and the PA sets out further Israeli withdrawals, but implementation is halting. 2000 - The Camp David summit between Israeli PM Ehud Barak and Yasser Arafat fails to reach a final-status agreement. In September, the Second Intifada (Al-Aqsa Intifada) begins after Ariel Sharon’s visit to the Temple Mount. Violent Israeli-Palestinian clashes leave thousands dead. 2001 - Ariel Sharon becomes Israeli prime minister. The US “roadmap for peace” is proposed. The Palestinian Islamic group Hamas carries out suicide bombings inside Israel. 2002 - Israel reoccupies areas of the West Bank during Operation Defensive Shield, following a series of suicide bombings. Construction of the Israeli West Bank barrier begins. The UN, US, Russia, and EU form the Quartet on the Middle East. 2003 - The Quartet presents the Roadmap for Peace, calling for a two-state solution. Palestinian PM Mahmoud Abbas resigns after 100 days amid infighting. 2004 - Yasser Arafat dies in a French hospital. Mahmoud Abbas succeeds him as PLO chairman and later PA president. 2005 - Israel unilaterally withdraws from the Gaza Strip, dismantling all settlements and military installations. The Palestinian Authority takes control, but its grip is weak. 2006 - Hamas wins the Palestinian legislative elections. International donors cut aid. Tensions between Hamas and Fatah escalate. In July, Hezbollah fighters cross the border from Lebanon, capturing two Israeli soldiers. A 34-day war follows, ending with a UN-brokered ceasefire. Over 1,000 Lebanese and 160 Israelis are killed. 2007 - Hamas takes over the Gaza Strip after fierce clashes with Fatah. Mahmoud Abbas dissolves the Hamas-led government, declaring a state of emergency. Israel and Egypt impose a blockade on Gaza. 2008 - Israel launches Operation Cast Lead in Gaza, a 22-day military campaign, in response to rocket attacks. Over 1,400 Palestinians and 13 Israelis are killed. 2009 - Benjamin Netanyahu returns as Israeli prime minister. He gives a speech at Bar-Ilan University endorsing a demilitarised Palestinian state, but with conditions. 2010 - Israeli commandos board the Gaza-bound flotilla, the Mavi Marmara, killing nine Turkish activists. The event strains Israeli-Turkish relations. The PA begins state-building efforts. 2011 - The UN recommends state-building progress. President Abbas submits a bid for UN membership for a Palestinian state; it fails to get Security Council approval. The PA gains membership in UNESCO. 2012 - November: Israel launches Operation Pillar of Defense, assassinating Hamas military chief Ahmed Jabari. An Egyptian-brokered ceasefire halts eight days of violence. The UN General Assembly upgrades the PA’s observer status to “non-member observer state”. 2013 - US Secretary of State John Kerry launches a peace initiative. Talks resume but collapse in 2014. 2014 - Israel launches Operation Protective Edge in Gaza after Hamas rocket attacks and the killing of three Israeli teenagers. The 50-day war kills over 2,100 Palestinians and 73 Israelis. Hamas is severely weakened, but Gaza’s blockade continues. 2015 - Palestinian stabbing, shooting, and car-ramming attacks increase in Jerusalem and the West Bank. Israel responds with security measures and home demolitions. 2016 - The UN Security Council passes Resolution 2334, declaring Israeli settlements in occupied territories a “flagrant violation” of international law. The US abstains. 2017 - President Donald Trump recognises Jerusalem as the capital of Israel and moves the US embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. Palestinian leaders boycott US peace efforts. 2018 - Violent weekly protests along the Gaza-Israel border, the “Great March of Return”, are met with Israeli force. Dozens of Palestinians are killed. In May, the US embassy opens in Jerusalem; dozens of Palestinian protesters are killed on the same day. 2019 - The US announces its peace plan, stalled by Israeli political crises. Three inconclusive elections take place in Israel. The International Criminal Court (ICC) opens a preliminary examination into alleged Israeli war crimes in the occupied territories. 2020 - The US unveils its “Peace to Prosperity” plan, which envisions a disjointed Palestinian state and Israeli annexation of parts of the West Bank. The plan is rejected by Palestinian leaders. In August, the UAE and Israel agree to normalise relations (Abraham Accords), followed by Bahrain, Sudan, Morocco. Israeli annexation plans are put on hold. 2021 - In May, tensions escalate in East Jerusalem over the eviction of Palestinian families from Sheikh Jarrah and Israeli police actions at Al-Aqsa Mosque. Hamas fires rockets; Israel retaliates with heavy airstrikes on Gaza. An 11-day war kills over 260 Palestinians and 13 Israelis. A ceasefire holds. 2022 - Israeli-Palestinian violence surges in the West Bank, with Israeli military raids into Palestinian areas and Palestinian attacks on Israelis. The UN records the highest number of Palestinians killed in the West Bank since 2005. A fragile calm is maintained in Gaza. 2023 - In October, Hamas launches a massive, unprecedented attack on southern Israel, killing around 1,200 Israelis and taking over 250 hostages. Israel responds with a devastating military offensive in Gaza, causing widespread destruction and a humanitarian crisis. The death toll in Gaza passes 40,000 by late 2024. International calls for a ceasefire intensify, but the conflict continues into 2025. 2024 - The war in Gaza persists. The ICC issues arrest warrants for Israeli and Hamas leaders. The UN General Assembly votes overwhelmingly for an immediate ceasefire. Israel faces growing isolation. Diplomatic efforts by the US, Egypt, and Qatar fail to secure a lasting truce. The humanitarian situation in Gaza is described as catastrophic. 2025 - As the year begins, the conflict shows no signs of resolution. The Israeli military remains in Gaza. Hezbollah and Israel trade fire along the Lebanon border. The West Bank sees its deadliest period in decades. The two-state solution appears more distant than ever, while voices for a single democratic state gain some traction. The international community remains divided on how to proceed.

title: Pastor Terry Jones shares a name with one of the Monty Python troupe, and the scene outside his Gainesville church is undoubtedly a circus.
text_ai: In the searing Florida heat I counted at least 20 television satellite trucks (yes, including one used by the BBC); plus assorted technicians, camera crews and glistening correspondents (including me). On the main road, a small group of banner-waving protesters denounced the pastor's views on everything from Islam to abortion to homosexuality. The pastor himself, a man in his early 60s with a shock of white hair and a fixed, almost theatrical smile, emerged briefly from the small white church building — the Dove World Outreach Center — to address the media scrum. He spoke of a "moral obligation" to speak out against what he calls the "scourge of Islam", and promised a new protest, this time outside a local mosque, timed to coincide with the anniversary of the 9/11 attacks. His words were met with a chorus of boos from the counter-protesters, who had gathered in numbers far exceeding his own dwindling congregation. Inside the church, the atmosphere was markedly different. A handful of elderly parishioners sat in plastic chairs, fanning themselves with hymn sheets, while a large digital clock counted down the hours until the planned demonstration. Mr Jones, who shot to notoriety in 2010 when he threatened to burn the Quran on the anniversary of the 9/11 attacks — a plan he later carried out in a reduced form — seems to thrive on the attention. "The media is our megaphone," he told me, his voice cracking slightly under the Florida humidity. "Without you, nobody would know about the danger we face." But many in Gainesville are tired of the spectacle. Local businesses have reported a drop in footfall on days when Mr Jones protests. The city's mayor, Lauren Poe, described the pastor's activities as an "unwelcome distraction" and urged residents to ignore him. "We are a community of faith, tolerance and diversity," Mayor Poe told the BBC. "This man does not represent us." Yet the circus shows no sign of leaving town. Police have erected barriers and deployed extra officers, anticipating possible clashes. The local Islamic centre has been given additional security. Its imam, Dr Hassan al-Jamal, said the community had learned to live with Mr Jones's provocations. "He is a tiny minority with a loud voice," he said. "We will not be intimidated." The broader question, however, is why a man with a dwindling following commands such global attention. Media analysts point to the perfect storm of provocative language, the anniversary of a national trauma, and the endless appetite for 24-hour news. "It's a feedback loop," one academic told me. "Each broadcast fuels his sense of purpose, and each broadcast confirms to his critics that he is dangerous." As the sun set over Gainesville, the television lights flickered on. The pastor, flanked by a small security team, was preparing for his evening media round. A young woman in a headscarf walked past the church, carrying a shopping bag. She did not look up. In the distance, a police helicopter began its slow, rhythmic patrol. The circus, it seemed, would continue.

title: A council is set to drop plans to merge a Welsh-language school with a mixed language one after the High Court ruled its proposals "hopelessly flawed".
text_ai: Denbighshire council wanted to create a new bilingual school by shutting Ysgol Pentrecelyn and Ysgol Llanfair Dyffryn Clwyd in Ruthin and opening a new site. Pentrecelyn parents had campaigned vigorously against the plan, saying the school's Welsh character would be lost. Councillors have been advised to keep the school when they vote later. The High Court judge last month ruled that the consultation process leading to the proposal was "so procedurally flawed as to be unlawful". He said the council had failed to give proper weight to the unique Welsh-medium character of Ysgol Pentrecelyn, which teaches entirely through the medium of Welsh. Parent campaign group Rhieni Dros Addysg Gymraeg said the judgement was a "victory for common sense and for Welsh language education". Meirion Edwards, a parent who led the campaign, said the council had "consistently ignored the deep attachment of the community to this school". The council had argued the merger was necessary because of falling pupil numbers and the need to provide a sustainable bilingual education for the area. But the judge said the consultation was "biased" and had "prejudged the outcome". Council leader Hugh Evans said he respected the court's decision. "We have listened carefully to the views of parents and the community," he said. "The advice now before councillors is to halt the merger process and to retain Ysgol Pentrecelyn as a separate Welsh-language school." A report to the council's education scrutiny committee says a fresh consultation would be required if any future merger were to be considered, and recommends that no further action be taken on the current proposals. The Welsh Language Commissioner had also raised concerns about the plan, saying it could undermine the Welsh-medium education sector in Denbighshire. In a statement, the commissioner said the High Court ruling reaffirmed the importance of "robust and fair consultation" when changes to Welsh-medium schools are proposed. Ysgol Pentrecelyn currently has around 65 pupils. Despite a small drop in numbers in recent years, parents argued the school was financially viable and popular within the local community. The council vote is expected to be a formality, with the leaders of all three main parties on the council having already indicated they will support the recommendation to drop the merger. If approved, the council will be required to formally withdraw its statutory notice to close the school. The two schools will then continue as separate entities — Ysgol Pentrecelyn as a Welsh-medium school and Ysgol Llanfair Dyffryn Clwyd as a dual-stream school offering both Welsh and English education. Parents at Ysgol Pentrecelyn said they would remain vigilant, but welcomed the council's change of heart. "We hope this marks the end of years of uncertainty for our children and our community," said Mr Edwards. "The Welsh language is alive and well here."

title: Celtic had to rely on two late strikes before overcoming dogged part-timers Alloa Athletic and reach the semi-finals of the Scottish League Cup.
text_ai: While the Premiership leaders dominated the first half, home goalkeeper Craig Gordon was fortunate to escape with a yellow card for a foul on Greig Spence. Kieran Tierney fired against the Alloa bar, while keeper Neil Parry made some fine stops for the League One leaders. But the home side's resilience finally crumbled in the closing stages as Celtic struck twice in the space of three minutes to book their place in the last four of the competition. It was a ruthless display of character from the Scottish champions, who had been frustrated for long periods by a well-organised Alloa defence that refused to buckle under relentless pressure. ## Second-half frustration grows The second half followed a similar pattern to the first, with Celtic enjoying the lion's share of possession but struggling to carve out clear-cut chances against a deep-lying Alloa block. The visitors' game plan was evident: absorb pressure, hit on the counter, and rely on set-pieces to cause problems. For much of the half, it worked. Alloa almost took a shock lead on the hour mark. A long ball over the top caught the Celtic defence flat-footed, and Greig Spence raced through on goal. He dragged his shot wide of the post, but the warning signs were there for the Premiership leaders. Moments later, a corner from the right found Kevin Cawley unmarked at the back post, but his header was straight at Gordon, who gathered comfortably. Celtic responded with a flurry of pressure. Callum McGregor, who had been orchestrating play from midfield, saw a long-range effort tipped over by Parry. Then, a sweeping move involving Daizen Maeda and Jota ended with a curling shot from Matt O'Riley that whistled just past the post. Alloa's defence, marshalled by the experienced Andy Graham, stood firm. The visitors' goalkeeper, Neil Parry, was having the game of his life. He denied Kyogo Furuhashi with a flying save after the Japanese striker had been played through by a clever backheel from Maeda. Parry also got down well to smother a low drive from Liel Abada, who had replaced the ineffective James Forrest just after the hour mark. As the clock ticked towards the 80th minute, the tension inside Celtic Park began to mount. The home fans, who had been patient, grew restless. Chants of "We want goals" echoed around the stadium. Celtic manager Ange Postecoglou, usually calm on the touchline, was becoming increasingly animated, urging his team to increase the tempo. ## Breakthrough at last The breakthrough finally came in the 82nd minute – and it was a moment of individual brilliance. Abada, who had injected pace and directness down the right flank, picked up the ball on the wing, cut inside onto his left foot, and unleashed a curling shot that beat Parry at his near post. The ball nestled into the bottom corner, sending the home fans into raptures. It was a goal that had been coming, but the manner of it – a moment of quality from a substitute – was typical of Celtic's strength in depth. Parry had no chance; the shot was perfectly placed. Alloa's heads did not drop, however. They pushed forward in search of an equaliser, leaving gaps at the back. Celtic exploited them ruthlessly. Just three minutes later, a quick break from a corner saw McGregor release Maeda down the left. The Japanese winger drove to the byline and pulled the ball back for *substitute* David Turnbull, who arrived late in the box to sweep the ball past Parry with a clinical first-time finish. The stadium erupted again. It was a goal that sealed the tie, and Turnbull's celebration – a clenched fist and a roar – showed just how much it meant. Celtic had finally broken the stubborn resistance of the League One leaders. ## Late drama and a red card There was still time for further drama. In the 88th minute, Alloa's Andy Graham was sent off after a second yellow card for a cynical foul on Turnbull as he raced towards goal. The defender had been booked earlier for a trip on Jota, and the referee, Kevin Clancy, had no hesitation in brandishing the second yellow. Alloa finished the game with 10 men, but they had already given everything. Their manager, Brian Rice, could have no complaints about the result, though he was proud of his side's performance. "Against a team like Celtic, you have to be almost perfect," he said after the match. "We were for 80 minutes, but a lapse in concentration and a moment of magic from their substitutes was the difference. We'll take the positives from this." ## Postecoglou's praise Celtic manager Ange Postecoglou was relieved but not entirely satisfied. "It was a difficult game, as we expected," he said. "Alloa came here with a plan and executed it very well. We had to be patient, keep our belief, and eventually our quality showed. The goals came from the bench, which shows the strength of the squad. We're delighted to be in the semi-finals." He also praised the performance of Neil Parry. "Their goalkeeper was outstanding. He made several great saves, and we had to work very hard to get past him. But in the end, we found a way." Postecoglou confirmed that Craig Gordon had apologised to Greig Spence after the incident in the first half when he escaped with only a yellow card for a last-man foul. "Craig knows he was lucky. He made a mistake, but he came out and made a crucial save later. He's an experienced goalkeeper, and he'll learn from it." ## Analysis: A test of character This was a match that could have been a banana skin for Celtic. Alloa, top of League One and unbeaten in their previous nine games, came with a clear plan and executed it well. They defended in numbers, frustrated Celtic's attacking players, and posed a genuine threat on the counter-attack. For long periods, they looked capable of taking the tie to extra time. But Celtic's strength in depth proved decisive. The introduction of Abada and Turnbull changed the game, adding energy, directness, and composure in front of goal. Postecoglou's ability to change a game from the bench has been a hallmark of his time at the club, and this was another example. Equally important was the defensive work of Cameron Carter-Vickers and Carl Starfelt, who dealt with the limited but dangerous threats from Alloa's forwards. Gordon, despite his early indiscretion, made a crucial save at 0-0 and claimed a clean sheet. ## What next for Celtic? The draw for the semi-finals will take place on Monday. Celtic will be joined by Rangers, Hearts, and Kilmarnock, who have also reached the last four. For Postecoglou, the objective is clear: win the League Cup for the second season in a row. "We want to win this trophy. It's our first opportunity of the season, and we're determined to get there," he said. "But we know it'll be tough. Every team left in the competition is strong. We'll take it game by game." ## Alloa's pride For Alloa, this was a valiant effort. They may have lost, but they can take immense pride in their performance. Their fans, who made up a noisy contingent in the away end, applauded their players off the pitch. The team is still top of League One and has a real chance of promotion this season. Brian Rice added: "We've got a big league game next week, and we need to recover quickly. But the players can hold their heads high. To come to Celtic Park and push them all the way shows what this group is capable of." The cup run has also brought financial rewards for the part-time club, and they will hope to build on this momentum. ## Match statistics - Possession: Celtic 67% - 33% Alloa - Shots on target: Celtic 12 - 2 Alloa - Corners: Celtic 8 - 3 Alloa - Fouls: Celtic 6 - 14 Alloa - Yellow cards: Celtic 1 (Gordon) - Alloa 3 (Spence, Graham, Cawley) - Red cards: Alloa 1 (Graham) ## Player ratings **Celtic:** Gordon 6, Johnston 7, Carter-Vickers 8, Starfelt 7, Tierney 7, McGregor 8, Hatate 6, O'Riley 6, Jota 7, Maeda 7, Kyogo 6. *Subs:* Abada 8, Turnbull 7, Haksa 6. **Alloa:** Parry 9, Taggart 7, Graham 7, Bene 7, MacDonald 6, Cawley 6, Hetherington 6, Scougall 6, Kilday 6, Spence 7, Sammon 6. *Subs:* Robertson 6, Thomson 6, King 6. ## What they said **Celtic midfielder Callum McGregor:** "We knew it would be tough. Alloa made it very difficult for us. But the team showed great character and patience. The subs came on and made a big difference, which is what you need in these games." **Alloa captain Andy Graham:** "I'm gutted with the red card, but more so with the result. We matched them for 80 minutes. That gives us confidence going forward. We'll learn from this." ## The road to Hampden The semi-finals will be played at Hampden Park in November. Celtic, aiming for a 21st League Cup title, will be confident of reaching the final. But as Saturday's match showed, there are no easy games in this competition. Alloa's cup journey ends here, but they have earned the respect of everyone at Celtic Park. For 80 minutes, they were the equal of the Scottish champions. It was only in the final moments that the gap in class and depth really showed. The late strikes from Abada and Turnbull were brutal but fair. Celtic, as so often under Postecoglou, found a way to win. And that, ultimately, is the mark of a champion.

title: Paul Nuttall's press officer has offered to resign after saying she was to blame for "mistakes" in statements about the UKIP leader's involvement in the Hillsborough disaster.
text_ai: Mr Nuttall earlier admitted claims on his website that he had lost close friends in the 1989 tragedy were false. "I take full responsibility for these mistakes and I have offered my resignation to Paul," she said. "He has accepted it." "To use the dead and the bereaved for personal political gain is shameful," she told the BBC. "He should have known better than to make such claims without checking the facts." He has previously faced questions over his claims to have lost a close friend in the 1996 Dunblane massacre, as well as his assertion that he had a PhD – which turned out to be an honorary doctorate. Labour’s shadow home secretary, Diane Abbott, said the episode showed a "pattern of dishonesty" from Mr Nuttall. "The people of Liverpool will not forget this," she said. Conservative chair Brandon Lewis said the UKIP leader had "serious questions to answer" about his integrity. Within UKIP, there were signs of internal unease. "We cannot afford these kinds of errors in a general election year," they said. However, other party officials rallied behind him, insisting he had been let down by his staff. Ms Roughley, a long-time UKIP activist and former parliamentary candidate, said she had "no excuse" for the errors. In a statement, she said: "I was the one who wrote and authorised those press releases. Paul trusted me, and I let him down. I am deeply sorry for the distress this has caused to the Hillsborough families and to the people of Liverpool." The press officer’s resignation is not expected to end the matter. "A written apology is not enough," Mr Rotheram said. "He needs to look them in the eye and explain himself." Mr Nuttall has not yet indicated whether he will accept that invitation. An inquest jury in 2016 ruled that the 96 victims were unlawfully killed, and that a police cover-up had contributed to the tragedy. For many in Liverpool, any attempt to exploit the disaster for personal or political gain is seen as a profound betrayal. As the fallout continues, the focus will now shift to whether Mr Nuttall can rebuild trust with voters and his party. For the bereaved families, however, the damage may already be done. title: Delays for motorists going to Dover have eased but some disruption could last for weeks, police have warned.
text_ai: Kent Police said traffic was back at normal levels, after drivers had queued for up to 14 hours because of extra French security checks at the port. The additional checks are expected to continue, which means we could see further disruption in the coming weeks as the Easter holidays approach and traffic volumes increase.” The Port of Dover said in a statement: “We are pleased to report that the backlog has been processed and there are no longer queues at the port. We thank customers for their patience. However, French border controls remain in place, and we strongly advise all passengers to allow at least three hours before their scheduled departure time, particularly over the weekend and bank holiday periods.” The port also urged drivers to check the latest updates from ferry operators and ensure they have the correct travel documents, including passports and, where required, visas for entry into the Schengen area. One driver, Paul Harris from Manchester, told the BBC he had been stuck for more than 13 hours with his wife and two young children. “It was absolutely horrendous — no warning, no updates, just sitting in traffic with the kids getting restless. We missed our ferry by six hours and had to be rebooked onto a later one. I understand security is important, but people need to know what’s happening,” he said. The AA said the situation highlighted the fragility of cross-Channel travel. “When there are sudden changes at the border, the knock-on effect can be immediate and severe,” said a spokesman. “Drivers should plan for the worst, carry supplies, and consider alternative routes or timings.” Transport experts warned that the additional checks could become a recurring issue. Professor John Preston of Southampton University said: “Post-Brexit, the UK is now a third country from the EU’s perspective. French authorities have every right to carry out enhanced checks, but this can place enormous strain on a port that was not designed for such procedures. The Road Haulage Association said some drivers had faced delays of up to six hours. “This is not just about people trying to get away for the weekend — it’s about supply chains and the economy,” said a representative. A police spokesperson added: “We are working with all partners to minimise disruption. But we must be realistic: if French security procedures continue at this level, there will be days when the port cannot process vehicles quickly enough, and that means queues. Our advice is to plan ahead, allow extra time, and expect the unexpected.” The Port of Dover confirmed it had held talks with French officials about streamlining the checks, but no immediate changes were expected. A spokesman said: “The safety and security of all passengers and staff is our top priority. We will continue to liaise with border authorities to find ways to speed up processing without compromising security.” For now, travellers are urged to stay informed via official channels and avoid non-essential travel during peak times if possible. One driver, finally boarding his ferry after a 14-hour wait, summed up the mood: “I’m just glad to be moving. But I certainly won’t be doing this again next week.”

title: A crofter has lost a damages claim he had raised against Highland Council after he tripped on a paving slab.
text_ai: Iain Pocock, who lives near Tomich in the Highlands, caught a foot on a raised slab and fell during a visit to Inverness on 9 February 2012. The claim was dismissed by Sheriff Keith Grant at Inverness Sheriff Court on Friday, after a three-day hearing. The court heard that Mr Pocock, 67, a former engineer who now runs a small crofting enterprise, had been walking along Rose Street in the city centre when he caught his foot on a paving slab that had been raised by a tree root. He fell heavily, sustaining a complex fracture to his left tibia and fibula. The injury required multiple surgeries and left him with a permanent limp and chronic pain. Mr Pocock argued that Highland Council had failed in its duty of care to maintain the pavement in a safe condition. He pointed to the fact that the slab had been raised by approximately two centimetres — a height he claimed was a known trip hazard. His legal team presented photographic evidence taken shortly after the accident, showing the slab’s uneven surface, and argued that the council had been aware of the issue for months, as residents had previously reported the problem. However, the council’s defence contended that the slab’s displacement was minimal and that it had a reasonable system of inspection in place. They said the pavement had been inspected within the statutory timeframe and no defect had been noted. The council argued that Mr Pocock’s own failure to observe where he was walking contributed to the accident. Sheriff Grant, in his written judgment, said he accepted that Mr Pocock had suffered a serious injury and that his pain was genuine. But he concluded that the council had not breached its duty. “The evidence does not satisfy me that the defect was of such a nature or magnitude that the council ought to have known about it and taken action before the pursuer’s fall,” he wrote. “The inspection regime was reasonable and proportionate given the resources available.” The sheriff also noted that Mr Pocock was a “careful and cautious witness” but that he could not be sure the slab was raised to the extent claimed on the day of the accident. “Photographs taken months later do not necessarily reflect the exact condition on the date in question,” the judgment said. Outside court, Mr Pocock said he was “deeply disappointed” with the outcome. “I’m not a litigious person,” he said. “I just wanted the council to acknowledge that they had a responsibility to make the pavements safe. Now I’m left with a permanent injury and no help.” He added that the legal costs, which could run into tens of thousands of pounds, would be “devastating” for him and his family. He said he was considering an appeal. A Highland Council spokesman said: “We are pleased with the sheriff’s decision. The council takes road safety very seriously and has a robust inspection and repair programme. We sympathise with Mr Pocock’s injury but we must balance the needs of all pedestrians with the resources available.” The case has reignited debate about the liability of local authorities for pavement defects. In Scotland, councils are protected by a “three-year rule” for claims, but the threshold for proving negligence remains high. Legal experts said the ruling was a reminder that a trip alone is not enough to secure compensation — claimants must show that the council knew or ought to have known of the danger. Mr Pocock’s 2013 BBC documentary, “The Last Crofter”, charted his efforts to revive a traditional Highland smallholding. It showed him working the land despite his injury, using a walking stick. “I’ve always been determined,” he said. “But this has knocked me back more than I expected.” The injury has also curtailed his ability to carry out heavy crofting work. He now relies on neighbours and volunteers to help with fencing and livestock. He said he hoped the publicity from the case might encourage councils to do more preventative maintenance. Inverness Sheriff Court is currently dealing with a backlog of personal injury cases, many involving trip claims. The court heard that Highland Council receives around 200 pavement defect claims a year, most of which are settled or withdrawn before trial.

title: Consumers in the UK could save billions of pounds thanks to major changes in the way electricity is made, used and stored, the government has said.
text_ai: New rules will make it easier for people to generate their own power with solar panels, store it in batteries and sell it to the National Grid. If they work, consumers will save £17bn to £40bn by 2050, according to the government and energy regulator Ofgem. The plans, outlined in a joint document from the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero and Ofgem, aim to create a far more flexible energy system. Currently, the grid is designed around a one-way flow of power from large, centralised power stations to homes and businesses. Under the proposed reforms, households and businesses will be able to play an active role in balancing supply and demand. Central to the proposals are "dynamic" time-of-use tariffs, already being trialled by some suppliers. These would see electricity prices vary throughout the day, incentivising consumers to run appliances like washing machines or electric vehicle chargers when demand is low and renewables are plentiful – typically overnight or on windy, sunny afternoons. "I think this is a genuinely transformative moment for how we think about energy," Energy Secretary Claire Coutinho will tell the BBC later. "For too long, consumers have been passive bill-payers. We want them to become active participants in our clean energy transition, saving money and helping to keep the lights on." Ofgem estimates that if just half of British households adopt some form of flexibility – such as shifting their energy use away from peak times or installing a battery and solar panels – the system-wide savings could reach up to £40bn by 2050. That figure is derived from avoided costs for building new power stations, reinforcing the grid, and reducing the need for expensive gas imports. However, critics warn the benefits may not be evenly shared. The upfront cost of solar panels – typically £5,000 to £7,000 – and home batteries – £4,000 or more – remains prohibitive for many. Consumer group Which? has cautioned that low-income households, who spend a larger proportion of their income on energy, could be left behind. "Unless there is targeted support, we risk creating a two-tier system where the well-off can generate their own cheap power while those in fuel poverty continue to pay high prices," said Rocio Concha, the group's director of policy and advocacy. The government insists it is aware of these risks. It is consulting on a "flexibility guarantee" to ensure vulnerable customers are not penalised, and points to existing schemes such as the Energy Company Obligation, which provides grants for insulation and heating upgrades to low-income homes. The plans also envisage a boom in local energy trading. In future, neighbourhoods with solar panels and batteries could form "virtual power plants", selling excess power to the grid or directly to neighbours. Digital platforms would match buyers and sellers in real time, with revenues shared among participants. Industry body Energy UK welcomed the direction of travel but stressed the need for clear regulation. "Consumers need to be confident that these new products and tariffs are safe, reliable and deliver real savings," said its deputy director, Simon Cran-McGreehin. "Mis-selling scandals in the past have damaged trust – we must not repeat those mistakes." The reforms come as the UK struggles to meet its 2030 target for a fully decarbonised electricity grid. While renewable generation has surged – wind and solar provided nearly half of Britain's electricity last year – the lack of storage means power is often wasted when generation exceeds demand. Batteries, pumped-storage hydro and even hydrogen could help, but progress has been slow. Looking ahead, the government expects more radical changes could come within a decade. Smart meters – already in over 30 million homes – will become essential hubs, automatically shifting appliance use to the cheapest times. Electric vehicles, with their giant batteries, are seen as a key part of the solution: plugged in when not in use, they could feed power back to the grid during evening peaks. A consultation on the proposals will run until April, with final rules expected by the end of the year. If all goes to plan, the way Britons heat, light and power their homes will look fundamentally different – and cheaper – within a generation.

title: A cup of coffee in the evening may be keeping you awake for more reasons than you realise, scientists say.
text_ai: Their study, in Science Translation Medicine, showed caffeine was more than just a stimulant and actually slowed down the body's internal clock. A double espresso three hours before bedtime delayed the production of the sleep hormone melatonin by about 40 minutes, making it harder to nod off. The researchers, from the University of Colorado Boulder and the Medical Research Council's Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge, carried out a series of experiments to unpick exactly how caffeine interferes with our natural sleep-wake cycle. In one part of the study, five volunteers spent 49 days in a laboratory with no windows, clocks or any other external cues about the time of day. Their sleep patterns were carefully monitored under controlled conditions. On days when they were given a double espresso three hours before their usual bedtime, the release of melatonin – the hormone that signals to the body it is time to sleep – was not only delayed but also suppressed in total amount. “Caffeine doesn’t just keep you awake by blocking the receptors that make you feel sleepy,” said Dr John O’Neill, a co-author of the study from the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology. “What we’ve shown is that it also acts directly on the core machinery of the body’s internal clock, delaying its ticking. That’s a completely different mechanism from the well-known stimulant effect.” The internal clock, or circadian rhythm, is a roughly 24-hour cycle that governs everything from sleep and appetite to hormone release and body temperature. The team found that caffeine essentially resets this clock, making it run slightly longer and thus delaying the natural urge to sleep. The effect appears to be dose-dependent, the researchers say. A single double espresso three hours before bedtime was enough to push back the internal clock by about 40 minutes, but stronger doses or multiple cups could amplify the delay. The study also found that the timing of caffeine consumption is crucial. The closer to bedtime it is consumed, the more pronounced the effect. But even a morning coffee, while less disruptive, still has a small influence on the body’s circadian rhythm, the scientists noted. The findings help explain why many people find it so difficult to fall asleep after an evening coffee, even if they do not feel particularly alert. “People often think they can have a coffee and still fall asleep, but they may not realise that their quality of sleep is compromised and their internal clock is being thrown out of sync,” said Dr O’Neill. Over time, chronic disruption of the circadian rhythm is linked to a range of health problems, including obesity, diabetes, heart disease and depression. The researchers emphasise that the study does not mean coffee is harmful, but rather that timing matters. “If you want a good night’s sleep, the best advice is to avoid caffeine in the late afternoon and evening,” said Dr O’Neill. The team also notes that individual sensitivity varies, partly due to genetic differences in how quickly the body breaks down caffeine. Some people may be able to tolerate a later cup without significant effect, while others may notice a disruption even from a morning brew. Ultimately, the study underscores that caffeine is a powerful drug that acts on multiple systems in the body. For anyone struggling with sleep, the solution might be as simple as moving their last coffee of the day a few hours earlier. As Dr O’Neill put it: “We’re not saying don’t drink coffee. We’re saying be aware of when you drink it.” The research adds to a growing body of evidence that what we consume can directly influence not just wakefulness but the fundamental rhythms of our biology.
