title: Oscar Romero - the Roman Catholic archbishop murdered during the 1980-92 civil war - has been beatified at a ceremony in El Salvador attended by huge crowds.
text_ai: At least 250,000 people have filled the streets of the capital San Salvador for the ceremony. It is the last step before Archbishop Romero is declared a saint. He was shot dead by a sniper as he celebrated Mass in a hospital chapel on 24 March 1980. The ceremony, led by Cardinal Angelo Amato, the Vatican's saint-making prefect, took place in the capital's central square, known as Plaza Salvador del Mundo. Thousands more watched on giant screens erected across the city. Many held banners reading "Saint of the Poor" and "Romero, Presente." Archbishop Romero was killed by a single bullet to the heart while elevating the chalice during Communion. His assassination came a day after he had appealed in a sermon to soldiers to stop killing their fellow citizens. "In the name of God, in the name of this suffering people whose cries rise to heaven more loudly each day, I implore you, I beg you, I order you: stop the repression," he had said. His murder occurred at the start of El Salvador's brutal 12-year civil war, a conflict that claimed at least 75,000 lives. Right-wing death squads and government forces waged a dirty war against leftist guerrillas and anyone suspected of sympathising with them. Romero had become a powerful voice for the poor and an outspoken critic of the military regime, denouncing human rights abuses from the pulpit. For decades, his beatification was stalled by conservative Catholic factions who viewed him as a leftist figure, even a Marxist. Pope John Paul II, though sympathetic, was cautious. It took the election of Pope Francis, the first Latin American pontiff and a fellow Jesuit, to unblock the cause. In 2015, Francis recognised that Romero had been killed "out of hatred for the faith" – a key requirement for martyrdom – bypassing the need for a miracle attributed to his intercession for beatification. Crowds began gathering before dawn, many having walked for days from rural areas. "I was a child when he was killed, but my mother told me he was the voice of the voiceless," said Maria Santos, 57, who travelled from the northern province of Chalatenango. "Now the church has recognised what we always knew: he is a saint." The beatification Mass was celebrated under a blazing sun. Cardinal Amato read the apostolic letter declaring Romero a "blessed" martyr, and a tapestry bearing Romero's image was unveiled on the façade of the Metropolitan Cathedral, where his tomb now lies. Relics – including a bloodstained alb – were presented to the congregation. Not everyone welcomed the ceremony. Some conservative Catholics and members of El Salvador's ruling party, Arena – a political descendant of the forces that fought the leftist guerrillas – have long opposed Romero's elevation. They argue he was a political figure, not a true martyr for the faith. But the crowds on the streets were overwhelmingly celebratory. Julio Cesar Lopez, 82, a former guerrilla fighter who lost two brothers in the war, wiped tears from his eyes. "He is our saint," he said. "He died because he defended the poor. The rich and powerful feared him. Now he is finally where he belongs." The archbishop's beatification is the second-last step before canonisation, which usually requires a verified miracle. Church officials say several cases are being investigated. For the faithful of El Salvador, however, this day was already a miracle. "He was killed on 24 March 1980. Today, 35 years later, he is blessed," said Father Jose Alas, a close friend of Romero. "Justice is slow, but it comes." The ceremony concluded with the crowd singing the hymn "Firmes y Adelante" – Onward, Christian Soldiers. Many wept. For a nation still scarred by civil war, the beatification offered a moment of reconciliation – a step toward healing wounds that have never fully closed. Oscar Arnulfo Romero, once a shy, conservative priest who grew into a prophet of the poor, was at last being embraced by the church he served unto death.

title: Democrat Hillary Clinton and Republican Donald Trump have both won the most states on the biggest day of the race for the US presidential nominations.
text_ai: Alabama, Georgia, Tennessee and Virginia were among the states where both triumphed. Mr Trump was defeated by Ted Cruz in Texas and Oklahoma. Democrat Bernie Sanders won four, including his home state of Vermont. Super Tuesday sees 11 states voting on the biggest single day ahead of the 8 November presidential election. The night’s results reshaped the contours of the Republican and Democratic races, cementing front-runner status for Trump and Clinton while exposing persistent vulnerabilities for both. For Trump, victories in the Deep South and the Mid-Atlantic states demonstrated a broad appeal that his rivals have struggled to counter. He won decisively in Alabama, Georgia, Tennessee and Virginia – states with vastly different demographics and political cultures. Yet the losses in Texas and Oklahoma, where Senator Cruz capitalised on his home-state advantage and a network of evangelical and conservative activists, underscored the limits of Trump’s coalition. Cruz’s victories were decisive: in Texas, he won by more than 20 points, carrying nearly every county; in Oklahoma, he outperformed Trump by a similar margin, fuelled by strong support from rural and faith-based voters. The Texas senator, speaking to supporters in his home state, framed the results as a turning point. “Tonight is a victory for conservatives who want a nominee who will actually beat Hillary Clinton and who will keep his promises,” Cruz said, his voice hoarse from weeks of non-stop campaigning. “We have a choice: a candidate who will stand for principles, or one who will say anything to get elected.” Trump’s campaign, meanwhile, touted his national strength. “Look at those numbers,” he told a crowd at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida. “We won everywhere – except where some people wanted to play games. But that’s fine. We’re going to win the nomination, and we’re going to win the White House.” On the Democratic side, Hillary Clinton swept through the South with overwhelming margins among African-American voters, a bloc that has proved crucial to her strategy. She won Alabama, Georgia, Tennessee, Texas and Virginia by wide margins, often surpassing 70% of the vote in heavily black precincts. In Tennessee, she delivered a particularly stinging blow to Sanders, winning by a margin of 30 points. But Sanders, the Vermont senator, claimed four states – Colorado, Minnesota, Oklahoma and his home state of Vermont – demonstrating his enduring appeal among younger voters and liberals. His victory in Oklahoma was especially remarkable: a state where Clinton had been expected to win after leading in polls. Sanders’ campaign argued that the results proved his message of economic populism could resonate beyond the solidly Democratic states where he had previously won. “I am grateful to the people of Oklahoma, Minnesota, Colorado and Vermont for standing with us,” Sanders told supporters in Burlington. “Our campaign is about building a movement that will transform this country. We are winning the votes of young people, and we are winning the debates. And we are in this to win the nomination.” The delegate count told a more nuanced story. By the end of Super Tuesday, Clinton had added roughly 500 delegates to her tally, including nearly all of the 232 so-called “superdelegates” who have publicly endorsed her. Sanders had won about 300 pledged delegates. With 2,383 delegates needed to secure the nomination, Clinton’s lead was formidable but not insurmountable. The night also offered a glimpse of the general election to come. In Virginia, a key swing state, both Trump and Clinton performed strongly, signalling that the state – which Barack Obama won in 2008 and 2012 – could remain competitive in November. Trump’s victory there came despite a vigorous effort from the state’s Republican establishment to back Marco Rubio, who had hoped to emerge as the mainstream alternative to the front-runner. Rubio’s campaign, which had invested heavily in Virginia, ended the night with a disappointing third-place finish in his home state of Florida – a state that Trump is expected to win when it votes in two weeks. The Florida senator, speaking to a subdued crowd in Miami, vowed to continue. “We are going to take our message to every corner of this country,” he said. “We are not giving up. We are fighting for the soul of the Republican Party.” But the arithmetic was against him. Trump now leads the overall delegate count with more than 300, followed by Cruz with about 250, and Rubio with roughly 120. The field – which also includes Ohio Governor John Kasich and neurosurgeon Ben Carson – is increasingly winnowed, though none of the candidates has signalled an imminent exit. For the front-runners, Super Tuesday underscored both strengths and weaknesses. Trump’s appeal among white working-class voters and those without a college education remained solid, but his inability to win in states with large evangelical populations – like Texas and Oklahoma – suggested a ceiling to his support that Cruz hopes to exploit. Clinton’s dominance among black voters was a powerful asset, but Sanders’ strong showing in white, liberal states highlighted her continued problem with younger voters, who are sceptical of her ties to Wall Street and twenty years in the political spotlight. The next major tests will come in March, when states like Michigan, Florida, Ohio and Illinois vote. For now, both races are far from decided. But the contours of the battle – and the candidates who will shape it – are now much clearer.

title: Crews have taken a first look inside the Hoegh Osaka cargo ship, which had run aground in the Solent.
text_ai: The Hoegh Osaka was towed to Berth 101 at Southampton docks by four tugs, from a point between East Cowes and Lee-on-the-Solent, on Thursday. Opening the rear door on Friday revealed one of the pieces of heavy machinery it had been carrying. The crane, a yellow JCB excavator, was still secured to the deck, its tracks gripping the steel plating. It was one of around 100 pieces of plant machinery and luxury cars – including Jaguars and Land Rovers – that had been destined for export to the Middle East. The ship's interior was described as "stable" by salvage experts, but the cargo had shifted significantly during the incident on 3 January, when the 51,000-tonne vessel was deliberately beached on the Bramble Bank to prevent it capsizing after a dangerous list developed off the Isle of Wight. Hugh Shaw, the secretary of state's representative for maritime salvage and intervention, said the initial inspection was "encouraging". He told the BBC: "We've been able to get a full view of the main deck and some of the lower hold. The structure appears intact, and there are no signs of any significant leaks of fuel or oil. That's excellent news for the Solent's environment." The Maritime and Coastguard Agency confirmed that salvage teams had pumped out the water that had flooded the engine room soon after the grounding. The ship's ballast tanks were also being adjusted to keep it upright and stable while investigations continued. Attention now turns to the cause of the near-catastrophe. title: Over the past few months Democratic presidential hopeful Bernie Sanders has packed arenas for campaign appearances around the country.
text_ai: His speech before a crowd of 12,000 at Liberty University in Lynchburg, Virginia, on Monday was the first such event to start with a Christian rock band and multiple group prayers, however. His speech before a crowd of 12,000 at Liberty University in Lynchburg, Virginia, on Monday was the first such event to start with a Christian rock band and multiple group prayers, however. This evangelical university in the foothills of central Virginia's Blue Ridge mountains is certainly an unusual venue for the self-proclaimed "democratic socialist" senator from Vermont. Armed with a carefully crafted message of economic justice and moral responsibility, Sanders aimed to bridge a chasm that has long defined American politics: the divide between the secular left and the religious right. "Very rarely do I get invited to a place like this," Sanders began, his voice echoing off the arena's steel rafters. "And I want to thank you for allowing me to be here." The crowd, initially wary, offered a polite but cautious applause. Some students wore "Make America Great Again" hats; others clutched Bibles. He spoke at the conservative Liberty University during the 2016 presidential campaign, drawing a similarly large and mixed response. But this visit, coming just days before the crucial South Carolina primary and a month before Super Tuesday, felt different. It was part of a broader, calculated strategy to reach voters who have long been written off by progressive candidates — white evangelical Christians, a demographic that overwhelmingly supported Donald Trump in 2016 and remains a core Republican voting bloc. The event, hosted by the university's student government and Republican club, was billed as a "conversation" rather than a rally. But the trappings of a campaign stop were unmistakable: staffers distributed Sanders-branded stickers and buttons; volunteers held signs reading "Bernie 2020" and "Medicare for All"; and the senator's wife, Jane, sat in the front row, nodding along to his remarks. For nearly an hour, Sanders wove a narrative that blended his trademark proposals — a $15 minimum wage, tuition-free public college, universal health care — with a moral imperative rooted in the teachings of Jesus. He quoted Amos, the Old Testament prophet, who condemned those who "trample on the poor" and "turn aside the needy." He cited Matthew 25, in which Jesus instructs his followers to feed the hungry, clothe the naked and visit the imprisoned. And he invoked Pope Francis's encyclical on the environment, Laudato Si', which calls for a global response to climate change. "Poverty and economic justice are not just political issues," Sanders told the students, his voice rising. "They are moral issues. They speak to the very soul of our nation." It was a deft rhetorical move — one that sought to reclaim the language of morality from the religious right, and to frame his progressive agenda as a natural extension of Christian compassion. But the audience's reaction was mixed. Some students nodded along; others sat stone-faced. A few whispered to one another during his arguments for government-funded healthcare, a concept that many in the audience likely view as socialized medicine. "I don't agree with him on almost anything," said Caleb, a 19-year-old business major from Texas, who stood outside the arena after the speech. "But I appreciated that he came here. It shows he's willing to talk to people who don't agree with him. That's more than most politicians do." That sentiment was echoed by many students, even those who said they would never vote for Sanders. The senator's willingness to engage with conservative audiences — and his refusal to demonize them — has earned him a measure of respect among some unlikely admirers. "He's genuine," said Lydia, a 20-year-old nursing student from Virginia. "I think he really believes what he says. I just don't think it would work in practice." The event was not without its tensions. During a question-and-answer session, a student asked Sanders about his stance on abortion — a topic that the senator has long navigated cautiously. "I am pro-choice," Sanders said, drawing a smattering of applause and some audible groans. "And I believe that a woman has the right to control her own body. But I also believe that we can work together to reduce the number of abortions by making sure that every child is wanted and loved." The answer, careful and diplomatic, did little to bridge the gap. Nonetheless, his decision to appear at Liberty University speaks to a larger shift in the Democratic primary. By framing his economic policies in moral terms, he hopes to chip away at the wall that has separated the left from religious voters, particularly younger ones who may be more open to progressive ideas on healthcare and inequality. "The future of the Democratic Party lies in building a multi-racial, multi-generational coalition that includes people of faith," said Rev Dr. Susan Brooks Thistlethwaite, a professor of theology at the University of Chicago and a longtime observer of religion in politics. "Sanders understands that if he can't reach white evangelicals, he can't win the general election. But he's also signalling to the broader electorate that he's willing to engage with people he disagrees with — and that's a powerful message." Sanders has also spoken at the liberal evangelical Wheaton College in Illinois, and his campaign has hired faith outreach directors in early voting states. He has released a video in which he talks about his Jewish faith and its influence on his political views. And he has repeatedly cited the moral imperative behind his policies, from the Green New Deal to universal healthcare. For his supporters, the visit was a triumph of principle over pragmatism. "This is what real leadership looks like," said Emma, a 22-year-old student from the University of Virginia who drove two hours to attend the event. "He's not just preaching to the choir. He's going into the lion's den and talking about the things that matter." But critics, including some Democratic rivals, argue that Sanders's outreach to evangelicals is a fruitless exercise. "Bernie Sanders is not going to win over the religious right," said the Rev Dr. William Barber, a prominent progressive Christian leader and co-chair of the Poor People's Campaign. "But what he is doing is important: he is reclaiming the moral narrative from those who have twisted it to justify greed and exclusion." The event also underscored a broader question about the role of religion in American politics. For decades, the religious right has aligned itself with conservative economic policies, often citing biblical principles to justify deregulation and tax cuts. Sanders, by contrast, argues that the Bible's teachings on poverty and justice demand a different approach — one that prioritises the needs of the vulnerable over the interests of the wealthy. "It is not enough to say, 'I have a personal relationship with Christ' and then go and trample on the poor," Sanders said, echoing a line he has used before. "Faith without works is dead." The speech was not without its critics on campus. Some students walked out midway through, and others booed during his defence of abortion rights. But many stayed, and Sanders shook hands with students for nearly an hour after the event, posing for selfies and answering questions. "I might not vote for you, but I respect you," one student told him, as the senator smiled and thanked him. As the crowd slowly filtered out into the cool Virginia evening, the Vines Center fell quiet. The Christian rock band had long since packed up, and the stage lights dimmed. Outside, students debated the merits of Sanders's proposals, some animated, others reflective. It was, in many ways, the kind of dialogue that American politics so often lacks — civil, engaged, and rooted in a recognition that the other side, however wrong or misguided, is still made up of people. Whether this conversation will translate into votes remains to be seen. Sanders is not expected to win South Carolina, where African-American voters dominate the Democratic primary and have shown more support for Joe Biden. Nor is he likely to carry the evangelical vote in a general election, should he become the nominee. But by standing in the heart of the evangelical establishment and making his case, he has done something that few politicians on either side have managed: he has forced a conversation about the moral foundations of American policy. And for a candidate who has spent much of his career on the political fringe, that is no small achievement.

title: A deal has been reached between the British and Irish governments and Northern Ireland's two largest parties to resolve the current crisis.

title: Councils have welcomed an increase in the amount of money the government plans to give them in the coming year - but few are celebrating.

title: Court documents suggest the FBI paid a Geek Squad technician who located images of child abuse on a customer's computer $500 (Â£412).
text_ai: Companies that carry out computer repairs are legally required to report such images, but a warrant is required for actively searching for material. The revelation has emerged in a pre-trial motion filed by defence lawyers representing a man charged with possessing and distributing indecent images of children. The suspect, whose name is protected by a court order, had taken his computer to a Geek Squad service centre in Broomfield, Colorado, in 2018 after it began malfunctioning. According to the motion, a technician named Benjamin "Ben" Bond examined the hard drive and discovered a folder containing thumbnail images that appeared to depict child sexual abuse. Bond then allegedly contacted the FBI, which had previously trained Geek Squad staff on how to recognise such material. Over the following months, the government says Bond was paid a total of $500 in "finder's fees" for three separate cases, including this one. Defence attorneys argue that the payment transformed Bond from a private repairman fulfilling a legal obligation into a de facto government agent—one who actively searched for evidence without a warrant, in violation of the Fourth Amendment. "The FBI cannot outsource its constitutional obligations by paying a civilian to do what law enforcement would need a warrant to do," the motion states. The case has attracted attention from civil liberties groups, who see it as part of a broader pattern of law enforcement using private companies to bypass constitutional protections. "This is a classic end-run around the warrant requirement," said Hanni Fakhoury, an attorney with the Electronic Frontier Foundation. "If the government directs or incentivises a private party to search, that party becomes an agent of the state, and any evidence found must be suppressed." Federal prosecutors, however, deny that Bond was acting on their orders. In court filings, they maintain that the Geek Squad technician was simply fulfilling his company's own reporting obligations under the US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) guidelines. "The technician's actions were not directed by the FBI," the government wrote. "He independently identified the images and voluntarily contacted law enforcement." Best Buy, which owns Geek Squad, has said it has strict policies requiring employees to report any suspect material immediately and not to conduct further searches. The company says it requires repairs only to the specific problem reported by the customer, unless a technician accidentally encounters illegal content. The FBI has also defended the payment, describing it as a nominal reward for assisting investigations, not an inducement to search. Similar payments are common in other areas of law enforcement, from tips about fugitives to information about drug trafficking. Legal experts say the case could set a vital precedent about the limits of private-public partnerships in digital evidence collection. "The key question is: did the FBI's training and payment effectively deputise the technician?" said Professor Jennifer Daskal of Arizona State University's law school. "If so, then the search was warrantless and likely unlawful." A hearing on the motion to suppress the evidence is expected later this month. If the judge rules in favour of the defence, it could jeopardise not only this case but potentially dozens of others where Geek Squad technicians have received payments from the FBI since the programme began in 2016. The issue is particularly sensitive given the central role private companies play in policing online content. Under US law, tech firms must report apparent child exploitation material to NCMEC, but they are not required to actively seek it out. Critics say that paying repair technicians blurs the line between passive reporting and active searching, creating a system where profit can incentivise privacy intrusions. The defendant remains in custody pending trial. A spokesperson for the FBI declined to comment further on the ongoing litigation.

title: Chinese stocks have plunged for a second day after worries over China's slowing growth triggered a global sell-off.
text_ai: The Shanghai Composite, China's main stock exchange, fell 7.6% on Tuesday - after losing 8.5% on what state media have called China's "Black Monday". Analysts said the sell-off reflected deepening fears about the health of the world's second-largest economy, which has been showing clear signs of a slowdown. China's growth rate has dipped below 7% for the first time since the global financial crisis, and recent manufacturing data has pointed to weakening demand both at home and abroad. The rout on Tuesday began in Asia, with Hong Kong's Hang Seng index falling 5.2% and the Shenzhen Composite dropping 7.4%. European markets followed suit: London's FTSE 100 fell 2.4%, Frankfurt's DAX lost 2.8%, and Paris's CAC 40 dropped 2.9%. In New York, the Dow Jones Industrial Average opened sharply lower, shedding more than 400 points in early trading before recovering slightly. Investors appeared to be reacting to a combination of factors. The Chinese government's attempt to stabilise the market over the weekend - including cutting interest rates and easing reserve requirements for banks - had failed to quell selling pressure. Many traders believed the measures were too little, too late, and that the underlying economic problems were more deep-seated than officials had acknowledged. "The market is now pricing in a much more pessimistic outlook for China," said Daniel Morris, senior investment strategist at BNP Paribas in London. "The authorities have lost credibility in their ability to manage the slowdown, and the spillover to global markets is a sign of how interconnected the world economy has become." The falls also reignited concern about China's vast shadow banking sector, which has been a source of hidden debt. On Tuesday, the People's Bank of China injected a further 150bn yuan ($24bn) into the banking system in an attempt to ease liquidity pressures, but it did little to reassure markets. In a sign of the growing anxiety, the Chinese central bank said it was closely monitoring the situation and stood ready to take further action. However, analysts warned that Beijing's room for manoeuvre was limited, as further stimulus could fuel asset bubbles and increase financial instability. The sell-off came against a backdrop of broader global uncertainty. The US Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates as early as September, which could further tighten financial conditions and put additional pressure on emerging markets. "The combination of a Chinese slowdown and a Fed tightening is a dangerous cocktail," said Louise Cooper, a markets analyst at CooperCity. "We haven't seen this kind of synchronised risk-off move for years." As trading closed in Shanghai, state media sought to calm nerves, with the official Xinhua news agency running an editorial insisting that China's long-term fundamentals remained strong. But for many investors, the message of reassurance was drowned out by the scale of the losses - and the fear that the worst may yet be to come.

title: One of the world's largest pulp and paper producers announced on Wednesday that it had stopped clearing forests as part of its operations - but the battle to stop deforestation is still far from won, as Alice Budisatrijo reports from Jakarta.
text_ai: The firm, April, controls a million hectares of forests in Indonesia, and has now said it will allocate nearly half of it for conservation. The environmental group Greenpeace, which has previously been a fierce critic of the company, now called it a "champion" and vowed to closely monitor the implementation of the new policy. The firm, April, controls a million hectares of forests in Indonesia, and has now said it will allocate nearly half of it for conservation. The environmental group Greenpeace, which has previously been a fierce critic of the company, now called it a "champion" and vowed to closely monitor the implementation of the new policy. But for many Indonesian and international campaigners, the announcement is long overdue – and they warn that the company's track record of breaking promises means the real test lies in enforcement. April's decision follows years of pressure from environmental groups and consumer campaigns that targeted major buyers of its pulp, including household names in the stationery and tissue industries. The company had been accused of clearing vast tracts of rainforest, including peatland critical for storing carbon, and encroaching on the habitats of endangered species such as the Sumatran tiger and elephant. The new policy commits April to "no deforestation, no peat development, and no exploitation" – known in the industry as NDPE. It covers all of its suppliers and third-party wood sources, meaning the company will not accept fibre from any land cleared of natural forest after 1 September 2019. April's chief executive, Praveen Singhavi, told the BBC that the move was "a natural evolution of our business towards sustainability". He acknowledged that the company had previously "not done enough to address the concerns of our critics", but said the new policy was "comprehensive and irreversible". Yet the scale of the challenge is immense. Indonesia has the world's third-largest area of tropical forest, but deforestation rates have risen sharply in recent years, driven largely by the expansion of palm oil and pulp plantations. President Joko Widodo has pledged to halt the clearing of primary forests and peatlands by 2030, but observers say enforcement is patchy and corruption rife. April's announcement is a significant step, but it does not cover all of its holdings. The company will continue to operate in plantations established before the cut-off date, which environmentalists say could still involve the conversion of degraded forests with high conservation value. And there are concerns about how the policy will be verified, especially given the complexity of supply chains that involve many smallholder farmers and intermediaries. Greenpeace Indonesia's forest campaigner, Kiki Taufik, said: "This is a big win for the millions of people who have been fighting to protect Indonesia's forests. But we have seen many bold commitments before that have not materialised. April must now prove it can walk the talk." The company has set up an independent monitoring mechanism, with regular audits and a grievance procedure for communities and environmental groups. It has also invited NGOs to join a stakeholder advisory group. But some remain sceptical. "The devil is in the detail," said Bustar Maitar, head of the Indonesian environmental group Auriga. "The definition of deforestation is crucial. If April still allows the clearing of 'degraded' or 'secondary' forests, the impact could still be significant. We need to see the maps and the timelines." April's move comes at a time when global demand for sustainable products is rising, particularly in Europe and North America. Many of the company's customers are under pressure from their own consumers to prove that their supply chains are free from deforestation. The new policy could help April retain and attract buyers. But the battle to stop deforestation is far from won. In Indonesia, the pulp and paper industry still accounts for a significant share of forest loss. April's main competitor, Asia Pulp & Paper, made a similar commitment in 2013, but campaigners say it has been slow to implement it fully. Meanwhile, other companies continue to clear land with little accountability. Across the border in Malaysia, the story is much the same. Conservationists point out that April's policy only covers its own operations, and does not address the wider problem of illegal logging or the expansion of palm oil plantations that are often carved out of rainforest. For the activists who have spent years documenting April's impact on the ground, the announcement feels like a victory – but a fragile one. "We are cautiously optimistic," said one campaigner who asked not to be named. "We have seen these pledges before, and we have seen them broken. The only way this will work is if there is real transparency and real consequences for non-compliance." As the sun sets over the Sumatran rainforest, the sounds of chainsaws have not fallen silent. But for the first time in years, there is a glimmer of hope that one of the world's biggest destroyers of forests is trying to become its protector. The question now is whether April's conversion is genuine – and whether others will follow.

title: A drug addict who killed an aspiring child actor and his aunt during a police chase has been jailed.
text_ai: Joshua Dobby, 23, was out of jail on licence when he knocked over Makayah McDermott, 10, and Rozanne Cooper, 34, in Penge, south London, last August. Dobby had previously denied manslaughter but changed his plea last month at the Old Bailey. The court heard that Dobby, who had a string of previous convictions for theft and drug offences, had been released from prison just weeks before the fatal crash. He was driving a stolen Ford Fiesta at up to 70mph in a 20mph zone when he mounted the pavement, striking the victims outside a McDonald's restaurant. Makayah, a promising young actor who had appeared in commercials and a feature film, had been on a day out with his cousin and aunt Rozanne Cooper, a mother of three. Two other children - Makayah's younger brother and another relative - were also seriously injured in the collision. Prosecutor Oliver Saxby KC told the Old Bailey that Dobby had taken cocaine and cannabis before getting behind the wheel. He had been spotted by police driving erratically and attempted to evade them, reaching speeds of nearly three times the limit before losing control. "This was a catastrophic and entirely avoidable tragedy," Mr Saxby said. "The defendant's selfish and reckless actions have destroyed two families." In a victim impact statement read to the court, Makayah's mother described her son as a "kind, gentle and brilliant boy" who dreamed of becoming a professional actor. She said: "He had so much life ahead of him, so many plans. Now all we have are memories and a gaping hole in our lives." Rozanne Cooper's sister said the family had been left "broken beyond repair", adding: "She was taken in a senseless act of violence, and we will never get her back." Dobby, who wept in the dock as the statements were read, had initially claimed he swerved to avoid a cyclist - a defence the prosecution dismissed as a lie. He later admitted two counts of manslaughter, as well as causing serious injury by dangerous driving, aggravated vehicle taking and driving while disqualified. Sentencing, Judge Simon Mayo KC described Dobby's driving as "arrogant, dangerous and utterly selfish". He said that Dobby had shown "a complete disregard for the safety of others" and that his decision to drive while disqualified and under the influence of drugs was "a catastrophic failure of judgment". The judge added: "You knew the risks, yet you chose to take them. Two innocent people are dead because of that choice." The court also heard that Dobby had been handed a suspended sentence for robbery in 2019, then jailed for a further offence in 2020. He was released on licence in July 2022 - just weeks before the crash. The judge noted that Dobby had been given multiple chances to turn his life around, but had "repeatedly squandered them". Outside court, Detective Chief Inspector Dave Whellams of the Met Police said the case "serves as a stark reminder of the devastating consequences of drug-driving and fleeing from police". He added: "We hope this sentence brings some measure of closure to Makayah and Rozanne's families, though nothing can ever make up for their loss." Dobby was sentenced to life imprisonment with a minimum term of 16 years before he can be considered for parole. He was also disqualified from driving for life. As he was led away, members of the victims' families sobbed in the public gallery. The judge offered his condolences, saying: "The pain and grief your actions have caused will last a lifetime."

title: A football star made a marriage proposal with a specially-made babygrow for his newborn baby at Wishaw General Hospital's maternity unit.
text_ai: Hamilton Accies Greek centre-back, Georgios Sarris, asked maternity staff to dress baby Nancy in an outfit that said: "mummy will you marry my daddy?". "I had the babygrow made specially by a friend who runs a printing business in Motherwell," he explained. title: Reports from Nigeria say at least two bombs have ripped through two bus stations in the northern city of Gombe.
text_ai: At least 29 people have been killed in the blasts, a Red Cross official told the Reuters news agency. Earlier in the day, suicide bombers killed at least 11 people in neighbouring Cameroon. The group has frequently targeted bus stations, markets and places of worship in its campaign to establish a caliphate. Gombe, the capital of Gombe State, lies on the frontline of the conflict, with the group holding territory in the surrounding countryside. Despite repeated claims by the Nigerian military that Boko Haram is "technically defeated", the attacks demonstrate the group's continued ability to strike at soft targets. Rescue workers were still pulling bodies from the wreckage early on Monday. A local Red Cross official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told the BBC that the death toll could rise further as many of the injured are in critical condition. Hospitals in the city are overwhelmed, with medical staff struggling to cope with the influx of casualties. The bombings come just days after neighbouring Cameroon suffered a suicide attack in the northern town of Kolofata, where at least 11 people were killed and dozens wounded. That attack was also attributed to Boko Haram, which has carried out cross-border raids from its strongholds in Nigeria's Borno State. The United Nations has condemned the latest violence, calling for an end to "senseless killings of civilians". In a statement, the UN Secretary-General's spokesman urged the Nigerian authorities to ensure that those responsible are brought to justice. "The government says they are winning the war, but we are the ones dying." title: One of the men credited with the successful election of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is urging British Indians to reconnect with the Labour Party.
text_ai: Manoj Ladwa, a London-based political strategist, is the founder of Indians for Labour, a platform for Indians in Britain to talk to Labour politicians and policy makers. Mr Ladwa, Mr Modi's director of communications during India's general election in 2014, says Labour needs to do more to appeal to aspirational Indian voters in the UK following its disastrous election result. Now, as the party licks its wounds after a heavy defeat in the July general election, Mr Ladwa is warning that Labour has lost touch with a key demographic that once formed part of its core support. "British Indians are aspirational, entrepreneurial and increasingly socially conservative," he told the BBC in an interview. "The Labour Party under Jeremy Corbyn failed to speak to those values. It was seen as too metropolitan, too focused on identity politics, and not enough on economic opportunity and family values." Mr Ladwa, who cut his political teeth in the UK before returning to India to work with Mr Modi, is among a growing number of voices within the Indian diaspora urging Labour to rebuild bridges. He argues that the party's decline among British Indians mirrors a broader global trend where centre-left parties have struggled to connect with upwardly mobile ethnic minority communities. The numbers are stark. In the 1997 general election, Labour won an estimated 72% of the British Indian vote. By 2019, that figure had fallen to around 60%, and according to some polls, it dropped further to 54% in this year's contest. The Conservatives, by contrast, have steadily increased their share, particularly among Hindus and Sikhs from India, who now make up the largest ethnic group in the UK after white Britons. Mr Ladwa points to what he calls the "Modi factor" at home and abroad. "British Indians are proud of India's rising global stature under Prime Minister Modi. They see a leader who champions economic growth, national security and cultural pride. Labour, in contrast, has been seen as critical of India's policies - on Kashmir, on citizenship laws, and on human rights." He adds: "When Labour MPs and councillors criticised the Indian government's handling of the pandemic or its stance on religious freedom, many British Indians felt their own culture and heritage were being attacked. That's a dangerous path for the party." The Labour leadership, under Sir Keir Starmer, has made tentative moves to mend fences. In recent months, senior figures have visited Indian temples and community centres in Leicester, London and Birmingham, and the party has launched a new network for British Indian supporters. But Mr Ladwa argues these are cosmetic and that the party needs a deeper strategic shift. "Labour must stop treating British Indians as a single, homogenous block with fixed political loyalties," he says. "They are not. There are differences between Hindus, Sikhs, Muslims and Christians. There are differences between first-generation migrants and their children. Labour needs to listen to all of them, not just the loudest voices on the left." His call is echoed by other influential figures in the Indian diaspora. Lord Dolar Popat, a Conservative peer and former minister, told the BBC that Labour's problem with British Indians predates Mr Corbyn but has become entrenched. "The party has allowed itself to become captured by a small, radical fringe that is hostile to India and to Hindu culture. That is a strategic error of monumental proportions." But not all agree with Mr Ladwa's analysis. Some Labour insiders point to the party's strong performance in areas with large Indian populations, such as Harrow West and Ilford South, where local MPs have retained their seats. They argue that the headline figures hide a more nuanced picture, with younger British Indians moving back towards Labour on issues like climate change and the cost of living. "The idea that British Indians are a natural Conservative vote is a myth," said a senior Labour strategist who spoke on condition of anonymity. "Yes, some have shifted, but many others remain loyal. The challenge is to articulate a vision that speaks to their aspirations without abandoning Labour's core principles." Mr Ladwa founded Indians for Labour in 2023 as a non-profit platform to foster dialogue between the British Indian community and the party. It organises roundtables, policy forums and cultural events. So far, it has held meetings with shadow cabinet members including the party's Treasury spokesperson and its home affairs team. "The response from Labour has been positive," Mr Ladwa said. "But positivity is not enough. We need concrete action: more British Indian candidates selected for winnable seats, more representation in the shadow cabinet, and a policy platform that reflects the values of hard work, family and enterprise." He is also planning a series of events across the UK in the coming months, including a major conference in Birmingham aimed at rebuilding trust. "This is not about endorsing Labour uncritically," he said. "It's about telling the party: you cannot take the Indian vote for granted. You have to earn it." The challenge is significant. On the ground, British Indian voters describe a feeling of being taken for granted by Labour and courted only at election time. "I've voted Labour all my life," said Rajesh Patel, a 54-year-old pharmacist in North West London. "But this time, I didn't. They stopped listening to people like me." As Labour embarks on a prolonged period of reflection and renewal, voices like Mr Ladwa's are likely to become harder to ignore. The party's relationship with its ethnic minority base will be one of the defining tests of its recovery. For now, the message from one of the men who helped make Narendra Modi's electoral machine tick is clear: reconnect, or lose a crucial part of the old coalition for good.

title: Clashes between security forces and protesters have continued for a third day in the Pakistani capital Islamabad.
text_ai: The army has denied suggestions it is backing anti-government groups, insisting it is "apolitical". title: Prime Minister Theresa May has ordered a full public inquiry into the fire that engulfed a west London block of flats, killing at least 17 people.
text_ai: That figure is expected to rise, as fire chiefs do not expect to find any more survivors in the burnt-out Grenfell Tower in north Kensington. The PM said people "deserve answers" as to why the fire spread so rapidly. The first victim has been named by the Syria Solidarity Campaign as Syrian refugee Mohammed Alhajali, 23. The 23-year-old, who had been living in Britain for two years while studying civil engineering at the University of West London, was trapped on the 14th floor. His brother, Omar Alhajali, who escaped the blaze, told the BBC he had lost contact with Mohammed in the chaos. "I called him many times, but he didn't answer," he said. "I prayed he would be okay. But now I know he is gone." Friends described Mohammed as a kind, hard-working man who had fled the war in Syria and dreamed of rebuilding his home country. The Syria Solidarity Campaign said the family had been "torn apart by this horrific tragedy". The Metropolitan Police said formal identification of victims was ongoing, but warned that the death toll could rise further. Commander Stuart Cundy said the fire, which began in the early hours of Wednesday, had caused "unprecedented" devastation. "We have to be prepared for the fact that the number of those who have died may be higher than 17," he said. "The building is still being searched floor by floor, and it is a painstaking and distressing process." The announcement of a public inquiry came after mounting pressure from survivors, opposition MPs and local residents. Speaking outside Downing Street, Theresa May said she was "appalled" by the tragedy and that those affected "deserve answers". "The public inquiry will investigate the cause of the fire and the circumstances surrounding it, including concerns raised by residents about the safety of the building," she said. The prime minister added that the government would also review fire safety regulations for all high-rise residential buildings across the country. The decision to launch a full public inquiry – rather than a judge-led review – means it will have the power to summon witnesses under oath and compel the release of documents. It is likely to take months, if not years, to complete. Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn said the inquiry must "get to the truth quickly" and that residents' warnings about safety had been ignored for years. "People died because they were not listened to," he said. At the heart of the questions is the role of the building's cladding. Grenfell Tower underwent a major £8.6m refurbishment completed in 2016, which included fitting aluminium composite panels. Experts have suggested that these panels may have accelerated the spread of the fire. The BBC has learned that several other high-rise blocks in London and other cities are covered in similar material. The London Fire Brigade said it had tested a sample of cladding from the tower and found it to be "not compliant with building regulations". The government has now launched a national test of all such cladding on public housing estates. Residents of Grenfell Tower had repeatedly raised concerns about fire safety. The Grenfell Action Group, a residents' group, had warned for years that the building was a "death trap". In a 2016 blog post, they described a fire risk assessment that found "the fire policy, procedures and fire safety management are not robust enough". The Kensington and Chelsea Tenant Management Organisation, which managed the block, said it had "robust" procedures. But survivors say they were ignored. "We told them again and again – no one listened," said one resident, who asked not to be named. "Now our neighbours are dead." The political fallout has been swift. Councillors from the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea have faced angry protests from residents. The council's leader, Nick Paget-Brown, said the authority would co-operate fully with the inquiry but acknowledged that "trust has been broken". He added: "We are deeply sorry for the suffering that has been caused." Labour's leader in the council, Robert Atkinson, called for the immediate suspension of the tenant management organisation. Echoes of the 2009 Lakanal House fire, in which six people died, were present in many discussions. In that incident, a coroner called for changes in fire safety law – but critics say little was done. An inquest found that fire doors, smoke alarms and escape routes had all failed. Since then, campaigners have pressed for sprinklers to be installed in all high-rise blocks. Grenfell Tower had no sprinklers, only a single staircase, and fire doors that many survivors said did not close properly. Survivor accounts paint a harrowing picture of the inferno. Edward Daffarn, a resident who managed to escape, described the fire as a "disaster waiting to happen". "We saw the fire start in a neighbour's flat. Within minutes it had spread to the cladding and was racing up the side of the building," he said. "The smoke was thick, black and toxic. People were hanging out of windows, screaming for help. Some jumped – they had no choice." Others described using mobile phones as torches to feel their way down smoke-filled corridors, and passing children hand-over-hand down the stairs. The response from emergency services was praised, but questions have been raised about why those trapped were told to stay in their flats. The London Fire Brigade said its standard procedure is to advise residents to stay put if the fire is in another part of the building – a policy designed to limit panic and keep escape routes clear. But experts say that policy may have been disastrous in a fire that spread so rapidly. Professor Jose Torero, a fire engineering expert at University College London, said the "stay put" advice should not apply to buildings with flammable cladding. "If the fire can travel up the exterior of the building, the entire structure is at risk," he said. "The policy needs to be reviewed as a matter of urgency." A nationwide audit of similar high-rise blocks is now under way. Local authorities and housing associations have been told to test cladding, check fire doors, and confirm that fire risk assessments are up to date. The government has also pledged £1m in emergency funding for the Grenfell Tower victims. A charity appeal has raised over £4m. In the shadow of the charred tower, community vigils have been held. Thousands have gathered in silence, laying flowers and lighting candles. At one vigil, a local priest said the tragedy had "ripped the heart out of our community". Banners reading "Justice for Grenfell" have been draped over nearby railings. The anger is palpable, but it is tempered by grief. The search for the missing continues. Police are using drones, sonar and sniffer dogs to check the inside of the building, which is still smoking days later. Structural engineers are assessing whether the tower could collapse – the intense heat may have weakened its concrete frame. The area remains cordoned off. The name Mohammed Alhajali is the first to be publicly confirmed. His brother Omar has appealed for privacy for his family, but also for answers. "How did this happen?" he asked. "Why did the fire spread so fast? We want to know, so no one else has to die." The public inquiry will attempt to answer those questions. But for the families of the dead and the survivors of the living nightmare, the answers cannot come soon enough. The nation is left to mourn, and to demand a reckoning over how a tower block in the heart of London became a tomb.

title: Colin Kennedy, whose actions at the Crofting Commission were the source of a row, has been unsuccessful in being re-elected after losing by two votes.
text_ai: Last year, the commission's board apologised for its handling of a dispute with crofters over the management of common grazing land. Board members also asked Mr Kennedy to resign as convener. He refused to do so. The count for the commission elections was held in Stornoway on Lewis. Mr Kennedy, who had served as convener for five years, was defeated by his opponent, Alasdair MacLeod, by a margin of 214 votes to 212. The result, announced by the Scottish Government, which oversees the commission, means Mr Kennedy will vacate his seat with immediate effect. The row that overshadowed Mr Kennedy's tenure centred on his handling of a dispute over the management of common grazing land in the Isle of Skye. Crofters had complained that the commission failed to consult them properly before approving a new grazing committee. The board's apology last year acknowledged that "processes were not followed" and that "trust had been broken". In a statement following the election result, a commission spokesperson said: "The Crofting Commission acknowledges the outcome of the election and thanks Mr Kennedy for his service. The board is committed to moving forward and rebuilding confidence among crofters." However, the dispute has left deep divisions. One crofter from Skye, who asked not to be named, told the BBC: "This was a case of the system failing us. The board apologised, but Mr Kennedy never did. I think the voters have spoken." Mr Kennedy, who is also a crofter on Lewis, has previously defended his actions, insisting he acted within the rules and that the dispute was "blown out of proportion". He has not commented on the election result. The Crofting Commission is a non-departmental public body responsible for regulating crofting in Scotland. It manages the registration of crofts, the approval of changes to tenancies and the administration of common grazings. The convener is elected by the crofting commissioners – a panel of eight elected crofters and five appointed members. Mr Kennedy's defeat has raised questions about the future direction of the commission. Some crofters have called for a root-and-branch review of how the body handles disputes. The Scottish Government has said it will consider any proposals for reform. The election itself saw a higher than usual turnout, with 426 votes cast – a significant increase on previous elections. Officials said this reflected the level of interest in the outcome. Now that Mr Kennedy has lost his seat, the commission is expected to elect a new convener from among its remaining elected members. A date for that meeting has not yet been set. For the time being, the board will continue its work under the interim leadership of vice-convener Morag MacKenzie, who has been praised for her conciliatory approach. She said: "We have lessons to learn. I want to work with crofters across Scotland to rebuild trust and ensure our processes are fair and transparent." The row over common grazings in Skye is not yet fully resolved. The grazing committee appointed by the commission remains in place, but some crofters have threatened legal action if their concerns are not addressed. The Scottish Crofting Federation, which represents crofters, said it hoped the change in leadership would lead to a "fresh start". Chairman John MacKay said: "This election result is a clear message that crofters want accountability. We urge the new convener to prioritise listening to crofters and acting in their interests." The election of the new convener will be watched closely by the entire crofting community, which relies on the commission for the smooth running of one of Scotland's most distinctive land management systems.

title: Police have reopened a 10-year-old investigation into sexual abuse at a former County Durham detention centre, which saw two staff jailed.
text_ai: Church minister Neville Husband, who worked at Medomsley juvenile detention centre as a prison officer and store man Leslie Johnson were jailed in 2003. The pair, both now dead, were convicted of sexually abusing inmates. Durham Police has now reopened the investigation after a former inmate claimed he was also abused. The force said the new allegation had been made by a man who was held at the centre in the 1970s, and that it was "reviewing the circumstances" to see if any further offences had been committed. Medomsley, which operated from 1961 to 1987, held boys aged between 14 and 17, many of whom had been sent there for minor offences or because they were deemed to be in need of care and protection. Husband, a Church of England minister, was jailed for six years in 2003 after being found guilty of 12 indecent assaults on boys aged 15 and 16. He had been a prison officer at Medomsley from 1978 to 1982. Johnson, a store man, was jailed for three years in 2004 after being convicted of five indecent assaults on boys. He worked at the centre from 1974 to 1987. Both men died in 2019 – Husband aged 77 and Johnson aged 82 – having never faced the full extent of allegations made against them. The reopening of the investigation is likely to fuel further calls for a wider public inquiry into abuse at Medomsley. A previous independent review, commissioned by Durham Police in 2013, identified more than 2,000 potential victims who had come forward with claims of physical and sexual abuse. That review, published in 2014, found that "systemic" failures had allowed abuse to go unchecked, with staff turning a blind eye or actively covering up for their colleagues. The force said the new allegation was being treated "very seriously" and that specialist officers from the Durham Constabulary's safeguarding unit were now examining the claim. "We are committed to ensuring that all victims of abuse are listened to and that any new evidence is thoroughly investigated," said Detective Superintendent Paul Goundry, who is leading the inquiry. "This will be a careful and sensitive investigation, and we will keep the complainant updated on progress." The development comes amid growing pressure on the government to establish a full public inquiry into historic child sexual abuse in institutions, including Medomsley. The county's police and crime commissioner, Joy Allen, said she was "deeply concerned" by the new allegation and urged anyone with information about abuse at the centre to come forward. "Medomsley has cast a long shadow," she said. "Every survivor must know that their voice matters and that we will pursue justice wherever possible." The force has set up a dedicated hotline and email address for anyone wishing to report abuse or provide information. Officers are also liaising with support groups for survivors of Medomsley. The investigation is at an early stage, and police have not said whether they expect any further criminal proceedings, given the deaths of the two main perpetrators. But they emphasised that the inquiry was not closed and that they would follow any new leads.

title: St Helens scored four of their five tries after the break as they came from behind to win at Castleford.
text_ai: The 2014 Super League champions were twice behind before finally seeing off depleted Castleford at the Jungle. Second row Joe Greenwood scored two of their tries, while Jonny Lomax followed up his two tries on his comeback against Leeds with Saints' final try. Castleford had taken the lead through a well-worked try from winger James Clare, who finished smartly in the corner after a lovely offload from Jake Trueman. The hosts, playing without several key players due to injury, continued to defy the odds when half-back Danny Richardson – on loan from St Helens – dropped a goal to extend their advantage to 7-0. Saints looked uncharacteristically disjointed in the first half, struggling to break down a stubborn Tigers defence that had conceded heavily in recent weeks. But the visitors emerged from the interval with renewed purpose. Within three minutes of the restart, Greenwood crashed over from close range after a sustained period of pressure, with Lachlan Coote converting to level the scores. The pendulum swung again, however, when Castleford scrum-half Jordan Rankin – another player with a point to prove against his former club – sliced through a gap and sent Greg Eden over in the corner. Richardson’s conversion made it 13-6. That setback sparked St Helens into life. Greenwood struck again, this time pouncing on a loose ball ten metres out after a crunching tackle from James Roby had forced a knock-on. Coote’s goal tied the scores once more. Then, on the hour mark, centre Kevin Naiqama barged over from dummy half after quick ruck speed caught the Tigers napping, and Coote’s conversion put Saints ahead for the first time. Castleford refused to wilt. Richardson landed a penalty to reduce the deficit to 20-16, setting up a tense final quarter. But Lomax, who had been a constant threat with his jinking runs, sealed the win with ten minutes remaining. He collected a pass from Theo Fages 30 metres out, stepped inside the covering defence, and showed a clean pair of heels to the line. Coote added the extras for a 26-16 lead. “We didn’t start well, but we showed real character to fight back,” said Saints coach Justin Holbrook. “Castleford made it very difficult for us, especially with the injuries they’ve got. But we stuck at it and our class showed in the end.” Castleford coach Daryl Powell lamented his side’s failure to capitalise on their first-half dominance. “We played some great stuff in that first 40 minutes and should have been further ahead,” he said. “To lose the game when you’ve been in front twice is disappointing, but the effort was there.” St Helens’ victory maintains their pursuit of league leaders Warrington, while Castleford remain in the bottom half, their play-off hopes hanging by a thread. Saints will host Huddersfield next Friday, while the Tigers travel to Hull Kingston Rovers.

title: An 80-year-old man has been jailed for 18 years for masterminding an acid revenge attack on his teenage ex-girlfriend.
text_ai: Mohammed Rafiq was convicted on 12 December of inflicting grievous bodily harm on Vikki Horsman, 20. Ms Horsman was left scarred by the attack in April, when she was 19. Rafiq, of Cheshire Road, Smethwick, paid two men Â£50 to attack her after she ended their relationship, Wolverhampton Crown Court heard. The court heard that Rafiq, who was 78 at the time of the attack, had become obsessed with Ms Horsman after they met through a mutual friend two years earlier. She initially felt sorry for the lonely pensioner, but when she tried to end the relationship in March 2024, Rafiq became "vengeful and controlling", prosecutor Andrew Wallace said. "He told her: 'If I can't have you, no one will,'" Mr Wallace told the court. "He then set about planning a brutal punishment for the rejection he felt so keenly." On the evening of 22 April, Ms Horsman was walking home from her part-time job at a local supermarket in Smethwick when two men, paid £25 each by Rafiq, approached her from behind. One of them threw a corrosive substance - later identified as a strong drain cleaner - directly into her face. The attack lasted only seconds, but its consequences have proved permanent. Ms Horsman suffered deep chemical burns to her face, neck and right arm. She underwent multiple skin grafts and reconstructive surgeries. In a victim impact statement read to the court, she described how she now avoids looking in mirrors and has had to give up her dream of becoming a nursery nurse because the scarring makes children frightened of her. "I feel like a prisoner in my own body," she said. "I can't go outside without people staring. The man I trusted destroyed my life because I wouldn't stay with him. He was old enough to be my grandfather. I hope he spends the rest of his days in a cell." Sentencing Rafiq, Judge Richard Powles said the attack was "calculated, cold-blooded and motivated by pure selfishness and malice". "You were prepared to have a young woman's face burned off for the price of a round of drinks," the judge told him. "You exploited two younger men to do your dirty work, offering them a pittance for a crime that has caused lifelong harm. Your age does not mitigate your culpability - in many ways, it makes it worse. You should have known better." The two attackers - aged 19 and 21, both from the Birmingham area - were earlier sentenced separately after pleading guilty to wounding with intent. One received nine years, the other seven. Rafiq showed no emotion as the sentence was passed. He had denied the charge throughout, claiming that Ms Horsman had fabricated the story after he refused to buy her a car. The jury rejected his account after a seven-day trial. Detective Constable Sarah Evans of West Midlands Police called the attack "one of the most cruel and cowardly" she had ever encountered. "This was a man who thought he could use money to control a young woman's life," she said. "He failed. She will carry the scars, but she has shown remarkable courage throughout." Outside court, Ms Horsman's mother told reporters her daughter was "relieved justice has been done" but added: "Eighteen years can't undo the damage. He will be in his late 90s if he ever comes out. Vikki has to live with this for the rest of her life." Rafiq will serve two-thirds of his sentence in prison before being considered for release on licence. He was also given an indefinite restraining order banning him from contacting Ms Horsman.

title: A girl buried 3,400 years ago in Denmark, who became one of the country's best-known Bronze Age relics, was probably born in Germany, scientists have discovered.
text_ai: The so-called Egtved Girl was discovered in 1921 in a burial mound in the Jutland Peninsula, along with the cremated bones of a young child. She was estimated to have been between 16 and 18 when she died. It was assumed she was Danish, but this research has challenged that view. The research, led by Dr Karin Frei of the National Museum of Denmark, used strontium isotope analysis on the girl’s teeth and hair to trace her origins. Strontium is a naturally occurring element found in soil and rocks; it enters the body through food and water, and its isotopic signature varies by region. By comparing the levels in her remains with those of modern groundwater and archaeological finds, the team concluded she spent her childhood in the Black Forest region of south-west Germany – roughly 500 miles from where she was buried. “She was not a local,” Dr Frei explained. “Her teeth show she grew up outside Denmark, probably in the area of present-day Stuttgart. Then, within the last two years of her life, she moved to the Jutland region.” The analysis also revealed a striking detail about her final months. Sections of her hair, which had grown in the months before her death, contained high levels of strontium consistent with southern Jutland. But shorter sections – closer to the scalp – showed a sudden spike in a different isotopic ratio, suggesting she had made a long journey shortly before she died. “She travelled a great distance in her last year – possibly more than once,” said Dr Frei. “This is not a story of a single, final move. It is one of mobility and connection across Bronze Age Europe.” The Egtved Girl’s burial was unusually rich. Laid in an oak coffin, she was dressed in a short woollen tunic and a string skirt – a garment that left her waist bare, which scholars believe was a mark of her high status. By her side lay a bronze belt disc, intricately decorated with a spiral pattern, and a box of small personal items, including a comb and a dagger. At her feet were the cremated remains of a child, aged about five or six. The relationship between the two remains unclear, but the child’s teeth also show non-local strontium levels, though from a different region – possibly the Baltic island of Bornholm. This discovery challenges long-held assumptions about Bronze Age life. Previously, archaeologists thought most people in this period lived and died within a small area, with long-distance movement reserved for traders or warriors. The Egtved Girl’s story suggests that high-status women – perhaps sent for marriage alliances, or as part of a religious network – could travel widely. “She was not a farmer’s daughter,” said Dr Erik Jørgensen, an archaeologist at Aarhus University who was not involved in the study. “She was a traveller, a link between distant communities. This rewrites our understanding of how the Bronze Age world worked.” The research also raises new questions. Why was a young woman from Germany buried in a Danish mound with such elaborate ceremony? And who was the child? One theory is that she was a bride in a political marriage, perhaps from a powerful family in the Unétice culture of central Europe, which had trade links with Scandinavia. Another is that she was a priestess or a trader’s daughter. “We may never know her exact role,” said Dr Frei. “But we know she was important. Her burial was a statement – and it says something about the society that wanted her among them, even after death.” The findings, published in the journal *Scientific Reports*, are part of a broader effort by the National Museum to re-examine Bronze Age remains with modern scientific techniques. Similar isotopic studies on other Danish burials have revealed that many individuals – not just the elite – had travelled widely, suggesting a more mobile and interconnected society than previously imagined. For now, the Egtved Girl remains in Denmark, her oak coffin preserved in a climate-controlled room at the National Museum. But her story is no longer purely Danish – it is a European one, a tale of a young woman who crossed borders three and a half millennia ago, leaving a trace in the soil of a foreign land.

title: Housing is "too expensive" for would-be buyers to take advantage of the government's Help to Buy Isa (HTB Isa), savers have told the BBC.
text_ai: A BBC investigation found found in many areas the average price of a starter home exceeds the maximum purchase cap permitted under the scheme. Here we share your stories. Claire Etheridge, from Greenwich, south-east London, works in the capital but cannot afford to buy a home there. "I've been saving into a Help to Buy Isa for three years," she says. "I put away £200 a month, and the government bonus is a nice addition. But when I look at properties in my area, even the smallest flats go for £350,000 to £400,000. The scheme caps the purchase price at £250,000 in London. So I'm essentially locked out. It feels like a cruel joke." Claire is not alone. The BBC spoke to more than three dozen savers across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Their stories echo a common frustration: the property they can afford with the Isa's bonus is simply not available within the price ceiling set by the scheme. The Help to Buy Isa, launched in 2015, allows first-time buyers to save up to £200 a month, with the government adding a 25% bonus on savings up to £12,000 – meaning a maximum top-up of £3,000. The bonus is paid when the saver completes a home purchase. However, the property must be priced at or below £250,000 in London, or £450,000 elsewhere in the UK. In practice, those limits have not kept pace with house price inflation. According to the Office for National Statistics, the average first-time buyer home in London now costs over £500,000 – double the Isa cap. Even in more affordable regions, such as the North West, the average starter home is currently around £205,000, dangerously close to the £250,000 ceiling. In some parts of the South East, properties under £250,000 have become extremely scarce, particularly in desirable commuter towns. Sarah Jenkins, 34, from Reading, told the BBC she had been saving diligently for four years. "I've got about £8,000 saved, plus the government bonus, so I'd have over £10,000 for a deposit. But the only options under £250,000 in my area are tiny studio flats that need complete renovation – or flats with 999-year leases but exorbitant ground rents. The house I could actually live in costs £280,000. That's just £30,000 over the cap, but it might as well be a million for how impossible it makes things." The government has acknowledged the frustration. A Department for Levelling Up, Housing and Communities spokesperson said: "The Help to Buy Isa has supported over 400,000 completions since its launch. We keep all schemes under review to ensure they remain effective. However, the housing market is complex, and we cannot simply raise the caps without considering the broader impact on affordability and public finances." Critics argue the scheme has become a victim of its own success – but also of its rigidity. "The caps were set when the market was very different," says Neil Bennett, a housing analyst at the Centre for Policy Studies. "In 2015, the average London home cost just over £400,000. Now it's above half a million. The Isa hasn't moved. Meanwhile, the newer Lifetime Isa has a cap of £450,000 across the country, which is more generous but still insufficient in the South East." For many savers, the Help to Buy Isa has turned into a long-term waiting game. "I'm using mine like a regular savings account now," says James McLeod, 29, from Manchester. "I've got £6,000 in it, but I don't even check house prices anymore. The bonus is nice, but it's not making homeownership possible. I need a 15% deposit and a salary that keeps up with inflation." Some have given up entirely. Anna West, 31, from Birmingham, closed her Isa and used the money for a car. "The bonus was only £600 after three years. I looked at houses under £250,000 and they were all in areas I wouldn't want to live. It felt pointless." The BBC investigation also found that in 12 of the 20 largest local housing markets, fewer than one in five properties for sale fell under the relevant cap. In parts of London, that figure drops to below one in 20. The government is currently running a review of first-time buyer support schemes, with a decision expected in the autumn. Savers like Claire say they want action, not analysis. "I have the savings, I have the bonus, I have the commitment – but I don't have a home. That's the one thing the Help to Buy Isa cannot give me."
prefix: A BBC investigation found found in many areas the average price of a starter home exceeds the maximum purchase cap permitted under the scheme. Here we share your stories. Claire Etheridge, from Greenwich, south-east London, works in the capital but cannot afford to buy a home there.

title: A group of Native American actors have walked off the set of an Adam Sandler comedy, claiming the film is "totally disrespectful" of Apache culture.
text_ai: Nine actors quit the set of Western satire The Ridiculous Six this week over its portrayal of Native Americans. But Netflix, which commissioned the film, said it was a "broad satire" intended to send up stereotypes. "The movie has 'ridiculous' in the title for a reason: Because it is ridiculous," a Netflix statement said. The walkout, which occurred on Tuesday in New Mexico, involved actors from the film’s Native American cast who objected to scenes they said mocked Apache customs and traditional dress. Among them was actor Loren Anthony, a member of the Navajo Nation, who told the BBC he felt “humiliated” after seeing the script’s depiction of a medicine man and a scene in which Apache women were portrayed as sexually promiscuous. “We were told this would be a comedy that poked fun at Hollywood’s old Western tropes,” Anthony said. “Instead, it was just the same old stereotypes dressed up in a modern production. The joke was on us.” The Ridiculous Six, directed by Frank Coraci and co-produced by Sandler’s Happy Madison Productions, is described as a satirical take on classic Westerns. It features Sandler as an outlaw who assembles a team of misfits to track down his father. The film’s title itself is a nod to the 1960s film The Magnificent Seven. But critics of the walkout argue that satire can only work if the audience recognises the absurdity—and that the Apache portrayals were not clearly framed as parody. Native American advocacy groups have long criticised Hollywood for historical misrepresentation. Jacqueline Keeler, a writer and activist with the Navajo Nation, said the walkout was “a long-overdue stand”. She added: “Netflix’s claim of ‘broad satire’ is a weak defence. The industry needs to listen to the people whose stories are being trivialised.” Netflix did not confirm whether production would be delayed but insisted the film’s intent was “to entertain, not to offend”. A source close to the production said Sandler had been “genuinely surprised” by the reaction and had offered to rework the offending scenes. However, Anthony said the actors were not given a chance to provide input before the walkout. “We were hired as background performers, not consultants,” he said. “If they want authenticity, they should have brought us in from the start. Instead, they assumed we would just go along with it.” The incident comes amid a broader reckoning in Hollywood over the treatment of minority communities. Last year, the film Pan faced backlash for casting Rooney Mara as a Native American character. And earlier this year, Disney’s Moana was praised for its cultural consultation but still drew criticism for some depictions. The Ridiculous Six is set for release later this year. Whether the walkout will prompt lasting changes—or simply be dismissed as another Hollywood tempest—remains to be seen. For now, the actors who left are waiting to see if the studio will take their concerns seriously. “We’re not asking for special treatment,” Anthony said. “Just basic respect for a culture that has been mocked for far too long.”

title: A vast and hidden field of small black holes predicted to be near the centre of our galaxy could be revealed as a giant gas cloud passes by.
text_ai: The G2 cloud is as large as our Solar System, and bound for a "supermassive" black hole at the Milky Way's core. On the way, it should encounter many black holes just tens of km across.
