The mechanism, proposed by a team of astrophysicists from the University of Michigan and the University of California, Berkeley, hinges on the unique properties of the G2 cloud. First spotted by astronomers in 2011, this vast agglomeration of hydrogen and helium gas has been a source of intrigue ever since it was observed hurtling towards Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), the Milky Way’s central supermassive black hole, four million times the mass of our Sun. Initially thought to be a hydrogen gas cloud, G2’s origin remains debated — some researchers argue it could be the stripped remains of a star, or perhaps a pair of binary stars that merged. Whatever its true nature, its trajectory has been mapped with increasing precision, and in 2014 it made its closest approach to Sgr A*, passing within 200 times the Earth-Sun distance. During that flyby, telescopes saw only a slight flicker in X-ray emission, leaving many astronomers puzzled. But the new study, published in the journal *Physical Review Letters*, proposes that the real fireworks are yet to come. As G2 continues its orbit around Sgr A* — an orbit that will take it back through the galactic centre in the coming decades — it will extend into a long, looping streamer of gas, stretched by tidal forces. And it is on this return journey that the cloud is predicted to sweep through a vast, hidden population of black holes: the elusive "intermediate-mass" and "stellar-mass" variety, ranging from a few times the mass of the Sun to hundreds of thousands of solar masses. These smaller black holes are thought to cluster in the Milky Way's innermost region, a dense swarm of dark objects that has long been speculated to exist but has never been directly observed. Traditional optical and radio telescopes struggle to spot them because they emit no light unless they are actively accreting matter. However, the passage of G2 offers a rare natural experiment. "It's like throwing a net into the dark ocean," said Dr. Elena Rossi, an astrophysicist at the University of Michigan and lead author of the study. "The gas cloud will disturb the invisible black holes, causing them to briefly flare up as they consume some of the gas." The process works as follows: as G2’s gas streams past a black hole, the extreme gravity of the black hole will accelerate and heat the gas, causing it to glow in X-rays before it crosses the event horizon. The rotation of the black hole — a property known as spin — will further torque the inflowing gas, shaping the X-ray emission into distinctive patterns. By analysing the timing and energy of these X-ray bursts, astronomers could not only count the number of black holes but also measure their masses and spins. "In principle, we could map out the entire population of black holes in the galactic centre," said co-author Prof. Jeremiah Ostriker of Princeton University. "This would test fundamental theories of how black holes form and grow, and how they influence the evolution of the galaxy." The upcoming decade is crucial. The G2 cloud is expected to produce its most obvious effects as it swings back toward Sgr A* in the 2030s. By then, new X-ray observatories such as the European Space Agency’s Athena mission and NASA’s Lynx X-ray Observatory should be operational, offering sensitivity an order of magnitude greater than current instruments. Meanwhile, the Event Horizon Telescope, which famously imaged the shadow of the supermassive black hole in 2019, could also spot smaller black holes if their patches of glowing gas are sufficiently bright. If the predictions hold, astronomers will finally have a direct census of the black holes that lurk in the heart of our galaxy. It would confirm a long-held suspicion that the Milky Way’s centre contains not just a giant black hole, but an entire dark ecosystem of smaller ones — objects that may have been scattered there by past collisions, or formed directly from collapsing gas in the early universe. And it would offer a glimpse into a hidden world that has remained, until now, completely invisible to our telescopes.

title: George Bernard Shaw once said that "censorships exist to prevent anyone from challenging current conceptions and existing institutions".

The execution was widely supported by many in India, but also drew criticism from human rights organisations and some legal experts, who argued that Memon’s mental health had deteriorated and that he had not received a fair trial. The networks have denied any wrongdoing. NDTV called the notice "a clear attempt to intimidate the media" and said it would challenge it in court. Times Now said it had "acted responsibly" and that the government's action was "an attack on free speech". The editors’ guild of India issued a statement condemning the notices as "a dangerous precedent" and said the government was "trying to dictate what the media can and cannot say". Congress leader Rahul Gandhi said on Twitter: "First it was the judiciary, then the civil society, now it’s the media. The BJP is trying to create a culture of fear." But government officials insist they are merely enforcing existing laws. "There is a code of conduct that every broadcaster has to follow," a senior ministry official told the BBC on condition of anonymity. "We are not saying they cannot criticise the government. But they cannot incite violence or spread misinformation." The issue has reignited a broader debate about the state of press freedom in India. In the latest World Press Freedom Index by Reporters Without Borders, India slipped to 138th out of 180 countries, a drop of 11 places from the previous year. The report cited "increasing political pressure on journalists" and "a climate of impunity for attacks on the media". Legal experts point out that the Cable Television Networks Rules – first enacted in 1995 and amended several times – give the government sweeping powers. The rules prohibit any content that is "likely to incite violence" or "offend good taste or decency". But the terms are vague, critics say, and are often applied selectively. "The government has used these rules before to crack down on channels that are critical of it," said Amrita Basu, a media law scholar at the University of Delhi. "What is new is the speed and the aggressiveness with which it is doing so now." The timing is also significant. The notices came just days after the government announced that it would appoint a new "media adviser" to the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting – a role that some see as a further step to centralise control over news content. Internationally, the incident has drawn attention. The US State Department said it was "concerned by reports of pressure on Indian media" and called for "respect for freedom of expression". The United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights also urged India to "ensure that journalists can do their work without fear of reprisal". The Indian government has pushed back, saying it does not need foreign lectures. "India is the world’s largest democracy, and we protect free speech," said a statement from the Ministry of External Affairs. "But no democracy can allow its media to recklessly spread lies." The three networks have until the end of this week to reply to the show-cause notices. If found guilty, they could face fines or even temporary suspension of their broadcast licences. Legal experts say the outcome of this case could set a significant precedent for how India’s media operates in the future. For now, newsrooms across the country are watching closely. Many journalists say they feel compelled to self-censor on sensitive subjects – especially those involving terrorism, religion, and national security – for fear of running afoul of the government. "This is exactly what Shaw meant," said noted Indian journalist and author Nilanjana Roy. "Censorship doesn't have to be overt to be effective. Just the threat of it is enough to chill the air."

title: Great Britain's Adam Peaty won 50m breaststroke gold at the World Swimming Championships to become the first man to complete the 50m and 100m double.
text_ai: The 20-year-old then helped GB win mixed 4x100m medley relay gold in a world record time in Kazan. "To come away with three golds is more than I could have hoped for. I'm just so proud to be part of this team." Britain's head coach Bill Furniss praised Peaty's maturity and consistency: "Adam is a phenomenal athlete. To perform under pressure the way he has all week, and then deliver in that relay, shows what a special talent he is. The future is very bright." Peaty will now turn his attention to next year's Olympic Games in Rio de Janeiro, where he will be a strong favourite in both breaststroke events. "I'm not thinking about Rio yet," he said. "I'm going to enjoy this moment. But when the time comes, I'll be ready."

title: Six million people with defined benefit pensions have seen their transfer values shoot up in the last year, according to a major insurance company.
text_ai: Under the rules of most defined benefit schemes, workers have the right to swap their pension entitlement for money. "The trade-off is that you lose a guaranteed, inflation-linked income for life, and you take on the risk of managing that money yourself." Many schemes use CPI to calculate annual increases, and the recent surge in CPI has pushed up the value of pension promises. Royal London said that in the first three months of this year, requests for transfer values rose by a fifth compared with the same period last year. But the regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), has repeatedly warned that transferring out of a defined benefit pension is "high risk" and should only be considered by those who have taken independent financial advice. Since 2015, it has been illegal for anyone to transfer a pension worth more than £30,000 without taking advice. The FCA's own figures show that the number of people transferring out of such schemes has fallen sharply since tougher rules were introduced in 2015, but that the sums involved have risen as transfer values have increased. "At first glance, an extra £50,000 in your pocket might seem very attractive," said Sir Steve Webb, a former pensions minister and now a partner at LCP. "But you are trading a secure income that will last as long as you do for a lump sum that you have to manage yourself, and which might run out in your lifetime." As a result, the amount they are willing to pay to get rid of the liability has increased. But for individual members, the decision is rarely straightforward. However, only a handful of such schemes have been set up so far. In a statement, Royal London said: "Pension transfer values have risen sharply over the past year, and in some cases have reached levels not seen since 2015. But it is essential that anyone considering a transfer takes independent financial advice, and weighs up the risks carefully." For the vast majority of people, the advice from experts will be to stay put. "A defined benefit pension is the gold standard of retirement income – it's guaranteed, index-linked and pays out for life," said McPhail. "Transferring out is a big decision, and should only be taken after very careful consideration."

title: Given his record of recent years, and his surprising last minute split from Yamaha, all eyes will be on Michael Dunlop at the 2015 Isle of Man TT.

He eschews social media, rarely gives interviews, and treats each lap as a battle against the 37.73-mile Mountain Course. His father, Robert, also a TT winner, died in a racing accident in 2008, and Michael carries that legacy with a fierce independence. "I don't do politics," he once said. "I just want to go fast." The Superbike class is stacked: McGuinness, Hutchinson, Bruce Anstey, Gary Johnson, and Guy Martin – all have won here. But Dunlop's raw pace on the Flying Finn – as he calls his BMW – is unnerving. Dunlop is entered in all five solo classes: Superbike, Superstock, Supersport (two races) and Senior. His best chance might be the Superstock race, where he has dominated – winning it in 2012, 2013 and 2014. But the Senior remains the ultimate prize. "You can't ignore his record," said McGuinness. "On any given day, Michael can beat anyone. The question is whether the late change unsettles him." There are also whispers about the BMW's electronics versus the Yamaha's. Dunlop insisted the BMW's set-up "suits my style – I can feel the front tyre, I can push harder." However, some rivals suggest the Yamaha had more top-end power. "Maybe it does," Dunlop replied, "but the TT isn't a drag race. It's about confidence through the bumps and over the mountain." The island itself is buzzing with the drama. Fans line the paddock, hoping for a glimpse of the man who might become Ulster's next TT king. His uncle Joey holds 26 wins; Michael has 11. "People keep talking about records," he said. "I just focus on the next corner." For now, all eyes are on Dunlop – not just for his speed, but for his nerve. As the first race approaches on Saturday, the 26-year-old knows that one mistake on the Mountain Course can be fatal. But that is the gamble he has taken, swapping a factory contract for a familiar machine – and the chance to prove that in this most dangerous of sports, instinct and talent can still triumph over planning.

title: A judge has criticised paedophile hunters after the trial of an alleged sex offender collapsed.

title: Groups offering mental-health support to children and young people are to receive a multi-million-pound funding boost from April, the government says.

"This additional funding is a vital lifeline for families who often feel they have nowhere else to turn," she said. The government must ensure this is not just a one-off boost, but part of a sustained commitment." title: A touring version of Dirty Dancing has been criticised for cutting musicians and using a recorded backing track.

title: Saturn's ice-crusted moon Enceladus may now be the single best place to go to look for life beyond Earth.

The assessment comes on the heels of new observations at the 500km-wide world made by the Cassini probe. It has flown through and sampled the waters from a subsurface ocean that is being jetted into space. Cassini’s chemistry analysis strongly suggests the Enceladean seafloor has hot fluid vents - places that on Earth are known to teem with life. "For the first time, we have direct evidence that hydrothermal activity is occurring on another world, far beyond our own," said Dr Hunter Waite, the lead author of a study published in the journal Science. "This is a monumental step forward in the search for habitable environments in the Solar System." The Cassini spacecraft, which has been orbiting Saturn since 2004, has made several dramatic discoveries at Enceladus. In 2005, it spotted towering plumes of water vapour and ice particles erupting from the moon's south polar region. Later flybys revealed that the plumes originate from a vast subsurface ocean, kept liquid by tidal heating from Saturn's gravitational pull. And now, the most tantalising find yet: the chemical fingerprint of hot water reacting with rock on the ocean floor. Cassini's instruments detected molecular hydrogen (H2) in the plume material. On Earth, hydrogen is produced when hot water percolates through iron-rich rocks, such as those found in hydrothermal vent systems. These vents, like those in the Lost City field in the Atlantic or the black smokers of the Pacific, are oases of life in the deep sea, supporting complex ecosystems entirely independent of sunlight. "The hydrogen is a key piece of evidence," explained Dr Waite. "It tells us that the water-rock reactions are occurring, providing a chemical energy source that could potentially power living organisms. We are essentially looking at the chemistry of a deep-sea hydrothermal vent from afar." The implications are profound. For decades, scientists have argued that any search for extraterrestrial life should focus on places with liquid water, a source of energy, and a stable environment. Enceladus now offers all three. Moreover, the Cassini data suggest that the ocean is likely in direct contact with a rocky core, creating the chemical gradients necessary for life to emerge. "Hydrothermal systems on Earth are thought to be the crucibles of life," said Dr Sarah Hörst, a planetary scientist at Johns Hopkins University. "The conditions we see on Enceladus are remarkably similar to those that may have given rise to the first organisms on our own planet. This makes it one of the most promising targets for future exploration." The discovery also raises the possibility that Enceladus could host a biosphere today. The plumes continuously vent material into space, meaning that a future spacecraft could sample the ocean without having to land or drill through the icy crust. This has already been demonstrated by Cassini, which, during its final flybys, flew directly through the plume and analysed its composition. But Cassini's mission is ending. The spacecraft is running low on fuel and will be deliberately crashed into Saturn's atmosphere in September 2017 to avoid any risk of contaminating Enceladus or the other potentially habitable moon Titan. However, its legacy will shape the next generation of space exploration. Several missions have been proposed to follow up on Cassini's findings. One concept, called Enceladus Life Finder (ELF), would carry more sensitive instruments to detect organic molecules, amino acids, and even evidence of microbial life. Another, the Enceladus Explorer (EnEx), would send a robotic probe to drill through the ice and explore the ocean directly. NASA and the European Space Agency are evaluating these and other proposals. "The case for Enceladus is now stronger than ever," said Dr Jonathan Lunine, a planetary scientist at Cornell University and a member of the Cassini team. "The presence of hydrothermal activity, combined with the ocean's chemistry and the availability of energy, makes it the single best place to look for life outside Earth in our Solar System." The search for life elsewhere has long focused on Mars, with its dried-up riverbeds and buried ice. But Enceladus offers a more immediate and accessible target. Its plumes allow remote sampling, and the ocean is likely vast and stable, providing a long-term habitat. Even if no life is found, studying Enceladus will shed light on the limits of habitability and the processes that underpin life's emergence. "Every time we think we have a complete picture, the Solar System surprises us," said Dr Carolin Krieger, a planetary scientist at the University of Cologne. "Enceladus is a tiny moon, but it has an outsized potential to answer the biggest question: are we alone?" As Cassini prepares for its final plunge, the data continues to be analysed. The findings from the plume will keep scientists busy for years, modelling the ocean's chemistry and its potential to sustain life. Already, there are hints of other complex organic molecules in the plume, though their origin remains uncertain. "If we can detect a clear signal of biological processes in the plume, it would be a game-changer," said Dr Waite. "We are not there yet, but we have the tools to find out. The next step is to send a dedicated mission to search for life." The international scientific community is now rallying around Enceladus. A recent workshop at the University of Colorado brought together planetary scientists, astrobiologists, and mission designers to discuss the best approach. The consensus was clear: Enceladus is the priority target for the next decade. "We have a window of opportunity," said Dr Hörst. "The science is compelling, the technology is within reach, and the public appetite for discovery is huge. We should seize it." The discovery of hydrothermal vents on Enceladus does not prove that life exists there, but it dramatically increases the odds. And for a species that has long gazed into the night sky wondering if we are alone, that might be the most exciting news of all. The little moon orbiting Saturn, once just a dot in the distance, has become a beacon of hope in the search for our cosmic companions.

title: A leading malaria control expert has said efforts to contain the disease may be jeopardised by the Ebola crisis.
text_ai: Dr Fatoumata Nafo-Traoré, who heads the Roll Back Malaria (RBM) Partnership, said after visiting west Africa: "Understandably, all the health workers' attention is on Ebola." Now, experts fear that the gains made against malaria over the past decade could be reversed as health systems buckle under the strain of the Ebola outbreak. The World Health Organization (WHO) has warned that the number of malaria cases and deaths in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone could surge if treatment is interrupted. "We are extremely concerned," said Dr Pedro Alonso, director of the WHO's Global Malaria Programme. "If people with fever are not tested and treated promptly, we risk seeing a resurgence of malaria deaths on top of the Ebola crisis." The problem is twofold: health workers are overwhelmed by Ebola cases, and local populations are fearful of visiting clinics where the virus is present. Dr Nafo-Traoré described how mothers in Sierra Leone were keeping children with high fevers at home, terrified of catching Ebola. "They would rather risk malaria than risk Ebola," she said. This is catastrophic because malaria can kill within 24 hours if untreated, especially in young children. Data from the WHO shows that in the three most-affected countries, there were an estimated 6.6 million malaria cases in 2012, with roughly 7,000 deaths. But this year, with Ebola having killed more than 5,000 people in the region, the health infrastructure is crumbling. Clinics that once offered free malaria testing and treatment have closed or are functioning with skeleton staff. The distribution of insecticide-treated bed nets has stalled, and thousands of children have missed vital doses of preventive treatment. International health organisations are trying to adapt. The RBM Partnership has launched an emergency appeal for $35m (£22m) to support malaria control in the three countries. The funding would go towards mass drug administration – treating entire communities regardless of symptoms – and providing protective equipment for health workers dealing with fever cases. "We can't let malaria become a silent epidemic behind the Ebola crisis," Dr Nafo-Traoré said. But the logistical challenges are immense. In some areas, malaria is now the leading cause of fever, and distinguishing it from Ebola without a test is difficult. Ebola can present with similar symptoms: high fever, headache and body aches. This overlap has led to misdiagnosis and further strain on limited testing capacity. "Every fever is now a suspected Ebola case," said Dr Alonso. "That slows down the response to both diseases." Meanwhile, malaria control programmes across sub-Saharan Africa are watching nervously. The region accounts for 90% of global malaria deaths. The WHO has warned that any disruption to malaria services in the three Ebola-hit countries could lead to a ripple effect, with drug-resistant strains emerging and mosquitoes breeding unchecked. Dr Nafo-Traoré urged the international community not to forget malaria in the midst of the Ebola response. "We must treat the two diseases together," she said. "A child who dies of malaria today is just as dead as a child who dies of Ebola. And we have the tools to save them." The next few months, as the rainy season peaks and malaria transmission intensifies, will be critical. Without urgent action, the legacy of Ebola may include a deadly resurgence of a disease the world had begun to conquer.

title: Scientists have begun to predict the animals that may become extinct in the next century because of climate change.
text_ai: Researchers at Brown University in the US have combined predictions of climate change with the geographic ranges of well-studied amphibians. The study, published in the journal *Nature Climate Change*, is one of the first to account not only for long-term shifts in temperature and rainfall but also for the erratic, short-term "weather noise" that can prove even more disruptive. "We know that animals will try to track their preferred climate as it moves towards the poles or up mountainsides," said Dr. Justin Nowakowski, the lead author and a postdoctoral researcher at Brown. "But what we’ve shown is that even if the long-term trend looks favourable, a single unusually hot year or a sudden cold snap can create a barrier that they simply cannot cross. It’s like trying to run a marathon with hurdles that keep appearing at random." They found that when short-term climate variability is factored in, the number of species predicted to be at risk of extinction rises sharply—by roughly 10 to 15 percent compared to models that only consider average warming. Amphibians are particularly vulnerable because they have moist, permeable skin and complex life cycles that depend on specific water conditions. Frogs, salamanders and caecilians are already among the most threatened groups on the planet, with around 40 percent of species considered at risk. The new study suggests that climate change will accelerate their decline, especially in tropical regions where biodiversity is highest. "The assumption has been that if we protect large enough areas and allow for corridors, species can move on their own," explained co-author Dr. Phoebe Zarnetske, a community ecologist at Michigan State University. "But when you add in year-to-year variability, those corridors can become impassable at critical times. A species might be perfectly capable of dispersing over a decade, but if it faces a lethal dry season two years in a row, it never gets the chance." The study has significant implications for conservation policy. In the past, "assisted colonisation"—the deliberate translocation of species to more favourable environments—has been controversial. Critics argue that it can introduce invasive species, disrupt existing ecosystems, and risk failure if the new habitat proves unsuitable. But the Brown team says that in a rapidly changing world, the risk of doing nothing may be greater. "There are species that will not survive without human help," said Dr. Nowakowski. "We need to be proactive and think about moving them now, while they still have viable populations to draw from, rather than waiting until they are on the brink." After that, if their current habitats become uninhabitable and they cannot reach new ones, extinction becomes almost inevitable. Not all scientists agree. Dr. Mark Schwartz, a conservation biologist at the University of California, Davis, who was not involved in the study, cautioned that assisted colonisation is "an extreme intervention" that should only be used after thorough risk assessment. "We have to be careful not to cause more harm than good. Moving a frog could accidentally introduce a disease to a naïve population, or it could outcompete native species," he said. Nevertheless, the Brown study adds weight to a growing consensus among ecologists that traditional conservation—such as creating national parks and wildlife corridors—must be supplemented by more aggressive strategies. For amphibians, the outlook is especially grim. Their decline is already being called the "sixth mass extinction" in microcosm, and climate change is accelerating it. The new research suggests that if we fail to act quickly, the next century will see the loss of some of the planet's most charismatic and ecologically important creatures—from the poison dart frogs of the Amazon to the giant salamanders of East Asia. "These are the animals that control insect populations, cycle nutrients, and serve as indicators of ecosystem health," said Dr. Nowakowski. "Losing them is not just a tragedy in itself—it will have cascading effects on entire habitats." As the world warms, the question may no longer be whether humans should intervene, but how—and how soon.

title: He's fallen out with judges, journalists and intelligence agents, and his approval rate is a measly 41% among all adults in the US.
text_ai: But there's one group of people with whom President Donald Trump is still hugely popular. It represents a depth of partisan loyalty that has reshaped the contours of American politics, and it is a force that the president and his strategists are betting will carry him through the turbulence of his second term. To understand this bond, you have to look beyond the policy wins, the executive orders on energy and immigration, or even the judicial appointments. For a core of the Republican electorate – perhaps a third of the party’s voters – the connection is almost totemic. They do not see a man who has fallen out with judges over court orders blocking his travel bans. They see a warrior willing to take on a system they believe is rigged against them. “He says what we’re all thinking,” is a phrase repeated in diners from rural Pennsylvania to the exurbs of Phoenix. The fights with journalists, whom many on the right have long viewed as a liberal priesthood, are a feature, not a bug. The dismissal of intelligence assessments on Russia or North Korea is framed not as recklessness, but as a necessary corrective to what they see as a “deep state” bureaucracy that tried to undermine his first term. Polling conducted by the Pew Research Center in recent weeks shows that even among Republicans who describe themselves as “moderate” or “somewhat conservative”, the president’s approval rating hovers around 75%. Among “very conservative” Republicans, it is effectively unanimous – 97%. This is not a hollow popularity. It translates into a fundraising machine that has already collected more than $150m for his 2026 midterm campaign efforts, far outpacing any potential primary challenger. It also insulates him from the kind of congressional backlash that has historically plagued presidents with low overall numbers. Republican lawmakers, facing their own primaries, know that crossing Trump is akin to career suicide. Yet the gulf between his national and partisan approval is historically dramatic. Trump’s current 86% among Republicans is the highest for any president of either party at this stage in their term since modern polling began – eclipsing even the sky-high numbers enjoyed by Barack Obama among Democrats in his first quarter of 2009. Political scientists offer several explanations. One is the phenomenon of “affective polarisation” – the idea that party identity has become an all-encompassing social identity, akin to a tribe. In this environment, any attack on a tribal leader is seen as an attack on the tribe itself. “The president has effectively weaponised his unpopularity,” says Dr Jennifer Merolla, a political scientist at the University of California, Riverside. “Every time a judge blocks an order, every time a journalist criticises him, he can point to that as proof that the establishment is out to get not just him, but the people who voted for him. It’s a self-reinforcing cycle.” But there is also a substantive, policy-driven dimension. The president’s early moves – an aggressive tariff on foreign steel, the revival of the Keystone XL pipeline, a sweeping tax cut that disproportionately benefits high earners and corporations – are deeply popular with the GOP base. The tariffs, in particular, have won him praise from blue-collar workers in the Rust Belt who felt abandoned by free-trade deals. “I don’t care if he fights with the media or the courts,” said Tom Ruddell, a welder from Youngstown, Ohio, in a recent interview. “He’s the first person in the White House who actually gave a damn about manufacturing jobs.” This support, however, is not unconditional. The 86% figure conceals a fault line within the party. Among college-educated Republicans – a group that includes many suburban voters who fled the party during the Trump era – approval is noticeably lower, around 65%. These voters are more likely to be troubled by the president’s chaotic style, his legal troubles, and his attacks on democratic norms. They may not desert him in a general election, but they are uneasy. And in a country where the president’s overall approval is stuck at 41%, any erosion of his base could be lethal. The challenge for the White House is to maintain the loyalty of the hard core while reaching out to the broader electorate that currently views him unfavourably. The president’s team is keenly aware of the numbers. In private briefings, they have emphasised a strategy of “relentless messaging” on the economy and border security – two issues where Trump still polls well, even among some independents. But they also know that the national disapproval number – 54% in some recent surveys – is a drag on their legislative agenda and a warning sign for the 2026 midterms. History is not kind to presidents with below-50% approval ratings. Jimmy Carter, George H.W. Bush, and Donald Trump himself in his first term all suffered midterm losses after being stuck in the low 40s. The difference this time, say White House strategists, is the depth of Republican support. “We don’t need to win the popular vote,” one senior adviser told the BBC on condition of anonymity. “We need to turn out our base. And right now, the base is fired up.” There is a risk, however, that the base is a gilded cage. The very policies that thrill the 86% – the tariffs, the aggressive immigration enforcement, the withdrawal from international agreements – are the ones that turn off the independent and moderate voters needed to win a national election. The president’s approval among independents is currently 32%, a figure that has barely budged despite a buoyant stock market and low unemployment. For now, the president seems content to lean into the divide. His recent rally in Georgia drew 20,000 people and featured the familiar refrains: “They’re after you, and I’m just in the way.” The crowd roared. The cameras captured the adulation. But back in Washington, the intelligence community is still bruised, the journalists are still emboldened, and the judges are still ruling against him. The 86% may be a fortress, but even a fortress needs supplies from the outside. As the second term enters its second year, the question is not whether President Trump can keep the loyalty of his party. The polls have already answered that. The real question is whether any president can govern effectively when nearly three in five Americans – and a majority of the nation’s most powerful institutions – are arrayed against him. The 86% is a source of strength. But it is also a measure of how profoundly divided the country has become. And in that division, there is little room for the kind of broad consensus that history suggests is needed to sustain a presidency beyond the next election.

title: Solicitors have lost a legal challenge against government plans to cut by more than half the number of duty lawyers attending magistrates' courts and police stations in England and Wales.
text_ai: Solicitors' associations warn that cutting the number of contracts from 1,600 to 527 will lead to inadequate access to legal advice for defendants. But judges in London's High Court ruled the plans were not legally flawed. The Ministry of Justice said savings had to be made in the legal aid system. The High Court challenge was brought by the Law Society of England and Wales, the Criminal Law Solicitors' Association (CLSA) and the London Criminal Courts Solicitors' Association (LCCSA). They argued that the Ministry of Justice's decision to reduce the number of duty solicitor contracts was "irrational" and failed to comply with a legal duty to consult properly. In a detailed judgment, Mr Justice Julian Knowles and Mrs Justice Jefford dismissed all grounds of the challenge. They found that the consultation process – which ran from November 2021 to February 2022 – was fair and that the Ministry had provided sufficient evidence to justify the cuts. The judges noted that the government had considered the risk of "advice deserts" – areas where defendants might struggle to access a solicitor – and had introduced a "market sustainability" mechanism to monitor and address any gaps. "The court is satisfied that the Secretary of State acted within the bounds of his discretion," the ruling stated. "The decision was not one that no reasonable minister could have reached." The controversial reforms, first announced in 2021, will see the number of contracts for duty solicitor work – which covers representation at police stations and magistrates' courts – fall from 1,600 to 527. The Ministry of Justice says the changes will save around £20m a year from the legal aid budget, which totals approximately £2bn annually. It insists the new system will be "more efficient" and will ensure that contracts are awarded to firms that can deliver high-quality services, rather than being spread thinly across hundreds of smaller practices. But the solicitors' bodies fear that the cuts will particularly hit rural and coastal areas, where firms are already struggling to recruit and retain criminal defence lawyers. They point to a chronic shortage of duty solicitors: according to the Law Society, the number of solicitors doing criminal legal aid work has fallen by more than 40% over the past decade. Lubna Shuja, the president of the Law Society, said the ruling was "deeply disappointing" and warned of consequences for the justice system. "This is a bitter blow for anyone who values access to justice," she said. "These cuts will make it harder for people – especially the most vulnerable – to get legal advice when they are arrested or appear in court. We have seen the erosion of criminal legal aid over many years. This will accelerate the crisis." CLSA chair Bill Wymers said the changes would create "postcode lotteries" where defendants in some areas would have to wait hours for a solicitor, or travel long distances to see one. "The government has pressed ahead despite overwhelming opposition from the profession and from magistrates, who know that justice delayed can be justice denied," he said. The Ministry of Justice acknowledged the professional concerns but argued that the current model was unsustainable. "We have made £10m available to support firms in remote areas, and will keep the market under constant review," a spokeswoman said. "The legal aid system must deliver value for money while maintaining quality. These reforms are necessary to ensure that the most vulnerable defendants still have access to a solicitor when they need one." The three-judge panel also rejected a separate argument that the Ministry had failed to conduct a proper equality impact assessment. The judges said the Ministry was entitled to conclude that any adverse effects on protected groups – such as people with disabilities or from ethnic minorities – would be mitigated by the oversight arrangements. The solicitors now face a decision on whether to seek permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal. They have 21 days to lodge an application. If no appeal is brought, the new contract regime will be phased in from 2025, with the full reduction expected by 2026. Legal aid practitioners warn that the exodus from criminal defence work may continue unless funding is substantially increased, leaving the most vulnerable defendants without effective representation. The justice system, they say, is already buckling under pressure – and this ruling may only hasten the decline.

title: Yahoo has denied that it has made it deliberately difficult for customers to migrate to another email provider.
text_ai: It follows the disabling of an email-forwarding feature which allows people to migrate automatically. Yahoo said it was a "temporary" move while it worked on improvements. The firm is dealing with fallout from a massive breach of customer data and accusations that it allowed the US government to spy on emails. The controversy erupted after users attempting to switch to rivals such as Gmail or Outlook found the auto-forward function disabled. Yahoo acknowledged the feature was turned off on 3 October for "some" customers, but insisted it was merely a short-term measure to enhance security following the 2014 data breach, which compromised the details of 500 million accounts. "This is not a retention tactic," a Yahoo spokesperson told the BBC. "We are working to restore the feature as quickly as possible, and we apologise for any inconvenience. The temporary removal is part of a broader effort to protect our users' data and ensure a secure transition." However, critics remain sceptical. The decision comes at a sensitive time for the internet giant, which is in the midst of a $4.8bn (£3.9bn) acquisition by Verizon. The telecoms firm has indicated it may seek to renegotiate the deal in the wake of the security breach and revelations that the company complied with a secret US government surveillance programme that scanned all incoming emails. Privacy campaigners argue that Yahoo's move is a deliberate attempt to lock in customers. "It's no coincidence that disabling email forwarding happens just when users have most reason to leave," said Jim Killock, executive director of the Open Rights Group. "This looks like a cynical ploy to hold people hostage, not a security upgrade." Security experts, however, offer a more nuanced view. "While the timing is highly unfortunate, there are genuine technical reasons for pausing automatic forwarding after a breach of this magnitude," said Prof Alan Woodward, a cybersecurity specialist at the University of Surrey. "Attackers could exploit the feature to redirect mail without the user's knowledge. Yahoo needs to ensure the system is safe before reactivating it." Yahoo has not yet given a date for when the forwarding service will be restored. Meanwhile, users who want to move their email manually must download their messages via the web interface, a time-consuming process that can take days for those with large archives. The company also charges a fee for exporting data via its paid service. The episode is the latest blow to Yahoo's battered reputation. The breach – which the company initially confirmed in September 2016 – was one of the largest in internet history. It was later revealed that the attack had occurred in 2014, and that Yahoo had been aware of it but failed to disclose it to users or regulators promptly. In addition, leaked documents from former NSA contractor Edward Snowden showed that Yahoo complied with a secret court order to scan all incoming emails for a specific string of characters, effectively allowing US intelligence to monitor the communications of millions of users. The company has said it was legally compelled to comply. The combined fallout has left many users questioning whether to stay with Yahoo. For those determined to leave, the path is now steeper – but not impossible. "You can still move your email – it just takes more effort," said one industry analyst. "But for a company trying to rebuild trust, making things harder is the last thing you want to do." Yahoo has insisted it is committed to transparency and security, and that the email-forwarding feature will return soon. For now, however, many users feel trapped.

title: A local authority has lost its legal bid to prove that adult members of an extended family intended to take four children to live in war-torn Syria.
text_ai: Sir James Munby, president of the High Court's Family Division, said he had not been persuaded by the "central core of its case against any of the adults". He also said a significant part of the adults' evidence was "untruthful". The council had taken action to remove the children from their parents because of fears they were in danger. In his ruling, Sir James Munby said the local authority had failed to prove that any of the adult family members – including the children’s parents, an uncle and a grandmother – planned to take the youngsters, aged between two and 11, to conflict zones in Syria. The judge acknowledged the council had genuine concerns about the children’s welfare, but concluded those fears were not supported by the evidence presented. “This is not to say that the adults have been entirely candid,” Sir James said. “A significant part of their evidence I found to be untruthful. But untruthfulness about peripheral matters does not equate to proof of the central allegation.” The case, heard in the Family Division of the High Court in London, revolved around a family with strong ties to Syria. The local authority had intervened after intelligence reports suggested the adults were radicalised and intended to travel to the country – which remains gripped by a devastating civil war – with the children. Social workers obtained emergency protection orders last year, and the youngsters were placed in foster care. During the hearing, the council pointed to social media posts, phone records and witness testimony that it argued showed a concerted plan to leave the UK. One of the adults had previously expressed sympathy for jihadist groups, the court heard. However, the family’s lawyers countered that the material was ambiguous and that the adults’ sole motive was to visit relatives in a different part of Syria, far from active fighting. Sir James said the local authority’s case suffered from “a lack of direct evidence” and that its interpretation of the intelligence was “speculative”. He noted that one key witness had since recanted their statement, and that other evidence had been “mischaracterised” by the council. The judge also criticised the speed of the local authority’s intervention, saying it had acted “precipitately” in some respects, though he acknowledged the difficult decisions social workers face in such cases. The ruling does not mean the children will automatically return home. A separate welfare hearing will now consider what is in their best long-term interests. The local authority said it would “carefully consider the detailed judgment” before deciding on next steps. A spokesperson for the council said: “Our primary concern has always been the safety of these children, and we will continue to work with all parties to ensure they are protected.” The case has raised broader questions about how the family courts assess intelligence-led evidence in cases involving national security concerns. Legal experts say the judgment underscores the high bar required to prove an intention to take children to a war zone. One family law barrister, speaking on condition of anonymity, said: “Courts are rightly cautious before making findings that could separate families for years. The burden of proof remains on the local authority.” No application for permission to appeal has been made, but sources indicated the council may consider its options. Meanwhile, the children remain in foster care, awaiting the next chapter in this complex and sensitive case.

title: A little over a decade has passed since Ryan Giggs' final game for Wales yet, even at 43 years old, the former Manchester United winger can still be devilishly elusive.
text_ai: He has been enjoying a first year off in a career which has spanned more than a quarter of a century, starting with his United debut in 1990 and coming to a temporary halt when he left the club as a coach 12 months ago. That decision to step away from the dugout, announced in June 2022, allowed Giggs a rare moment of stillness in a life that had, until then, been measured in seasons, substitutes and silverware. He spent the summer watching his son, Zach, play for Altrincham's academy, attending concerts with friends and, for the first time in memory, waking up without a training regime dictating his day. "It was strange," he admitted in a rare interview with a Welsh language programme last autumn. "I had to learn that doing nothing is actually doing something. It's not easy when you've been programmed for 30 years." But inactivity, for a man of Giggs' restless energy, was never going to be a permanent state. Behind the scenes, he has been quietly shaping a new chapter - one that does not involve a whistle or a tactics board, but which draws directly on the two decades of elite-level experience that made him the most decorated player in British football history. **A life in motion** The numbers alone are staggering. 963 appearances for Manchester United. 13 Premier League titles. Two Champions League triumphs. Four FA Cups. Three League Cups. And, on the international stage, a record 64 caps for Wales - a figure that stood as a national record for 13 years until broken by Chris Gunter. Yet Giggs has always been uneasy with cold statistics. He prefers to talk about moments: the 1999 FA Cup semi-final replay against Arsenal, when he weaved through the Gunners' defence like a ghost through a graveyard; the 2008 Champions League final in Moscow, where he captained United to victory and became the competition's oldest outfield player to lift the trophy at 34. That ability to reinvent himself - from raw, shaggy-haired teenager to composed midfield metronome - is what Sir Alex Ferguson once described as "the mark of a true professional". And it is that adaptability, those who know him say, that will define his next move. **The coaching conundrum** Giggs' managerial ambitions are no secret. He applied for the Swansea City job in 2016, the first of several approaches that did not materialise. His interim spell at Manchester United in 2014, after David Moyes' sacking, was brief but instructive - four games, two wins, one draw, one defeat. At the time, he spoke of "enjoying the pressure" and "learning every day". But the permanent role went to Louis van Gaal, and Giggs settled for a place on the Dutchman's coaching staff, a position he described as "frustrating at times" in his 2020 autobiography. The pattern repeated under Ole Gunnar Solskjær. Giggs, who had by then taken charge of the Wales national team in November 2018, was often mentioned as a potential United manager. But when Solskjær was sacked in November 2021, the call did not come. Instead, Ralf Rangnick was parachuted in as interim, and Giggs' role at Old Trafford effectively ended. He left the club the following June, having spent the final months of his contract working remotely due to ongoing legal proceedings. **The legal shadow** That shadow - the trial at Manchester Crown Court on charges of controlling and coercive behaviour and assault against an ex-girlfriend - has inevitably shaped the public perception of Giggs in recent years. He has consistently denied the allegations. In August 2023, after a retrial was ordered following a hung jury, the Crown Prosecution Service announced it would not seek a third trial. Giggs was formally cleared, but the case had already taken a toll. The Football Association of Wales (FAW) placed him on leave from his role as national team manager in November 2020, and he officially resigned in June 2022, saying he did not want to "distract" the squad ahead of their first World Cup in 64 years. In the aftermath of the acquittal, Giggs released a statement thanking his legal team and expressed a desire to "rebuild my life". Those close to him say the experience has been "humbling" and "sobering", but also clarifying. "He knows who his real friends are now," one former United teammate told BBC Sport. "He's not the kind of person to wallow. He'll find a way forward." **A new pitch** And that way forward may well involve the Welsh national team - in a different capacity. Sources close to Giggs indicate he has held informal talks with the FAW about a possible ambassador role, one that would allow him to remain connected to the game he loves without the day-to-day pressures of management. The FAW has made no public comment, but the organisation is known to value his experience in developing young players, particularly given the current crop of Welsh talent - Brennan Johnson, Kieffer Moore, Ethan Ampadu - who emerged under his tenure. Giggs' record with Wales is often understated. Of the 20 matches he oversaw, he won 12, drew three and lost five - a win rate of 60%. He led the team to the brink of World Cup qualification, narrowly missing out on the 2022 tournament after a play-off defeat to Poland. His successor, Rob Page, eventually took them to Qatar, but Page has acknowledged the "foundation" Giggs laid. "The players trusted him," Page said in a 2022 press conference. "He gave them belief. You can't underestimate what he did for the culture of that squad." **The elusive legacy** It is that legacy - part glittering, part contested - that Giggs is now trying to curate. He has been spotted at youth matches across the northwest of England, offering advice to teenagers who were not yet born when he made his Premier League debut. He has also been working with a sports psychologist, exploring how to translate his own competitive drive into a new context. "I'm not ready to write my final chapter yet," he told a small gathering of journalists at a charity event in Manchester last month. "I've still got things to give." What those things are remains deliberately unclear. But those who have watched him over the years know better than to write him off. The same elusiveness that made him a nightmare for defenders down the left flank is now being deployed off the pitch. He moves through the football world without a fixed address, turning up where least expected, leaving people guessing. **A different kind of match day** On a recent wet Tuesday evening, at a non-league ground in Cheshire, a small crowd watched a pre-season friendly between Altrincham and a local side. In the stands, wearing a plain black jacket and a cap pulled low, sat Ryan Giggs. He was there to watch his son, Zach, but he also spent the half-time interval deep in conversation with a youth coach, drawing diagrams on a napkin. When the final whistle blew, he lingered, signing autographs for a handful of fans who recognised him, shaking hands with the referee, and then disappeared into the night. It was a scene that summed up his current existence: visible, yet peripheral; engaged, yet detached. For a man who has spent his entire adult life in the glare of floodlights, the dimmer switch of anonymity is something he is still learning to master. But if his first year off taught him anything, it is that the most difficult opponent is sometimes yourself - and that beating him requires patience, perspective, and a willingness to change. It has been a decade since he last played for Wales. In many ways, he has not been seen clearly since. But Ryan Giggs, at 43, is still moving. And the next move, whatever it is, promises to be worth waiting for.

title: High Street food chain Greggs has reported a rise in both sales and profits, but it warned it is facing increased inflationary pressures and greater economic uncertainty.
text_ai: Total sales rose by 7% to £894.2m last year, while pre-tax profits hit £75.1m, up from £73m in 2015. But the company said the consumer outlook was "more challenging" than it had been. Greggs is shifting from being a bakery business to focusing on food-to-go. The shift, which has included opening more shops in travel hubs and expanding its café-style seating, helped drive a 14.5% increase in like-for-like sales in its company-managed shops during the second half of the year. However, the Newcastle-based chain cautioned that cost pressures, particularly from higher wage bills, ingredient prices and energy costs, would persist into 2024. "The consumer outlook is more challenging than a year ago," said chief executive Roisin Currie. "We are not immune to the broader economic headwinds, but our value-for-money proposition and the resilience of our supply chain give us confidence." Greggs announced plans to open between 140 and 160 new shops this year, building on a net addition of 145 in 2023. It also opened its first 24-hour drive-thru in Manchester and its largest UK shop in Birmingham. The company expects to invest between £60m and £70m in its estate and infrastructure during 2024. Pre-tax profit rose by 2.9% to £75.1m, though analysts had expected a slightly higher figure. Total sales reached £894.2m, up 7% compared with the previous year. The company described the performance as "solid" against a backdrop of "significant cost inflation". Greggs has been reshaping its menu to appeal to breakfast and evening customers, with items such as pizza slices and hot wraps now available after 4pm. It has also expanded its vegan range and introduced a loyalty app with more than 800,000 active users. But the broader economic uncertainty meant the company was cautious about the months ahead. "We are planning for a more moderate sales growth in 2024," Ms Currie said. "But we believe our focus on convenience, quality and price will continue to attract customers who are looking to make their money go further." Shares in Greggs fell 1.5% in early trading as the market digested the warning, though the company's long-term strategy was praised by retail analysts. Shore Capital described the results as "robust" and said Greggs remained "well-positioned in the fast-growing food-to-go market". The firm employs more than 28,000 people across nearly 2,400 shops. It said it was working to offset cost increases through improved efficiency and better procurement, but acknowledged that margin pressure would remain a theme for the year ahead.

title: So-called Islamic State (IS) lost almost a quarter of its territory in 2016, according to new analysis.
text_ai: The group gave up almost 18,000 sq km (6,900 sq miles), its territory being reduced to some 60,400 sq km, just less than the size of Florida, security and defence analysts IHS Markit reported. IHS Markit predicted the recapture of Mosul by Iraqi government forces by the middle of the year. The loss of territory marks a significant blow to the group's self-declared caliphate, which at its height in 2014 controlled an area roughly the size of the UK. IHS Markit analyst Columb Strack said the group's collapse in Iraq had been "much faster" than anticipated, driven by sustained coalition air strikes and the grinding advance of Iraqi forces, aided by Shia militias and Kurdish peshmerga fighters. In Syria, the picture is more complex. IS has been squeezed by rival forces: the Syrian army backed by Russian air power, and US-backed Kurdish-led fighters. The group lost the key border town of Jarablus in August, but still holds the de facto capital Raqqa. The UK-based Syrian Observatory for Human Rights estimates IS controls about half of Syria's oil and gas fields, though their revenue has been hit hard by coalition bombing. The financial toll has been severe. IHS Markit calculates the group's monthly revenue has fallen from about $81m (£65m) in mid-2015 to around $56m now, as it loses access to smuggling routes and extortion networks. "They are now a shadow of the revenue-generating machine they once were," Strack noted. "But they remain a potent insurgency threat, even if they lose all their territory." The prediction of Mosul's recapture by mid-2017 – the article was written in late 2016 – appears prescient. Iraqi forces, backed by US-led coalition air support, launched the operation to retake the city in October 2016, and after months of intense urban fighting, Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi declared victory in July 2017. At the time of the IHS report, Iraqi troops had already begun encircling the city, cutting off key supply routes. The analysis also highlights the group's shifting strategy. As its conventional forces have been degraded, IS has increasingly turned to guerrilla tactics, including suicide bombings and assassinations, both inside Iraq and abroad. The attacks in Paris, Brussels and Istanbul were partly aimed at proving it remains a viable global threat. Western intelligence agencies have warned that even if the caliphate is dismantled, the ideology will persist, with foreign fighters returning to their home countries. The report's findings underscore the coalition's progress, but also the long-term challenge ahead. As one British defence official put it, "Territory can be taken back. But the idea is far harder to kill."

title: Four more city workers have been charged in the investigation into the lead-tainted water crisis in Flint, Michigan, state prosecutors said.
text_ai: Former state-appointed emergency managers Darnell Earley and Gerald Ambrose were charged for failing to protect residents from the toxic water. Two city employees were also charged with felony counts related to the case. Flint's drinking water became contaminated with lead in 2014 after the city changed its water supply. The charges, announced by Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, bring the total number of individuals indicted in the long-running probe to 15. Earley and Ambrose, who served as emergency managers during the period when the water switch occurred, are accused of failing to prevent the disaster despite having clear authority to do so. They face multiple counts of misconduct in office and wilful neglect of duty. The two city employees charged are former Flint water plant operators – one of whom is accused of tampering with evidence. Both are alleged to have manipulated water quality reports to downplay the danger. Prosecutors say their actions – or inactions – directly contributed to a public health catastrophe that exposed more than 100,000 residents to dangerous levels of lead. Flint’s crisis began in April 2014 when the city, under the control of state-appointed emergency managers, switched its water source from Lake Huron – via the Detroit system – to the Flint River to save money. The river water was not treated with corrosion inhibitors, causing lead to leach from ageing pipes into the supply. The contamination was initially hidden by officials who insisted the water was safe, despite mounting evidence of sickness and elevated lead levels in children. The scandal has become a symbol of government malfeasance and environmental injustice, with the majority-black city suffering disproportionately. In 2017, criminal charges were filed against several officials, but many were later dropped or dismissed. The current round of charges represents a renewed effort by the attorney general’s office to hold high-level decision-makers accountable. Earley, who served as Flint’s emergency manager from 2013 to 2015, has previously argued that he inherited the city’s problems and did not make the decision to switch water sources. Ambrose, the city’s emergency manager in 2015, has similarly denied responsibility. Critics, however, say their refusal to reverse course or order proper treatment amounted to criminal negligence. The two water plant employees now face up to 20 years in prison if convicted on the tampering charges. Their lawyers have not yet commented on the allegations. Residents of Flint, many of whom still do not trust tap water and rely on bottled supplies, expressed cautious hope that the latest charges signal a turning point. “It’s about time someone with real power is held responsible,” said Melissa Mays, a local activist. “But this doesn’t bring back the health of our children.” The investigation continues, with prosecutors vowing to pursue all those who “failed in their duty to protect the people of Flint.” The water crisis is expected to cost the state hundreds of millions of dollars in long-term health care and infrastructure repairs.

title: Across the world there has been a decline in piracy and sea robbery, but one precarious expanse of ocean waters in South East Asia is bucking that trend, as maritime defence expert Swee Lean Collin Koh explains.
text_ai: There was a time when news of pirates and kidnap-for-ransom dramas in the waters off Somalia dominated global news headlines. In 2011, at the height of the crisis, a total of 237 incidents were reported in the area. Since 2012, global maritime piracy has steadily fallen, driven by improved naval patrols, onboard security measures, and diplomatic efforts. The International Maritime Bureau's Piracy Reporting Centre recorded 132 incidents worldwide in 2023, the lowest figure in over two decades. Yet against this backdrop of progress, a troubling hotspot has emerged in the waters of Southeast Asia – specifically, the Sulu and Celebes seas that straddle the maritime borders of Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines. It is here, in this chokepoint of scattered islands and porous coastal communities, that a stubborn and violent strain of piracy has taken root. Unlike the opportunistic theft of cargo that plagues other regions, the attacks in this area are increasingly linked to kidnapping for ransom, often involving armed groups with political or extremist affiliations. The modus operandi is chillingly familiar: small, fast skiffs overpower slow-moving fishing vessels or tugboats hauling barges, seizing crew members before melting into the labyrinth of mangrove swamps and coral atolls that make navigation and pursuit a nightmare. "It's a very different threat environment from what we saw off Somalia," says Swee Lean Collin Koh, a research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore. "The Somali pirates were essentially criminals of opportunity, seeking quick financial gain from ship ransoms. What we have here in the Sulu-Celebes sea is a more complex, hybrid threat – where organised crime and local insurgency blend together, and the proceeds of piracy directly fund militant activities." The numbers, while modest in absolute terms, tell a worrying story. According to the Regional Cooperation Agreement on Combating Piracy and Armed Robbery against Ships in Asia (ReCAAP), the number of incidents in the Sulu and Celebes seas rose from just 2 in 2017 to 21 in 2023, with a further spike in reported abductions so far this year. Most of the attackers are believed to be affiliates of the Abu Sayyaf Group (ASG), an Islamist militant organisation based in the southern Philippines that has pledged allegiance to the Islamic State. Though weakened by sustained military operations, ASG retains the capacity to launch maritime kidnap raids, using the proceeds to buy weapons and maintain its networks. The human cost is acute. In May 2023, gunmen seized five Indonesian fishermen off the coast of Sabah, Malaysia, demanding a ransom of 20 million pesos (about £280,000). Two months later, a Vietnamese cargo ship was attacked near the Philippine island of Basilan; the captain was killed when he resisted, and three crew members were abducted. They remain missing. These attacks have profound implications for regional security and maritime trade. The Sulu-Celebes sea sits astride vital shipping lanes that connect the Indian Ocean to the Pacific, with an estimated 40% of global maritime trade passing through the nearby South China Sea. Shipping companies are increasingly wary of transiting the area, and some have begun rerouting vessels at significant extra cost. "The economic disruption is real," says Koh. "Insurance premiums for ships operating in this zone have risen sharply, and some shipping lines now insist on armed guards or enhanced surveillance. In 2022, the Philippines passed a new maritime security law that designates the Sulu and Celebes seas as a "piracy-prone area", providing legal cover for more aggressive interdiction and allowing for the detention of suspects without charge for up to 30 days. But challenges remain. The region's geography – thousands of islands, weak governance in remote communities, and deep-rooted poverty – provides ideal conditions for pirates to operate. "You can't patrol every estuary or every village," notes Koh. "The simple reality is that the returns from piracy are still attractive compared to the alternatives. Many of these fishermen earn less than £200 a month, and a single successful kidnapping can bring in ten times that amount. Until you address the underlying socio-economic drivers, you will never fully eliminate the problem." International partners have also stepped in. The United States, under a longstanding security agreement with the Philippines, provides training and intelligence support to Philippine marine units. Japan has supplied patrol boats and radar systems. The European Union's naval force, Operation Atalanta, shares information on piracy trends and has conducted joint exercises with Southeast Asian counterparts. Yet Koh cautions against a purely militarised approach: "We need a holistic strategy that combines law enforcement, economic development, and community engagement. Otherwise we are just treating the symptom, not the disease." Of particular concern is the emerging nexus between piracy and more conventional criminal networks. Intelligence agencies have detected links between pirate groups and drug traffickers, who use the same routes and maritime corridors to move methamphetamine from the Golden Triangle to markets in Australia and East Asia. "The pirates are not operating in a vacuum," says Koh. "They are part of a broader maritime crime ecosystem that includes illegal fishing, smuggling, and human trafficking. Disrupting one element can sometimes push the others into more violent or sophisticated behaviours." The global decline in piracy elsewhere offers both lessons and caution. The success stories – the drop in Somali piracy following the deployment of armed guards and the stabilisation of the country's political situation – show that targeted interventions can work. But they also highlight the importance of sustained commitment. "Once the international community's attention shifted away from Somalia, the residual threat remained, and we are now seeing a small resurgence in the Gulf of Aden," Koh notes. "In Southeast Asia, the question is whether the governments involved can maintain the political will and the resources over the long haul." For the thousands of seafarers who cross the Sulu and Celebes seas every year, the threat is all too real. Many now travel in convoys, carry satellite phones, and receive training on how to respond to an attack. Some fishing cooperatives in Malaysia have pooled funds to hire private security boats. But for the crews of smaller vessels, who lack the budget for such precautions, the risks remain high. The coming months will test the region's ability to stem the tide. A new five-year anti-piracy action plan, drawn up by the ASEAN Maritime Forum, is due to be approved later this year. It calls for better data sharing, joint prosecution guidelines, and a regional fund to compensate victims' families. But critics argue that it lacks enforceable targets and does not address the underlying grievances that fuel piracy in the first place. As Swee Lean Collin Koh puts it: "The trend is bucking the global picture, and that should worry everyone. In an interconnected world, no maritime highway is safe if a single stretch of water remains lawless. The question is whether the nations of Southeast Asia can turn the corner before the problem escalates further." For now, the pirates of the Sulu-Celebes sea continue to operate with impunity, their small boats slipping through the channels of history, as the world watches the numbers climb once again.

They had hosted endless bilaterals in which European counterparts politely inquired whether "the decision" could be reversed. They had rewritten cables, adjusted strategies, and quietly prepared for the possibility of a no-deal exit that would leave British nationals stranded abroad and supply chains in tatters. Yet here, in the Locarno rooms—named after the 1925 treaties that had sought to guarantee peace in Europe—Hammond was not offering a mea culpa. Instead, he outlined a vision of "Global Britain" that was to be aggressive, optimistic, and unapologetic. He spoke of deepening trade ties with India, of a new partnership with the Gulf states, of a special relationship with the United States that was not simply transactional but deeply rooted in shared values. He mentioned the Commonwealth, not as a sentimental relic but as a "network of opportunity" that could rival the EU's internal market. The diplomats nodded, but their eyes betrayed a certain wariness. They had heard this before, from Boris Johnson, from Liam Fox, from David Davis. It was a speech that could have been given—and probably had been—by any Conservative minister since 2016. But then Hammond did something unexpected. He acknowledged the elephant in the room. "I know that some of you feel the Foreign Office has been sidelined in the Brexit process," he said, his voice dropping. "That the negotiations have been driven by Number 10 and the Department for Exiting the European Union, with little input from those who understand the nuance of European diplomacy. One senior ambassador, who had served in Paris for a decade, later told me he felt as though a weight had been momentarily lifted. "We don't expect sympathy from government," he said, his voice low. "But we do expect to be listened to." The speech lasted twenty-seven minutes. When Hammond finished, the applause was genuine—if measured, as was the Foreign Office way. Sir Simon McDonald returned to the podium, thanked the foreign secretary, and then opened the floor to questions. The first came from a veteran diplomat who had served in Moscow. He wanted to know about Russia, about the Skripal poisoning, about the expulsion of twenty-three Russian diplomats that had taken place just months earlier. Hammond was robust. "We will not tolerate the use of chemical weapons on British soil," he said. "And we will not allow the Kremlin to destabilise our allies through disinformation and interference." The diplomat nodded, but pressed further: what about the long-term? What about the need for a new architecture of arms control? Hammond’s answer was careful, non-committal. The meeting moved on. The next question was from a female ambassador who had just returned from a posting in the Middle East. She asked about the government's commitment to the Iran nuclear deal—the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action—which the United States had abandoned the previous month. "We remain a party to the deal," Hammond said, "and we will continue to uphold our commitments, so long as Iran does the same." It was a diplomatic tightrope walk, and everyone in the room knew it. Britain was trying to maintain a relationship with Washington while also saving a deal that the White House had declared dead. The ambassador did not push further. She knew the constraints. Throughout the session, one theme kept recurring: resources. The Foreign Office, like much of the British civil service, had faced a decade of austerity. Its budget had been cut, its staff reduced, its embassies shuttered in less strategic locations. The diplomats in the room could see the cracks in the edifice. They had to compete with the Ministry of Defence for influence, with the Department for International Trade for credit, with the Prime Minister's own team for the ear of the public. Hammond, when asked about funding, gave a carefully worded answer about "efficiencies" and "priorities." It was not the reassurance many had hoped for. Lunch followed—a modest spread of sandwiches and salads, served by waiters in white gloves. The diplomats mingled, formed clusters of regional expertise, exchanged whispered observations. The European ambassadors gathered near the windows, their conversation laced with French and German phrases. The Middle East hands stood by the fireplace, debating the prospects of a post-war Syria. The South Asia team huddled near the door, discussing the upcoming elections in Pakistan. It was a microcosm of British foreign policy: fragmented, specialised, and quietly proud. Later that afternoon, the conference broke into smaller groups for roundtable discussions on topics ranging from cyber threats to climate diplomacy. A young diplomat from the policy planning staff presented a paper on "the arc of instability from the Sahel to the Hindu Kush." It was met with polite interest, but the real energy was in the informal chats over coffee. Here, the diplomats could speak freely, without the burden of official minutes. The consensus, as one seasoned hand put it, was that Britain was "still in the game, but playing on half a board." As the day wore on and the chandeliers began to dim, the diplomats filed out into the London evening. They had been reminded of the scale of the challenge, but also of the resilience of their institution. The Foreign Office had survived the Suez crisis, the end of empire, the Iraq war. It would survive Brexit, too. But the question, lingering in the air like the last notes of a distant piano, was: at what cost? And for what purpose? The answers, like the next year's conference, lay somewhere on the horizon, obscured by the fog of uncertainty that had become the defining feature of British statecraft.

title: With the Australian Open now over, it is not only tennis players and fans who are casting a keen eye towards the start dates of the next two Grand Slams in Europe.
text_ai: Staff at Roland Garros in Paris, and at the All England Lawn Tennis Club (AELTC) in London, will be fine-tuning their preparations over the spring, so that when they open their doors for two weeks of tennis everything is pitch perfect. For years, players have called for a more rationalised calendar, with longer gaps between majors. But the reality is that broadcasters and sponsors have their own timetables, and the Grand Slams are the crown jewels of the sport’s revenue. It’s about creating a rhythm that works for everyone—within the constraints we have.” Those constraints are also keenly felt at Wimbledon, where the All England Club has its own set of traditions and expectations. The grass-court season is notoriously short, squeezed between the French Open and the summer hard-court swing. Wimbledon’s start date—always the last Monday in June—is fixed by a century-old convention, but the club has become more flexible in recent years. The introduction of a roof over Centre Court in 2009, and later over No. 1 Court, has reduced rain delays, but the grass surface itself remains vulnerable to wear and tear. “We have a very specific window to prepare the courts,” said Neil Stubley, head of courts and horticulture at the AELTC. “The grass is grown from a rye grass and fescue mixture, and it needs the right balance of moisture, sunlight and temperature. If the spring is unusually cold or wet, that can delay the growth. We then have to roll, cut and mark the courts to a precise standard.
