Unlike the clay at Roland Garros, which can be re-rolled and re-wetted, or the hard courts at the Australian and US Opens, which are consistent by design, grass is a living surface. It degrades during the tournament, especially around the baseline, creating unpredictable bounces that test even the most accomplished players. For the top seeds, who often play the later rounds on the main show courts, the surface can be markedly different from the first Monday to the final Sunday. This year, the scheduling of the two European Slams will also be influenced by the Olympic Games in Paris, which will take place at Roland Garros in late July and early August. The tennis event at the Olympics is a separate entity, but the clay courts will need to be preserved and then prepared for a second phase of play. The FFT has already announced that it will begin laying the clay earlier than usual, to give the surface time to settle before the French Open, and will then re-lay a fresh layer for the Olympics. This dual-use of the venue adds a layer of complexity—and cost—but also provides a unique opportunity to showcase the sport on one of its most iconic stages. For players, the Olympic tournament is a chance to win a medal for their country, but it also disrupts the already congested calendar. Some top names may choose to skip the Olympics if they feel the physical toll is too great, especially with the US Open beginning just a few weeks later. The ATP and WTA tours have not yet formalised any exemptions for Olympic participants, but discussions are underway about potential adjustments to ranking points or entry rules. “We are in a new era where players are more vocal about their wellbeing,” said former world number one and BBC tennis correspondent, Tracy Austin. “The days of playing 25 tournaments a year are over for most top players. Something has to give.” The broader context of the tennis calendar is also shaped by the growing influence of the Middle East and Asia. The early-season swing through Doha, Dubai and Adelaide has become increasingly lucrative, and the Australian Open now sits at the end of a long summer stretch that begins in late December. While 2024 saw a return to full capacity, the financial pressures remain. The FFT has invested heavily in upgrading the infrastructure at Roland Garros, including a new court showing and improved fan zones, but the costs have been substantial. Ticket prices have risen, and the tournament has introduced dynamic pricing for certain sessions, a move that has drawn criticism from some fans. “We want to keep tennis accessible, but we also have to cover our costs,” Mauresmo said. “It’s a difficult balance. We are exploring new ways to engage younger audiences, including digital content and social media features, but the core experience—the tennis itself—must remain the priority.” At Wimbledon, the AELTC has taken a different approach. The club has kept ticket prices relatively stable, but the demand far outstrips supply. The public ballot for tickets is notoriously oversubscribed, and the resale market sees prices soar. The club has introduced a new queuing system for unreserved seats on Court 1 and 2, and has increased the number of grounds passes available, but the exclusive atmosphere remains a defining feature. “Wimbledon is a brand, but it’s also a living tradition,” said Richard Doughty, a former tournament director. “The challenge is to modernise without losing what makes it special. The white dress code, the lack of sponsorship on the courts, the quietness of the crowd—these are all part of the magic. But the world changes, and so does tennis. At Wimbledon, the roof has allowed play to continue into the night, creating a new atmosphere under the floodlights. At Roland Garros, the roof has been used sparingly, but its presence has given organisers the confidence to schedule night sessions. Yet for all the preparations, the biggest variable remains the players themselves. The 2025 season is still in its infancy, but the early signs are that the men’s and women’s draws are as competitive as ever. Sinner and Sabalenka are the defending champions in Melbourne, but the chasing pack includes Carlos Alcaraz, Iga Swiatek, Coco Gauff and a host of rising stars. The players who succeed are those who can adapt quickly and consistently. It’s not just about your best tennis; it’s about your best tennis on three different stages.” As the spring approaches, the staff at Roland Garros and the AELTC will continue their meticulous work. The soil will be tested, the grass will be measured, the lights will be checked. And when the first balls are struck in May and June, the years of planning will be put to the ultimate test. For the players, the fans and the thousands of people behind the scenes, the countdown has already begun.

title: An appeal for information has been made after the discovery of the body of a rare bird of prey in south-west Scotland.

title: Science is being squeezed out of English primary schools, with a third not providing the recommended two hours of teaching a week, research suggests.
text_ai: The Confederation of British Industry study also suggests science has become less of a priority in many schools. title: After watching the tragedy of the Aberfan disaster unfold on television, photojournalist Chuck Rapoport left his home in New York to capture the aftermath.
text_ai: But to the grief-struck villagers he was "just another man with a camera". Little did they know he would change their lives and become a lifelong friend. Curators have worked closely with the photographer, now 77 and living in California, to ensure the story is told with the sensitivity it deserves. "What struck me most was not the mud or the wreckage," he recalled. "It was the silence. The silence of a village that had stopped breathing." His photographs show rescue workers in overcoats and flat caps digging through the black slurry; a lone woman standing by a gate, her face a mask of disbelief; a small row of wellington boots lined up outside a chapel, waiting for children who would never wear them again. But there are also images of ordinary life continuing: a milkman making his rounds, a man sweeping his front step, a group of women huddled together in a kitchen, drinking tea. "That's what I wanted to show," said Mr Rapoport. "Not just the tragedy, but the dignity. These were people who had been dealt the worst possible blow, and yet they still got up every morning." The friendship that began with a camera lens has endured for half a century. On every anniversary, Mr Rapoport returns to Aberfan, staying with families he first met in those terrible October days. He has attended weddings, christenings and funerals. He has become, as one villager puts it, "one of us". "At first, we didn't trust the press," said Margaret Jones, whose six-year-old daughter, Sarah, was among the dead. "They came from everywhere – London, Manchester, even America. They took their pictures and they left. But Chuck stayed. He came back year after year, not to take more photographs, but just to be with us." It is a sentiment echoed by the exhibition's curator, Dr Helen Davies of the National Museum Wales. "Chuck's work is unique because it was born out of compassion, not sensation," she said. "He didn't exploit the pain – he sat with it. That's why his images are still so powerful today." The Aberfan disaster, which killed 116 children and 28 adults, remains one of the worst mining-related catastrophes in British history. The collapse of a colliery spoil tip onto the village school has been the subject of numerous inquiries, books and documentaries. Fifty years on, many of the same faces appear in Mr Rapoport's later photographs: older, greyer, but still carrying the same weight. "I don't think you ever get over it," he said. "You just learn to carry it with you." The exhibition includes a short film in which Mr Rapoport speaks directly to the camera, his voice still cracking with emotion. "I went to Aberfan thinking I was going to be a photojournalist," he says. "I left knowing I had found a family."

title: HSBC is the first big UK bank to explain in detail how it intends to get round the new European Union prohibition on big bonuses and continue to pay its top people many millions of pounds each.

In a statement, the bank said the allowance is not a bonus – it is a fixed component that can be reduced or revoked only for "exceptional" reasons, such as gross misconduct. A spokesperson said: "We expect all firms to comply with both the spirit and the letter of the remuneration rules." However, the PRA has so far stopped short of ordering HSBC to change course. Other UK banks – including Barclays, Lloyds and RBS – are reportedly examining similar schemes. If the EU fails to act, the cap could become a dead letter. If it does act, the result may be a prolonged legal battle – one that tests the limits of the EU's authority over global financial institutions. title: A wide range of disorders and problems in school-age children have been linked to delayed fatherhood in a major study involving millions of people.
text_ai: Increased rates of autism, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, suicide attempts and substance abuse problems were all reported. For example, less than 1% of children born to older fathers developed schizophrenia, but the relative risk was roughly double. Unlike eggs, which are all present at a woman’s birth, a man’s sperm-producing stem cells divide repeatedly throughout his lifetime – roughly every 16 days. title: Scotland ended their summer tour with a disappointing defeat by Fiji in Suva.

"In the Premiership, you can't afford to get drawn into a frantic tempo, especially against a side with Hibs' quality. We had to absorb some pressure, but I thought we were the better side in spells, particularly in the first 45." The half-time whistle brought a sense of frustration among the home support, who had expected goals from a County side that had scored six in their previous two group matches. But this was a different Hibernian – organised, compact, and dangerous on the break. Manager Lee Johnson had made four changes from the team that beat Queen's Park, resting key men such as Christian Doidge, but his side retained a fluid shape that often suffocated County's attacking rhythm. The second half followed a similar pattern. Hibs pushed forward with intent, and Josh Campbell – playing in a more advanced role – twice went close, first with a header that drifted just wide, then with a fierce drive that Laidlaw did well to parry. At the other end, Jordan White – a late inclusion after an injury to Murray – proved a handful in the air, but his finishing lacked the requisite composure. On one occasion, he rose above the Hibs defence to meet a Dhanda cross but could only guide his header straight at the grateful David Marshall. The crowd, numbering just over 4,000 – a respectable turnout for a midweek group fixture – grew increasingly restless as the clock ticked towards the 90-minute mark. Both managers made substitutions in search of a winner, but the game's final acts were more about control than chaos. Hibs' best opportunity came in the 85th minute when a sweeping move ended with Boyle's low cross being touched onto the post by the sliding Joe Newell. The ball trickled agonisingly across the goal line before being cleared by Nightingale, who had a superb defensive display. And so, for the second time in the group stage, a penalty shootout would decide the bonus point. Earlier in the week, County had edged past Elgin City on spot-kicks, and the experience of that win was a clear psychological advantage. "We practice penalties every week," said Mackay. "It's not luck; it's repetition and nerve. The boys were confident." Marshall, the Hibs goalkeeper, had a reputation as a penalty specialist, having saved two in the previous season's group stage. But County's takers were composed. Ben Purrington stepped up first, sending Marshall the wrong way with a low strike into the corner. Josh Sims followed suit, his powerful effort grazing the underside of the bar before nestling in the net. Keith Watson, the veteran defender, made no mistake from the third kick, drilling his shot high into the centre of the goal. Hibs' penalty takers showed less composure. Newell's opening effort was saved by Laidlaw, who guessed correctly and dived to his right. Campbell then scored after a stuttering run-up, but Jake Doyle-Hayes saw his shot hit the post and bounce clear. Boyle, usually so reliable, blasted his attempt high over the bar to leave County 3-1 up with two penalties to spare. After David Carson – who had been substituted on specifically for his penalty-taking prowess – slotted home the decisive fourth kick, the home side erupted in celebration. "To be honest, it's a sickener," admitted Johnson. "We dominated long spells, had the better chances, and I thought we deserved to win in normal time. But football is cruel. We have to learn to be more clinical, and we have to be better from 12 yards. It's a missed opportunity." The result lifts County to the top of Group D on seven points, three ahead of Hibs, who are now second with four points. Airdrieonians, who have a game in hand, could yet make the qualification race interesting, but County have placed themselves in a commanding position. They face a tough trip to Airdrie in their final group game, while Hibs host Elgin City. For Mackay, the bonus point could prove invaluable. "In group stages, every point counts," he said. "We have a strong squad, and we're finding ways to win without playing at our best. That's the sign of a good team." The verdict? Ross County's resilience and penalty prowess have earned them a crucial advantage in the race for the knockout stages. Hibernian, meanwhile, will rue another expensive shootout failure – a recurring issue that Johnson must address if his side are to challenge for silverware this season. Next week's final group fixtures will determine who advances, but for now, the Highlanders are celebrating a gritty, determined win that could define their cup campaign.
prefix: County had won their first two Group D games and Hibs had taken full points from their only other game. But, despite some exciting play, especially in the opening half, chances came and went in the first group game to involve two Premiership sides.

title: Women's rights activists in Afghanistan say they fear the advances made by women over the past decade could be reversed if a peace deal is done with the Taliban.
text_ai: The Taliban came once for Fawzia Koofi, and she knows they could come again. This prominent member of parliament - and mother of two - survived a hail of bullets last year. She is among a growing number of Afghan women who fear that the progress of the last two decades may be traded away in exchange for peace. When the Taliban ruled from 1996 to 2001, women were barred from education, forced to wear the full-body burqa, and could not leave home without a male guardian. Public executions and beatings were routine. Today, girls can go to school, women hold seats in parliament, and female judges and prosecutors serve in the judiciary. "But every time there is talk of peace, I feel like the ground is moving beneath my feet. The sacrifices of my mother's generation are being forgotten." The United States and the Taliban signed a landmark agreement in Doha in February 2020, setting the stage for the withdrawal of foreign troops and the start of intra-Afghan negotiations. The deal included a commitment by the Taliban to prevent extremist groups from using Afghan soil, but it made no specific mention of women's rights. While the Taliban have said they will respect women's rights within the framework of Islamic law, activists say that phrase is a blank cheque. "Islamic law can mean many things," said Koofi, who is also a women's rights advocate. "For the Taliban, it means a return to the 1990s." The negotiations between the Afghan government and the Taliban have been sluggish and fraught. A key sticking point is the very nature of the future Afghan state. The Taliban insist on an "Islamic system", while the government demands a continuation of the democratic republic, including protections for women and minorities. In the meantime, fear stalks the streets of major cities. Female judges have been gunned down. Schoolgirls have been poisoned. Women activists have disappeared. One such case is that of Nafisa, a 28-year-old journalist who received death threats after writing a column criticising the Taliban's educational policies. She now lives in a safe house in Kabul, unable to visit her family in the provinces. "I am a prisoner in my own country," she said. "But I would rather be a prisoner than silent. Silence is what they want." The Taliban have denied targeting women, but the evidence suggests otherwise. According to the UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan, in the first three months of 2021 alone, 37 women were killed and dozens more wounded in targeted attacks. The perpetrators remain largely unknown, but the pattern is clear: women in public life are being systematically intimidated. The international community has offered reassurances. US Secretary of State Antony Blinken has said that women's rights will be a "central focus" of any peace deal. But activists remain sceptical. They point to previous agreements, such as the 2015 peace talks in Murree, Pakistan, where women's participation was marginalised. "We hear the words, but we need to see the action," said Dr. Sima Samar, a former human rights commissioner and one of the first female ministers in Afghanistan. "If the Taliban are serious about peace, they must demonstrate it. Not by statements, but by allowing girls to go to school without fear." The Taliban's track record is not encouraging. In areas under their control, they have imposed restrictions on women's mobility, banned female education above primary level, and forced women to wear the burqa. In the southern province of Helmand, girls' schools have been burned down. In Ghazni, female health workers have been threatened. "This is not about culture or religion," said a women's rights lawyer in Kabul who preferred to remain anonymous. "This is about power. They want to erase us from public life." Yet many Afghan women are not waiting for the outcome of negotiations. They are organising, speaking out, and building networks of resistance. In Herat, a group of female lawyers has launched a hotline for women facing domestic violence. In Mazar-i-Sharif, women's cooperatives are training female entrepreneurs. In Kabul, a secret school for girls operates in a basement, hidden from the Taliban's gaze. "We will not go back," said Sahra, a 19-year-old student who attends the underground school. "My mother could not read. I want to be a doctor. And if the Taliban come, I will teach other girls in secret. They cannot kill all of us." The resilience is inspiring, but it is also a sign of desperation. The international community, activists say, must not abandon Afghanistan again. "We made a promise after 2001," said Koofi. "We said we would not leave. Now we are leaving, and the women who believed in that promise are being left behind." As the last American troops prepare to withdraw by September, the clock is ticking. For Fawzia Koofi, the bullets that tore through her car were a warning. But she continues to travel the country, meeting with women, listening to their fears. "I know the Taliban want me dead," she said. "But if I stop, they win. And I cannot let them win." But the walls are closing in again." She spoke in a whisper, her gaze fixed on the mountain paths that once carried the Taliban fighters. "We are afraid," she said. "But we are also watching. We will not surrender."

title: Government offices have been shut and streets have emptied in Iraq as summer temperatures hit 53C (127F), nearing the highest recorded in the country.
text_ai: The heat has been compounded by chronic power shortages, depriving homes of electricity for large parts of the day. The conditions have placed a particular strain on Iraqis displaced by an assault on Falluja, a UN official said. Average temperatures in June were the highest recorded worldwide - a rise attributed to greenhouse gas emissions. The heatwave has forced many to seek refuge in the few air-conditioned spaces that remain operational, such as shopping centres and mosques. In Baghdad, residents describe melting asphalt on roads and staggering electricity bills for those able to afford private generators. "We have no water, no electricity—only heat," said Umm Ali, a mother of four in the city's outskirts. "The government talks about solutions, but nothing changes." The power deficit is particularly acute in camps for the displaced. More than 50,000 people have fled the recent offensive against militant strongholds in Falluja, west of Baghdad, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM). In the camp of Al-Hajaj, near the city, temperatures inside makeshift tents have exceeded 50C. "The elderly are collapsing, children are suffering from dehydration," said Lise Grande, the UN Humanitarian Coordinator for Iraq. "This is a health emergency on top of a displacement crisis." The Iraqi government has responded by shifting working hours in state offices to early morning and evening. But the broader infrastructure remains inadequate. Years of war and neglect have left the national grid unable to meet demand, and corruption has hampered repairs. "Every summer is a crisis," said Mohammed al-Shammari, a local engineer. "But this one feels different—the heat is relentless." Climate scientists warn Iraq is on the front line of global warming. June's record global average temperature was 1.3C above pre-industrial levels, according to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa). The World Bank predicts Iraq could experience a 20% drop in water resources by 2050, exacerbating agricultural collapse and further displacement. For now, the priority is survival. On the streets of Falluja, a few vendors sell ice and cold drinks from carts, their voices hoarse from shouting. "We live hour by hour," one said. The heat shows no sign of easing.

title: A stand-off between loyalists and republicans in north Belfast has ended.
text_ai: A crowd of about 200 gathered at the Ardoyne shops after a return Orange Order feeder parade passed off without serious incident. Tensions had been high throughout the afternoon, as flags and banners were brandished on both sides of the interface. Police negotiators worked behind the scenes to ensure the parade could proceed without violence, and a visibly increased security presence — including Land Rovers and officers in riot gear — lined the route. By early evening, the crowds began to disperse. The stand-off, which had threatened to reignite sectarian tensions in the area, was over. Superintendent Nigel Grimshaw of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) confirmed that a robust policing operation had been in place. He added: "The people of Ardoyne have had enough of disruption and division. They want to live in peace." The Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) also urged restraint, with assembly member William Humphrey stating that "everyone has a right to parade, but no one has a right to impose violence". The parade had been the focus of intense controversy in recent weeks, with the Parades Commission imposing restrictions on the return leg — requiring it to pass the Ardoyne shops by 4pm. The lodge that did turn up complied, and the only incident reported was a minor altercation involving a small group of youths, quickly dealt with by police. Residents on both sides expressed relief. One republican observer, who asked not to be named, said: "I'm just glad it's over. We don't need another summer of confrontation." A loyalist parade supporter echoed the sentiment: "We made our point. Now let's get home safe." The PSNI said no arrests were made and no injuries reported. title: An independent review of UK economic statistics has said moving the Office for National Statistics (ONS) out of London has made its output worse over the last decade.
text_ai: The interim report by former Bank of England deputy governor Sir Charlie Bean said the ONS should have more staff in London to engage with users. It also says that a cultural change is needed that will make the ONS better able to cope with a changing economy. The report, commissioned by the Treasury, is highly critical of the decision taken a decade ago to relocate the ONS's headquarters from central London to Newport in South Wales. Sir Charlie, who led the review alongside Professor Sir David Hendry of the University of Oxford and Professor Sir John Aston of the University of Cambridge, said the move had "undoubtedly weakened the ability of the ONS to engage effectively with the users of its statistics". "Proximity matters," the report states. "The ONS's principal users – the Treasury, the Bank of England, and many of the leading economic commentators and researchers – remain overwhelmingly based in London. The physical distance has made informal, day-to-day contact much harder. It has also made it more difficult for the ONS to attract and retain the most skilled analysts and data scientists, who are often reluctant to relocate." The review's interim findings come amid growing unease in Whitehall and in financial markets about the reliability of key economic data. In recent years, the ONS has been forced to revise its estimates for GDP, employment and inflation repeatedly, sometimes months after initial publication. Critics argue that the quality of official statistics has deteriorated just when policymakers need them most – to navigate the fallout from Brexit, the pandemic and the cost-of-living crisis. "The UK economy is undergoing profound structural change," the report continues. "The rise of digital services, the shift to remote work, and the increasing complexity of global supply chains all place new demands on the statistical system. The ONS has not kept pace. It has been too slow to adopt modern data sources, too reliant on ageing survey methods, and too insular in its culture." Among the most striking recommendations is a call for the ONS to "substantially increase" the number of senior staff based in London, perhaps by establishing a second major office in the capital. The report stops short of demanding a full-scale move back, acknowledging the investment made in the Newport campus and the benefits of having a presence outside the South East. But it warns that without a "significant London footprint", the ONS risks becoming "increasingly disconnected from the community it serves". Sir Charlie told the BBC the situation was "fixable", but required "bold leadership and a willingness to change". He added: "The ONS has many talented people, but they are not being deployed in the right places, and they are not being given the right tools. We need a cultural shift – away from a mindset of 'we produce the numbers, and it's up to you to interpret them' – towards one that is much more collaborative and responsive to user needs." The review also highlights a lack of diversity in the ONS's workforce, particularly at senior levels. Despite being based in a city with a large minority ethnic population, the ONS's leadership team remains overwhelmingly white and male. "This is not just a matter of equity," the report notes. "It affects the quality of the statistics. A workforce that does not reflect the society it measures is less likely to identify blind spots in its methodology or to anticipate new data needs." The ONS has already taken steps to address some of the criticisms. Earlier this year, it launched a recruitment drive for data scientists and announced a new partnership with the Alan Turing Institute to improve its use of machine learning. But the review suggests these efforts have been "too modest in scale" and "too focused on short-term fixes". The Treasury, which commissioned the review in response to the former Bank of England governor Mark Carney's public concerns about data quality, said it would "carefully consider" the interim report. A Treasury spokesperson said: "Accurate and timely statistics are vital for economic decision-making. We are committed to ensuring the ONS has the resources and the structure it needs to deliver world-class outputs." However, the report has also drawn a sharp response from the unions representing ONS staff. The Public and Commercial Services union said it was "deeply concerned" that the review's recommendations could lead to job losses in Newport. A union spokesperson argued: "Relocation is not the magic bullet. The real issue is chronic underfunding and a lack of investment in technology. Staff in Newport are just as capable as those in London – they are being let down by a lack of support from the top." The ONS itself, in a statement, said it welcomed the "constructive challenge" and would work with the review team ahead of the final report, due in the autumn. ONS chief executive Sir Ian Diamond said: "We are committed to improvement. The world of data is changing fast, and we are changing with it. But we recognise there is more to do, and we will take the review's findings very seriously." The interim report also recommends that the ONS establish a formal "user council" – a panel of economists, business leaders and policymakers – to provide regular feedback on the relevance and timeliness of official statistics. In addition, it calls for a more systematic use of "nowcasting" techniques – using real-time data such as credit card transactions, traffic flows and online job adverts – to produce faster estimates of economic activity. "This is not about replacing official surveys," Sir Charlie explained. "It's about supplementing them with new sources that can give us a much more up-to-date picture. The ONS has been too cautious in embracing these methods. Other countries – Estonia, New Zealand, Canada – are well ahead." The review marks the most significant external critique of the ONS since the 2000 report by Lord Moser, which led to the creation of the UK Statistics Authority. It is likely to fuel the ongoing debate about the concentration of institutional knowledge in London, versus the government's long-standing policy of relocating civil service jobs to other parts of the UK. The final report, expected in November, will set out a detailed roadmap for reform. But Sir Charlie has already made clear that he believes the clock is ticking. "The economy is not going to wait for the ONS to catch up," he said. "If we want to make the right decisions – on interest rates, on tax, on public spending – we need the right numbers. And right now, we are not getting them."

title: Girls who eat a lot of meat during childhood tend to start their periods earlier than others, a study suggests.
text_ai: UK researchers compared the diets of more than 3,000 12-year-old girls. They found high meat consumption at age three (over eight portions a week) and age seven (12 portions) was strongly linked with early periods. Writing in Public Health Nutrition, the researchers said a meat-rich diet might prepare the body for pregnancy, triggering an earlier puberty. The study, led by researchers at the University of Bristol, used data from the Children of the 90s project, which has tracked the health of thousands of families in the Avon area since the early 1990s. Girls were classified as having "early" periods if they started menstruating before the age of 12 — roughly the point at which the average girl in the UK now reaches puberty. A total of 21% of the girls in the study fell into this category. The team found that those who ate the most meat at age three — more than eight portions a week — were almost twice as likely to have started their periods early compared with those who ate the least. At age seven, girls eating 12 or more portions a week were 75% more likely to have an early menarche. The link remained strong even after the researchers took into account other known influences on puberty timing, such as the girl's body mass index (BMI), the mother's age at first period, and the family's social background. "We believe this is a genuine association," said Dr Imogen Rogers, one of the study's authors from the University of Brighton. "Meat is a rich source of zinc and iron, as well as protein — all nutrients that are important for growth and development. It may be that a high-meat diet provides the body with a signal that conditions are favourable for reproduction." However, she stressed that the findings did not prove cause and effect. "It could be that girls who eat more meat also have other dietary patterns or lifestyle factors that we haven't fully accounted for," she added. Other experts welcomed the research but urged caution. Professor Tim Key, a cancer epidemiologist at the University of Oxford, said: "This is an interesting observation, but it is based on parents reporting what their daughters ate many years earlier, which is not always reliable. Early puberty has been linked to an increased risk of breast cancer and other health issues, so understanding its causes is important, but we need more research before changing dietary recommendations." The study also found that girls who ate more meat at age three tended to have a higher BMI by age seven, and that part of the link between meat and early periods might be explained by body fat. Meat consumption is known to be associated with higher intakes of animal fat and protein, which can promote growth and weight gain. Commenting on the findings, dietitian Dr Carrie Ruxton said: "Meat is a valuable source of iron, which is especially important for teenage girls. But the message for parents is not to cut out meat — rather to ensure a balanced diet with plenty of fruit, vegetables and whole grains. Early puberty is influenced by many factors, including genetics and overall calorie intake." The researchers plan to investigate further whether the type of meat — red, white or processed — makes a difference, and whether the effect is also seen in boys in relation to their timing of puberty. For now, they advise moderation: meat in childhood is fine, but perhaps not in excessive quantities from a very young age.

title: Speaking at the annual Munich Security Conference at the weekend, Russian Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev claimed that Europe was "rapidly rolling into a period of a new cold war".
text_ai: "Russia," he said, "has been presented as well-nigh the biggest threat to Nato, or to Europe, America and other countries. "I am sometimes confused," he went on. "Is this 2016 or 1962?" Just a few days earlier in Washington, the director of the US National Intelligence Agency, James Clapper, was giving evidence on "worldwide threats" to the influential Senate Armed Services Committee. Speaking before the committee, Mr Clapper painted a stark picture of the global landscape. "Russia is a full-scope cyber actor," he said. "It is a competitor and an adversary in many domains." He described Moscow's willingness to use military force to achieve its goals, pointing to the conflict in Ukraine and the annexation of Crimea in 2014 as the primary examples. Mr Clapper's assessment, part of an annual review of threats facing the United States, also highlighted a "heightened level of tension" along Nato's eastern flank. The juxtaposition of Mr Medvedev's speech in Munich and Mr Clapper's testimony in Washington underscores a deepening chasm in perceptions between Moscow and the West. For many in European capitals, Mr Medvedev's language—strikingly reminiscent of the rhetoric of the early 1980s—was a deliberate attempt to reframe the narrative. By invoking the spectre of 1962, the year of the Cuban Missile Crisis, he appeared to be warning his audience that the current stand-off risked a similar, potentially catastrophic, miscalculation. But analysts were quick to point out that the comparison was, at best, incomplete. In 1962, the United States and the Soviet Union were the two dominant superpowers, each commanding vast nuclear arsenals and spheres of influence. Today, the world is far more multipolar. China's rise, the resurgence of Islamist terrorism, and the proliferation of non-state actors have fundamentally altered the strategic environment. Nato, meanwhile, far from being a monolithic bloc, has struggled to maintain unity on issues from defence spending to relations with Turkey. Nevertheless, Mr Medvedev's remarks tapped into a genuine unease that has been building across Europe since the election of Donald Trump. The American president's repeated criticism of Nato as "obsolete", his equivocal stance on Article 5—the alliance's mutual defence clause—and his unorthodox overtures to Vladimir Putin have fuelled anxiety among many allies. In Munich, European leaders were forced to confront the uncomfortable possibility that the transatlantic partnership, the bedrock of post-war security, might no longer be as reliable as it once seemed. "We are seeing a fundamental shift in the geopolitical tectonic plates," said Wolfgang Ischinger, the veteran German diplomat who chairs the Munich Security Conference. "The question is not whether a new cold war is beginning, but whether we are prepared to manage it without it turning hot." His sentiment was echoed by the French Defence Minister, Jean-Yves Le Drian, who warned against "sleepwalking" into a conflict that nobody wanted. The Russian Prime Minister's speech, however, was not merely a critique of Nato. It was also a carefully calibrated appeal to European nations to break ranks with Washington. He made a pointed distinction between the "reasonable" European partners Russia had once hoped to engage with—Germany, France, Italy—and what he described as the "aggressive, expansionist" agenda of the United States and its allies in Central and Eastern Europe. "We are ready to cooperate with anyone who wants honest and equal partnership," he said. "But we will not accept ultimatums." That message found a receptive audience among some far-right and populist parties across Europe, many of which have long argued for a rapprochement with Moscow. Yet it also provoked a sharp response from Nato's Secretary General, Jens Stoltenberg, who said that any suggestion of a new cold war was the result of Russian actions, not Western policy. "Russia has repeatedly violated international law," Mr Stoltenberg told reporters. "It has used force to change borders in Europe. It has interfered in the democratic processes of other countries. This is not about Nato's posture. This is about Russia's behaviour." The question of who is to blame for the current impasse is, of course, deeply contested. Western intelligence agencies have documented a pattern of Russian interference in elections—from the US in 2016 to the French presidential campaign of 2017 and the Brexit referendum. Moscow has also ramped up its military exercises, including snap drills on Nato's borders, and deployed new missile systems in Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave sandwiched between Poland and Lithuania. From the Kremlin's perspective, however, Nato's eastward expansion—encompassing former Warsaw Pact states and even, in 2008, promising membership to Ukraine and Georgia—represents a direct threat to Russia's sphere of influence. "My gravest concern is the disconnect between the two narratives," said Sir Andrew Wood, a former British ambassador to Moscow. "Each side sees itself as the aggrieved party. And each has enough evidence to maintain that belief. The danger is that this mutual grievance escalates into a crisis that no one intended." He pointed to the deployment of anti-aircraft systems in Syria, the increased flights of Russian bombers near Nato airspace, and the growing number of close encounters between ships and planes as "accidents waiting to happen". Meanwhile, economic ties between Russia and Europe remain significant, despite the sanctions imposed after Crimea. Germany, in particular, has been reluctant to sever energy links—most notably the Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which would bring Russian gas directly to its shores. That project has become a lightning rod for tensions: Washington sees it as a means for Moscow to exert political leverage, while Berlin insists it is purely a commercial matter. Against this backdrop, Mr Medvedev's speech can be seen as a shot across the bow, designed to rattle an alliance already under strain. But whether it heralds the dawn of a new cold war, or merely reflects the continuation of an old one that never truly ended, remains an open question. What is certain is that the tone and content of the language now being used—on both sides—carry echoes of a past that many had hoped was consigned to history. The conference in Munich, a city synonymous with both appeasement and the post-war order, provided a fittingly sombre venue for the debate. As the delegates filed out of the conference hall, the word on everyone's lips was "containment"—a strategy from the 1940s that might just need to be reinvented for the 21st century. The challenge, as one senior European diplomat put it, is to find a formula that deters aggression without provoking confrontation. "We need to be firm," he said, "but we also need to talk. And at the moment, there is very little talking going on."

title: With more money coming into the game of rugby union than ever before, coaches and players have never been under such pressure.
text_ai: Although not quite at football-type levels, sackings certainly do happen, while many players live on a constant tightrope, hoping they have done enough each season to earn another year or two on the contract. The same applies to referees, who have seldom been under more scrutiny. In the professional era, the margin for error has shrunk to almost nothing. A single poor season can cost a director of rugby their job, a handful of costly mistakes can end a player’s international career, and one controversial decision can leave a referee vilified across social media for weeks. The financial stakes have risen dramatically in recent years, with broadcast deals, private equity investment and global sponsorship pouring unprecedented sums into the sport. Yet with that money comes an unforgiving demand for results. Take the coaching carousel. In the past 12 months alone, six Premiership clubs have changed their head coach – either by dismissal or mutual agreement. In the United Rugby Championship, four have gone. In France’s Top 14, the turnover is even more relentless. The average tenure of a professional rugby head coach now stands at less than three years, according to a study by the Rugby Players’ Association. Compare that to the amateur era, when a man like Jim Telfer could lead Scotland for more than a decade, or Carwyn Jones could mould a generation at Llanelli. The modern coach is hired to deliver immediate success, not long-term development. “The pressure is immense,” says former England fly-half Stuart Barnes, now a pundit for Sky Sports. “You’re only as good as your last result. If you lose three in a row, the whispering starts. After four, the board gets nervous. After five, you’re gone. There’s no time to build anything because the money demands immediate returns. Club owners are not philanthropists – they have investors, sponsors, season-ticket holders to satisfy.” That pressure trickles down to the players. The average salary in the Premiership is around £110,000 a year – decent money, but not life-changing when careers last only a decade at best, and often far less due to injury. Contracts are typically short, many for just one or two seasons. Players know that one serious injury, one dip in form, or one young prospect emerging from the academy can end their time at a club. The physical toll is enormous: studies show that professional rugby players suffer, on average, three to four concussions over a career, while the incidence of osteoarthritis in retired players is significantly higher than in the general population. “You never feel safe,” says a Premiership player who spoke on condition of anonymity. “You go into every season knowing that if you don’t play well, you might not get a new contract. But you also have to play through injuries because if you miss games, someone else takes your spot. It’s a brutal cycle. And the mental side is just as hard as the physical.” The mental health of players has become a growing concern. In 2022, the Rugby Players’ Association launched a wellbeing programme after a survey found that nearly 40% of current professionals had experienced symptoms of anxiety or depression. The issue is compounded by the relentless calendar. The introduction of the Nations Championship, the expanded World Rugby Sevens series, and the increasing demands of domestic competitions mean that elite players can now be involved in up to 40 matches a year. Player burnout has become a talking point in every boardroom, yet little has changed. “We are asking players to perform at an elite level almost every week for 10 months of the year,” says Dr James Brown, a sports psychologist who has worked with several Premiership clubs. “That is unsustainable. The body needs rest. The mind needs rest. But the revenue demands more games. There is a fundamental tension between the commercial growth of the sport and the welfare of those who make it possible.” Referees are not immune to the pressure. In the past, officials were largely anonymous figures, respected for their authority. Today, they are scrutinised by television cameras, slow-motion replays, and a chorus of social media commentators. In April, World Rugby announced it was reviewing its officiating protocols after a series of high-profile errors – including a missed forward pass in a Champions Cup quarter-final that prompted an outcry. Referees now attend media training, learn to manage abuse online, and undergo psychological support sessions. “The scrutiny is unlike anything we’ve seen,” says former international referee Nigel Owens, who officiated the 2015 Rugby World Cup final. “When I started, you’d get a letter in the post from a fan. Now you get thousands of tweets, some of them threatening. You have to develop a thick skin. But also, the game has become far more complex. The laws are intricate, the ruck is a mess, and every decision is magnified. You make one mistake and it’s all anyone talks about.” The financial landscape has changed irreversibly. In 2018, CVC Capital Partners acquired a 27% stake in Premiership Rugby for £200m. Two years later, it invested £365m into a new company controlling the Six Nations and autumn internationals. The message was clear: rugby is no longer a gentleman’s hobby – it is a billion-pound industry. Clubs have responded by chasing commercial partnerships, expanding stadiums, and raising ticket prices. But the cost base has also soared. Player wages have risen by 30% in the last five years in the Premiership, while coaching staff have doubled at some clubs. Yet the returns are not guaranteed. Two Premiership clubs – Wasps and Worcester – went into administration in 2022, shedding hundreds of jobs and leaving players and staff unpaid. Both had overspent in pursuit of success, gambling on short-term glory that never materialised. “The sport is in a dangerous place,” says former England captain Will Carling. “There is too much money chasing too few results. Clubs are borrowing against future revenue streams that may not materialise. The structure is fragile.” The international game faces its own pressures. The Rugby World Cup remains the sport’s financial engine, but the four-year cycle leaves nations scrambling to fill the gaps. Emerging rugby nations like Georgia, Portugal and Chile struggle to fund competitive programmes, while traditional powers like England and New Zealand face declining domestic audiences. World Rugby has proposed a global calendar reform that would reduce the number of international windows, but progress has been slow, with unions unable to agree on revenue sharing. “The sport is at a crossroads,” says journalist and author Tom English. “Do we continue down the path of hyper-commercialisation, with ever more matches and ever greater pressure? Or do we step back and think about what rugby is for? It’s supposed to be a game, not just a business. But the genie is out of the bottle.” For players, the uncertainty is a constant companion. Many now employ agents to negotiate clauses that protect their earnings in case of injury or release. Others take out insurance policies against career-ending events. Some have started businesses or completed degrees while still playing, preparing for the day when the contract runs out. “You can’t rely on rugby forever,” says the anonymous Premiership player. “Even the best players end up broke sometimes. You have to plan for the end from the very beginning.” The pressure is not only financial. Social media has given fans a platform to voice their frustrations directly – and often viciously. Players are targeted after poor performances, coaches are called out after defeats, and referees are subjected to online pile-ons. In 2021, the Rugby Football Union launched a campaign against online abuse, but the problem persists. “It’s become part of the game,” says former Wales captain Sam Warburton. “You have to learn to ignore it. But that’s easier said than done. We are human.” As the sport prepares for the 2023 Rugby World Cup in France, the stakes have never been higher. The tournament is expected to generate more than £400m in revenue, with broadcast deals reaching new heights. But for those on the inside – the coaches, the players, the referees – the prize is not just financial. It is survival. In a game where the margin for error is measured in millimetres and the pressure is measured in dollars, success is fleeting and failure is permanent. The men and women who make rugby run understand this better than anyone. They live it, week in, week out. And they know that in modern professional rugby, the only guarantee is uncertainty.

Philip Rankin, who has died at his home in Ballachulish at the age of 99, led the construction of Scotland's first ski tow in Glen Coe in the 1950s. His vision helped transform the remote Highland glen into a winter sports destination that would draw generations of skiers. "Without Philip, Scottish skiing as we know it today simply wouldn't exist," said Heather MacRae, chair of the Glen Coe Ski Club. "He saw the potential in our mountains when most people thought skiing was something you only did in the Alps. He was a true trailblazer." Rankin, an engineer by trade, was part of a small group of enthusiasts who founded the Glen Coe Ski Club in 1949. The following year, they began work on a 600-foot rope tow powered by an old lorry engine, a contraption that could haul skiers up the lower slopes of Meall a' Bhuiridh. The tow opened in 1951, just as a heavy snowfall brought hundreds of skiers to the area, many of whom had never seen a ski lift before. "It was a Heath Robinson affair," recalled local historian Alistair MacKay. "There were constant breakdowns, and the rope would ice up. title: A suntan is a sign of skin damage, not glowing health, NHS England and the Met Office are reminding parents in Britain just days after a heatwave.
text_ai: A survey suggests a third of parents mistakenly believe going brown is good for children. A quarter have even encouraged their children to tan. A few said they had allowed their children to use sun beds. The findings come from interviews with 1,000 parents with children aged 11 and younger. "A suntan is not a sign of good health – it is a sign that your skin has been damaged by the sun," he said. Parents need to be aware that children's skin is particularly sensitive and that sunburn in childhood can double the risk of developing melanoma later in life." Chief meteorologist Steve Ramsdale said: "Even on cloudy days, UV levels can be high enough to cause damage. We are urging people to protect their skin by using sunscreen with at least SPF 30, wearing a hat and sunglasses, and staying in the shade between 11am and 3pm when the sun is strongest." Around 100 new cases of melanoma are diagnosed in the UK every day, according to Cancer Research UK, and the disease kills about 2,300 people each year. Although skin cancer rates are higher in older adults, experts warn that cumulative sun exposure from childhood is a key risk factor. The survey also highlighted a lack of awareness about the dangers of sun beds. Dr Adrian Thompson, a consultant dermatologist at the Royal Marsden Hospital, said: "Using a sun bed before the age of 35 increases the risk of melanoma by up to 75%. A spokesperson said: "We want to make sure families have the right information to protect their children. This is not about scaremongering – it's about simple, practical steps that can save lives." For now, the NHS and Met Office are urging parents to check the UV index before heading out, to apply sunscreen liberally and frequently, and to remember that a tan is not a souvenir of a happy day – it is evidence of injury. As Prof Powis put it: "No tan is worth that risk."

title: With hot tubs, lake swimming and yoga sessions as well as headliners Bjork and George Clinton, Wilderness, which took place in Oxfordshire this weekend, is among a new breed of festivals offering more than just music.
text_ai: While most festivalgoers want to be entertained, ticket-holders at Wilderness are likely to be roped in to be part of the entertainment themselves. Wilderness, which began in 2011, has positioned itself at the vanguard of this movement, offering a programme that is as much about personal enrichment as it is about musical discovery. They want to learn something new, to challenge themselves, to connect with others in a meaningful way." In one corner, a group of festivalgoers are learning the basics of silversmithing under a canvas awning, their faces lit by concentration and the glow of small blowtorches. Nearby, a crowd gathers for a foraging walk through the surrounding woodland, led by a local expert who points out edible mushrooms and wild herbs. Wellness has become a major draw, with the festival's "Sanctuary" area offering everything from gong baths to sound healing sessions. The lake, once a simple aesthetic feature, now hosts wild swimming classes at dawn, with instructors guiding nervous participants into the cool water. "It's about pushing your boundaries in a safe environment," said one attendee, wrapped in a towel after her morning dip. "I never thought I'd be swimming in a lake at a festival, but here we are." The culinary offering is equally ambitious. Rather than the usual burger vans, Wilderness features a "Feast" tent where Michelin-starred chefs prepare multi-course banquets using locally sourced ingredients. On Saturday evening, a long table seating 200 guests was laid out under fairy lights, with diners sharing dishes of slow-cooked venison and foraged nettle soup. The music line-up, while still central, has been curated to complement this ethos. Bjork's headlining set on Friday was a sensory experience in itself, with the Icelandic singer performing against a backdrop of immersive visuals and experimental soundscapes. George Clinton's Parliament-Funkadelic on Saturday brought a different energy, but one equally focused on spectacle and audience participation. Yet perhaps the most telling indicator of this new direction is the festival's approach to families. Unlike many events where children are an afterthought, Wilderness offers a dedicated "Kids' Kingdom" with workshops in circus skills, storytelling and bushcraft. "We wanted to create something that families could enjoy together, not just endure," Furness said. The commercial logic is clear: by offering a diverse range of activities, the festival can attract a broader demographic and encourage longer stays. VIP areas have been replaced by "Glamping" zones with real beds and hot tubs, catering to those who want comfort without sacrificing atmosphere. However, some purists argue that this shift dilutes the core festival experience. "It's becoming more like a holiday camp than a music festival," said one veteran attendee, nursing a pint of local ale. But for many, that is precisely the appeal. As the sun set over the lake on Sunday, a group of festivalgoers gathered for a final yoga session, their silhouettes framed against the orange sky. It was a scene that would have been unthinkable at Glastonbury a decade ago – but here, it felt entirely natural.

title: TV presenter and comedy writer Denis Norden has spoken for the first time about his "accidental" visit to the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp.
text_ai: Norden, who was serving in the RAF during World War Two, went to the liberated camp in northern Germany to find lighting for a show he was putting on. He went with fellow performers the late Eric Sykes and Ron Rich and none of them had any idea what the camp had been used for. Speaking to the BBC for a new documentary, Norden, who died in 2018 aged 96, recalled the surreal moment he found himself inside one of the most notorious Nazi death camps. "We had no idea," he said. "None of us had heard of Bergen-Belsen. We were just told there was a camp nearby where there might be some electrical fittings we could borrow for the stage lights." It was 23 April 1945, barely a week after the camp had been liberated by British forces. The full horror of what the Allies had discovered was still unfolding. Norden, then a 23-year-old aircraftman, had been tasked with organising entertainment for troops ahead of a concert party. He and his colleagues drove to the camp in a jeep, expecting little more than a disused military facility. What they found was beyond comprehension. Bodies lay unburied, stacked like cordwood. Emaciated survivors, little more than skeletons, shuffled through the mud. The stench of death and disease hung thick in the air. "It was a landscape of utter desolation," Norden recalled. "We walked in and I remember thinking, 'This is not a place for a show. This is a place for a funeral.'" The trio quickly realised their mistake. They were not at a supply depot but at a site of industrialised murder. The camp, originally a prisoner-of-war camp, had been converted into a concentration camp in 1943. By the time of liberation, an estimated 50,000 people had died there, most from typhus, starvation and exhaustion. Among the victims was Anne Frank, who perished just weeks before the camp was freed. Norden never forgot the sight. He said the experience "seared itself into my memory" and shaped his entire worldview. "You cannot see that and remain unchanged," he told the documentary makers. "It makes you realise how thin the veneer of civilisation really is." The comedian, best known for hosting the long-running shows *It'll Be Alright on the Night* and *Looks Familiar*, rarely spoke publicly about his wartime experience. He said he had not wanted to appear to be trading on tragedy. "It felt almost like a violation to talk about it," he explained. "I was a witness, but I was also an intruder. I had no business being there." His account sheds new light on the chaotic days following the liberation of the camps. Many British soldiers and servicemen were unprepared for what they encountered. The British Army had to draft in medical teams, burial units and interpreters. Survivors were given food, but many died from refeeding syndrome – their bodies unable to cope with sudden nutrition. Norden said he and his companions left within an hour. They never found the lighting equipment. "We just got back in the jeep and drove away in silence," he remembered. "There was nothing to say. What could you say?" Later in life, he visited the site of the camp once more, this time as a tourist. He found a memorial and a museum. "It was clean and orderly and very moving," he said. "But it wasn't the same. The real Bergen-Belsen was the one we stumbled into by accident." The documentary, which airs on BBC One next week, also includes interviews with historians and survivors. They praise Norden for his honesty. Dr Emily Mayhew, a historian of the Second World War, said his account was "unusually raw" because it came from a man who had not been trained to process such trauma. "He was a comedian, a performer, a man of wit and lightness," she said. "He was the last person you would expect to be a witness to the Holocaust. And yet he was." Norden's testimony is a reminder that the horror of the camps was not confined to the victims and their liberators. It spilled over into the lives of ordinary servicemen, who carried those images with them for the rest of their lives. For Norden, the memory never faded. "It is always there," he said. "Just below the surface. You try to move on, but you never truly leave."

title: Former Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak has been released from prison after appealing against his detention.
text_ai: He was taken by helicopter from Cairo's Tora prison to a hospital and is later expected to be put under house arrest. Mr Mubarak, 85, still faces charges of corruption and complicity in the killing of demonstrators during the protests that toppled him in 2011. The helicopter touched down at a military hospital on the outskirts of Cairo shortly before midday local time. Security sources said the former president would remain under heavy guard in a private suite, with access restricted to his doctors and immediate family. His lawyer, Fareed El Deeb, had earlier confirmed that Mr Mubarak would be transferred to house arrest at his villa in the upmarket Heliopolis district once medical assessments were completed. The release marks the latest twist in a tumultuous legal saga that has seen Mr Mubarak shuttled between prison, hospital and courtrooms for more than six years. He has been in custody since April 2011, two months after he was ousted from power following 18 days of mass protests that convulsed Egypt and the wider Arab world. His detention was originally ordered on charges of corruption and ordering the killing of protesters – a case that was later overturned on appeal but subsequently retried. Mr Mubarak was acquitted of murder charges in a retrial in 2014, but the public prosecutor appealed. That appeal was eventually dropped by a lower court in 2015, but a separate corruption case – concerning the alleged embezzlement of public funds earmarked for presidential palaces – continued to hold him in custody. Earlier this month, his legal team filed a request for his release after the maximum pre-trial detention period for that case expired. The public prosecutor did not object, and a judge granted the order on Wednesday. The former president still faces a retrial on separate charges of complicity in the deaths of demonstrators, after a court in 2015 ordered a retrial of a retrial. That case is ongoing, but Mr Mubarak's lawyer insisted that his client's release does not mean he has been cleared. "He is still under investigation in several cases," Mr El Deeb told reporters outside the hospital. "But the law is the law. He has served the maximum period of pre-trial detention permitted by Egyptian law." The decision to free Mr Mubarak has drawn sharp reactions. Some Egyptians, particularly those who took part in the 2011 uprising, expressed anger and dismay. "It feels like the revolution is being undone," said Ahmed Harara, who lost an eye during the protests. "He is not a sick old man – he is a symbol of the old regime, and his release sends a terrible message." Others welcomed the move, arguing that Mr Mubarak had already suffered enough and that the country should move on. The political context is significant. Mr Mubarak's release comes as President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's government faces mounting international criticism over human rights abuses and a sweeping crackdown on dissent. Hundreds of political prisoners – including activists, journalists and Islamists – remain behind bars. Mr Mubarak, once a close ally of the West, was overthrown by his own military in a move that later paved the way for Mr Sisi's rise. Many analysts see the former president's release as a quiet gesture of reconciliation with the old guard. Security officials said Mr Mubarak's health remains fragile. He suffered a heart attack during the early days of his trial and has undergone several surgeries, including gallbladder removal. His medical team at the military hospital described his condition as "stable but in need of continuous monitoring". A senior security source, speaking on condition of anonymity, told the BBC that the former president was not expected to hold any press conferences or public appearances. The fate of Mr Mubarak's two sons, Alaa and Gamal, remains unclear. They were also convicted on corruption charges but released in 2015 after serving time. They have been barred from travel and remain under investigation for other allegations. For many Egyptians, Mr Mubarak's release closes a chapter in the country's turbulent post-revolution history – but it does not answer the deeper questions about accountability and justice that the 2011 uprising demanded. Rights groups have criticised the Egyptian judiciary for handling high-profile cases in a manner they say prioritises political expediency over legal consistency. The helicopter flight from Tora prison to the military hospital symbolised the former president's unique status – no longer a prisoner, not yet a free man, but a figure who continues to cast a long shadow over Egypt's political landscape.

title: After a week of disturbing headlines, is Islamic State winning?
text_ai: It depends where. In Syria, where Islamic State (IS) captured Palmyra and is said to have murdered large numbers of people in its usual bloodthirsty fashion, it looks as though the regime of Bashar al-Assad is getting into serious trouble. Its army is no longer so effective at fighting his battles. But the picture across the wider Middle East is more nuanced. In Iraq, for example, IS has lost significant territory since its lightning offensive in 2014. The Iraqi security forces, backed by US-led coalition air power and Shia militias, have recaptured Tikrit, Ramadi and, most recently, Fallujah. The battle for Mosul, the group's de facto capital in Iraq, is looming. Yet the group remains a potent threat, able to carry out devastating suicide bombings in Baghdad and elsewhere. In Libya, IS has been largely driven out of its stronghold of Sirte by local forces loyal to the UN-backed government. But it has not been eradicated; fighters have melted into the desert or sought refuge in other parts of the country. In Afghanistan, the group's Khorasan Province affiliate has been squeezed by both US airstrikes and Taliban offensives, but it continues to carry out high-profile attacks in Kabul and elsewhere. So the question – is Islamic State winning? – demands a more careful answer. The group is losing ground in its core heartlands, but it is also adapting, morphing into a more resilient, diffuse and decentralised organisation. Its physical caliphate, once a source of immense propaganda value, is shrinking. But its ideological reach, its ability to inspire or direct attacks far beyond the battlefield, may be growing. The recent spate of attacks in Europe – in Paris, Brussels, Nice, Berlin – suggests a shift in tactics. IS has called on its followers to strike wherever they are, using whatever means are available. This is not the result of a master plan from its central command; it is a strategic response to military pressure. The group is no longer able to pour resources into large-scale, coordinated operations abroad as it once did. Instead, it has become a franchiser of terror, encouraging lone-wolf actors and small cells to act in its name. This is precisely what makes IS so difficult to defeat. Coalition airstrikes and local ground forces can retake cities, but they cannot eradicate an idea. The ideology of IS – a brutal, apocalyptic vision of a puritanical Islamic state – continues to attract recruits and sympathisers, even as its territorial holdings shrink. The group's sophisticated media apparatus, though damaged, still operates, pumping out videos, magazines and online propaganda, often in multiple languages. Furthermore, the root causes that allowed IS to flourish remain unaddressed. In Iraq, the sectarian policies of former Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki alienated the Sunni minority, creating a fertile recruitment ground. In Syria, the brutal repression of the Assad regime, and the subsequent vacuum left by a failed state, provided IS with space to expand. In Libya, the collapse of the state after the 2011 Nato intervention opened a new front. As long as these conditions persist, IS or a similar group can regenerate. The coalition strategy has been to degrade and ultimately destroy IS by targeting its leadership, finances and infrastructure. There have been successes: hundreds of senior and mid-level commanders have been killed; oil revenues have been slashed; weapons factories have been bombed. But the group has proved adept at replacing its losses. The US military estimates that IS still has tens of thousands of fighters, many of them hardened veterans. Moreover, the fight against IS is also a war of narratives. The group portrays itself as the defender of Sunni Muslims against a hostile coalition of Crusaders, Shia apostates and puppet regimes. Each time a US-led airstrike kills civilians – and such incidents, though carefully avoided, do happen – IS uses it as propaganda. Each time the Iraqi government or the Syrian regime commits atrocities against Sunnis, IS gains credibility. One of the most troubling developments is the way IS has managed to outlast the attention span of the international community. The world was horrified by the beheadings of Western hostages, the enslavement of Yazidi women, the massacre of Shia prisoners. But as the group's territory shrinks, so does the headlines. The danger is that complacency sets in, allowing IS to regroup and reorganise in the shadows, much as al-Qaeda did after the surge in Iraq a decade ago. Yet there are reasons for cautious optimism. The coalition has learned from past mistakes. The campaign is no longer solely military; it includes efforts to stabilise recaptured areas, provide humanitarian aid, and promote local governance. In Iraq, the government in Baghdad is making tentative steps towards reconciliation with the Sunni community. In Syria, the fall of Palmyra may be a setback, but it does not change the overall trajectory: IS has lost half the territory it once controlled in the country. But the war against IS is not a conventional conflict with a clear victory. It is a generational struggle, one that will require sustained political, economic and ideological effort. The group is not winning in the sense of expanding its territory or building a functioning state. But it is surviving. It is adapting. And it is still capable of causing immense suffering and inspiring violence across the globe. In the end, the answer to the question depends on which metrics you use. On the ground, in Syria and Iraq, IS is on the back foot. But in the broader war of ideas, and in its ability to exploit chaos and grievance, the group remains a formidable threat. The battle is far from over. And as the frontlines shift, the question itself may become less relevant than the need for a more sophisticated, long-term strategy to tackle not just the militants, but the conditions that give rise to them.

title: Scotland's first minister has congratulated Donald Trump on his surprise election win despite admitting it was "not the outcome I wanted".
text_ai: Nicola Sturgeon publicly backed Hillary Clinton ahead of the presidential vote. But she said the result of the election should be respected, and that Scotland valued its relationship with the US. On the other, the US is Scotland's largest international trading partner outside the European Union, and the Trump Organisation has significant commercial interests in the country. The president-elect owns two golf courses in Scotland – the Trump International Golf Links in Aberdeenshire and the Trump Turnberry resort in South Ayrshire. In 2014, he invested heavily in the latter, which features a luxury hotel and two championship courses. His mother, Mary Anne MacLeod, was born on the Isle of Lewis, giving him a direct family link to the country. During the campaign, Mr Trump described his Scottish ancestry as "very important" and vowed to "cherish" the relationship if elected. But his previous comments about Muslims prompted Ms Sturgeon to strip him of his role as a business ambassador for Scotland in 2015, drawing a sharp rebuke from the billionaire businessman, who called her a "failed politician". Now, with Mr Trump set to take office in January, the Scottish government faces the challenge of maintaining a constructive relationship while holding to its values. Ms Sturgeon acknowledged this tension in her statement: "I hope and expect that our two countries will continue to work together in the years to come on shared interests such as trade, security, and the fight against climate change. However, I have been clear about my concerns about some of his campaign statements, and I will continue to speak out when I believe fundamental principles are at stake." The first minister's approach echoed that of other European leaders, who offered congratulations while voicing reservations. But for Scotland, the stakes are arguably higher. The country is in the midst of a renewed push for independence, and the outcome of Brexit negotiations could have a profound impact on its future. The US relationship is a key part of that calculation. Scottish exports to the US were worth £5.4bn in 2019, accounting for 14% of all international sales. Key sectors include whisky, financial services, and life sciences. Any disruption to trade – whether from tariffs, immigration policy, or political tensions – would be felt keenly. "We are a small, open economy with a global outlook," said Professor Sir Anton Muscatelli, principal of the University of Glasgow and an adviser to the UK government on trade. "The US market is vital for many Scottish firms, particularly in food and drink. If the new administration pursues protectionist policies, it could have a significant negative impact." During the campaign, Mr Trump floated the idea of a 45% tariff on Chinese goods, but he also threatened to renegotiate trade deals with partners such as the UK and the EU. "If the US imposes tariffs on EU goods post-Brexit, and the UK is still in the single market at that point, Scotch whisky could be caught in the crossfire," said Karen Betts, chief executive of the Scotch Whisky Association. "We would urge the UK government to ensure that any future trade deal with the US protects the sector." Mr Trump's victory also has implications for the independence debate. "An independent Scotland would need to be a strong and dynamic player in the world," said Dr Kirsty Hughes, director of the Scottish Centre on European Relations. "If the US is perceived as a less reliable partner, that could make the case for independence more fraught, or conversely, it could reinforce the idea that Scotland needs to be part of a larger European bloc to have influence." The Scottish Conservatives, who oppose independence, seized on the result to attack Ms Sturgeon's previous criticism of Mr Trump. Scottish Tory leader Ruth Davidson said: "The first minister spent years trying to burnish her progressive credentials by attacking Donald Trump. Now she has to work with him. Ms Davidson added that the UK government, not the Scottish government, was responsible for international trade and foreign policy. "Nicola Sturgeon cannot pick and choose which aspects of the US relationship she wants to engage with while claiming to want a separate Scottish state that would have to handle these issues from day one." Ms Sturgeon pushed back against the criticism, saying her concerns about Mr Trump's policies were shared by many across the world. "I will never apologise for standing up for the values of tolerance, diversity, and human rights," she said. "But that does not mean I cannot work constructively with the US administration on issues of mutual interest." The first minister also pointed to the importance of the Scottish diaspora in the US, estimated at around 6 million people. Many are concentrated in states such as North Carolina, Texas, and California, and they have long been a source of cultural and economic ties. "There are deep bonds between Scotland and America that go far beyond any one political leader," Ms Sturgeon said. "Our shared heritage, our language, and our history of migration mean that the relationship is resilient. I am confident that it will endure." The first minister is expected to speak to US officials in the coming days and to seek a meeting with Mr Trump when he visits Scotland – though such a meeting may not be straightforward given their past exchanges. "Scotland should be doing much better." Since then, the two have traded occasional barbs. In July 2020, Ms Sturgeon criticised Mr Trump's handling of the pandemic, saying his suggestion that testing was being overdone was "dangerous". Mr Trump responded by tweeting that she was "a disaster" and that Scotland was "wasting its time" with lockdowns. Despite these tensions, diplomatic sources suggest that both sides will seek to keep relations pragmatic. "The US is a superpower, and Scotland is a small country within a larger state," said Professor John Curtice, a political scientist at the University of Strathclyde. "Ms Sturgeon cannot afford to snub him. She needs to be seen as a responsible leader who can engage with the realities of global politics." The prime minister, Boris Johnson, has already spoken to Mr Trump and is expected to push for a trade deal. But if the US prefers to deal directly with the UK government, the SNP's argument that Scotland needs its own voice on the world stage may be undermined. "Scottish independence is fundamentally about sovereignty, and sovereignty means being able to sit at the table with countries like the US," said Prof Curtice. title: Scottish Power has been rated worst for customer service in a ranking of the UK's biggest brands.

title: Among Pyongyang's recent inflated threats, the announced intention to "readjust and restart" its nuclear facilities is the most worrisome.
text_ai: If implemented, North Korea will be producing both kinds of fissile material that can create nuclear explosions: plutonium and highly enriched uranium. "By restarting both tracks, North Korea is telling the world it will not be constrained by any commitments it made in 2018–19. The Yongbyon freeze agreed with the Trump administration is dead in all but name." The timing is also revealing. title: The Catholic Archbishop of Durban, Wilfrid Fox Napier, has described paedophilia as a psychological "illness, not a criminal condition".
text_ai: The South African cardinal told the BBC that people who were themselves abused as children and then abused others needed to be examined by doctors. title: Sea creatures in all our oceans are getting bigger.
