title: Tourists recreating a scene from Bond movie Skyfall have been accused of causing damage in a Highlands glen.
text_ai: The film from 2012 has Dame Judi Dench's M and Daniel Craig's 007 standing side by side looking out over the landscape of Glen Etive. Social media campaign, Glen Etive the Dirty Truth, blames visitors to the same spot for causing erosion. The campaign, run by local residents and outdoor enthusiasts, has published photographs showing bare, rutted earth where visitors have repeatedly parked or stood to capture the iconic view. One image shows tyre tracks cutting across fragile moss and heather, while another reveals a wide, muddy patch where vehicles have churned up the ground – a stark contrast to the sweeping, pristine vista seen in the film. "It's heartbreaking," said Fiona MacLeod, a founder of the campaign and a hillwalker who has frequented Glen Etive for decades. "People come here wanting to recreate that perfect James Bond moment, but they don't understand they're trampling over a fragile ecosystem that takes years to recover. We're not anti-tourist – we're anti-destruction." The problem is not new. Glen Etive, a remote valley in the Scottish Highlands north of Glen Coe, has seen a surge in visitors since Skyfall's release, with many seeking the precise vantage point where M and Bond pause during their journey to the fictional Skyfall Lodge. But the damage has accelerated in recent years, fuelled by a rise in staycationing and social media sharing. Parking is a particular flashpoint. The single-track road winding through the glen offers only informal lay-bys, and visitors often abandon cars on grass verges or block access to farm tracks. "We've had people driving right up to the riverbank to get a selfie," said John Stewart, a local crofter. "It's not just the erosion – it's the litter, the toilet waste, the disturbance to wildlife." The Scottish Outdoor Access Code allows responsible use of land, but campaigners argue that the sheer volume of visitors seeking the Skyfall view has overwhelmed the glen's capacity. NatureScot, the government agency responsible for Scotland's natural heritage, has acknowledged the issue and is working with the local community to explore solutions, including improved signage and potential designated parking areas. A spokesperson said: "We recognise the pressure that increased tourism is placing on sensitive sites like Glen Etive. We are committed to working with partners to promote responsible access and protect these landscapes for future generations." But for local campaigners, the solution must also involve a shift in visitor behaviour – a move from simply replicating a film still to genuinely respecting the land that made it famous. As Fiona MacLeod put it: "You can take a photo without leaving a scar."
prefix: The film from 2012 has Dame Judi Dench's M and Daniel Craig's 007 standing side by side looking out over the landscape of Glen Etive. Social media campaign, Glen Etive the Dirty Truth, blames visitors to the same spot for causing erosion.

title: European leaders are billing their new proposal to deal with the refugee and migrant influx as a "game-changer", but the scheme is not agreed yet and there are doubts about whether it it is practical or even legal.
text_ai: The centrepiece is a plan to take any refugees and migrants who cross the sea to Greece in smugglers' boats and return them, directly, to Turkey. European Union officials say whatever is finally agreed "will comply with both European and international law". The blueprint, hammered out in Brussels ahead of a summit of EU and Turkish leaders on Monday, would see all irregular arrivals on the Greek islands — including those claiming asylum — returned to Turkey. In exchange, the EU would accelerate the resettlement of Syrian refugees from Turkish camps, taking in one person for every one sent back. Ankara would also receive a doubling of the €3bn (£2.3bn) already pledged, faster progress on visa liberalisation for Turkish citizens, and renewed momentum in its long-stalled membership talks. “This is not a simple readmission agreement,” a senior EU official insisted, speaking on condition of anonymity. “It is a comprehensive package designed to break the smugglers’ business model. If you know that arriving in Greece means being sent back to Turkey, you will not pay a trafficker to take you.” Yet the plan rests on a fundamental legal and logistical assumption: that Turkey is a “safe third country” for Syrian refugees and other migrants. Under both the 1951 Geneva Refugee Convention and the EU’s asylum procedures directive, states cannot return people to a place where they face persecution or torture. Human rights groups, the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR), and many legal scholars argue that Turkey does not meet that standard. **Legal minefield** Turkey does provide temporary protection for Syrians — more than 2.7 million are registered there — but it maintains a “geographical limitation” to the refugee convention, granting full refugee status only to those fleeing events in Europe. Non-Europeans, including Syrians, are given “conditional refugee” status, which does not guarantee long-term protection or the right to family reunification. Moreover, reports of Syrians being deported back to war zones, though denied by Ankara, have fuelled concerns. “Legally, this is highly questionable,” said Judith Sunderland, associate director for Europe at Human Rights Watch. “The EU knows that returning people to a country that does not offer full refugee protection could violate their rights under European and international law. The European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg has already suspended a previous EU-Turkey readmission deal over similar concerns.” The EU insists it will not carry out returns on an individual basis without assessing each case. “Every person will have their asylum claim examined individually by Greek authorities under EU law,” the senior official said. “No one will be automatically returned without due process.” But with an average of nearly 2,000 migrants and refugees arriving daily on Greek islands, critics question whether Greece’s overstretched asylum service can conduct fair, timely assessments. **Logistical nightmare** Even if the legal hurdles were cleared, the practical obstacles are daunting. Greece has already seen its reception system buckle under the weight of more than 850,000 arrivals since 2015. On Lesbos alone, some 15,000 people are crammed into a camp with a capacity of 3,000. Processing individual claims for all those who arrived after the deal is announced would require a huge expansion of staff and infrastructure. The plan also depends on the willingness of Turkey to accept rapid returns. Ankara has signalled it is ready to cooperate, driven by its own geopolitical and financial interests. President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has demanded progress on visa-free travel for Turkish citizens and fresh accession talks, both of which many EU member states, including Germany, are hesitant to grant. “Turkey is not doing this out of kindness — it wants concrete returns,” said Sinan Ülgen, a former Turkish diplomat and visiting scholar at Carnegie Europe. “The EU may have overestimated how easy it will be to move forward on visa liberalisation given the political climate in several member states.” Moreover, the EU has no legal mechanism to compel Turkey to abide by the deal if it decides to walk away. “This is not a formal treaty,” a second EU diplomat noted. “It is a political statement of intent. Its success depends entirely on mutual trust.” **Reactions from frontline states** Among EU member states, the proposal has divided opinion. Germany and Austria, which have borne the brunt of secondary movements from Greece, see it as a potential lifesaver. “We have to break the vicious circle of people dying in the Aegean and criminal gangs making billions,” said German Chancellor Angela Merkel. “This plan is our best hope.” But Greece, despite its desperate need to stem the flow, has raised concerns about the pressure put on its own asylum system. “We cannot become the buffer zone of Europe,” a Greek official said. “If the returns are not implemented quickly and efficiently, we will be left with thousands of people stuck on our islands, with no legal way forward.” Greece has also complained that the EU’s relocation scheme, agreed last year, has moved only a fraction of those it pledged to relocate. Eastern European states, led by Hungary and Poland, have been openly sceptical. “This plan rewards Turkey — an authoritarian government that is already holding millions of refugees — while punishing EU countries that want to protect their borders,” Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán said. “It will not stop the flow. It will only create more bureaucracy.” **NGOs and humanitarian groups** Aid organisations have been among the most vocal critics. Amnesty International called the plan “a Trojan horse for collective expulsions”. Save the Children warned that children would be returned to a country where many have no access to education and live on the streets. The UNHCR has publicly stated that Turkey should not be considered a safe third country for Syrians, and that the EU must maintain the right to seek asylum. “You are talking about returning people to a country that is already overwhelmed,” said Melissa Fleming, a UNHCR spokesperson. “More than 70% of Syrian refugees in Turkey live below the poverty line. There are massive gaps in education and healthcare. The EU cannot simply outsource its refugee problem and claim it is upholding international law.” **The Kurdish dimension** There is another complication: Turkey’s ongoing military operations against Kurdish forces in southeastern Turkey and northern Syria. Many asylum seekers from that region, including ethnic Kurds, have fled specifically to avoid being caught up in the conflict. Under the proposed deal, they would be returned to Turkey, where some claim they face detention, harassment, and even torture. The EU has acknowledged this concern. “We will ensure that no one is returned to a country where they face serious harm,” the senior official said. “That includes individuals from conflict zones in Turkey.” But critics argue that such a case-by-case approach is impossible to implement at the scale required, especially when thousands are arriving daily. **A political gamble** In the run-up to Monday’s summit, European Council President Donald Tusk warned that “time is running out” for a united EU response. The bloc has been divided for months over how to share the burden of the migrant crisis. The German-led push for mandatory quotas has been blocked by Eastern Europeans. The closure of the Balkan route has left Greece as the main entry point, and the country has threatened to block all transit if the EU does not provide more help. “This proposal is a high-stakes political gamble,” said Professor Andrew Geddes, director of the Migration Policy Centre at the European University Institute. “It tries to solve a series of problems at once: reducing arrivals to Greece, winning Turkish cooperation, and satisfying domestic populist pressures in EU states. But it risks creating new problems: violating refugee rights, overburdening Turkey, and alienating European courts.” **What happens next** The plan must be formally endorsed by EU leaders at the summit. Even then, its implementation would take weeks, possibly months. EU officials are working on a “fast-track” legislative mechanism to allow Greece to process returns speedily, but any law that restricts asylum rights could be challenged in the European Court of Justice. Meanwhile, the flow of migrants shows no sign of abating. In the 48 hours before the summit, more than 4,000 people crossed the Aegean to Greek islands. Smugglers have slashed their prices, warning that the window to reach Europe is closing. “The traffickers are selling this as the last chance,” said a Greek coastguard official. “They are telling people: ‘Go now, before the deal closes the door.’” As dawn broke over Lesbos on Sunday, a rubber boat carrying 50 Syrians, including a pregnant woman and half a dozen children, made landfall near the village of Skala Sikaminias. They were met not by European officials or Turkish police, but by a handful of Greek coastguards and volunteers from Médecins Sans Frontières. One of the volunteers, a young German doctor, shook his head. “They don’t know what’s coming,” he said. “They don’t know that the road ahead is just as hard as what they’ve left behind.”

title: The morning after the EU referendum - before she had even been to bed - Scotland's First Minister Nicola Sturgeon said she thought another independence referendum was "highly likely".

The Scottish Government's own Growth Commission report, published in 2018, painted a cautious picture of a transitional period requiring years of fiscal restraint before an independent Scotland could stabilise its finances. The Scottish Conservatives, with their new leader Douglas Ross at the helm, have made the case that the country should focus on recovery from the pandemic rather than a "divisive" referendum. Labour, too, under Anas Sarwar, has sought to reposition itself as the party of "federalism" within the UK, hoping to offer an alternative to independence without being seen as simply defending the Westminster status quo. It would not be fair to the people of Scotland, and it would be irresponsible to the people of the whole United Kingdom." The Scottish Government's own legal advice, published last year, argued that Holyrood could pass legislation for a referendum without Westminster's consent, though most constitutional lawyers dispute that contention. A legal challenge would almost certainly follow, and the Supreme Court would be asked to rule on whether the Scottish Parliament has the power to legislate for such a vote. The outcome of any legal battle is uncertain, but the political stakes are enormous. A Supreme Court ruling against Holyrood could leave Ms Sturgeon - and the independence movement - in a constitutional cul-de-sac, forced to rely on the outcome of the next general election as a proxy mandate. Winning a majority of Scottish seats in a UK-wide vote, while politically significant, would not automatically compel Westminster to grant a referendum, raising the spectre of a prolonged confrontation between Edinburgh and London. The mood in the independence movement itself is increasingly impatient. Younger voters, who backed independence heavily in 2014 and were among the strongest Remain supporters in the EU referendum, are frustrated by what they see as cautious incrementalism. Pro-independence grassroots groups, such as the newly formed "Yes Scotland" campaign - a rebranded successor to the 2014 campaign - have urged Ms Sturgeon to push ahead regardless of the legal obstacles. Yet the First Minister has shown a characteristic caution. She knows that while the passion of the pro-independence base is essential, the route to a sustainable Yes vote must also win over the uncommitted, the "soft No" voters who are open to persuasion but who balk at the idea of a leap in the dark. Running headlong into a legal battle and losing, she calculates, could set the cause back a generation. As the autumn session of the Scottish Parliament begins, the question of timing remains the most delicate strategic calculation. The First Minister has hinted that the "highly likely" moment may come sooner rather than later. But in the same breath, she has acknowledged that the public's appetite for another constitutional clash, after two years of pandemic and the cost-of-living crisis, is limited. "People want us to get on with the job of government," she told the BBC earlier this month, "but they also want their future to be decided by the people who live here, not by Boris Johnson." That tension - between the desire for stability and the demand for self-determination - will define Scottish politics for years to come. And for as long as the opinion polls remain static, Ms Sturgeon will have to navigate it with the same care she has shown since that sleepless morning in June 2016. The only certainty, perhaps, is that the question she posed then will not simply go away.

title: The dollar value of individual bitcoins may have fluctuated wildly since their creation but there is one facet of the virtual currency that has only ever accrued more and more interest - the question of who invented it.
text_ai: For the first two years of the project, the originator of Bitcoin's core ideas, who adopted the name of Satoshi Nakamoto, was very active on the cryptography forums where the underlying code of the protocol was critiqued, tested and improved. The dollar value of individual bitcoins may have fluctuated wildly since their creation but there is one facet of the virtual currency that has only ever accrued more and more interest - the question of who invented it. For the first two years of the project, the originator of Bitcoin's core ideas, who adopted the name of Satoshi Nakamoto, was very active on the cryptography forums where the underlying code of the protocol was critiqued, tested and improved. They engaged with developers, responded to suggestions, and even published a nine-page white paper in 2008 outlining the concept of a peer-to-peer electronic cash system. Then, in April 2011, Satoshi sent a final email to a fellow developer, stating simply: "I've moved on to other things." The messages stopped. The pseudonymous creator vanished, leaving behind a legacy of digital currency but an enduring mystery. The identity of Satoshi Nakamoto has become one of the most tantalising puzzles of the internet age. For more than a decade, journalists, amateur sleuths and even intelligence agencies have combed through every scrap of digital evidence, hoping to unmask the person—or group—behind the name. The stakes are high: if the real Satoshi is still alive, they are almost certainly a billionaire. Bitcoin wallets linked to the earliest mining activity are estimated to hold roughly one million coins, worth tens of billions of dollars at current prices. But the creator has never touched those funds, and the silence has only deepened the enigma. Several candidates have been proposed over the years. In 2014, *Newsweek* claimed to have identified the inventor as Dorian Nakamoto, a Japanese-American physicist living in California. Dorian vehemently denied any involvement, and the story collapsed under scrutiny. Then, in 2016, Australian entrepreneur Craig Wright publicly declared himself to be Satoshi, offering technical proof that was quickly dismissed by the Bitcoin community. Lawsuits followed, and Wright's claims remain a subject of bitter dispute, with a UK High Court judge ruling in 2024 that Wright is not Satoshi—a verdict that effectively shut down one of the most persistent narratives. Other theories point to cryptographers such as Nick Szabo, creator of the earlier "bit gold" concept, or Hal Finney, the first person to receive a Bitcoin transaction. Both have denied being Satoshi. Finney died in 2014, and Szabo has repeatedly distanced himself from the claim. Some researchers have suggested a collective authorship—a team of developers who together wrote the Bitcoin code and then dissolved, leaving no trace. But no convincing evidence has emerged. The mystery endures partly because of the careful design of the original system. Satoshi never registered a domain under a real name, never used a traceable IP address, and communicated only through encrypted channels and forum posts. Linguistic analysis has proven inconclusive: the white paper and forum comments are written in idiomatic British English, but with occasional American spellings. The timing of Satoshi's posts—often during the early hours in the US or late evening in the UK—has spawned theories about time zones, but nothing definitive. Why did Satoshi vanish? Some speculate that the creator wanted to protect both themselves and the decentralised nature of Bitcoin. A living figurehead would have concentrated power and influence, contradicting the very philosophy of the currency. Others suggest that Satoshi feared legal or personal repercussions, given Bitcoin's association with dark web markets and money laundering. A more sombre possibility is that the inventor is no longer alive. The question of Satoshi's identity is not merely a curiosity. It has profound implications for Bitcoin's governance and future. If the creator's wallets were ever moved, it could destabilise the market, or alternatively, if they were to reveal themselves, they might influence the direction of the cryptocurrency. The community remains divided: some argue that the search is pointless and distracts from Bitcoin's utility, while others insist that the world deserves to know who gave it such a transformative technology. As interest in Bitcoin continues to grow—driven by institutional adoption, regulatory scrutiny, and its role as a speculative asset—the mystery of Satoshi Nakamoto shows no signs of fading. It has become a modern legend, a tale of genius, anonymity, and the power of an idea that escaped its creator's control. And so the search goes on. New leads emerge, are debunked, and are replaced. The blockchain itself provides no answers—only a permanent, silent record of a digital ghost who built a revolution and then disappeared into it.

title: The healthiest way to cook mushrooms is to microwave or grill them to preserve their goodness, researchers say.

title: Electronic producer Moby has returned with a new project and pseudo-political manifesto Moby and the Pacific Void Choir.
text_ai: In the press release for the new record The Systems Are Failing, the musician writes: "We're destroying the world, and we're still miserable. Fat, sick, stupid and anxious are no ways to live. "These systems are failing. Let them fail. Change or die." What makes this different from a Moby album? The answer, Moby explains in a follow-up phone conversation, lies in the collective. "The Pacific Void Choir isn't a band in the traditional sense," he says. "It's a loose affiliation of musicians, activists, and data scientists who contribute to a shared sonic and political architecture. "We're not just saying 'the world is ending, let's dance'. We're saying the dance is a form of resistance, a way of rehearsing the world we want to build. The Systems Are Failing is a manual, not a dirge." The record, released today on his own Little Idiot imprint, is Moby's first full-length since 2020's *All Visible Objects*, and his most overtly political work since 1999's *Play* — albeit with a very different mode of address. Where *Play* sampled old blues and gospel recordings to create a haunted, melancholic dance-pop, the new album is deliberately abrasive, its textures built from field recordings of protests, granular synthesis of government speeches, and loops of ambulance sirens. The single *Permission to Die* opens with a distorted reading of a World Health Organisation report on antibiotic resistance, before collapsing into a nine-minute ambient drone punctuated by a single, repeated piano chord. "It's not easy listening," admits reviewer Jenna K. Thomas, who covers experimental electronic music for *The Wire*. "But that's the point. Moby is deliberately refusing the comfort of his earlier sound. He's saying: if you want to dance your way through the apocalypse, you have to first acknowledge that the floor is on fire." The Pacific Void Choir itself is a fluid entity. Core members include London-based sound artist Rika Tobin, whose work focuses on sonifying climate data, and Berlin vocalist Nils Andersson, who provides the only human voice on the album — a wordless, keening countertenor that cuts through the noise. "Moby wanted the choir to be truly decentred," Tobin explains. "No lead singer, no single identity. We contribute remotely, share stems, argue about mix decisions in a Signal group chat. The result is collaborative but also conflictual. That's the sound of disagreement, which is itself political." The accompanying manifesto, released as a 32-page PDF and a limited edition zine, is a dense, sometimes contradictory text. It calls for the abolition of private aviation, the nationalisation of streaming platforms, and a "universal basic creative income" for artists. It also advocates for a return to "slow music" — tracks that cannot be consumed via TikTok or algorithmic playlists. "We want to make music that demands time, attention, and discomfort," Moby writes in the introduction. This posture has already drawn criticism. Some observers note that Moby himself has a net worth estimated at $25m, much of it derived from the very streaming economy he now excoriates. "It's easy to romanticise obscurity when you're already famous," wrote music journalist Alex Petridis in *The Guardian* this morning. "Moby's version of 'slow music' arrives with a full PR campaign and a press junket. That's not an argument against the system; it's a career move within it." Moby is characteristically unapologetic. "I'm aware of the contradictions," he says. "But we don't get to opt out of the system's contradictions. We can only use our positions to point at them. I'm not trying to be a saint — I'm trying to make a noise that startles people into thinking." The project's genesis lies in a series of essays Moby wrote during the pandemic, originally posted on his personal blog. These meditations on ecological grief, technological alienation, and the failure of liberal democracies were read by Tobin, who reached out to suggest a collaboration. "I'd been working on a piece about the sound of melting glaciers," Tobin recalls. "And I thought: Moby has a platform, but he also has a willingness to be wrong. That's rare." The resulting album was recorded in what Moby calls "a deliberately low-fidelity way" — using a single microphone, a laptop, and a cracked copy of Pro Tools. It was partly funded by a small grant from the Arts Council England, which Moby donated back to a community radio collective in Bristol. "I didn't want the record to feel like a product," he says. "I wanted it to feel like a leak." Reviews have been mixed. *Pitchfork* gave the album a 6.5, noting that "for all its conceptual rigour, *The Systems Are Failing* occasionally forgets to be music". *Resident Advisor* was more enthusiastic, calling it "a brave, if uneven, experiment in political sound". But the most interesting response may be the one Moby himself anticipated: silence. Streaming numbers for the album's first 24 hours were low — barely 10,000 plays across platforms. Moby claims this was intentional. "If we'd released a pop single, we'd be complicit in the very machinery we're critiquing," he says. "We're asking: what does success mean in a failing system? Maybe success is just the act of making the thing, and letting it exist on its own terms." That may be a luxury few can afford. But Moby, now 58, seems comfortable with the paradox. "I've been famous, I've been obscure, I've been a punchline and a prophet," he says. "This project is not about my career. It's about using sound to map the collapse. And then to imagine what comes after." What comes after, the manifesto suggests, is a kind of collective creativity — a world where music is not a commodity but a common good. "We don't need more albums," Moby writes in its final pages. "We need more choirs." Whether anyone will join this particular choir, or whether it will remain a lonely voice in the void, remains to be seen. But as the systems continue to fail — politically, ecologically, emotionally — the urgency of the question is hard to deny.

title: The number of first-time buyers relying on the "bank of mum and dad" for financial help has hit a record high, according to new research.

"The banks need fresh capital, not just a promise of future revenue." With parliament now expected to vote on Tuesday, President Anastasiades faces an agonising choice. For the rest of the eurozone, the Cyprus crisis raises uncomfortable questions about the future of the single currency. The European Commission has long argued for a comprehensive framework to wind down failing banks without exposing taxpayers to huge losses. But the Cyprus levy shows how difficult that is in practice – and how quickly it can undermine confidence in the very safety net that is supposed to protect savers. The usual bustle of a Mediterranean capital has given way to anxious conversations in cafes and queues outside bakeries. For the past 16 years, the electoral map for US presidential elections has been variations on a familiar theme. Ohio and Florida are the key battlegrounds. A handful of other states - including New Hampshire, Virginia, Colorado and Iowa - count as smaller prizes in the quest to the reach the magic number of 270 electoral votes. Yet beneath this surface of apparent stability, a quiet but profound realignment has been under way. The tectonic plates of American politics have shifted, fracturing old coalitions and forging new ones with such force that the map of 2024 may bear little resemblance to the one that first took shape in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. What was once a predictable two-tier system – a handful of swing states surrounded by solidly blue or red territory – is now a more fluid and volatile landscape. And at the heart of this transformation lies a simple but disruptive question: which voters, and which places, will decide the next president? To understand the scale of the change, it helps to look back at the Obama years. In 2008, Barack Obama not only won Ohio and Florida, but also Indiana, North Carolina, and Virginia – states that had been reliably Republican for decades. It was a landslide built on a coalition of young voters, minorities, and college-educated whites, especially in the suburbs. But that coalition proved fragile. Just four years later, Obama lost Indiana and North Carolina, and barely held on to Ohio and Florida. The Republican Party, meanwhile, had begun its own transformation under the influence of the Tea Party movement, which pulled it further to the right and deepened its reliance on rural and non-college white voters. Donald Trump’s victory in 2016 shattered the old map entirely. He flipped Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin – states that had voted Democratic since the 1980s and were considered part of the “blue wall.” He also won Ohio and Florida by comfortable margins, and came within a whisker of winning Minnesota and New Hampshire. The familiar battlegrounds of the previous decade were suddenly joined by a new set of Rust Belt states, where economic anxiety and cultural resentment had overwhelmed traditional party loyalties. The suburban voters who had flocked to Obama in 2008 and 2012, particularly women and college graduates, began to drift away from the GOP, while working-class white voters in the industrial Midwest moved decisively toward Trump. By 2020, the map had shifted again. Joe Biden rebuilt the blue wall, winning Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, and added Georgia and Arizona – two states that had not voted Democratic since the 1990s. He also held on to Nevada, New Hampshire, and Minnesota. But he lost Ohio and Florida by wider margins than Hillary Clinton had, and he narrowly lost North Carolina. The story of 2020 was one of suburban backlash against Trump, especially among women and older voters, and a surge in turnout among Black and Hispanic voters in key cities and exurbs. Yet it was also a story of how deeply the country remained divided. Biden’s popular vote margin was about 4.5 percentage points – larger than Trump’s in 2016 but smaller than Obama’s in 2008 and 2012. And the Electoral College continued to favour Republicans, as Biden’s narrow wins in Georgia, Arizona, and Wisconsin were enough to secure the presidency despite losing states like Ohio and Florida by significant margins. So where does that leave us in 2024? The conventional wisdom, once again, points to a handful of familiar states. But that wisdom is increasingly outdated. Ohio, once the bellwether of American politics, has trended so heavily Republican that many analysts now consider it a red state – or at least a light-red one. It voted for Trump by 8 points in 2016 and by 8 points again in 2020, and its Senate races have followed a similar pattern. Its demographics – older, whiter, more rural, and less educated than the national average – have pushed it out of the swing-state category. Florida, too, has moved decisively to the right. Once the ultimate toss-up, it is now governed by a popular Republican governor, Ron DeSantis, and voted for Trump by three points in 2020 after being the closest state in the nation in 2000 and 2012. Its demographic mix – with large Cuban-American and Puerto Rican communities, as well as a growing population of retirees from the Northeast and Midwest – no longer guarantees a close race. Republicans have made significant gains among Hispanic voters, particularly in Miami-Dade County, while Democrats have struggled to mobilise their base in the state. The real battlegrounds of 2024 are likely to be further north and west. Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin are once again at the centre of the electoral map. All three were decided by less than one percentage point in 2020, and all three have seen significant demographic and political changes since then. Michigan has seen a surge in Democratic turnout in its suburban counties – especially Oakland County, outside Detroit – while its rural and working-class counties have moved further right. Wisconsin remains a near-perfect 50-50 state, with its conservative WOW counties (Waukesha, Ozaukee, Washington) offsetting the liberal city of Milwaukee and Dane County. Pennsylvania is perhaps the most volatile of all, with its eastern suburbs of Philadelphia and the western city of Pittsburgh pulling in opposite directions, and its vast rural middle leaning sharply Republican. Beyond the Rust Belt, a new tier of swing states has emerged. Arizona, once a conservative stronghold, has become a perennial battleground. Its fast-growing population, particularly in Maricopa County (Phoenix), includes a large number of transplants from other states, many of whom are moderate or liberal. The state’s rapidly diversifying electorate – with a growing Hispanic and Native American population – has also helped Democrats. However, Republicans have retained a strong base in the state’s rural areas and among older white voters. The result is a state that has voted for the Democratic candidate in three of the last four presidential elections, but by margins so narrow that a shift of a few thousand votes could flip it back. Georgia is another state that has moved from safe Republican to toss-up. Its transformation has been driven by two major forces: the suburbanisation of Atlanta and the mobilisation of Black voters, particularly women. In 2020, Biden became the first Democrat to carry Georgia since 1992, and the state has since elected two Democratic senators. But its political geography remains deeply divided. The metro Atlanta area – including Fulton, DeKalb, Cobb, and Gwinnett counties – is overwhelmingly Democratic, while the rest of the state, especially the rural and small-town south, is heavily Republican. The outcome in Georgia, like Arizona, will depend on turnout in the suburbs and among voters of colour. Nevada, too, remains a key battleground, though its electoral college votes are smaller. The state has voted Democratic in every presidential election since 2008, but by shrinking margins. Its economy – heavily dependent on tourism and gaming – has made it particularly sensitive to national economic conditions, and its large Hispanic and Asian American populations are not reliably Democratic. In 2020, Biden won Nevada by just over two points, and the state has since seen a surge in Republican registration. Perhaps the most intriguing new battleground is North Carolina. It has voted Republican in every presidential election since 1980, except for Obama’s narrow win in 2008. But its margins have been shrinking. In 2020, Trump won by only 1.3 points, and the state’s rapidly growing population is becoming more diverse, with large influxes of Hispanic and Asian American residents, as well as transplants from the Northeast. The suburban counties around Charlotte and the Research Triangle are becoming more Democratic, while the rural east and west remain strongly Republican. North Carolina has become a state where both parties invest heavily, and it could be the tipping point in a close election. What unites these new battlegrounds is a common demographic and geographic story: the suburban revolt against Trumpism, the growing power of non-white voters, and the polarisation of the electorate along educational lines. College-educated voters, especially white women in the suburbs, have moved sharply toward Democrats since 2016. Non-college voters, both white and non-white, have moved toward Republicans, though the shift is more pronounced among whites. The result is an electoral map that looks less like a chessboard and more like a patchwork quilt, with a hundred smaller battles being fought in state legislative districts, county commissions, and even precincts. At the same time, the old faithfuls are changing. The once-reliable red states of the South – Texas, South Carolina, and Mississippi – are becoming more competitive at the margins, though not yet truly competitive. Texas, in particular, is a long-term concern for Republicans. Its growing Hispanic population and fast-expanding metropolitan areas, especially around Houston, Dallas, and Austin, have made it more Democratic in recent cycles. In 2020, Trump won Texas by less than six points – the smallest margin for a Republican since 1996. Democrats, however, have yet to build the infrastructure and turnout machinery needed to win statewide, and the state’s restrictive voter-ID laws and gerrymandered congressional districts remain significant obstacles. Meanwhile, the once-solid blue states of the Northeast and West Coast are also shifting. New York, California, and Illinois have seen their Democratic margins shrink slightly in recent elections, as Republican voters have become more concentrated in rural and exurban areas. But these states remain safely Democratic at the presidential level. More notable is the trend in states like New Mexico, Colorado, and Virginia, which have moved from purple to light blue. All three now have Democratic governors and legislatures, and are reliably Democratic in presidential elections. Colorado, in particular, has seen a surge in Democratic registration, driven by the influx of young, educated workers to the Denver metro area. The implications for 2024 are profound. If the election is close, the outcome will likely hinge on a handful of states that were not even considered battlegrounds a decade ago. Arizona, Georgia, and North Carolina will be joined by Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. States like Nevada, New Hampshire, and Minnesota – while still competitive – may be less decisive simply because they have fewer electoral votes. And the perennial battlegrounds of Ohio and Florida, once the twin pillars of the electoral map, are now firmly in the Republican column, leaving Democrats to search for new paths to 270. That search is not easy. To win without Ohio and Florida, a Democratic candidate must hold all the states that Biden won in 2020 and then flip a red state like North Carolina or Georgia. Or they must hold every blue-wall state and then win a Sun Belt state like Arizona or Georgia. The same is true for Republicans: to win without Ohio and Florida, they would need to hold all the states Trump won in 2020 and then flip a blue-wall state like Michigan or Pennsylvania. Either path requires a candidate who can appeal to the specific coalition of voters in those states – and that coalition is different in each place. In many ways, the electoral map of 2024 will be a referendum on two competing visions of America’s future. One vision is urban and suburban, diverse and educated, global in outlook and tolerant in culture. The other vision is rural and exurban, white and working-class, nationalist in orientation and traditionalist in values. Both visions find expression in the battleground states, but they do so in different proportions. In Pennsylvania, the divide is between Philadelphia and Pittsburgh, and the sprawling suburbs that have grown up around them. In Georgia, it’s between Atlanta and the rest of the state. In Arizona, it’s between the Phoenix metro and the vast desert counties to the north and south. What makes the 2024 contest so uncertain is that neither party has yet found a formula to win consistently in all of these battlegrounds. The Republicans have a strong advantage in rural areas and among working-class voters, but they struggle in suburbs and among college-educated women. The Democrats have a strong advantage in cities and among minority voters, but they struggle in small towns and among non-college whites. The result is an electoral map that is both deeply polarised and highly fluid – a map where a shift of a few thousand votes in a handful of counties can determine the next president. For the past 16 years, the electoral map for US presidential elections has been variations on a familiar theme. But that theme is changing. The old battlegrounds are fading, the new ones are rising, and the forces of demographic change, economic dislocation, and cultural conflict are redrawing the lines of American politics. The map of 2024 will be different from the map of 2008 – and it may be different again by 2028. The only certainty is that the quest for 270 electoral votes will remain the most high-stakes contest in the world.
prefix: Ohio and Florida are the key battlegrounds. A handful of other states - including New Hampshire, Virginia, Colorado and Iowa - count as smaller prizes in the quest to the reach the magic number of 270 electoral votes.

title: Flights in southern England have suffered minor delays because of air traffic control computer problems.

A BA spokesperson said: "We are sorry for any inconvenience caused to customers and thank them for their patience." EasyJet also confirmed minor disruptions at Gatwick, with some departures held on the ground while the system was restored. The airline urged passengers to check their flight status before travelling to the airport. Social media users reported long queues at security and information desks at several airports, though the disruption appeared to be short-lived. By midday, Nats confirmed the system was fully operational and that normal service had resumed. The so-called "rogue flight plan" – an erroneous or improperly formatted flight plan that can confuse the computer system – is a known but rare occurrence in air traffic control. Nats said it would review the incident to prevent a recurrence. Wednesday's glitch comes on the anniversary of a far more serious Nats computer failure in August 2023, when a technical fault led to the cancellation of hundreds of flights and left thousands of passengers stranded. That failure, which lasted several hours, prompted a review by the Civil Aviation Authority. Industry experts noted that while Wednesday's incident was comparatively minor, it underscored the pressure on the UK's air traffic control infrastructure. A CAA spokesman said the regulator had been "in contact with Nats to understand the cause and ensure appropriate measures are in place". The Department for Transport said it was monitoring the situation but did not comment further. Passengers affected by the delays were advised to check with their airlines for rebooking options, though most were expected to reach their destinations within an hour of their original schedules.

title: The death of a forestry worker after a log pile became unstable was a tragic accident, a sheriff has found.
text_ai: Andrew Marshall, 71, died from a head injury and compression of his chest after becoming trapped under a fallen wooden log. A post-mortem examination confirmed the cause of death as blunt force trauma to the head and chest compression. "We found that the employer had provided appropriate training and had a system of work in place," he said. "There was no evidence to suggest any breach of health and safety legislation." The sheriff acknowledged that the incident had occurred in a remote location and that the log pile had been disturbed prior to the collapse by the removal of several logs for processing. However, he concluded that no individual or organisation was to blame for Mr Marshall's death. Speaking after the hearing, Mr Marshall's family said they were left with "unanswered questions" about the safety of working alone in such conditions. In a statement, they described him as "a dedicated and hard-working man who loved the outdoors" and said they hoped lessons would be learned from the tragedy. title: The death of a close, elderly relative can often mean a sombre weekend or two going through old things, sorting through photographs, donating old clothes to charity.
text_ai: But in an age when so much of our lives are online, little thought has been given to how we handle a person's digital world when they are no longer with us. It is a question that families, lawyers and tech companies are only beginning to wrestle with: what happens to the emails, the social media profiles, the cloud-stored photos, the online banking and the streaming subscriptions when someone dies? For most people, the answer is a messy, often painful scramble. Relatives may know a password, or they may not. They may have a list of accounts, or they may spend weeks trawling through inboxes and browser histories. And by then, bills may have gone unpaid, subscriptions may have auto-renewed, and precious digital memories may have been permanently locked behind a two-factor authentication wall. The scale of the problem is enormous. According to a 2023 study by the Digital Legacy Association, roughly 84% of UK adults have some form of online presence, and 43% have never discussed what should happen to it after they die. The result is a growing backlog of "digital orphans" — accounts that are effectively abandoned, their contents inaccessible to anyone. "It’s a new kind of grief," says Dr Helen Cartwright, a psychologist specialising in bereavement at the University of Bristol. "Families are already dealing with the emotional loss, and then they’re confronted with a technical puzzle. You can’t just put a photo album in a box anymore. The album might be in a cloud service that you can’t log into." The legal landscape is equally murky. In the UK, a person’s digital assets are not explicitly covered by traditional inheritance law. The courts have yet to produce a clear ruling on whether an email account or a Facebook profile is property like a house or a car, or something more personal — a form of communication that dies with the user. Tech companies, for their part, have different policies. Google offers an Inactive Account Manager, which can be set up to grant access to a trusted contact after a period of inactivity. Apple, by contrast, requires a court order and a death certificate before it will unlock a device. Meta allows users to designate a "legacy contact" for Facebook and Instagram, but that contact can only manage a limited set of functions — they cannot read private messages. "There is no one-size-fits-all solution," says James Driscoll, a solicitor specialising in digital estate planning at a London firm. "I advise all my clients to make a digital will. Write down every account, every password, and what you want done with each. And then store that document securely — not on your phone." The problem is that few people do. A survey by the insurer Direct Line found that only 7% of UK adults have included digital assets in their will. The rest assume their families will figure it out. But figuring it out can be traumatic. For Sarah, a 34-year-old teacher from Manchester, the death of her mother meant not only sorting through physical belongings but also decoding a digital life she never knew existed. "She had multiple email addresses — one for shopping, one for work, one for family. She had a PayPal account with a few hundred pounds in it. She had a Pinterest board she’d never told me about. I had to guess passwords. I had to use her phone to reset logins. It took months." Sarah’s experience is not unusual. Tech-savvy relatives might fare better, but even they can hit walls. Two-factor authentication, biometric locks, and encryption are designed to protect against hackers — and they do. But they also protect against grieving heirs. Some companies are beginning to respond. Last year, Apple introduced a Digital Legacy feature for iPhones and iPads, allowing users to add up to five legacy contacts who can request access after death. Microsoft offers a similar "next of kin" process. But these are voluntary systems, and the burden remains on the individual to set them up before they die. There is also a growing market for third-party digital vault services — companies like MyWishes, Keeper, or Everplans — that store passwords and instructions and release them to designated recipients upon proof of death. But these services are not regulated, and their long-term stability is uncertain. Beyond the practical and legal challenges, there is an emotional dimension that is often overlooked. What does it mean to read a dead person's emails? To see their unread messages, their drafts, their search history? Social media profiles can become shrines — or sources of pain. Some families want to keep a page active as a memorial; others want it deleted entirely. The choice is not always straightforward, and the platforms do not always respect it. "In the past, you had a funeral, you had a grave, you had a memory," says Dr Cartwright. "Now you also have a digital ghost. And that ghost doesn't have a set of instructions." Campaigners are calling for clearer legislation. The Law Commission of England and Wales is currently reviewing the probate process and has indicated it will consider digital assets. In the US, some states have passed laws allowing executors to access digital accounts, but the UK lags behind. Until then, the burden remains on the individual. Experts recommend the following: make a list of all online accounts and store it physically with your will. Set up legacy contacts where possible. Consider a digital executor. And talk to your family about it. "It feels morbid," says Driscoll. "But it’s a gift to the people you leave behind. Every password you write down is one less headache for them." For now, the digital afterlife is a frontier without a map. Families are left to navigate it in the dark, often learning the hard way that the things we leave behind are no longer just physical. They exist in servers, in encrypted files, in metadata. And they can be just as hard to let go of.

title: For most of her life, Jessie Stocks has been surrounded by four grey walls and machines in Sheffield Children's Hospital.
text_ai: It is the only world the two-year-old has known for the last 17 months after being diagnosed with leukaemia. Now her mum, Mel, is hoping to take her little girl on a trip around the world - in the form of postcards. From her cot, Jessie has watched the changing seasons through a window that frames a sliver of Sheffield sky. Her mother, Mel Stocks, 32, has spent countless nights on a pull-out chair beside her, memorising the pattern of the hospital’s linoleum floor. But now she is determined to give Jessie a taste of the world beyond those walls – one postcard at a time. The appeal, launched on social media last week, asks people from every corner of the globe to send a postcard addressed to Jessie at the hospital’s cancer ward. “I just want her to see that there’s more out there than beeping machines and isolation rooms,” Mel told the BBC. “She loves bright colours, animals, anything with a bit of glitter. I thought, if we can’t take her to the world, we’ll bring the world to her.” The response has been overwhelming. Within days, postcards arrived from as far afield as Australia, Japan, Canada and Brazil. A pensioner from Cornwall sent a picture of a sandy cove. A school class in Nairobi wrote a group message in Swahili. “Jessie can’t read yet, but we read them out to her,” Mel said. “Her face lights up when she sees a beach or a snow-capped mountain. It’s like a little window opening.” Jessie was diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in February 2023, when she was just nine months old. Since then, she has undergone multiple rounds of chemotherapy, blood transfusions and spinal injections. The treatment has left her immunocompromised, meaning even a common cold could be life-threatening. For months at a time, she has been confined to a side room on the hospital’s oncology unit, where every surface is wiped down with disinfectant and visitors are limited. “We’ve celebrated her first birthday in here, her first steps, her first words,” Mel recalled, her voice steady but heavy. “You try to make it as normal as possible, but it’s not. There are days when she just stares at the wall and I don’t know what to do.” The postcard campaign has given Mel a sense of purpose, and Jessie a daily dose of wonder. Staff on the ward have pinned the cards to a noticeboard by Jessie’s bed, creating a colourful collage that grows by the hour. “It’s become a real talking point for the other children and families too,” said nurse Claire Roberts. “It reminds everyone that there’s a whole world waiting out there.” Charities supporting families with childhood cancer have praised the initiative. “Simple acts of kindness can make a profound difference,” said Dr. Emma Turner, a paediatric psychologist at the hospital. “For a child who has lost so much normal life, receiving a postcard is a tangible connection to the outside world – a message that says ‘you are not forgotten’.” Mel now dreams of expanding the collection. She hopes to receive a postcard from every country on Earth – all 195. “It might take years,” she admits, “but Jessie is a fighter. If she can endure all those needles and treatments, the least I can do is chase some bits of paper.” As for Jessie, she doesn’t yet understand continents or stamps. But when her mother holds up a postcard from a stranger in a faraway land – a penguin in Antarctica, a panda in China – she reaches out with a tiny hand, touches the image, and giggles. For a moment, the four grey walls melt away.

title: England's most capped player Fara Williams has tipped strikers Beth Mead and Nikita Parris to earn their senior debuts in next month's European Championship qualifying opener.
text_ai: Sunderland's Mead, 20, is Women's Super League One's top scorer with 11 goals, while Manchester City's Parris, 21, has netted five times in all competitions. Mark Sampson's England side start their qualifying campaign in Estonia. "They're certainly two players he could look at," Liverpool's Williams said. "Both have been in outstanding form this season," the 31-year-old midfielder, who has 132 caps, told BBC Sport. "Mead is a natural goalscorer. She's quick, direct and has a real eye for goal. Parris is more of a wide player but she's got great pace and can beat defenders. They bring different qualities, but both are ready for the next step." Williams, who made her England debut aged 17, knows the challenge of breaking into a senior side that reached the semi-finals of last year's World Cup. "You don't want to throw players in at the deep end in a crucial qualifier, but Estonia away is a good opportunity. The expectation will be to win, but the pressure is not as intense as a World Cup qualifier." Mead's 11 goals in 13 league games have caught the eye of England coach Mark Sampson, who has been monitoring the Under-23s closely. Parris, meanwhile, has been a key part of Manchester City's run to the FA Cup semi-finals and their climb to second in WSL One. England's attacking options already include Ellen White, Jodie Taylor and Duggan, but Williams believes competition is healthy. "It keeps everyone on their toes," she said. title: The domestic rugby league season begins on Thursday, with 12 clubs all hoping to be crowned Super League champions in October.
text_ai: Are you a huge fan counting down the hours to your team's opening game? Or never seen the sport before and fancy something new? Here are 10 reasons to watch rugby league in 2015. Rugby league was catapulted into the sporting spotlight following Super League's Grand Final in October. Indeed, that Grand Final between St Helens and Wigan was a classic, drawing a record television audience and showcasing the sport at its most visceral. But as the new season dawns on Thursday night with Leeds Rhinos facing Warrington Wolves, there are even more compelling reasons to tune in – from a radical new league structure to a fresh cast of overseas stars. **1. The new league format** For years, critics said Super League lacked tension. Not any more. In 2015, the competition has been ripped up and remade. After 23 rounds, the 12 clubs split into three groups of four – the Super 8s, the Middle 8s and the bottom 8s. It is a winner-takes-all system designed to keep every match meaningful. The top eight fight for the title; the middle four battle to avoid relegation alongside the top four from the second-tier Championship; the bottom four are effectively consigned to the lower division. It is convoluted, yes, but it means no club can afford a mid-season slump. As Leeds coach Brian McDermott put it: “Every game has a consequence. That’s what rugby league is about.” **2. The return of the prodigal son** Sam Tomkins is back. After a disappointing stint with the New Zealand Warriors in the NRL, the most expensive player in British rugby league history has rejoined Wigan Warriors on a four-year deal. Tomkins’s ability to change a game from full-back – with his deceptive pace, audacious chip-and-chases and try-scoring instinct – makes him the league’s biggest box-office attraction. His first match against Leeds on Friday night is already sold out. “He brings a spark,” says Wigan coach Shaun Wane. “He’s a special player who gives everyone a lift.” **3. A golden generation of English talent** Tomkins is not alone. The domestic game is awash with home-grown stars. St Helens full-back Jonny Lomax, 25, has recovered from a series of injuries to become the most dangerous attacker in the league. Leeds captain Kevin Sinfield, despite being 34, remains a metronomic kicker and inspirational leader. And then there is the young prodigy: Zak Hardaker, now at Wigan after leaving Leeds, who was the 2014 Man of Steel. Hardaker’s physicality and speed make him a constant threat. This is a generation that could take England to World Cup glory. **4. The war of the Roses – and beyond** Nothing stirs the soul like a local derby. And 2015 offers a feast: St Helens vs Wigan, Leeds vs Bradford, Hull FC vs Hull KR – fixtures that are tribal, passionate and often violent. But the new format also creates cross-border rivalries as Championship sides like Leigh Centurions, with their noisy home crowd, get a shot at the big boys. The first Middle 8s round in August could feature Bradford – a club rebuilding after financial ruin – facing a Super League giant. That is the kind of underdog story that draws in the casual viewer. **5. The NRL stars arriving on these shores** The salary cap remains tight, but clubs have found room for some genuine marquee signings. Warrington have snared Australian Test forward Ben Currie? Actually, the biggest name is former NRL star and Samoa international Reni Maitua, plus ex-Canberra half-back Josh McCrone. But the most eye-catching is probably the signing of James Maloney? No, Maloney stayed in Australia. Instead, look for Hull FC’s new Australian half-back Leon Pryce (though he is English-born). Apologies for the confusion – the real highlight is the arrival in the Championship of former NRL star and Tonga international Feleti Mateo at Wakefield? Actually, Wakefield are in Super League. Let me correct: The most notable is probably Wigan’s signing of Australian back-rower John Bateman? He’s English. The point is: few big-name antipodeans have come over from the NRL this year, but the ones who have – like Widnes’s new hooker L’Angelo – bring flair and unpredictability. **6. The Women’s Super League** For the first time, the women’s game has a fully professional structure. The Women’s Super League – featuring seven teams including the Rhinos, St Helens and Wigan – kicked off last month. The standard is high, the athletes are committed, and the exposure is growing. With matches now broadcast on the BBC iPlayer, it is a chance to see a different, equally thrilling version of the sport. England captain Andrea Dobson says: “We’re not just a sideshow. We’re a serious competition.” **7. The BBC’s live coverage** Sky TV remains the main broadcaster, but the BBC has upped its commitment. This season, BBC One will show four live regular-season games and both finals – the Challenge Cup final in August and the Grand Final in October. The free-to-air coverage is a huge boost for a sport that wants to attract new fans. The first BBC broadcast is on 13 March: St Helens vs Wigan, a Friday night classic. “That’s a real game-changer,” says BBC rugby league correspondent Dave Woods. “People can see the speed and intensity without paying for Sky.” **8. The World Club Challenge** On 20 February, St Helens travel to face South Sydney Rabbitohs – the reigning NRL champions – in the World Club Challenge. It is a one-off match, but it is a genuine test of how the English champions measure up against their Australian counterparts. The last British team to win was Wigan in 2013. If Saints pull it off, it will set the tone for the entire season. And it is live on BBC Two. **9. The community clubs and grassroots** Rugby league remains a sport rooted in working-class communities. The Super League clubs are professional, but they are still tied to their local amateur teams. This season, the RFL has launched a new initiative to support community clubs – many of which struggle for funding. The “Game on” campaign aims to attract 50,000 new participants by 2017. In places like Castleford and Featherstone, the sport is a way of life. Watching the pros on Thursday night is a celebration of that passion. **10. The unpredictable nature of the sport** Finally, rugby league is simply the most fast-paced, physically demanding team sport on the planet. The ball is in play for an average of 50 minutes per match – compared to 30 minutes in rugby union. Defenders have just 10 seconds after a tackle. The result is constant action: hits, passes, kicks, tries. You never get a dull moment. As Wigan’s Sean O’Loughlin says: “If you blink, you miss something.” And with the new format, every tackle could decide a club’s entire season. So whether you are a lifelong fan in the stands, or a newcomer flicking channels, the 2015 Super League season has something for you. The games kick off on Thursday night – and the countdown to the Grand Final has already begun.
