title: Fifty years ago, direct from Manchester, Top Of The Pops made its debut on the airwaves.
text_ai: The weekly pop countdown ran for decades, racking up more than 2,000 episodes, featuring the likes of U2, Madonna, Kylie Minogue and Bob the Builder - sometimes on the same show. In fact, Top of the Pops is that rare beast: A programme which is still part of the BBC's annual Christmas Day ratings battle but was taken off the air due to unpopularity seven-and-a-half years ago. Yet the programme's enduring popularity – or at least its cultural resonance – is far from straightforward. For every viewer who recalls the thrill of seeing a new single premiered on a Thursday night, there is another who remembers the awkward dance routines, the mimed vocals, and the relentless promotion of whatever was number one. Top of the Pops was, in many ways, a barometer of the British music industry's health and its many frailties. It was a show that could make careers – and, some would argue, break them. The first episode, broadcast on New Year's Day 1964 from a converted church hall in Manchester, was a modest affair. Presented by Jimmy Savile – a name that would later become synonymous with scandal – the show featured acts like The Hollies, The Rolling Stones, and Dusty Springfield. There was no countdown then; simply a selection of the week's biggest hits, performed live or – more often than not – mimed to a backing track. The format was immediately recognisable: a studio audience of teenagers dancing awkwardly, the camera lingering on the performers, and a genial but slightly chaotic presentation style. It was Raw, rough around the edges, but undeniably compelling. Over the next four decades, Top of the Pops became a national institution. It was the only place on terrestrial television where viewers could reliably see their favourite bands, from The Beatles to Blur, The Clash to Coldplay. The show adapted to changing times – the glam rock glitter of the 1970s, the new wave of the 1980s, the rave and indie grooves of the 1990s. There were themed editions, such as the Christmas specials, which began in the 1960s and remain a fixture of the BBC One schedule to this day. The show also introduced innovations like the "Breakers" segment, where rising stars performed in a small booth, and the "Chart Rundown", which gave a quick spin through the rest of the top 40. But the show's relationship with its audience was always complicated. It was marketed as a pop chart programme, but the chart itself was a moving target. The BBC's decision to base Top of the Pops on the official UK singles chart – compiled by the British Market Research Bureau from 1969 onwards – gave the show a veneer of objectivity. Yet critics argued that the chart could be manipulated by record labels through bulk buying and payola. And the show's insistence on having artists perform live – or at least appear to perform – led to a litany of oddities: from the notoriously loose miming of the Sex Pistols in 1976 to the silent, empty-handed performance of Kate Bush in 1978, when she was forced to mime to a pre-recorded track because of a technical glitch. The golden era of Top of the Pops is often considered to be the 1970s and 1980s, when the show regularly attracted audiences of over 15 million. It was the programme that introduced the world to the concept of the "dance routine", with legions of young people in flared trousers and platform shoes jumping around in front of a psychedelic backdrop. The show also had a rotating cast of presenters – from DJs like John Peel, Alan Freeman, and Bruno Brooks, to pop stars like Gary Glitter and – at one point – a young, fresh-faced Chris Moyles. The presenters were as much a part of the show's identity as the music itself, though some were better than others. Yet for all its success, the show began to face existential challenges in the 1990s. The rise of cable and satellite television, with dedicated music channels like MTV Europe, eroded its monopoly on pop news. The internet, and then file-sharing, changed how people discovered and consumed music. The chart itself became a less reliable indicator of what people were actually listening to – the rise of multiple formats and download-only singles made the top 40 a more fragmented and less meaningful list. And as the show's ratings began to slide – from a peak of 19 million in the 1970s to around 5 million by the early 2000s – the BBC faced awkward questions about its relevance. In 2005, the BBC announced that Top of the Pops would be moved from its regular Thursday night slot to a late-night Friday position. The move was seen as a death sentence, and it was. The show's last regular episode aired on 30 July 2006, with a final chart-topper from Westlife and a performance from a group called Soundgirls. It ended not with a bang, but with a subdued, almost mournful, compilation of past glories. The BBC said it had decided to "rest" the show because of declining audiences, but many saw it as a brutal admission that the programme's time was over. The Christmas specials, however, survived. Indeed, they have become something of a tradition – albeit a somewhat anachronistic one. Each year, viewers can still tune in on 25 December to see a countdown of that year's biggest hits, often performed by the original artists or – more controversially – by modern-day pop stars covering old songs. The specials are a curious blend of nostalgia and commercialism: they attract viewers who want to relive the year's music, but they also serve as a promotional tool for the BBC's annual Christmas schedule. But the true legacy of Top of the Pops lies not in its Christmas specials, but in its vast archive. The BBC has carefully preserved most of the show's episodes, and they are now available – in part – on iPlayer and YouTube. For music historians, the archive is a treasure trove: it captures the fashions, the attitudes, and the sounds of half a century of British pop. It's a time capsule that shows how the country’s musical tastes evolved, and how the show itself evolved alongside them. The show's influence on subsequent music television is undeniable. Before Top of the Pops, there was no regular platform for pop videos. The show, in fact, helped to popularise the music video format, when it began featuring promotional films in the 1970s – a precursor to MTV. It also set the template for countless later shows, from The Chart Show to Hitlist UK. Even current formats like The Voice UK and Britain’s Got Talent owe a debt to the unspoken contract that Top of the Pops established: a regular, weekly appointment where the nation could gather to see who was number one. Yet the show also reflected some of the worst aspects of the music industry. Its reliance on miming encouraged a culture of fakery, and the show was often criticised for its lack of musical innovation. There were also scandals regarding the presenters: Jimmy Savile's abuse was not revealed until after his death, but his long association with the show now casts a shadow over its history. Other presenters, like Dave Lee Travis, were also accused of sexual misconduct. The BBC has attempted to address these issues, but they remain a sensitive part of the programme's legacy. Today, the question of whether Top of the Pops could ever be revived is a perennial one. The music industry is very different: streaming has changed how we consume music, and the chart is now a less cohesive entity. There is no longer a single, national radio station that plays a diverse range of pop music, and television viewing habits have fragmented across multiple platforms. A revival would need to be something quite different – perhaps an online-only show or a series of special events. But the BBC has, so far, resisted the urge. The 50th anniversary of Top of the Pops, then, is more than just a nostalgic look back. It's a chance to consider how we used to experience music as a collective culture, and how that experience has changed. The show was, for decades, a unifying force: a programme that parents and children could watch together, a barometer of national mood. It gave us The Jackson 5's "ABC", Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody", and the Spice Girls' "Wannabe" – all in the same iconic format. It also gave us Bob the Builder, and that's perhaps the best example of its democratic, inclusive vision: a children's character reaching number one, and appearing alongside Madonna and U2 on the same chart. As the BBC prepares to mark the milestone, there will be no grand revival, but there will be retrospectives, documentaries, and perhaps a few archive specials. And the Christmas edition will continue as before. For a programme that was killed off due to unpopularity, Top of the Pops has proven remarkably resilient. It lingers on in the collective memory, and in the many moments it captured on tape – moments that, for millions of viewers, were the soundtrack to their lives. It is fifty years since that first New Year's Day broadcast from Manchester. The show hasn't been a regular part of the weekly schedule for over a decade. But in the eyes of its fans, and in the dusty corners of the BBC's vast archive, Top of the Pops remains a living, breathing, occasionally awkward, but always essential part of British pop history. It is, in its own strange way, the programme that refused to die – even after it was taken off the air.
prefix: The weekly pop countdown ran for decades, racking up more than 2,000 episodes, featuring the likes of U2, Madonna, Kylie Minogue and Bob the Builder - sometimes on the same show. In fact, Top of the Pops is that rare beast: A programme which is still part of the BBC's annual Christmas Day ratings battle but was taken off the air due to unpopularity seven-and-a-half years ago.

title: They are a loose collective of hackers who once appeared to have no greater purpose than having some mischievous anarchic fun.
text_ai: But in recent times Anonymous has got serious. Earlier this month the collective targeted the Ku Klux Klan, publishing online a list of alleged sympathisers of the white supremacist group. Now they are pursuit of a much bigger prey, so-called Islamic State (IS). In recent days, the loose hacker network has declared a new front in its digital war, launching what it calls "Operation ISIS". The group has threatened to expose the online activities of fighters and supporters of the militant group, promising to publish personal data, email accounts and social media profiles of those linked to the so-called caliphate. Anonymous made its intentions known via a video posted on YouTube, featuring a masked figure in a black hoodie – the collective's signature symbol – speaking through a voice modulator. "We will track down your affiliated websites and accounts, from Twitter to YouTube, from Facebook to Pastebin," the figure declared. "We will take down your propaganda sites and we will expose your operatives and their sympathisers. You have declared war on humanity, and humanity will now respond." The video drew immediate attention from security experts and jihadist watchers, who offered a mixed assessment of what the campaign might achieve. On the one hand, supporters argued that exposing IS supporters online could help disrupt their recruitment networks and make it harder for the group to spread its message. On the other, sceptics cautioned that the hackers risked drowning in a sea of disinformation, while potentially alerting IS to vulnerabilities in its own security. "I would urge caution," said Dr Alia Brahami, a cybersecurity researcher at the University of London. "Anonymous is not a single entity. It is a loose affiliation of individuals with varying skills and motivations. Some are highly capable, but others are little more than script-kiddies who could easily be led into traps. Moreover, releasing personal data without proper verification could harm innocent people." Indeed, the group's track record is mixed. Its earlier campaign against the KKK saw it release a list of names it claimed were supporters of the white supremacist organisation. But some analysts noted that many of those names were already public – listed as donors to far-right causes – and that the authenticity of the entire list was difficult to confirm. Now, with Islamic State, the stakes are far higher. IS has already demonstrated its own formidable capabilities online, operating a sophisticated propaganda machine and using encrypted messaging apps to coordinate attacks. In response to the Anonymous threat, some IS supporters have taunted the hackers, daring them to try. Others have warned of retaliation, suggesting they would target Anonymous members in real life. The conflict has drawn in other actors. Shortly after the Anonymous video appeared, a pro-IS hacking group calling itself the "Caliphate Cyber Army" published a list of what it claimed were personal details of supposed Anonymous members. The authenticity of that list, too, remains unclear. In the background, Western intelligence agencies have watched the developments with a mixture of interest and concern. While any disruption to IS's online operations is welcome, there is unease about vigilante action that could blur legal lines or escalate tensions unpredictably. "Anonymous is not part of any government's counter-terrorism strategy," said Mark Fallon, a former US counter-terrorism official. "They are independent actors. Their actions could create confusion, or they could provide useful intelligence. But they also could jeopardise ongoing investigations. It's a double-edged sword." The BBC has learned that some UK police forces are monitoring the campaign, mindful that any data released might need assessment for intelligence value, but also wary of encouraging vigilantism. As the digital battle intensifies, one thing is clear: the line between hacktivism and counter-terrorism has blurred, and the world is watching to see whether this loose collective of pranksters can take on one of the most dangerous extremist groups on the planet. For now, the threat from Anonymous remains largely rhetorical. But its history shows it is not a group to be underestimated.
prefix: But in recent times Anonymous has got serious. Earlier this month the collective targeted the Ku Klux Klan, publishing online a list of alleged sympathisers of the white supremacist group. Now they are pursuit of a much bigger prey, so-called Islamic State (IS).

title: Editorials in Chinese state media have denounced the presence of a US warship in the South China Sea, and warned that Beijing is prepared to take action.
text_ai: While urging calm from both sides, media outlets also said the US was "harassing China" and that Beijing is "not frightened to fight a war". The USS Lassen sailed in the Spratly archipelago on Tuesday as a challenge to China's claim over the islands. The Chinese foreign ministry echoed the sentiment, stating that the navigation of the USS Lassen "undermines regional peace and stability". In a strongly worded statement, it called on Washington to "immediately stop such provocative acts" and warned that Beijing would "take necessary measures to safeguard its sovereignty". The vessel, an Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer, passed within 12 nautical miles of artificial islands built by China on the Subi Reef, according to US defence officials. The operation was conducted under the banner of "freedom of navigation" – a principle Washington insists applies to all states in international waters, including those within the exclusive economic zones claimed by China. Beijing, however, considers the Spratly archipelago, along with most of the South China Sea, as part of its "indisputable sovereignty" – a stance supported by a nine-dash line map that has been rejected by a 2016 international arbitration ruling. The tribunal in The Hague found that China's historic claims had no legal basis under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). China has refused to recognise the ruling. The state-run Global Times newspaper, known for its nationalist bent, declared in an editorial: "The US is deliberately escalating tensions. If it believes it can force China into submission through such muscle-flexing, it is gravely mistaken." It added that the Chinese military had been monitoring the USS Lassen and was prepared to respond "resolutely". An opinion piece in the People's Daily, the official newspaper of the Communist Party, struck a more measured tone but nonetheless emphasised resolve. "The Chinese people are not afraid of war, but neither do they seek conflict," it read. "What is clear is that any infringement upon our territorial integrity will be met with a proportional response." Regional reactions have been mixed. Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei and Taiwan all have overlapping claims in the South China Sea. While Hanoi has generally voiced concern over Chinese construction and militarisation of the islands, it has also sought to avoid direct confrontation with Beijing. Manila, under President Rodrigo Duterte, has pursued closer ties with China while cautiously acknowledging the US alliance. Analysts suggest the USS Lassen's transit was a carefully calibrated move – neither a full-scale challenge nor a mere diplomatic gesture. "It's a classic signal of commitment to allies and to the principle of freedom of navigation," said Dr. Rebecca Johnson, a maritime security expert at the Australian National University. "But it also risks miscalculation, especially if Chinese forces decide to shadow more aggressively or deploy countermeasures." In Washington, the Pentagon described the operation as routine. "The United States operates in the South China Sea on a daily basis," a spokesman said. "This mission was no different from many before it." Yet the timing, coming shortly after President Xi Jinping's state visit to the US, has raised eyebrows. Some see it as a deliberate test of China's resolve, others as a necessary reaffirmation of international law. The incident underscores the fragile nature of maritime security in the region. With Chinese fisheries patrols and naval vessels increasingly assertive, and US allies such as Japan and Australia conducting their own exercises, the potential for unintended escalation remains high. For now, both sides have kept their rhetoric below the threshold of open confrontation. But the editorial warnings from Beijing suggest that the patience of the world's second-largest economy may be wearing thin.
prefix: While urging calm from both sides, media outlets also said the US was "harassing China" and that Beijing is "not frightened to fight a war". The USS Lassen sailed in the Spratly archipelago on Tuesday as a challenge to China's claim over the islands.

title: During a year of anti-government protests throughout Ethiopia, its global diaspora, particularly that in the US, has been deeply involved - and not just vocally, writes Addis Ababa-based journalist James Jeffrey.
text_ai: Twitter and Facebook have been blocked since a six-month state of emergency was imposed last month as the government tries to restore order across the country's two most populous regions of Oromia and Amhara. The state of emergency, imposed on 4 February, followed weeks of deadly clashes between security forces and protesters in Oromia and Amhara, the country’s two largest regions. At least 50 people were reported killed in the unrest, which began after a regional power-sharing dispute in Oromia and later spread to Amhara over land and administrative boundary issues. Though the government insists the emergency is temporary and necessary to protect civilian lives, critics see it as a crackdown on dissent ahead of a possible election delay. For the diaspora, the social media blackout has been both a practical obstacle and a symbolic affront. Many rely on platforms such as Facebook and Twitter to coordinate fundraising, share information and amplify calls for reform. "The shutdown is an attack on our ability to speak truth to power," says Lemlem Hailu, a Washington-based organiser with the Ethiopian American Civic Action Group. "But it has not silenced us. We have found other channels." Indeed, the diaspora’s role has evolved far beyond sending remittances—Ethiopia receives over $4bn annually from its citizens abroad, the fifth-largest diaspora flow in Africa. Today, Ethiopian communities in the US, Europe and the Middle East are also key political players, using sustained lobbying, legal challenges and media campaigns to influence events back home. In the past year, groups have pressed US lawmakers to introduce resolutions condemning human rights abuses, funded independent journalism and even launched a satellite television channel. The US diaspora is particularly influential. It numbers at least 250,000 people, concentrated in Washington DC, Minneapolis, Los Angeles and Seattle. Many are highly educated professionals who have retained deep ties to Ethiopia. They have formed organisations such as the Ethiopian Diaspora Trust Fund and the Oromo-American Council, which combine advocacy with development projects. "We are not just observers. We are participants in Ethiopia’s future," says Dr Fekadu Mulugeta, a professor of African studies at the University of Maryland and a diaspora adviser to the Oromo opposition. This activism is not without controversy. During the protests, some diaspora figures have been accused by the government of inciting violence. In 2023, a federal prosecutor filed charges against two diaspora-based activists for allegedly financing and organising protests that turned deadly. The government has also warned foreign-based media outlets—including Ethiopian satellite channels run from Europe—that their broadcasts could be disrupted if they "spread false information". Yet many in the diaspora argue that the state of emergency is itself a sign of weakness. "The government is losing control, and it knows it," says Dr Mulugeta. "Blocking social media and arresting activists at home only drives the opposition abroad. They cannot arrest everyone in Minnesota." The emergency has also drawn attention to the wider web of diaspora-led networks. In the US, Ethiopian-owned businesses have been used to discreetly transfer funds into accounts of relief agencies that also help protesters’ families. Community centres in Minneapolis and Washington have become hubs for organising protests outside Ethiopian embassies and consulates. "Our voice on the street in Washington matters more than the government might think," says Jemal Ahmed, a Oromo organiser based in Minneapolis. "It puts pressure on the Ethiopian embassy, but also on US policymakers." US lawmakers have taken notice. In January, the House Foreign Affairs Committee held a hearing on the Ethiopian government’s record, focusing on the emergency and the social media crackdown. Several members, including Representative Michael McCaul, a Texas Republican who chairs the committee, voiced concern about the state of emergency’s implications for stability in the Horn of Africa. "It fuels the crisis," he said during the hearing. The Ethiopian government responded by accusing the US of "interfering in internal affairs". The diaspora’s influence is not limited to the US. In Europe, Ethiopian communities in Germany, Sweden and the UK have staged demonstrations outside embassies, while lobbying the European Union to suspend budget support until human rights conditions improve. In the Middle East, where hundreds of thousands of Ethiopian domestic workers are employed, there have been reports of labour activism—women organising to demand better conditions, often linking their cause to the protests at home. But the diaspora is far from monolithic. The government has its own supporters abroad, including members of the Ethiopian diaspora who align with the ruling Prosperity Party. They argue that the protests are driven by a small minority and that the emergency is necessary to prevent ethnic conflict. "They want to destabilise the country," says Berhanu Ayele, a diaspora leader in Texas who supports the government. "They don't live here anymore. They don't see what we see." This internal split has led to tensions. In some US cities, heated arguments have broken out at community events, and online forums have become echo chambers of polarised opinion. Still, the broad consensus among many diaspora figures is that the government’s actions are undermining its legitimacy. "The emergency is a short-term fix that will create long-term problems," says Lemlem Hailu. "It erodes trust. And once trust is gone, rebuilding takes years." For now, the immediate impact of the diaspora’s involvement is difficult to measure. The Ethiopian government remains in place, the emergency continues, and social media is still blocked. But the networks that have been built—the channels, the lobbying groups, the solidarity funds—are unlikely to vanish once the crisis subsides. "The diaspora has become a permanent third actor in Ethiopian politics," says Dr Mulugeta. "The question is whether that will push the country toward reform or toward deeper division." As the state of emergency enters its second month, the opposition inside Ethiopia faces severe restrictions. But from thousands of miles away, the diaspora is determined to keep the momentum alive. They have learned to work around the blocks, using encrypted messaging apps and virtual private networks. They are planning new campaigns. And they are waiting for the moment when the emergency lifts—knowing that, when it does, they will be ready.
prefix: Twitter and Facebook have been blocked since a six-month state of emergency was imposed last month as the government tries to restore order across the country's two most populous regions of Oromia and Amhara.

title: The last British resident being held in Guantanamo Bay, Shaker Aamer, could be released "within weeks" his lawyer has told Victoria Derbyshire.
text_ai: Clive Stafford Smith said various US government officials had told him Mr Aamer was going to be released in June. He has never been charged or been on trial and, since 2007, has been cleared for release twice by both President George Bush and Barack Obama. His continued detention has been a long-running source of diplomatic tension between London and Washington. The British government has repeatedly called for his return, arguing that there is no evidence to justify holding him any longer. Aamer, who moved to the UK in 1996 after marrying a British woman, was captured in Afghanistan in late 2001 and transferred to Guantanamo in 2002. He has always maintained his innocence, insisting he was a humanitarian aid worker, not a combatant. In a statement, his lawyer Clive Stafford Smith told the Victoria Derbyshire programme: “We've been told by multiple sources within the US government that the wheels are finally turning. Shaker could be home with his family in weeks, not months.” He added that the transfer had been delayed for years by bureaucratic hurdles, including a dispute over whether Aamer would face any restrictions on his movements once back in the UK. The case of Shaker Aamer has become a cause célèbre for human rights groups. He is one of the few remaining detainees at Guantanamo, which President Barack Obama pledged to close shortly after taking office in 2009. That promise has not been fulfilled, and the facility still holds about 40 men, many of whom have been cleared for release. Aamer was first cleared for transfer in 2007 under President George W. Bush, and again in 2009 under Obama. No charges have ever been brought against him. His health has deteriorated significantly during his 13 years of captivity. His lawyers have said he suffers from severe depression, post-traumatic stress disorder and has been on hunger strike several times to protest his detention. In 2013, he was force-fed for a period, a practice that has been widely condemned by medical and human rights organisations. Aamer’s family, including his wife of Pakistani origin and their four children – all British citizens – have campaigned tirelessly for his release. His wife, Zinab, said in a recent interview: “My children have never known their father outside of a prison cell. We just want him home.” The UK government has been pressing the Obama administration to expedite the transfer. However, under US law, any detainee cleared for transfer must still be sent to a country that will accept them and provide security assurances. For years, the sticking point was whether Saudi Arabia – of which Aamer is also a citizen – would take him, or whether he could be sent directly to Britain. The US has insisted on a bilateral agreement that would prevent him from returning to the battlefield – a standard provision. The UK has been reluctant to accept such a condition, arguing that it already has robust legal powers to monitor any terrorist suspect. Last month, the Foreign Office confirmed that talks with the US were “nearing a conclusion”. A spokesperson said: “We have always been clear that we want to see Shaker Aamer returned to the UK. We continue to work closely with the US administration to achieve that objective.” The BBC understands that security assessments have been conducted by both MI5 and the UK’s Home Office, and that no objections have been raised to his return. The potential release has also stirred political debate. Some Conservative MPs have expressed concern that Aamer might pose a security risk, despite having never been charged. But Stafford Smith dismissed such fears: “If there were any credible evidence against him, he would have been tried years ago. The US itself has said he is not a threat.” If released, Aamer would be the 11th former Guantanamo detainee to resettle in Britain. Some of those men have faced restrictions, including overnight curfews and limits on travel. It is unclear what, if any, conditions would be placed on Aamer. His lawyers say he simply wants to rebuild his life and see his children grow up. The family's local MP, John McDonnell, has also been vocal. He told the BBC: “This has been a bureaucratic and moral outrage. Shaker has been punished without charge for over a decade. It is time he came home.” As the June deadline approaches, Aamer’s supporters are cautiously optimistic. But after so many false dawns – he was reportedly close to release in 2010 and again in 2013 – no one is counting their chickens. “We’ve been let down before,” his wife said. “But this time feels different. The US and UK are finally working together.” The next few weeks will be critical. If the release goes ahead, it will mark the end of a long and painful chapter for one of the most prominent symbols of America’s post-9/11 detention policies. For Shaker Aamer, it would mean the simple but profound act of walking free.
prefix: Clive Stafford Smith said various US government officials had told him Mr Aamer was going to be released in June. He has never been charged or been on trial and, since 2007, has been cleared for release twice by both President George Bush and Barack Obama.

title: The founder of VR (virtual reality) firm Oculus has hand delivered the first Rift headset to a customer.
text_ai: Palmer Luckey handed over the headset a couple of days before the consumer version of the Rift is officially due to start reaching customers. The recipient was Ross Martin from Alaska who ordered the headset when pre-orders opened in January. Mr Luckey said he wanted the "satisfaction" of delivering the first Rift headset. The handover took place at a hotel in Anchorage, with Mr Luckey personally unboxing the device for the first time in front of a small gathering of journalists. The Rift, which costs $599 (£420) in the US, has been billed as the first major virtual reality headset aimed at consumers, sparking a new wave of interest in immersive technology. Mr Luckey, who sold Oculus to Facebook for $2bn in 2014, said the delivery marked a "significant milestone" for the industry. "We've been working on this for years, and to actually see it in the hands of someone who pre-ordered it months ago is incredibly rewarding," he told the BBC. "Ross is a true pioneer – he took a leap of faith, and I wanted to be part of that moment." For his part, Mr Martin, a 34-year-old software developer, said he had been following VR since the early prototypes. "It's been a long wait, but seeing the final product – it's worth it," he said, after putting on the headset for the first time. "The level of detail is stunning." The Rift, which requires a powerful PC to run, places users inside a fully immersive 3D world, with motion sensors tracking head movements in real time. It has been praised for its comfort and low latency but criticised for its high price and reliance on a high-end gaming computer. The launch comes amid rising competition from rivals such as HTC's Vive and Sony's PlayStation VR. However, Oculus has been accused of failing to deliver sufficient launch titles, with only around 30 games and experiences available at launch. Critics argue that a strong software library is crucial for mainstream adoption. Mr Luckey acknowledged the challenge, saying: "We're working closely with developers to ensure a steady stream of content. This is just the beginning." The consumer version of the Rift goes on sale officially on 28 March. Analyst forecasts suggest that around one million units may be sold in the first year, though some caution that the technology is still niche. Nonetheless, Mr Luckey remains bullish. "The revolution is here," he said. "Now we just need to show people what it can do."

title: The keyboard and mouse have long been the main bridge between humans and their computers.
text_ai: More recently we've seen the rise of the touchscreen. But other attempts at re-imagining controls have proved vexing. "It's one of the hardest problems in modern computer science," Michael Buckwald, chief executive and co-founder of Leap Motion, told the BBC. But is the mouse and keyboard really the best way to interact with our digital devices – or just the one we have settled for? From the clunky command-line interfaces of early computing to the graphical user interface (GUI) revolution ushered in by Apple's Macintosh, the history of human-computer interaction is littered with both breakthroughs and dead ends. Touchscreens, popularised by the iPhone in 2007, offered an immediacy that a mouse never could. Yet they come with their own compromises. "Finger fat," the problem of imprecise taps, remains a frustration. And for tasks requiring fine control – photo editing, writing code, or playing complex video games – touchscreens often feel like a step backwards. The quest for a new input paradigm is, as Mr Buckwald suggests, "one of the hardest problems in modern computer science". It is not simply a question of engineering a sensor that can detect a gesture. It is about building a system that is intuitive, lag-free, and works without requiring the user to learn a new vocabulary of movements. "The brain already has a very sophisticated model of how the physical world works," he explains. "The challenge is to map that onto a digital environment without friction." Numerous attempts have faltered. Microsoft's Kinect, launched as a motion-sensing accessory for the Xbox, allowed players to control games with whole-body movements. But it was often imprecise and required ample space. After initial buzz, it faded. Nintendo's Wii remote, while a commercial success, used simple accelerometer-based gestures – waving a hand to swing a tennis racket – which quickly felt gimmicky. Gesture control, in the living room at least, has not replaced the remote or the controller. "The difficulty is that the technology is either too coarse or too demanding," says Dr. Rachel Howard, a human-computer interaction researcher at University College London. "A system that can only recognise a few broad arm waves feels like a party trick. One that tries to track every finger at sub-millimetre precision often fails in real-world lighting or with different hand shapes." Voice control, too, has had a bumpy ride. Amazon's Alexa, Apple's Siri and Google Assistant have found homes in kitchens and cars, but are rarely used for sustained computing tasks. "Voice is wonderful for 'Set a timer' or 'What's the weather?'," says Dr Howard. "But try editing a spreadsheet by voice. It is painfully slow and cognitively demanding." She adds that the so-called "uncanny valley" of voice assistants – when they almost understand, but not quite – often leaves users more frustrated than if they had typed the query. This is where companies like Leap Motion are staking their claim. The San Francisco-based firm, founded in 2010, developed a small device that fits under a monitor and tracks the movement of both hands in three dimensions – all ten fingers, with remarkable precision. The technology uses two cameras and infrared LEDs to detect the position of each joint, updating 200 times per second. The latest iteration, the Leap Motion Controller 2, is designed to be embedded into virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) headsets. In VR, the problem is acute. Current systems rely on hand-held controllers that are tracked in space. Users press buttons and pull triggers to simulate actions. Leap Motion aims to remove the controller entirely. "In the real world, you interact with objects naturally," says Mr Buckwald. "You don't pick up a stick to press a button. Why would you want to do that in a virtual world?" Its technology, he says, allows users to see their own hands rendered inside the virtual environment, and to pick up virtual tools, type on a virtual keyboard, or draw with a virtual pen. The potential applications are broad. In automotive design, engineers at Ford have used Leap Motion's hand-tracking to manipulate 3D car models without a mouse. In medical training, it allows surgeons to practice delicate procedures on virtual anatomy. In music production, it lets producers gesture to adjust sound parameters – waving a hand to change a filter, for instance – in ways that a mouse could not replicate. Yet for all its promise, the technology is not yet mainstream. High processing demands, occasional tracking glitches in poor lighting, and the "gorilla arm" problem – holding your hands up for extended periods leads to fatigue – remain barriers. "We're not trying to replace the keyboard," says Mr Buckwald. "We're trying to add a new layer of interaction – for the moments when a mouse feels like too much friction, or a touchscreen feels too clumsy. And for 'immersive' computing, hand-tracking is essential." Beyond Leap Motion, other avenues are being explored. The FOVE headset uses eye-tracking to allow users to select objects with their gaze. Neural interfaces, pioneered by companies like Neuralink and Elon Musk's brain-machine interface venture, aim to read brain signals directly – but these raise profound ethical questions and remain experimental. Haptic feedback, which simulates touch through vibration or tiny motors, is improving but cannot yet convincingly replicate the texture of a surface. So what of the keyboard and mouse? Will they ever be more than a temporary bridge? "I think we'll see a diversification, not a replacement," says Dr. Howard. "Keyboards are still the most efficient way to input text – nothing beats a skilled typist. Mice are excellent for precise selection. But for the next wave of computing – augmented reality glasses, virtual offices, immersive gaming – we need something else." Mr Buckwald agrees. "Computing is leaving the desk. It's moving into space, into our environment. The keyboard and mouse were designed for a world where you sit still and stare at a screen. That is no longer the full picture." His firm's vision is one in which hand-tracking becomes as intuitive as touch – and as reliable as a mouse click. The path is long, but the prize is a world where the boundary between thought and action, between the physical and the digital, begins to dissolve. For now, the keyboard and mouse remain firmly in place – but the race to find their successor, or at least their companion, is accelerating. And as with many of computing's hardest problems, the solution will not be a single invention, but a suite of them. The bridge may be longer than we thought – but it is being rebuilt, one gesture at a time.

On 2 May 1998, at the old Wembley Stadium, the Challenge Cup final delivered a story that would be retold in pubs, terraces and rugby league documentaries for decades. Wigan, the most decorated club in the sport’s modern era, arrived as overwhelming favourites. They had won the previous three Challenge Cups, nine of the last ten, and fielded a team bristling with internationals: Andy Farrell, Jason Robinson, Kris Radlinski, and the legendary Shaun Edwards – a man who seemed to own the trophy. Their squad featured journeymen, cast-offs and a handful of emerging talents, led by the inspirational scrum-half Mark Aston, who also served as player-coach. He had devised a game plan that focused on patience, defensive discipline, and exploiting Wigan’s occasional tendency to over-elaborate. “They believed they only had to turn up to win,” Aston later recalled. “We knew we had to be perfect.” The day itself was quintessentially English cup final weather: grey skies, a light drizzle, and a Wembley pitch that had already hosted its share of wear and tear. Keep doing what we do.” The second half was a masterclass in composure. Sheffield’s defence, marshalled by the granite-like Paul Broadbent and the tireless Gary Lord, repelled wave after wave of Wigan attacks. Every tackle was desperate, every clean break blocked by a last-ditch ankle tap. On 52 minutes, a crucial moment: Wigan’s Irish prop, Phil Veivers, was sin-binned for a high tackle. The cup was returning to the DW Stadium. Yet Sheffield refused to break. They won a penalty from the restart, and Aston calmly slotted it to make it 8-8. The game entered a frenetic final ten minutes, with both sides exhausted and willing errors creeping in. Then, with just two minutes on the clock, came the defining play. Wigan, attempting to run from deep, were turned over 40 metres from their own line. Sheffield’s Darren Turner, a substitute brought on for his pace, pounced on the loose ball. He fed Sovatabua, who drew the last defender and offloaded to the supporting Paul Carr. The full-back raced 20 metres to score in the corner. Edwards opted to tap and go, but the resulting play was smothered. The final hooter sounded. Sheffield Eagles had won the Challenge Cup. Pandemonium erupted. It is a reminder that in rugby league, as in life, the underdog can have its day – and that the most dramatic scripts are rarely written by pundits. The 1998 Challenge Cup final has since been immortalised in books, documentaries, and the memories of those who witnessed it. For Sheffield, it was a moment of pure, unadulterated glory. For Wigan, a humbling lesson. For the sport, a classic. And for the thousands who packed Wembley, a story they would never tire of telling.

title: Expectations of a rise in interest rates has prompted a pick-up in mortgage activity, and unsecured borrowing has also increased.
text_ai: Although timing of any rate rise is far from certain, the British Bankers' Association (BBA) said "competitive" deals had driven increased lending. The rise in unsecured borrowing is a particular concern for policymakers at the Bank of England, who have repeatedly warned about the build-up of consumer credit. The Bank's Financial Policy Committee said in March that the level of unsecured debt posed a risk to financial stability, and that lenders should ensure they were not extending credit to households who could not afford to repay. But with the economy expected to slow following the triggering of Article 50, the timing of any move remains uncertain.

title: There were nine attempts to use drones to infiltrate prisons in England and Wales in the first five months of 2015, according to the Ministry of Justice.
text_ai: Among them was a drone carrying mobile phones and drugs that was intercepted by guards at Bedford Prison in March. In the remaining two cases, the drones were spotted but managed to escape before they could be intercepted. The figures, released to the Press Association under a freedom of information request, mark the first time the government has disclosed the scale of the problem. A spokesperson said the number of incidents was "relatively small" but acknowledged the technology posed a "serious and growing challenge" to prison security. Drones were used in an effort to smuggle a variety of contraband, including mobile phones, SIM cards, cannabis and even the synthetic drug Spice, which has become a particular problem inside prisons. In some cases, the aircraft were fitted with small release mechanisms designed to drop packages into exercise yards or land them on roofs. "This is an emerging threat that we are taking very seriously," Richard told the conference. "Prisons are having to adapt to new tactics from criminals who are constantly looking for ways to bypass our security measures." The MoJ said it was working with police and the Civil Aviation Authority to develop counter-measures, including the use of netting, signal-jamming equipment and drones equipped with net-firing technology to intercept them. A pilot scheme testing anti-drone systems is under way at several high-security jails. But critics have warned that the government is lagging behind the pace of technological change. "Prisoners are using sophisticated methods to get contraband inside, and drones are just the latest," said a spokesman. "We need a co-ordinated national response, not piecemeal measures." The nine attempts recorded between January and May of this year compare with only two confirmed incidents in the whole of 2014. Campaigners for prison reform expressed concern that the figures may be the tip of the iceberg, as many drone flights go undetected. A subsequent search uncovered a package containing mobile phones and drugs. No arrests have been made. The government has said it will legislate to make it a specific criminal offence to fly a drone within a prison perimeter, with penalties of up to two years in prison. Currently, such cases are prosecuted under existing laws on smuggling or endangering aircraft. The Home Office is also considering whether to extend the current no-fly zone around prisons to include small, unmanned aircraft. Prison governors have been given the power to search cellphones and other digital devices for evidence of drones being organised from inside. But the increasing sophistication of the devices means that even basic counter-measures can be circumvented. Some drones now come equipped with GPS navigation systems that allow them to follow pre-programmed routes, making them harder to detect. The Ministry of Justice said it was "determined to keep ahead of the threat" and would introduce new legislation "as soon as parliamentary time allows".

title: Animal rescue centres have warned of a steeper rise in the number of abandoned Staffordshire Bull Terriers.

"Many of these dogs are handed in by owners who say they can no longer cope—often due to financial pressures, housing issues, or simply because the dog has grown too strong or boisterous for them to manage." title: Donald Trump will hold his first press conference in almost six months on Wednesday, to talk about plans to avoid conflicts of interest involving his sprawling business empire while he's president.
text_ai: Meanwhile the US Congress is reviewing the nominations of a series of his top political nominees who are facing their own ethical questions, and concerns continue to swirl around several other high-level advisers. While Mr Trump will dominate the headlines, here's a look at some of the controversies that could dog those poised to serve under him. The spotlight on Mr Trump’s own business affairs, however, is only part of a wider ethical landscape that is drawing scrutiny from watchdogs and lawmakers alike. From conflicts of interest to questions of financial probity, the president-elect’s inner circle faces a gauntlet of potential controversies. **Jeff Sessions: Attorney General nominee** Senator Jeff Sessions of Alabama, Mr Trump’s pick for the nation’s top law enforcement officer, has already faced a contentious confirmation hearing. The 70-year-old Republican, known for his hardline stance on immigration and his role as an early Trump endorser, has drawn fire over his past statements on race and civil rights. In 1986, Sessions was denied a federal judgeship after allegations that he made racially charged remarks, including referring to a white civil rights attorney as a “disgrace to his race” and suggesting the Ku Klux Klan was “OK” until he learned they smoked marijuana. He has denied the most serious charges. But the questions now extend well beyond his record. Critics point to a potential conflict of interest in the Justice Department’s oversight of the Trump Organization. As attorney general, Sessions would oversee the FBI and the department’s criminal division, which might investigate any alleged financial wrongdoing tied to Mr Trump’s business empire. Sessions has said he would recuse himself from matters directly involving the president-elect, but transparency advocates argue the mere appearance of partiality is damaging. “The attorney general is expected to be the chief law enforcement officer independent of political pressure,” said Fred Wertheimer, president of Democracy 21, a campaign finance watchdog. “Having a Trump campaign surrogate in that role raises serious concerns.” Furthermore, Sessions has been a vocal critic of the civil rights division he would supervise. His past opposition to the Voting Rights Act and his support for restrictive voter ID laws have alarmed advocates who fear a rollback of protections. The NAACP has called for the Senate to reject his nomination. **Rex Tillerson: Secretary of State nominee** Rex Tillerson, the former ExxonMobil chief executive, brings decades of global deal-making to the State Department, but his ties to Russia have become a central flashpoint. Tillerson, 64, was awarded Russia’s Order of Friendship in 2013, a state honour given by President Vladimir Putin. His company, ExxonMobil, signed a major oil exploration deal with Rosneft, the Russian state-owned energy giant, in 2011 - a deal now under US sanctions over Moscow’s annexation of Crimea. Tillerson’s critics question whether he can credibly negotiate with a Kremlin he has done business with for years. The company says Tillerson ended his involvement with the Rosneft venture in 2013, questions persist about his financial holdings. To avoid conflict of interest, Tillerson has pledged to divest his ExxonMobil shares and sever ties, but ethical watchdogs say the process lacks transparency. “If he is to lead American foreign policy, he must be completely disentangled from any foreign government or company with interests before the US government,” said Senator Robert Menendez, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. Tillerson’s confirmation hearing last month exposed deep divisions, with some Republicans joining Democrats in expressing unease. **Betsy DeVos: Education Secretary nominee** Betsy DeVos, a billionaire Republican donor and school-choice advocate, faces intense opposition from teachers’ unions and civil rights groups over her lack of experience in public education and potential conflicts of interest. DeVos has pledged to sell off dozens of her investment holdings, including those in companies that could benefit from education policy changes, such as for-profit colleges and charter school chains. But ethics review documents released last month show she will retain some assets, including an interest in a company that operates a school voucher programme in Michigan – a programme she has publicly championed. The Office of Government Ethics has highlighted her failure to properly disclose certain holdings, though DeVos has since updated her filings. Critics argue that her family’s substantial investments in education-related businesses – the DeVos family has donated millions to promote school choice – create an inherent conflict. “The person running the Department of Education should not have financial interests in the very schools that would benefit from her policies,” said a statement from the American Federation of Teachers. Despite these concerns, her confirmation is all but assured given Republican control of the Senate. **Tom Price: Health and Human Services Secretary nominee** Representative Tom Price of Georgia, a physician and orthopedic surgeon, has built a reputation as a fierce critic of the Affordable Care Act, but his own financial dealings have cast a shadow over his nomination. During his time in Congress, Price traded hundreds of thousands of dollars in shares in health-care companies while sponsoring legislation that could affect those same firms. A 2016 investigation by the Wall Street Journal found that Price had bought and sold shares in a pharmaceutical company, then introduced a bill that would have delayed a Medicare rule that could have cut the company’s profits. He has denied any wrongdoing, saying all trades were made by professional brokers without his knowledge. Yet the pattern has sparked a criminal complaint from the Campaign Legal Center, which alleges that Price may have violated the 2012 Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge (STOCK) Act. The HHS secretary oversees Medicare and Medicaid, as well as the Food and Drug Administration, meaning Price’s decisions could have a direct impact on the companies in which he once held shares. He has promised to divest his health-care stocks, but critics say the process should be overseen by an independent ethics monitor. **Scott Pruitt: Environmental Protection Agency nominee** Scott Pruitt, the Oklahoma attorney general, has built his career challenging the environmental regulations he would be tasked with enforcing. According to campaign finance records, his political action committee accepted tens of thousands of dollars from energy companies, and he has been a vocal supporter of increased fossil fuel production. The EPA is responsible for regulating emissions and overseeing clean energy programmes. The first phase, a 38-hectare development on the larger of the two islands, is already under construction. Cranes rise from the muddy ground, and the skeleton of a luxury hotel is visible against the grey-green waters. The promoters say that when fully built out over the next 15 years, La Cite du Fleuve will house 150,000 people and provide 50,000 jobs. "It's not just about building homes," Mr Choudury explains, gesturing towards the site from a speedboat. "We are creating a city within a city. We have to build everything from scratch - the water treatment plant, the power station, the roads, the schools, the hospitals. It's like starting from zero." The project has a price tag of $5bn (£4bn), a sum that dwarfs the annual budget of many of the DRC's provinces. ## A Dubai vision in Central Africa The design, by the Dubai-based firm Al Jabber, is unmistakably Gulf-inspired. White, geometric buildings with sweeping curves and generous balconies rise from a network of palm-lined boulevards and man-made lagoons. Renderings show a futuristic skyline of glass and steel, with a monorail linking the islands to mainland Kinshasa. The ambition is to create a high-end, gated community that can rival the capitals of the continent's wealthiest nations. The development is the brainchild of a consortium of international investors, including French, Emirati and Chinese firms. The DRC government has granted a 99-year lease for the islands, which were previously uninhabited and used for illegal sand mining. In return, the government will receive a 10% equity stake in the project, plus a share of future revenues. ## A city of contradictions Kinshasa, a sprawling metropolis of at least 12 million people, is a study in extremes. Glossy skyscrapers and five-star hotels sit alongside vast, unplanned slums. The city's roads are choked, its power supply erratic, its water often unsafe. For many, La Cite du Fleuve represents a tantalising vision of what could be - a modern, orderly, functioning city. But for others, it is a symbol of the country's deep inequalities, a project that will benefit only the wealthy elite while doing nothing for the millions who struggle to survive. "I've seen the plans," says Professor Marie-Louise Kabongo, an urban planner at the University of Kinshasa. "They show a city that is disconnected from the rest of Kinshasa. There is a wall, a security perimeter, a private water supply and a private power grid. This is not a project for the people of Kinshasa. It's a project for rich foreigners and the Congolese elite." The developer rejects this characterisation. "We are creating jobs and economic activity that will benefit the whole city," says Mr Choudury. "The construction alone will employ thousands of Congolese workers. And the spin-off industries - the restaurants, the shops, the services - will create thousands more. We are also building a public transport link that will connect the islands to the mainland, which will be free for local residents." ## Environmental questions The project's location is a cause for concern. The islands sit at a point where the Congo River narrows and its current becomes fierce. During the rainy season, the river can rise by up to 8 metres, and the islands frequently flood. The developers say they have built a system of dykes and pumps to protect the site, but some environmentalists worry that the development could exacerbate flooding elsewhere. "We are not against development," says Jean-Pierre Nzita, a geologist and environmental activist. "But this project is being built in a zone that is naturally prone to flooding. If the dykes fail, the consequences could be catastrophic. And even if the dykes hold, the dredging and construction could alter the river's flow, affecting communities downstream." The developers say they have commissioned extensive environmental studies and are working with international consultants to minimise the impact. "We are using the latest technology to ensure that the islands are safe and sustainable," says Mr Choudury. "The dykes are designed to withstand a one-in-500-year flood. We are also planting thousands of trees and building green spaces to absorb rainfall." ## A test for the president The success of La Cite du Fleuve is closely tied to the political fortunes of President Felix Tshisekedi, who has championed the project as a symbol of his vision to transform the DRC into a regional economic powerhouse. The government has fast-tracked the planning permissions and offered tax incentives to attract investors. But the project has also become a lightning rod for criticism, with some accusing the president of prioritising a prestige project for the wealthy over the basic needs of the poor. "There is a perception that this government is more interested in building luxury developments than in fixing the roads, the hospitals or the schools," says Dr Kabongo. "People ask: Why is the government spending so much time and energy on a project that only a few will benefit from? It's a political risk." The developers are aware of the sensitivity. They have promised to build a certain number of affordable houses and to invest in community projects on the mainland. But the definition of "affordable" in a city where most people live on less than $2 a day is a matter of debate. A two-bedroom flat in La Cite du Fleuve is expected to cost around $100,000 - a sum that would take an average Kinshasa resident 50 years to earn. ## A glimpse of the future? Despite the doubts, the construction is proceeding. The first phase, which includes the hotel, a shopping centre and 2,000 apartments, is expected to be completed in 2027. The developers say they have already sold 40% of the units, mostly to overseas buyers from the diaspora and to wealthy Congolese. On the mainland, the reaction is mixed. "It's a good thing," says Faustin, a tuk-tuk driver who works near the ferry terminal. "They will create work. Maybe my son can get a job there." Fatima, a market vendor selling dried fish, is more sceptical. "This city is for the rich," she says, shaking her head. "We are just here to serve them." As the speedboat turns back towards the shore, Mr Choudury points to the skyline of Kinshasa in the distance. "Look," he says. "The city is growing. It's chaotic, but it has energy. We are not trying to replace it. We are just adding a new chapter. And I believe that in 20 years, people will look back and see this as the moment Kinshasa became a true world city." ## Similar stories across Africa La Cite du Fleuve is not the only mega-city project on the continent. In Kenya, the Tatu City development near Nairobi promises a similar vision of a self-contained, modern city, with mixed success. In Nigeria, the Eko Atlantic project on Lagos's Bar Beach has reclaimed land from the Atlantic Ocean and built a walled city for the wealthy. Each has faced criticism over affordability, environmental impact and social equity. But the DRC may face an even steeper challenge. A country with a history of corruption, conflict and weak institutions, the Congo is not the easiest place to build a $5bn luxury development. Yet the developers are undaunted. "We have strong political backing, international finance and a clear plan," says Mr Choudury. "The risk is real, but so is the opportunity." Standing on the muddy bank, with the sound of hammering and sawing behind him, Robert Choudury allows himself a rare moment of reflection. "You know, when I first had this idea, people told me I was crazy. And maybe I am. But if it works, this will be the most ambitious urban development in Africa. And that is a legacy worth fighting for."

Designed in Dubai, the new complex is expected to include thousands of flats, villas, offices, hotels and shopping centres. "It's a crazy idea," says Robert Choudury, the French-Indian promoter.

title: BBC Sport's football expert Mark Lawrenson is pitting his wits against a different guest each week this season.
text_ai: Lawro's opponent for this weekend's Premier League fixtures is Nobby Butcher - aka Sacha Baron Cohen, star of new comedy film 'Grimsby'. Butcher told BBC Sport: "I'm very experienced at the beautiful game and once had a trial with Grimsby United. Butcher, whose character in the forthcoming film is a loveable but hapless football fan from the Lincolnshire seaside town, went on to explain his credentials. "I've played for the Dog and Duck, the Black Lion and I once scored a hat-trick for the Rotary Club XI against the Ladies' Darts Team. Grimsby United might not have signed me, but I've got a left foot that could open a tin of beans from 40 yards." Lawrenson, a former Liverpool and Republic of Ireland defender turned pundit, has been making his weekly predictions for over a decade. Each season he invites a celebrity guest to challenge his expertise, with mixed results. This year, the stakes are higher than ever. "I've never been beaten by a man in a fake moustache," Lawro said with a grin. "But Nobby seems to think he knows his onions. We'll see if his Grimsby upbringing gives him any insight into the Premier League." The format is simple: Lawro picks a score for each of the weekend's 10 matches, and his guest does the same. Points are awarded for correct results and exact scores. Last season, Lawro finished with a respectable 52% success rate, but guests occasionally upset the odds. In 2018, actor and comedian James Corden managed a narrow victory, and in 2021, singer Olly Murs came within one point of Lawro's total. Butcher, however, is confident he can go one better. "I've been studying the form ever since I got the call," Butcher said. "I've watched every Match of the Day from the last three seasons, and I've even got a spreadsheet. My wife says I'm obsessed, but she doesn't understand the beautiful game. She's a badminton fan." The weekend's fixtures kick off on Saturday lunchtime with a mouth-watering clash at the Etihad Stadium, where Manchester City host Liverpool. Lawro, a former Liverpool player, is torn. "City are formidable at home, but Liverpool's attack is relentless. I'll go 2-2. Both teams will score, but neither will want to lose." Butcher disagrees. "Nah, City 3-1. They've got that Belgian fella, De Bruyne, and that new striker. Liverpool's defence leaks goals like a sieve. I've seen it down the pub - everyone says so." The next match sees Arsenal travel to Tottenham for the north London derby. Lawro predicts a tight affair. "Arsenal have improved under Arteta, but Tottenham at home are a different beast. I'll say 1-1. Kane will score for Spurs, and Saka will equalise." Butcher laughs. "Mate, you're living in the past. Arsenal 2-0. They've got pace, power and a manager who knows what he's doing. Spurs are a one-man team - and that man is Harry Kane, but even he can't do it all. Plus, their fans boo at half-time. That's not a good sign." Elsewhere, Chelsea host West Ham in a London derby with European implications. Lawro sees a home win. "Chelsea 2-0. Their midfield is stronger, and West Ham have struggled for goals away from home." Butcher is sceptical. "West Ham 1-1. They'll sit deep, frustrate Chelsea, and nick one on the break. I've seen it happen. My mate Dave is a West Ham fan and he says they always do well when nobody expects it." Leeds United face Manchester United at Elland Road, a fixture steeped in history and animosity. Lawro: "Leeds are unpredictable, but Manchester United have more quality. 2-1 to the visitors." Butcher shakes his head. "Leeds 3-2. They'll come out flying, the crowd will be like a twelfth man. And Bruno Fernandes goes missing in these games. I've got a feeling." Burnley host Brighton in a game that could define both sides' seasons. Lawro: "Burnley at home are tough to beat. 1-0 to the Clarets." Butcher: "Brighton 2-0. They pass the ball better than anyone outside the top six. Burnley just hoof it. It's 2023, not 1983." Wolves face Brentford at Molineux. Lawro: "Wolves have found some form. 2-1 home win." Butcher: "Brentford 1-1. They're organised and have that Thomas Frank. He's a genius. Wolves will struggle to break them down." Newcastle United host Leicester City at St James' Park. Lawro: "Newcastle are flying. 3-1 to the Magpies." Butcher: "Leicester 2-1. Jamie Vardy will score. He always does against big teams. And Newcastle might be good, but they're not that good." Southampton travel to Crystal Palace. Lawro: "Palace at home are difficult. 1-0 to the Eagles." Butcher: "Southampton 2-0. They've got a new manager bounce. Palace are too inconsistent." Finally, on Sunday, Everton host Aston Villa, and Watford face Norwich in a relegation six-pointer. Lawro goes for Everton 2-1 and Watford 3-1. Butcher predicts Villa 2-0 and Norwich 1-0. "I've done my homework," Butcher insisted. "I've even watched highlights of the Championship. I know my stuff. Lawro might be a legend, but I'm a Grimsby legend. That counts for something." Lawrenson smiled. "We'll see on Monday morning when the results come in. I've got a feeling this might be the week I get a perfect score. But if Nobby beats me, I'll eat my hat. And I don't even own a hat." For those wishing to follow the predictions, all of Lawro and Butcher's scorelines will be published on the BBC Sport website before each match. Viewers can also tune into Match of the Day on Saturday evening to see how their predictions compare with the actual results. Butcher, meanwhile, is already planning his victory speech. "I'll be wearing a Grimsby Town scarf and singing 'We're not really here' - it's a local chant. And I'll dedicate my win to all the underdogs out there. Especially those from Lincolnshire." Whether Nobby Butcher can truly challenge Lawro's expertise remains to be seen. But one thing is certain: the weekend's football will be entertaining, and so will the battle of wits between the former Liverpool defender and the man who once almost played for Grimsby United. To see how Lawro and Nobby Butcher get on, and to make your own predictions, visit the BBC Sport website or follow @BBCSport on social media. Don't forget to use the hashtag #LawroVsNobby. And if you fancy a laugh, catch Sacha Baron Cohen in 'Grimsby', out in cinemas nationwide from Friday. Just don't expect any footballing advice from the man himself - unless, of course, he wins this weekend.

title: Leicester City have won the Premier League title in one of the greatest sporting stories of all time.
text_ai: Tottenham's 2-2 draw at Chelsea on Monday confirmed a stunning achievement for Claudio Ranieri's side. Leicester started the campaign as 5,000-1 outsiders for the title after almost being relegated last season. As the final whistle blew at Stamford Bridge, a deafening roar erupted not in west London but 100 miles north, in a city that had dared to dream the impossible. For Leicester City, a club that had spent most of its history in the shadow of giants, the Premier League title was no longer a fantasy. It was reality. The 2-2 draw between Chelsea and Tottenham Hotspur on Monday night ensured that Claudio Ranieri’s side could not be caught at the top of the table, sparking scenes of jubilation that will be etched into football folklore forever. In the King Power Stadium's corridors, where the walls are lined with photographs of past glories, a different kind of picture was being framed. This was not a triumph built on vast oil wealth or decades of institutional dominance. This was a triumph of unity, of meticulous planning, of a manager who had been written off as a clown, and of players who had been discarded by bigger clubs. The 5,000-1 odds that bookmakers placed on Leicester at the start of the season now stand as a monument to the sheer improbability of it all – a statistical absurdity that has become a fairy tale. ## The moment it was confirmed Back in London, Tottenham's players knew they had let a golden opportunity slip. Trailing 2-0 at half-time, they had fought back to lead 2-1 through an own goal and a Harry Kane strike. But a late equaliser from Eden Hazard – a goal that Chelsea fans will never forget, even if it handed the title to their local rivals – sealed Leicester's fate. In the away end at Stamford Bridge, a small pocket of Leicester supporters who had travelled in hope rather than expectation began to sing. Their voices carried on the night air, a prelude to the celebrations that would soon sweep through the East Midlands. Back in Leicester, tens of thousands had gathered at the King Power Stadium, where a giant screen had been erected. They had come not to watch their own team – Leicester were not playing – but to witness history unfold. As Hazard's shot beat Tottenham goalkeeper Hugo Lloris, the stadium erupted. Strangers embraced. Grown men wept. Fireworks crackled overhead. The city, once known for its textiles and its foxes, had become the epicentre of the sporting world. ## The architect: Claudio Ranieri For Claudio Ranieri, this is the ultimate vindication. The 64-year-old Italian had been dismissed as a "tinker man" during his time at Chelsea, ridiculed for his constant changes and his inability to win the Premier League. He had been sacked by Greece after a humiliating defeat to the Faroe Islands. He had been seen as a safe pair of hands, a journeyman who would keep Leicester up – nothing more. But Ranieri had a vision. From the moment he took over in July 2015, he instilled a sense of calm and belief. He simplified the team's approach, telling his players to focus on the next game, the next opponent, the next three points. He famously rewarded them with pizza after their first clean sheet, a gesture that became a symbol of his man-management. "I said to the players, 'Why not us?'" Ranieri recalled after the title was confirmed. "They believed from the start. They worked so hard. This is for the city, for the fans, for everyone who dreams." His tactical acumen was often underestimated. Leicester's counter-attacking style, built on a solid defensive base and lightning-fast transitions, was a masterclass in efficiency. They conceded just 36 goals all season – fewer than any other team in the top four. And they scored 68, a testament to the potency of Jamie Vardy, Riyad Mahrez, and the midfield engine room of N'Golo Kanté and Danny Drinkwater. ## The heroes of the campaign Jamie Vardy's story is perhaps the most emblematic of Leicester's rise. Five years ago, he was playing non-league football for Stocksbridge Park Steels, earning £30 a week. He had a criminal record for assault, and many wrote him off as a troublemaker. But under Ranieri, he became the Premier League's top scorer, with 24 goals. His blistering pace, his relentless pressing, and his knack for scoring when it mattered most made him the heartbeat of the team. Then there is Riyad Mahrez. The Algerian winger was signed for just £400,000 from French club Le Havre. He was raw, inconsistent, and barely known outside of scouting circles. But this season, he was unstoppable. His dribbling, his vision, his ability to score from impossible angles – he was named PFA Player of the Year, and few could argue. Mahrez's performances against Southampton, Chelsea, and Manchester City were moments of pure artistry. And the unsung hero: N'Golo Kanté. The diminutive French midfielder covered every blade of grass, breaking up attacks, winning the ball back, and setting Leicester on the counter. His energy was phenomenal, his discipline impeccable. Chelsea had let him go as a youth player; now he was the Premier League's most influential midfielder. In the words of his teammate Danny Simpson, "He's like two players in one." ## The turning points Leicester's season was not without its moments of doubt. They lost to Arsenal in February, and many believed the wheels would fall off. But they responded with a six-match winning streak that took them clear of the chasing pack. The 3-1 victory over Manchester City in December was a statement of intent – a match in which Mahrez ran riot, and the defending champions were dismantled. The 1-0 win at Crystal Palace in March, secured by a Riyad Mahrez goal, felt like the moment belief turned into destiny. Perhaps the most significant game was the 1-1 draw with Manchester United in November. Leicester had taken the lead through Vardy, but United equalised. In previous seasons, that might have been a crushing blow. But this Leicester side refused to buckle. They held on, and they learned that they could compete with the elite. And then there was the match at the King Power Stadium on 3 May, when Leicester beat Southampton 3-1 to move within a whisker of the title. That night, the fans sang "We're going to win the league" with a conviction that no one could mock. They were right. ## The context: a league of giants This is a Premier League that has been dominated by the super-rich. Since its inception in 1992, only five clubs – Manchester United, Arsenal, Chelsea, Manchester City, and Blackburn Rovers – had won the title. The financial gap between the haves and the have-nots had grown ever wider. Transfer fees of £50m were commonplace, and wages of £200,000 a week were almost expected. Leicester's total wage bill was around £48m – less than what Manchester United paid Wayne Rooney alone. Their starting XI cost a combined £22m, a fraction of the £200m squads of their rivals. They did not have a superstar, a Galáctico, or a global brand. They had a team. In an era of data analysts, sports scientists, and multi-million-pound recruitment departments, Leicester's triumph was a throwback to a simpler time. It was a victory for scouting, for coaching, and for the power of collective endeavour. "We didn't need to spend £50m on a player," said director of football Jon Rudkin. "We needed to find the right players who fit our system and our culture." ## The fallout: what next? For Leicester, the challenge now is to build on this success. The team will inevitably be broken up – Kanté, Mahrez, and Vardy are all likely to attract interest from Europe's elite. But Ranieri insists the club will not sell unless they have to. "We want to keep all the players," he said. "But we are realistic. Every player has a price." The financial rewards are enormous. Qualification for the Champions League guarantees at least £30m, and the club's value will skyrocket. The owners, the Thai conglomerate King Power, have already hinted at ambitious plans to expand the stadium and improve the academy. But for now, the focus is on celebration. The players will parade the trophy through the streets of Leicester on Monday, a city that has waited 132 years for a top-flight title. The whole world will be watching, and as they do, they will remember that day in May 2016 when the impossible became possible. ## A wider significance This story transcends football. It is a story of hope, of resilience, of the belief that the underdog can still triumph in a world that seems stacked against them. It is the tale of a 64-year-old manager who refused to listen to his critics, of a striker who overcame a troubled past to become a national hero, of a winger who rose from obscurity to become the best in his country. It is also a reminder that sport, at its best, can unite communities and inspire generations. In a year dominated by political turmoil, economic uncertainty, and social division, Leicester City's triumph is a beam of light. It says that anything is possible if you work hard, stay together, and never stop believing. And so, as the champagne flows in the King Power Stadium, and as the city of Leicester turns blue, we are left with a simple truth: this was not just a title win. This was a miracle. And in the annals of English football, it will be remembered forever. Leicester City: champions of England. And the greatest story ever told.
