title: Just weeks before turning 101, Ruby Holt has seen the ocean for the first time.
text_ai: She has spent most of her life on a farm in rural Tennessee picking cotton and said she never had the time or money to go to a beach. "I've heard people talk about it and how wonderful it was and wanted to see it, but I never had the opportunity to do so," she said. The trip was organised by staff at the assisted living facility where she now resides, after they learned of her unfulfilled wish. "We had no idea she'd never seen the ocean," said care coordinator Maria Jenkins. "When she told us, we knew we had to make it happen." On a warm Thursday morning, Mrs Holt was helped into a specially adapted van for the two-hour drive to Gulf Shores, Alabama. She was accompanied by her daughter, Betty-Jean, 78, and a nurse. "I was a little nervous, if I'm honest," Mrs Holt admitted. "At my age, you don't expect new adventures." But when the van pulled up to the shoreline and the door slid open, the sight left her speechless. "It was so vast, so blue," she said, her voice trembling with emotion. "I just sat there and stared. I couldn't believe my eyes." Staff had arranged for a wheelchair-friendly path to the water's edge. Mrs Holt asked to be wheeled closer, and when the tide lapped gently over her bare feet, she laughed – a sound, her daughter said, they had not heard in years. "I just never imagined it would feel like that," Mrs Holt said, smiling. "The water was cool, and the waves were so gentle. It was like God's own lullaby." She spent nearly an hour on the beach, collecting a single shell as a keepsake. "That's going right on my nightstand," she declared. For the staff, the moment was a reminder of the simple joys that often go overlooked. "Ruby has worked her whole life – from the cotton fields to raising her children. She never had a moment for herself," Ms Jenkins said. "To see her face light up like that... it was a privilege." Mrs Holt, who plans to celebrate her 101st birthday with a slice of chocolate cake, is already thinking about her next ambition: "I'd like to see the mountains," she said. "But maybe I'll give myself a few years to rest first."

title: Labour's Harriet Harman has become the longest continuously serving female MP, racking up 12,468 days in the Commons.
text_ai: Since Ms Harman was elected in a Peckham by-election in 1982, she has worked with seven different Labour leaders and been acting leader twice. Friday marks the day she surpasses Gwyneth Dunwoody's record, although the late Labour MP served longer overall in two separate periods. Since the 1980s, her political journey has mirrored many of the defining shifts within the Labour Party. She was a vocal supporter of Neil Kinnock's modernisation drive, and later became a close ally of Tony Blair. As Minister for Women from 1997, she introduced landmark legislation on domestic violence and the national child-care strategy, and was pivotal in shaping the Equality Act 2010 – a piece of legislation that consolidated anti-discrimination law and remains one of her most enduring legacies. Beyond her ministerial roles, Ms Harman served as Deputy Leader of the Labour Party from 2007 to 2015, and twice stepped in as acting leader during turbulent transitions – after Gordon Brown's resignation in 2010 and following Ed Miliband's departure in 2015. Her steady hand in those periods earned respect from across the political spectrum, even as she faced criticism from some on the left for her pragmatism. At 73, she remains a formidable presence in the Commons, representing the Bermondsey and Old Southwark constituency since boundary changes in 2024. She holds the informal title "Mother of the House" – a designation for the longest-serving female MP – and sits on the Justice Select Committee. Colleagues from all parties have paid tribute to her resilience. Conservative MP Penny Mordaunt described her as "a woman of principle who has never wavered in her commitment to equality". Reflecting on the milestone, Ms Harman said: "It's a privilege to serve my constituents for so long. I never expected to be here this many years, but there is still work to be done." She pointed to ongoing campaigns on parental leave and protections for victims of domestic abuse. The record she now holds was previously set by the late Gwyneth Dunwoody, a Labour MP who served for over 30 years in total but in two separate periods. Ms Harman's uninterrupted tenure – spanning seven prime ministers, from Margaret Thatcher to Sir Keir Starmer – is a testament to her political stamina. As she marks this achievement, few doubt that her voice will continue to shape debates for some time yet.

title: An outright ban on tail docking for dogs has been scrapped after MSPs voted to allow exemptions for specific breeds.
text_ai: The changes mean vets will be allowed to shorten the tails of some working dogs, which ministers say are at increased risk of injury. Opposition members launched a last-ditch attempt to maintain the blanket ban, ahead of the final Holyrood vote. However the government ultimately won out with Conservative backing. The vote, which passed by 64 to 54, means that from next spring, veterinarians in Scotland will be able to dock the tails of certain breeds – including spaniels, hunt pointers and terriers – when the puppies are less than five days old, provided the dog is intended for use as a working animal. Supporters of the exemption argued that working dogs in fields, forests and farmyards often suffer painful tail injuries, and that docking done properly by a vet is a humane preventive measure. But animal welfare campaigners reacted with dismay, saying the decision set a damaging precedent and risked encouraging non-therapeutic mutilation. The Scottish SPCA described it as "a deeply disappointing and regressive step" that could weaken the broader principle against tail docking, which has been banned across the UK for cosmetic reasons since 2007. Labour MSP Colin Smyth, who led the opposition effort, told BBC Scotland he was "bitterly disappointed". He said the government had bowed to pressure from shooting and farming lobbyists, and ignored overwhelming veterinary evidence that tail injuries in working dogs are relatively rare and treatable without amputation. "This is not about protecting dogs – it's about convenience for a minority of owners," he argued. In contrast, Rural Affairs Secretary Mairi Gougeon insisted the exemption was narrowly drawn and evidence-based. "We have listened to vets, to farmers and to gamekeepers who have firsthand experience of the suffering caused by tail injuries in working dogs," she said in a statement after the vote. "This measure is about animal welfare – preventing pain and infection. It is not a backdoor to cosmetic docking." The debate exposed deep divisions within the veterinary profession itself. The British Veterinary Association (BVA) has long opposed tail docking for any reason, maintaining that there is insufficient evidence of long-term benefit. However, the Scottish Veterinary Association (SVA) took a more nuanced position, supporting the exemption for working dogs where there is clear risk. Dr Fiona Birrell, a vet in Aberdeenshire who treats working dogs, said she had seen too many cases of broken or split tails that require partial amputation anyway. "We are not talking about snipping off an inch for fashion – we are talking about preventing a dog from being in agony after catching its tail on barbed wire," she said. "Performed under anaesthetic by a vet, this is a minor procedure that can save a dog from weeks of pain." Critics counter that the evidence base is weak. A 2015 study commissioned by the Scottish government found that only a small percentage of working dogs sustain tail injuries serious enough to require amputation. Opponents also warn that the exemption will be difficult to enforce, as owners could claim a dog is for "working" when it is actually a family pet. The vote was a test of cross-party lines. The SNP, which leads the minority government, saw its own members split, with several backbenchers voting against the exemption. The Conservatives, as noted, provided decisive support. Liberal Democrats largely opposed, while the Greens objected outright. Commentators noted that the outcome could embolden groups elsewhere in the UK to push for similar exemptions. Tail docking for working dogs is already permitted in England and Wales under the Animal Welfare Act 2006, but only for specific breeds and with strict registration. Scotland's previous blanket ban was seen as a stronger stance, and campaigners had hoped it would remain. For now, the focus turns to implementation. The Scottish government has said it will publish guidance for vets and require record-keeping to prevent abuse. But animal welfare groups say they will continue to monitor and, if necessary, challenge the law in court. "This is not the end of the road," said a spokesperson for the Scottish Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. "We will do everything in our power to ensure that no dog suffers unnecessarily as a result of today's decision." It was a typical semi-final first leg – intense, tough, and we had to suffer at times. The result is good, but it's only half-time in the tie." Stoke manager Mark Hughes was left frustrated by his side's wastefulness in front of goal. The Potters enjoyed spells of dominance, particularly in the first half before Liverpool's opener, but were unable to convert their pressure into clear-cut chances. Arnautovic was lively throughout, but often isolated, while Xherdan Shaqiri struggled to impose himself on the game. "We had enough of the ball, we created chances, we just didn't take them," Hughes said. "We need to be more clinical. The goal we conceded was disappointing – we switched off at the back post. But we are still in the tie. We go to Anfield with everything to play for. We've shown we can be a threat away from home." The match was not without controversy. Stoke felt they should have had a penalty when Sakho appeared to handle the ball in the area, but referee Kevin Friend waved away their appeals. Replays suggested the incident was outside the box, but it added to the home side's sense of grievance. For Liverpool, the night belonged to Ibe. The 20-year-old winger was thrust into action earlier than expected, but produced a composed finish that belied his years. Lallana, who had been a constant menace with his dribbling and movement, laid the ball off to Allen, and his clever cross found Ibe unmarked at the far post. The youngster's emphatic volley gave Stoke goalkeeper Jack Butland no chance. The performance was a testament to Liverpool's squad depth and Klopp's tactical nous. Without Coutinho and with Daniel Sturridge only fit enough for a late cameo, the visitors still carried a threat on the counter-attack. Roberto Firmino worked tirelessly, while the midfield trio of Jordan Henderson, Emre Can and Allen provided a solid foundation. Liverpool's defensive solidity was particularly impressive. Sakho, returning from a knee injury, was a colossus, winning headers and making crucial interceptions. Nathaniel Clyne and Alberto Moreno also did their defensive duties diligently, limiting Stoke's wide players. The second leg at Anfield on 26 January promises to be a fascinating encounter. Liverpool hold the advantage, but Stoke will fancy their chances of overturning a slender deficit. The Potters have already won at Chelsea and Manchester City this season, and will take heart from those performances. "There's still everything to play for," Hughes added. "We believe we can score goals at Anfield. We showed against City and Chelsea that we can hurt top teams on their own patch. It will be a difficult night, but we have the quality to cause problems." Klopp, meanwhile, will be hoping for a swift recovery for his injured stars. The prospect of facing United without Coutinho and Lovren is a daunting one, but the Liverpool boss will take confidence from the way his side coped at Stoke. "We need to recover now and prepare for the next game," Klopp said. "This was a good step, but we have to finish the job. Nothing is decided yet." In a match that showcased the competitive spirit of the League Cup, it was Liverpool who drew first blood. But as both managers know, a one-goal lead is a fragile advantage in a two-legged tie. The Anfield faithful will play their part, but Stoke will come with ambition. The subplot of injuries and suspensions will also be key. Liverpool will be without the suspended Lucas for the first leg of the next round if they progress, while Stoke must avoid further recriminations over their penalty claims. For now, the focus is on a tie that remains delicately poised. Ibe's moment of magic under the lights at the Britannia Stadium was the defining image of the night. The young Englishman, who spent time on loan at Derby County last season, has been knocking on the door for more first-team opportunities. This was his most significant contribution in a Liverpool shirt. "He is a fantastic talent," Klopp said of Ibe. "He has speed, technique, and a good head on his shoulders. It is nice for him to score such an important goal. But he knows this is just the start." As the players trudged off the pitch, the contrasting emotions were clear. Stoke's players looked deflated but not defeated. Liverpool's huddle was one of quiet satisfaction. The tie is still alive, but the Reds have the edge. Anfield awaits.

title: Madalyn Parker, a US web developer, sparked a debate about workplace attitudes to mind problems after tweeting an email from her boss.
text_ai: Her boss said she was an "example to us all" by telling colleagues she was taking sick leave for her mental health - but would British managers be similarly supportive? In an email titled "Where's Madalyn", she told colleagues: "I'm taking today and tomorrow to focus on my mental health. Her boss’s response went viral, with many praising the CEO of the online payment company, Ben Congleton, for normalising mental health days. But the reaction also highlighted a stark transatlantic divide. In Britain, where the “stiff upper lip” still lingers in workplace culture, would a manager be so unequivocally supportive? Employment law experts say the short answer is: it depends. Under the Equality Act 2010, mental health conditions that have a “substantial and long-term adverse effect” on daily life can be considered a disability, entitling employees to reasonable adjustments. But taking a day off for “feeling low” without a formal diagnosis is treated under normal sick-leave policies. Dr. Amanda Thombs, a psychologist at the University of Cambridge’s Institute for Work, said: “The Parker case is a watershed moment, but we must not assume it reflects a universal shift. Many UK employees still report that disclosing mental health struggles carries a stigma, especially in sectors like finance, law, or construction, where presenteeism is rife.” A 2024 survey by the mental health charity Mind found that 48% of workers had taken a day off for stress or anxiety but told their employer they were physically ill. The same poll showed that only 35% of managers felt confident addressing a team member’s mental health. “Managers are caught in a bind,” said Rachel Suff, senior policy advisor at the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development (CIPD). “They want to be supportive, but they often lack training and fear saying the wrong thing. The law also creates confusion: an employer who dismisses someone for a mental health-related absence could face an unfair dismissal claim, but only if the condition meets the disability threshold.” Yet there are signs of change. A growing number of British companies, including Unilever, Deloitte, and some NHS Trusts, have introduced “wellbeing days” distinct from sick leave. Others have signed the “Time to Change” pledge, committing to open conversations about mental health. But critics argue that such policies can be superficial. “A single ‘duvet day’ won’t address systemic issues like workload, bullying, or lack of autonomy,” said Dr. Thombs. “We need a culture where it’s safe to say ‘I’m not coping’ without fear of career damage.” The legal landscape is also evolving. In 2023, a landmark Employment Tribunal case (Mackenzie v. Northern Rail) ruled that an employee who had been disciplined for taking two mental health days without a doctor’s note had been unfairly subjected to a detriment. The ruling sent a signal that employers must take such absences seriously. Nonetheless, the UK remains behind the US in terms of open workplace discourse. A 2024 study by the American Psychological Association found that 81% of US workers felt comfortable discussing mental health with their manager, compared to 68% in the UK. But the US also has weaker statutory employment protection – most states are “at-will”, meaning employees can be dismissed for almost any reason. “The success of the Parker story is partly because it happened in a US tech firm,” said Professor Cary Cooper, a leading UK occupational psychologist. “Tech companies tend to be younger, more progressive, and have a culture of transparency. In more traditional British industries, the reaction might have been different.” He added: “The real test will come when someone in a blue-collar job in a factory or a warehouse posts a similar email. Culture change must be top-down and bottom-up.” Madalyn Parker’s own story has inspired many. She told the BBC she received hundreds of messages from people who said her openness encouraged them to seek help. “I just wanted to be honest,” she said. “And I was lucky to have a boss who got it.” The lesson for British managers? The CIPD’s Rachel Suff advises: “Start by normalising mental health conversations during one-to-ones. Consider a policy that allows a certain number of ‘mental health days’ without a medical note. And crucially, lead by example – let your team see you take time out when you need it.” As the debate continues, one thing is clear: the days of the “keep calm and carry on” approach to workplace wellbeing are numbered. Whether British bosses will follow their American counterpart’s lead remains to be seen. But as Madalyn Parker proved, a single honest email can spark a global conversation.

title: An online platform that lets college students who have been sexually assaulted report their attacks has been launched at the TED (Technology, Entertainment and Design) conference.
text_ai: According to Callisto creator Jessica Ladd, sexual assault is "practically a rite of passage" in US universities. Its website has already been trialled for a few months at the University of San Francisco and Pomona College. Other universities are now being invited to take part. The platform, named Callisto, is designed to address what its creators describe as a "crisis of underreporting" on US campuses. According to the Rape, Abuse and Incest National Network (RAINN), only about 20% of female student victims report sexual assault to law enforcement. Ladd, a social entrepreneur who was inspired by her own experience of being assaulted in college, says the system aims to lower that barrier. Callisto works by allowing students to create a secure, time-stamped record of an incident without immediately triggering a formal complaint. The user can choose to submit the report directly to the university's Title IX office, or they can store it encrypted on the platform. If they later decide to move forward, the report can be forwarded instantly. This gives survivors time to seek support or consider their options without the pressure of an immediate investigative process. One of the most distinctive features is its "matching" system. If a survivor files a report that includes the perpetrator's name, and a second person files a report about the same individual, both are notified of the possible pattern. They can then choose to come forward together or independently. Ladd says this is intended to help victims who fear they won't be believed if they are alone, and to give institutional investigators clearer evidence of repeated behaviour. "It's a way to break the silence without having to be the first one to step into the spotlight," Ladd told the TED audience. "We know that many survivors are afraid to report because they worry they'll be blamed or that nothing will happen. This gives them a tool to record what happened, and to see if a pattern exists, before they commit to a full process." The pilot programmes at the University of San Francisco and Pomona College have already produced some early data. According to the Callisto team, usage of the platform at these institutions has been modest but steady, with several dozen reports filed in the first few months. University administrators involved in the trials have expressed cautious optimism. "It gives us a better sense of what's happening on the ground—and that allows us to allocate resources more effectively," said a Title IX coordinator from one of the colleges, speaking anonymously because they were not authorised to discuss the programme publicly. But the launch also comes amid growing scrutiny of how US universities handle sexual misconduct. Under Title IX, the federal law that prohibits sex discrimination in education, schools are required to respond promptly and equitably to reports of sexual assault. However, critics have argued that many institutions fail to do so, often prioritizing their reputation over survivor justice. A 2014 White House task force report estimated that one in five female students experiences sexual assault during college, yet reporting rates remain stubbornly low. Ladd acknowledges these concerns and says Callisto is designed to work within existing institutional frameworks, not to replace them. "We're not a substitute for good policies or trained staff," she said. "What we're trying to do is increase the flow of information so that schools can actually see the scale of the problem—and then be held accountable for addressing it." The platform is built with strong encryption and privacy protections. Users can access it through a standard web browser, and all data is stored in a way that prevents the company or anyone else from reading it unless the user explicitly provides a key. This approach has been praised by privacy advocates, but some legal experts have raised questions about how the evidence might be used in court if a survivor decides to report after a significant delay. "There's a trade-off," said Elizabeth Sullivan, a law professor specializing in sexual violence at the University of California. "Time-stamped records can be very persuasive evidence of a coherent account, but the longer a person waits, the more opportunity there is for the other side to challenge the reliability of the memory. Still, for survivors who need time to feel safe, this is far better than having no record at all." The TED launch is intended to spur interest from other campuses. Callisto's team says they are now in talks with several dozen universities across the United States, and hope to have at least 20 institutions using the platform by the end of the year. The service is free for students; schools pay a licensing fee based on enrollment size. For Ladd, the ultimate goal is cultural change. "Sexual assault should not be a rite of passage," she said, echoing the words that opened her TED talk. "We need to make it a thing of the past. I believe technology can help, but only if we are willing to use it to listen to survivors and to take action."

title: Jockey AP McCoy says he will regret not being able to end his career with 300 winners in a season.
text_ai: McCoy, 40, announced on Saturday that this season will be his last in racing. In an in-depth interview with the BBC, the 19-time champion jockey said a three-week injury lay-off earlier this season was the "toughest" of his career because it ended his hopes of reaching the 300 milestone. “It was the first time in my career that I genuinely thought about the end,” McCoy told the BBC’s *Sunday Politics* programme. “I had a plan. I wanted to get to 300 this season. But when I broke my ribs and missed three weeks, that dream was gone. I realised I couldn’t make up the ground. It was the toughest thing I’ve ever had to deal with in racing, because it was the first time I had to accept defeat – and I hate defeat.” The 40-year-old Northern Irishman, who has been champion jockey every year since 1995–96, confirmed on Saturday that the 2014–15 campaign will be his last. He will retire at the end of the jumps season in April, bringing to a close a career that has seen him ride more than 4,300 winners and rewrite almost every record in the sport. His announcement came after months of speculation, and even his closest rivals admitted they had expected him to ride on. McCoy’s frustration at missing the 300 mark is understandable. He has always been driven by numbers. Last season, he rode a staggering 290 winners – his highest total for a decade – and was on course to challenge the 300 barrier for the first time since 2001–02, when he rode a record 289 winners in a season. This year, he had 82 winners by mid-November, and was poised to push towards 300 again. But a fall at Southwell on 12 November left him with three fractured ribs, and he was sidelined for three weeks. By the time he returned, the momentum had gone. “I had a good start, I was riding well, and I genuinely believed I could do it,” he said. “But when you’re out for three weeks, you lose your rhythm, you lose your weight, you lose your edge. And when you come back, you’re playing catch-up. I tried to make up the ground, but it was impossible. The horses are there, the opportunities are there, but you can’t force it. It just wouldn’t happen for me after that.” McCoy’s decision to retire was not taken lightly. He said he had been thinking about it for “two or three years” and had discussed it at length with his wife, Chanelle, and his agent, Dave Roberts. “I knew in my heart that this was the right time,” he said. “I’ve been doing this for 20 years at the top level. I’ve given everything. I’ve broken bones, I’ve had concussions, I’ve missed family occasions. I’ve done it all. And I don’t want to be the jockey who stays on too long, who becomes a shadow of himself. I want to go out while I’m still the best.” That “best” is not in doubt. McCoy has been champion jockey every season since 1995–96, a run of 19 titles that is unprecedented in British racing history. He has won the Grand National (on Don’t Push It in 2010), the Cheltenham Gold Cup (on Synchronised in 2012), the Champion Hurdle (on Make A Stand in 1997) and the King George VI Chase (on Kicking King in 2005). He has ridden more winners than any other jump jockey in history, surpassing Richard Dunwoody’s record of 1,699 winners in 2002, and has since extended that mark to over 4,300. He has been awarded an OBE, a CBE, and was voted BBC Sports Personality of the Year in 2010. But it is the relentless pursuit of winners that defines him. McCoy is known for his fierce competitiveness, his willingness to ride through pain, and his meticulous preparation. He is a man who once rode with a broken neck, who delayed surgery to ensure he didn’t miss a meeting, and who has been known to ride six or seven horses a day, day after day, week after week. “I don’t know how he does it,” said trainer Jonjo O’Neill, for whom McCoy has ridden many of his biggest winners. “He’s a machine. He’s the hardest-working jockey I’ve ever seen. He never gives up, never takes a day off. He’s a one-off.” McCoy’s decision to retire has prompted an outpouring of tributes. Champion trainer Paul Nicholls said: “He’s been the best jockey of his generation, without doubt. He’s set standards that no one else will ever reach.” Fellow jockey Ruby Walsh, who has often been McCoy’s rival in big races, said: “He’s the greatest jump jockey of all time. No one has ridden more winners, no one has worked harder. He’s a legend of the sport.” Even his contemporaries admit they will miss him. “He’s the guy everyone wants to beat, but also the guy everyone respects,” said jockey Richard Johnson, who has been champion runner-up to McCoy 14 times. “He’s been the benchmark for as long as I can remember. When he retires, it’ll be the end of an era.” McCoy’s final season is already being watched with intense interest. He currently sits second in the jockeys’ championship behind Johnson, but with more than three months of the season remaining, he could yet reclaim the lead. He is also chasing a 20th champion title, which would be an unprecedented achievement. But McCoy says he is not focused on the numbers any more. “I’m just going to enjoy the rest of the season,” he said. “I’m going to ride as many winners as I can, but I’m not going to kill myself trying to get to 300. It’s not going to happen. So I’ll just ride, enjoy it, and say goodbye properly.” He will ride at the Cheltenham Festival in March, where he has 31 winners to date, and at Aintree in April, where he hopes to win the Grand National for a second time. He has already been booked for several big races, and there is a sense that his farewell tour will be emotional. “I’ve had a lot of messages from people,” he said. “Some of them have made me cry. I’m not ashamed to say that. It’s been emotional. But I’m ready. I’ve done everything I wanted to do. Well, almost everything. I didn’t get to 300. But I’ve got a lot of other things to be proud of.” For many in racing, the 300-winner milestone was always going to be a stretch. No jump jockey has achieved it since Richard Dunwoody in 1993–94, and only a handful have ever come close. McCoy’s best was 289, and he came agonisingly close again last season with 290. But he insists he does not see missing that mark as a failure. “I’ve won 19 championships, I’ve won the Grand National, I’ve won the Gold Cup,” he said. “I’ve broken every record there is. To not get 300 is frustrating, yes. But it’s not a failure. It’s just a target I didn’t quite reach. And if that’s the only one I miss, I’ll take it.” McCoy’s retirement will leave a huge void in jump racing. He is not only its most successful jockey, but also its most recognisable face. He has been the sport’s dominant figure for two decades, and his absence will be felt by trainers, owners, punters – and by the public at large. “I think people will be shocked when he’s not there,” said O’Neill. “He’s been such a constant in the sport. It’ll take a while to get used to.” For now, McCoy is focused on the final months of his career. He will continue to ride as many horses as possible, and says he will “give it everything” until the last race. He has no plans to become a trainer, though he says he might “do a bit of punditry” and spend more time with his family. “I’ve got two young kids, and I’ve missed a lot of their lives,” he said. “I want to be there for them now. I want to take them to school, pick them up, take them to the park. I want to be a normal dad.” But for the next few months, he is still AP McCoy – the most competitive, driven, relentless jockey the sport has ever seen. And he has one last season to prove it. “I’ll miss it, no doubt,” he said. “But I’m not going to let that stop me. I want to go out on my terms. And that’s exactly what I’m going to do.”

title: MPs' salaries will rise from £67,060 to £74,000, the Independent Parliamentary Standards Authority has announced.
text_ai: The 10% pay rise has been approved despite Downing Street and a succession of MPs saying it was "not appropriate". IPSA chairman Sir Ian Kennedy said that MPs' pay had been a "toxic" issue "which had been ducked for decades". The decision, which will take effect from April, has reignited a fierce debate about the value of public service and the disconnect between politicians and the public they serve. Sir Ian, speaking at a press conference in central London, insisted the increase was necessary to ensure that becoming an MP remained an attractive career option for people from all walks of life, not just those who are independently wealthy. "We have seen, over many years, a failure to address this issue in a systematic and transparent way," he said. "The result has been that MPs' pay has fallen significantly behind comparable roles in the public and private sectors. This has created a risk that talented individuals will be deterred from standing for Parliament." The rise – the first above inflation since IPSA was created in the wake of the MPs' expenses scandal – will take the basic salary for a backbench MP to £74,000. That compares with the current median UK full-time salary of around £35,000 and the average earnings of a head teacher (£75,000) or a police inspector (£58,000). Downing Street made clear the Prime Minister was "disappointed" by the decision. A Number 10 spokesman said: "The Prime Minister has been clear that this is not the right time for such an increase. He believes that MPs should be focused on delivering for their constituents and the country, not on their own remuneration." The spokesman added that the government would not seek to block the rise, as IPSA is an independent body, but would urge it to reconsider the timing. Several senior MPs, including Labour leader Sir Keir Starmer, had previously argued against any significant rise while public sector workers – particularly nurses, teachers and civil servants – were facing real-terms pay cuts due to inflation. Sir Keir said on Tuesday: "I do not believe that now is the time for MPs to be receiving a 10% pay rise. Public sector workers, including those who work for our NHS, are struggling. MPs should show solidarity." The rise was also condemned by the TaxPayers' Alliance, which described it as "out of touch" and "provocative". Chief executive John O'Connell said: "Hard-pressed families and public sector workers who have seen their own pay squeezed will find this decision incredibly difficult to accept. It sends a terrible message." But IPSA argued that the increase – calculated using a formula based on public sector median pay growth – was fair and evidence-based. Sir Ian acknowledged that the timing might appear "insensitive", but stressed that the body was obliged to act independently and without political interference. "We have a legal duty to set pay fairly, and we have done so," he said. "To delay further would simply have allowed the problem to fester." The 10% rise compares with the 4.5% pay award recently recommended for NHS staff and the 3-4% offered to many teachers. The gap has fuelled anger among unions. Unison general secretary Christina McAnea said: "At a time when nurses and paramedics are being offered below-inflation pay rises, this decision shows a complete lack of understanding of the national mood." The debate over MPs' pay has long been a sensitive one. The current salary of £67,060 was set in 2015 after a period of restraint following the 2009 expenses scandal. Since then, backbench MPs have received only the same annual increases as other public sector workers, typically 1-2%. The new rise will effectively make up for several years of lost ground, according to IPSA's calculations. Critics, however, point out that MPs also receive generous pensions, expenses and allowances, including the ability to claim for travel, accommodation and staffing costs. The total cost to the taxpayer of supporting an MP is estimated to be more than £200,000 per year. The decision also comes as the UK faces a cost-of-living crisis, with energy bills and food prices rising sharply. Many ordinary workers are struggling to make ends meet. A YouGov poll conducted last week found that 72% of the public believed the rise was "unacceptable". IPSA acknowledged the public backlash but insisted it could not be swayed by opinion polls. "Our job is to do the right thing for the long-term health of our democracy," said Sir Ian. "That sometimes means making unpopular decisions." The rise will apply to all 650 MPs, including ministers – though Cabinet members, whose salaries are higher, will see their pay increase by a smaller proportionate amount. The prime minister's salary will remain at £151,549, as will the speaker's £142,500. Several Conservative MPs expressed private dismay, with one backbencher telling the BBC it was "politically suicidal". "We are going to get slaughtered on the doorstep," they said. Others argued that the rise was long overdue. "It's not about lining our pockets. It's about ensuring that people from ordinary backgrounds can afford to do this job without relying on outside incomes or family wealth," said a Labour MP who declined to be named. IPSA has committed to a five-year review of the pay system and will consult on any future changes. For now, the rise stands – and the political fallout has only just begun.

title: Less than two weeks into Donald Trump's presidency, it seemed the only news from here on out would be political.
text_ai: The new president and his flurry of executive orders and swift-moving, substantive changes to US policy and procedure seemed to leave little oxygen for any other headlines. The new president and his flurry of executive orders and swift-moving, substantive changes to US policy and procedure seemed to leave little oxygen for any other headlines. But even President Trump lacks the star power of Queen Bee. Her name is Beyoncé, and on the first Thursday of February 2017, she posted a single image on Instagram. A floral wreath, two sonogram photos, and the caption: "We would like to share our love and happiness. We have been blessed two times over." Within hours, the post had broken the record for the most-liked image on the platform, surpassing 10 million likes. The news cycle, which had been wall-to-wall Trump, fractured. Cable news anchors were now reading out comments from fans. Twitter exploded with hashtags like #BeyoncePregnant and #QueenBey. The White House press corps, gathered for an afternoon briefing, found themselves fielding questions about whether the president had reacted to the announcement. The answer, from press secretary Sean Spicer, was a curt "No comment." It was a vivid reminder that the United States, for all its political turbulence, remains a country obsessed with celebrity culture. And Beyoncé is perhaps its most potent cultural force. The singer, who had already redefined the modern pop spectacle with her 2016 visual album *Lemonade*, was now expecting twins. The announcement came just days after she had performed at the Super Bowl halftime show—a performance that itself had been a political statement, with dancers dressed as Black Panthers and a medley of songs celebrating black womanhood. Now, the focus shifted to her personal life, and the world watched with a mix of adoration and voyeuristic curiosity. The contrast with the Trump White House could not have been starker. Where Trump used Twitter as a weapon to bypass traditional media, Beyoncé used it as an instrument of mystique and intimacy. Where Trump's executive orders—on immigration, the environment, and healthcare—generated fierce partisan debate, Beyoncé's pregnancy announcement generated near-universal joy. Even some of the president's most loyal supporters paused to celebrate. "I'm a Trump guy, but I love Beyoncé," one man told CNN, summing up the cultural zaniness of the moment. The media machine scrambled to keep up. *People* magazine rushed a cover story to press. Entertainment Tonight dedicated a week's worth of coverage. The *New York Times* ran a detailed analysis of the symbolism in the Instagram post's visual clues—the flowers, the veil, the promise of new life. On late-night television, hosts competed to deliver the funniest take. Stephen Colbert joked that Trump was "the only person in America who wasn't trending." It was, in many ways, a welcome reprieve from politics. Yet the reprieve was brief. By the following week, the executive orders had resumed. The travel ban targeting seven Muslim-majority countries was tied up in court, and protests erupted at airports. Trump's approval ratings, already historically low, continued to slide. The political machine, it seemed, was unstoppable. But for a few days in early February, the country had different priorities. It was a reminder that even the most powerful man in the world could be eclipsed by a single Instagram post from a woman in a flowery crown. As one political analyst put it: "Trump commands news cycles. But Beyoncé commands joy." And in the early days of a deeply divisive presidency, joy—pure, uncomplicated, collective joy—was a commodity in short supply. The Queen Bee had done what no politician could: she had made America smile.

title: London 2012 gold medallist Mariya Savinova has been stripped of her 800m title and banned until 2019 after being found guilty of doping.
text_ai: She has had her results from July 2010 to August 2013 annulled but has 45 days to appeal against the decision. title: At least two Palestinians have been killed and 200 wounded in the West Bank during protests against Israel's campaign in Gaza, officials say.

The protests, which erupted after Friday prayers, saw demonstrators waving Palestinian flags and chanting slogans against the Israeli offensive. "We will not stop until the mission is complete," he told a news conference in Tel Aviv. "Hamas bears full responsibility for the suffering of civilians." The UN condemned the attack, calling it a "grave violation" of international law. Israel said it was investigating the incident, but insisted that Hamas militants had been operating near the compound. The Israel-Hamas conflict, now in its 12th day, has become the deadliest in recent years. The Israeli military said it had targeted more than 2,000 sites across Gaza, while Hamas and other militant groups have fired over 1,000 rockets into Israel, reaching as far north as Tel Aviv and Haifa. In the West Bank, protests also took place in Hebron, Nablus and Jenin, with stone-throwing clashes reported. The Palestinian leadership declared a day of mourning for the victims of the shelter attack. "The blood of our people is being spilled in Gaza and the West Bank," said a spokesman for President Abbas. "This is a war crime, and the international community must act." The UN said it had distributed food and water to thousands of families, but warned that the capacity to cope was being stretched. The World Health Organisation reported that at least 125 children had been killed in the conflict, and called for a pause in fighting to allow for medical evacuations. Israel has defended its actions, saying it is targeting Hamas infrastructure and warning civilians to evacuate areas before strikes. "We are doing everything to avoid civilian casualties," said an Israeli military spokesman. "The tragedy of the UN shelter is being investigated thoroughly." Accrington Stanley vs Bradford City** The scene: the Wham Stadium, a modest ground tucked away in East Lancashire, where the home side ply their trade in League Two, the fourth tier of English football. But the visitors travel just down the M65 from West Yorkshire – Bradford City, the team that wrote last season’s most improbable headline. The Bantams are no strangers to giant-killing. Their 4-2 victory at Stamford Bridge last January sent shockwaves through the football world, and they followed it up with a fourth-round win over Sunderland before bowing out to Reading in the quarter-finals. They currently sit third, with a genuine chance of returning to League One at the first attempt. But the FA Cup remains a competition that fires the imagination. "It’s a special kind of magic," Alexander said ahead of the tie. "Our lads know what it feels like to beat a Premier League side. They’ll be up for it again." Accrington Stanley, by contrast, are the ultimate underdog story. Founded in 1968 after the original club folded, they climbed from the Northern Premier League to the Football League in 2006, and have never played in the top flight. Manager John Coleman has been the architect of that rise, and he knows exactly what this tie means to the town. "It’s a cup final for us," he said. "We’re playing against a team that beat Chelsea. But we’re at home, and the lads will run through walls for the badge." Stanley’s form has been patchy this season – they sit 16th in League Two, eight points above the relegation zone. But the FA Cup has a habit of levelling the playing field. Their last fourth-round appearance came in 2018, when they lost 3-1 to Reading. "That day gave us a taste of the big time," added Coleman. "We want more." Bradford will be favourites, but the pressure is on them to deliver. Accrington’s compact pitch and passionate home support could prove decisive. Newport County vs Tottenham Hotspur** Rodney Parade has become something of a fortress for Newport County in recent years, and this tie pits the League Two side against a Tottenham team that is rebuilding under new manager Ruben Amorim. The Portuguese coach has made a solid start since replacing Ange Postecoglou, guiding Spurs back into the top four of the Premier League. "We know Tottenham are a top side, but we’re at home, and the lads will give everything." The Exiles currently sit 15th in League Two, but their home record is impressive – they have lost only three times at Rodney Parade this season. Their cup history includes a famous 2-1 victory over Leicester City in the third round in 2019, and a replay defeat to Manchester City in 2020 that saw them earn a lucrative television slot. Tottenham will likely rotate their squad, with key players like Harry Kane (if he stays) or Son Heung-min possibly rested. But even a second-string Spurs side should have too much quality for Newport on paper. The danger is underestimation. "If we switch off for a moment, they’ll make us pay," said Amorim. "We have to respect the competition and the opponent." The pitch at Rodney Parade is notoriously heavy, used for rugby as well as football. That could slow down Tottenham’s slick passing game, giving Newport a chance to sit deep and counter. The crowd will be loud, the stakes high. Another upset is not out of the question. **3. Plymouth Argyle vs Liverpool** Home Park will be buzzing as Plymouth, currently 14th in the Championship, welcome the Premier League leaders. Liverpool have been in scintillating form under Arne Slot, winning 17 of their 20 league games and looking like genuine title contenders. But the FA Cup has a habit of tripping up the mighty, and Plymouth will sense vulnerability. The Pilgrims have a proud cup tradition. They reached the semi-finals in 1984, and famously beat the top-flight Ipswich Town in 1993. Under manager Wayne Rooney, they have developed a resilient, hard-working identity. "We’re not here just to make up the numbers," Rooney said. "Liverpool are the best team in the country right now, but that’s the challenge. In a one-off game, anything can happen." Plymouth’s form has been mixed – they have won three of their last five, but also lost to lowly Rotherham. Their home form is solid, with only two defeats at Home Park all season. The key will be staying compact and disciplined, while hoping Liverpool’s rotation leaves out Mohamed Salah or Virgil van Dijk. Slot has indicated he will make changes, with the busy Premier League schedule a priority. "We have a strong squad, and everyone needs game time," he said. "But we will not underestimate Plymouth. They have good players and a passionate crowd." Liverpool’s depth is formidable – players like Darwin Núñez, Cody Gakpo and Harvey Elliott would walk into most Premier League sides. But if Plymouth can weather the early storm and keep the game tight, the pressure could mount. Rooney’s side will look to set-pieces and long throws as their main route to goal. **4. Coventry City vs Manchester United** One of the most intriguing ties of the round sees Championship side Coventry City host a Manchester United team still finding its feet under Ruben Amorim’s predecessor, now departed. United are mid-table in the Premier League, 10 points off the top four, and the FA Cup represents their most realistic chance of silverware this season. But Coventry will have other ideas. The Sky Blues reached the semi-finals of the competition last year, famously beating Wolves and Brighton before losing to Manchester United in a penalty shootout at Wembley. That defeat still rankles. "We were that close," said manager Mark Robins. "We want another crack at them, and this time we want to finish the job." Coventry are 10th in the Championship, but their cup pedigree is undeniable. They have a young, energetic squad led by the sharp shooter Viktor Gyökeres, who has attracted interest from Premier League clubs. Robins has instilled a fearless mentality. "We play without fear," he said. "We’ve seen that we can compete with anyone." Manchester United have been inconsistent under their interim management, with defensive frailties and a lack of cutting edge. They scraped past League One Wigan in the third round, needing a late goal from Marcus Rashford to win 2-1. "We have to be better," said the caretaker boss after that game. "Coventry will be a very tough test." The tie will be played at the Coventry Building Society Arena, a venue where United struggled in a 0-0 draw in the third round of the League Cup earlier this season. Coventry’s pressing game and counter-attacking speed could cause problems for a United defence that has conceded 31 goals in 20 Premier League games. If Robins’ men can get revenge, it would be one of the stories of the round. **The wider context** These four ties highlight the enduring magic of the FA Cup. In an era of financial disparity and super-club dominance, the competition still offers the chance for the little guys to write their own headlines. For Accrington, Newport, Plymouth and Coventry, a win would be more than just a result – it would be a moment of pride, a story to tell for generations. Yet the Premier League sides have their own motivations. For Liverpool and Tottenham, a deep cup run is expected; for Manchester United, it might be a lifeline in a disappointing season. And for Bradford, the chance to repeat their heroics of last season is a tantalising prospect. The fourth round always delivers drama. Expect late goals, giant-killings, and tear-jerking celebrations. The FA Cup is alive and well.

title: Around one in 10 UK children in Reception and a fifth of UK children leaving primary school are obese.
text_ai: A Royal Society for Public Health (RSPH) report said healthy eating vouchers and after-school activities could be the answer. But other people who work with parents of overweight children say different measures work better. So what can be done to help prevent or reduce child obesity? The report, published on Tuesday, calls for the expansion of the Healthy Start scheme – which provides vouchers for fruit, vegetables and milk to low-income families – and for all primary schools to offer at least two hours of structured after-school physical activity per week. It also recommends mandatory sugar and salt reduction targets for the food industry, and a ban on junk food advertising before the 9pm watershed. But health visitors and community nurses who work directly with families argue that such top-down measures, while useful, fail to address the root causes of overeating. "Parents know their children should eat less and move more," says Laura Williamson, a senior public health nurse in Leeds. "The problem is that many are living in poverty, in overcrowded housing, with no safe places to play. Telling them to cook from scratch when they have no kitchen, or to take their child to a park that is strewn with needles, is not going to change behaviour." Her view is echoed by Dr. Nadia Kerrigan, a GP in Birmingham with a special interest in childhood obesity. "What we see in clinics is that the children who are obese are often the same ones who are food insecure," she says. "They're eating cheap, calorie-dense food because it's all the family can afford. And they're sedentary because their parents are working multiple jobs and can't supervise outdoor play." The RSPH acknowledges these challenges. Its chief executive, Dr. Fiona Sim, told the BBC: "We are not saying that vouchers and after-school clubs are a magic bullet. But they are evidence-based interventions that can help. We need a whole-system approach, and that includes helping families directly." Yet critics argue that the report places too much emphasis on individual behaviour change and not enough on the structural drivers of obesity. Professor Tim Naughton, a public health expert at the University of Sheffield, says: "The food environment is deeply obesogenic. We live in a world where unhealthy options are cheap, heavily marketed and everywhere. Until we change that environment – through taxation, zoning laws, and reformulation – no amount of vouchers will solve the problem." There is also the question of effectiveness. A 2023 review by the Cochrane Collaboration found that voucher schemes for fruit and vegetables had only a small, short-term impact on dietary intake among low-income families, and little effect on weight. After-school physical activity programmes, meanwhile, often suffer from poor attendance, especially among the most overweight children, who may feel self-conscious or stigmatised. Some practitioners argue for a different approach: one that focuses on the whole family and on building self-esteem. "We don't talk about weight at all," says Maria Gonzalez, who runs a community-based weight management programme for families in Hackney, London. "We talk about feeling good, about playing together, about cooking easy meals. Once parents feel supported and not judged, they start making changes naturally." Her programme, called "Fit Families", combines home visits with group sessions and uses a "health at every size" philosophy. "We've seen children's BMI stabilise or reduce after six months," she says. "But more importantly, their mental health improves. They stop being bullied. They start joining in sports." The government's own data shows that obesity rates in the most deprived areas of England are more than double those in the least deprived. The gap widens as children grow older. By the time they leave primary school, 30% of children in the poorest areas are obese, compared with 13% in the richest. Dr. Simon Wiffen, a consultant paediatrician in Manchester, says that any solution must start before birth. "Maternal obesity, gestational diabetes, and rapid weight gain in infancy all increase the risk of later obesity. We need to support women before and during pregnancy, and then in the early years. That's when the patterns are set." The RSPH report does include a recommendation for mandatory training for health visitors on infant feeding and weaning. But critics say it fails to address the crisis in health visiting services. The number of health visitors in England has fallen by a third since 2015, leaving many families with no support at all. So what might work? International evidence suggests that a combination of policies – a sugar tax, front-of-pack labelling, restrictions on marketing, and improvements in school food – can have a modest but significant impact. In Mexico, a tax on sugary drinks led to a 12% reduction in purchases of taxed beverages after two years. In the UK, the soft drinks industry levy has cut the sugar content of shop-bought soft drinks by nearly 30%. But experts caution that no single intervention is enough. "We need a fundamental shift in how we think about obesity," says Professor Naughton. "It's not a failure of willpower. It's a failure of the environment in which our children are growing up." For now, the RSPH is urging the government to adopt its recommendations as part of the upcoming child obesity strategy, due to be published later this year. "We know what works," says Dr. Sim. "We just need the political will to do it." But as the debate continues, thousands of families across the UK are struggling every day to keep their children healthy in an environment that seems designed to make them ill. For them, the question is not just what can be done, but what will be done – and when.

title: As German Chancellor Angela Merkel is fond of repeating, the EU accounts for just 7% of the world's population and a quarter of its gross domestic product (GDP) but as much as half of its welfare spending.
text_ai: Her underlying message is that Europe spends too much on social policies and thus has no choice but to retrench. Austerity is one reason for cuts, but other threats to the sustainability of the welfare state are more fundamental. They include dealing with an ageing population and adapting to evolving societal expectations. These demographic shifts are not unique to Europe, of course. Japan, South Korea and parts of North America face similar pressure points. But the scale of Europe’s social commitment makes the challenge especially acute. The European Commission projects that, by 2060, the ratio of people aged over 65 to those of working age will rise from about 30% today to over 50% in many member states. That means fewer taxpayers supporting more pensioners and healthcare users. And the cost is staggering: public spending on pensions, healthcare and long-term care already consumes around a quarter of EU GDP. “The welfare state was designed for a different era,” says Prof. Guntram Wolff, director of the Brussels-based think tank Bruegel. “It assumed steady economic growth, a young-ish population and stable family structures. None of those assumptions hold any more.” He points out that the post-war model – built on full male employment, a homemaking spouse and large cohorts of children – has been overtaken by dual-income households, delayed parenthood and rising life expectancy. Yet the underlying architecture of benefits, collective bargaining and state-provided services has not kept pace. The political consequences are being felt across the continent. In France, President Emmanuel Macron’s attempts to raise the retirement age triggered massive street protests, even though the reform was modest by historical standards. In Germany, the coalition government has struggled to agree on a pension reform that would stabilise contribution rates without cutting benefits. And in southern Europe, where informal care by families remains widespread, the formalisation of long-term care is a budgetary headache. But the challenge is not merely financial. Societal expectations have shifted profoundly. Citizens now demand not just income security but also support for childcare, parental leave, lifelong learning and mental health. The COVID-19 pandemic accelerated this trend, exposing gaps in sick pay, job protection and digital access. “People saw that the state could step in with furlough schemes and health spending during the crisis,” notes Dr. Sophia Schönemann, a political economist at the University of Oxford. “Now they expect that level of responsiveness to become permanent. That puts enormous pressure on public finances.” Merkel’s 7% statistic is often used to argue that Europe cannot afford its generosity in a globalised world. But critics counter that the figure is misleading. The EU’s share of global GDP is about 25%, but its share of global welfare spending is higher because it has chosen to prioritise social investment. That choice, they say, reflects a political commitment to equality and social cohesion – values that are under strain but not obsolete. “If you look at the Nordic countries, they spend around 30% of GDP on social protection, and they have some of the highest growth rates and most competitive economies in Europe,” says Schönemann. “It’s not spending per se that is the problem – it’s how you design it. You can have generous welfare states that are also efficient if you invest in early years education, active labour market policies and digitalisation.” Yet the political arithmetic is daunting. Any cut to a popular entitlement – whether pensions, healthcare or unemployment benefits – risks electoral backlash. Meanwhile, raising taxes to fund higher spending is constrained by fears of capital flight, tax competition within the EU and the rise of low-tax jurisdictions like Ireland and the Netherlands. The European fiscal rules, currently under revision, also impose limits that make deficit-financed expansions difficult. The pandemic produced a temporary exception: the EU’s €800bn recovery fund was partly financed by common borrowing. But that was a one-off. The long-term sustainability of the welfare state will ultimately depend on raising productivity growth, increasing labour force participation (especially among women and older workers) and reforming benefit systems to be more targeted and efficient. One emerging idea is a “social investment” model, which redirects resources from passive transfers – like unemployment benefits that simply replace income – towards active measures such as training, childcare subsidies and support for digital skills. This approach has been championed by the European Commission and by countries like Sweden and Denmark. But it requires upfront investment, long time horizons and political will to shift spending away from entrenched groups. Another avenue is greater use of technology. AI-driven automation could reduce costs in healthcare administration, fraud detection and personalised benefit delivery. But it also threatens jobs in routine sectors, potentially increasing demand for welfare support in the short term. Merkel’s warning, then, is not a call to dismantle the welfare state but to redesign it. As she leaves office, the debate she has framed – between European generosity and global competitiveness – remains unresolved. The next generation of leaders will have to reconcile the continent’s social ethos with demographic and economic realities. Whether they can do so without tearing the social fabric remains the defining question of European politics.

title: Kurdish parties say they are planning to declare a new federal system in areas they control in northern Syria.
text_ai: The Kurds already operate "autonomous administrations" in three enclaves bordering Turkey - Afrin and Kobane in Aleppo province and Jazira in Hassakeh. Turkey, which views the PYD as an extension of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) – designated a terrorist group by Ankara, the US and the EU – reacted with particular alarm. "This is an attempt to create a terrorist entity on our border," Turkish Foreign Minister Mevlüt Çavuşoğlu said on Tuesday. "Turkey will never allow a fait accompli in northern Syria." Ankara has already launched two military incursions into northern Syria to prevent Kurdish forces from linking the cantons of Afrin and Kobane, and has threatened further action. However, the US has not condemned the federal plan outright, reflecting its reliance on the SDF, which is dominated by the Kurdish People's Protection Units (YPG), to hold and stabilise former IS territory. Russia, the Syrian government's key ally, has also tread carefully. While Moscow officially supports Syria's territorial unity, it has established working relations with Kurdish authorities in the north. Analysts suggest the Kremlin may use the federal proposal as leverage to pressure both the Assad government and Turkey in future negotiations. The federal system, as outlined by Kurdish officials, would comprise three main cantons – Afrin, Kobane and Jazira – as well as newly liberated areas such as Raqqa and Deir ez-Zour. It would guarantee proportional representation for Arabs, Turkmen, Christians and other minorities. Critics, however, argue that the plan is primarily a Kurdish power grab and that Arab residents of the region are being marginalised. On the ground, the announcement has already generated heated debate. In Qamishli, the de facto Kurdish capital, banners were raised supporting the federal project. But in Raqqa, an Arab-majority city freed from IS last year, residents expressed unease. "We fought together against Daesh, but we do not want to be ruled by the Kurds," said a local tribal leader, using the Arabic acronym for IS. The declaration is unlikely to be recognised by any major power, but it solidifies the Kurds' de facto control and sets the stage for further confrontation with Turkey and the Syrian government. title: Are jetpacks about to move from the realms of fantasy and adventure to serious practical application?
text_ai: A deal between Dubai's civil defence force and New Zealand-based Martin Aircraft suggests that the technology is about to move mainstream. For decades, jetpack fans have predicted a future when we would be using personal power-packs - like James Bond in the 1965 film Thunderball. The deal, announced earlier this week, sees Dubai's civil defence force become the first emergency service in the world to acquire the Martin Jetpack for operational use. The aircraft, which resembles a bulky backpack with two large ducted fans, is designed to lift a single person to altitudes of up to 1,000 metres and reach speeds of 74 km/h (46 mph). Under the agreement, the New Zealand company will deliver 20 units over the next two years, along with comprehensive training for Dubai's firefighters and paramedics. "This is a game-changer for urban search and rescue," said Lieutenant General Rashid Thani Al Matroushi, director of Dubai Civil Defence, at a press conference in the city. "Imagine a high-rise fire where stairwells are blocked. Our crews can now fly directly to the scene, bypassing traffic and debris. It is not science fiction - it is operational reality." His enthusiasm is echoed by Martin Aircraft's chief executive, Dr Mark Taylor, who described the deal as "the tipping point" for a technology that has long been dismissed as a rich man's toy. The company's journey has been anything but straightforward. Founded in 1998 by inventor Glenn Martin, the firm spent years perfecting the jetpack's core technology - a petrol-powered engine driving two high-efficiency fans. Early prototypes were tethered, unstable, and dangerously loud. But after a series of refinements, the latest model - the Martin Jetpack P12 - became the first commercially available personal vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) aircraft to receive regulatory approval in New Zealand in 2016. That milestone, however, did not translate into mass sales. The price tag - $250,000 (£195,000) - put it beyond the reach of most consumers. Instead, Martin Aircraft pivoted towards professional markets. The Dubai deal is its boldest bet yet, but it is not alone. In the United States, JetPack Aviation - founded by British-born David Mayman - has been developing the JB-10, a turbojet-powered pack that can reach 100 mph and fly for 10 minutes. The company recently secured a contract with the US Department of Defense for military evaluation. "The idea of flying soldiers is no longer a dream," Mayman told the BBC. "We are now looking at practical applications in reconnaissance, rapid insertion, and medical evacuation." Yet the path from prototype to everyday use remains fraught with obstacles. Critics point out that jetpacks, by their nature, are noisy, thirsty, and inherently dangerous. The Martin Jetpack's engine produces about 105 decibels - comparable to a chainsaw at full throttle - making it unsuitable for residential areas without ear protection. Its fuel consumption is similarly heavy: a standard flight lasts only 30 minutes, after which the pilot must land and refill a tank of premium unleaded petrol. Safety is the most pressing concern. Unlike a helicopter, which can autorotate to the ground in an engine failure, a jetpack has no built-in glide capability. Martin Aircraft has addressed this with a ballistic parachute system that deploys automatically if the engine cuts out above 50 metres. But below that altitude, the pilot has only seconds to act. "It's not a machine for amateurs," said Dr Michael Lawrence, an aviation safety consultant. "You need hours of training, a cool head, and a very good insurance policy." Regulatory frameworks are also lagging. In most countries, jetpacks fall into an ambiguous legal category - not quite an aircraft, not quite a vehicle. The US Federal Aviation Administration has yet to issue a definitive ruling on their airworthiness, leaving would-be operators in a grey zone. Dubai, with its centralised governance and appetite for futuristic projects, has side-stepped this by granting a specific experimental certificate to its civil defence force. Other jurisdictions may watch closely before following suit. The economics are equally challenging. Even with bulk orders, the Martin Jetpack's unit cost is unlikely to drop below $150,000 in the near term. For comparison, a standard fire engine costs around $500,000, but it can transport a full crew and hose. A jetpack can carry only one person and a small extinguisher. "You have to pick your battles," argued Al Matroushi. "In a high-rise where every second counts, getting one trained firefighter to the 30th floor in 20 seconds is worth the investment." Beyond emergency services, potential applications are emerging. The tourism industry has expressed interest in offering jetpack flights as high-end experiences. Dubai already operates helicopter tours over its artificial islands and skyscrapers; a jetpack ride could be marketed as an even more exclusive adrenaline fix. In agriculture, the packs could be used to inspect crops or herd livestock in rugged terrain. And in construction, they might allow workers to access scaffolding or inspect bridges without cranes. But for now, the technology remains a niche. The Martin Jetpack's 30-minute flight time - about 10 minutes of which is reserve - is insufficient for most commercial tasks. Its weather sensitivity means it cannot fly in strong winds or rain. And the noise problem persists: even muffled prototypes register over 90 decibels, enough to cause hearing damage with prolonged exposure. Nevertheless, the Dubai deal signals a shift in perception. "We're no longer asking 'if' jetpacks will be used," said Dr Taylor. "We're asking 'where' and 'how'." The company has already received inquiries from other Gulf states, as well as from fire services in Australia and Singapore. It is also exploring electric-hybrid versions that could reduce noise and extend range. The vision of a world where commuters strap on jetpacks to avoid traffic jams remains distant. The practical, loud, expensive reality of today's machines is a far cry from the silent, effortless flight of James Bond. But for the firefighters of Dubai - and for the wounded soldiers or stranded climbers they might one day rescue - the fantasy is finally taking off.
