title: John Humphrys revisits Shirebrook in the East Midlands which, 10 years ago, saw the arrival of large numbers of workers from Eastern Europe.
text_ai: For generations immigration to the United Kingdom conjured up images of black and Asian people getting off boats and planes, finding their way to our great cities, setting up home in areas where many thousands of their compatriots were already settled. But the wave of immigration that swept into Shirebrook a decade ago was different. It was white, European, and largely invisible to the national conversation until it arrived in this former mining town in the heart of the Nottinghamshire coalfields. When I first came here ten years ago, the story was about a place in transition — a community that had lost its pits, its purpose, and its people. Now, as I walk the streets again, the transformation is stark, and the questions it raises are as urgent as ever. The first thing you notice is the noise. Not the rumble of coal trains or the clatter of pithead machinery — those have long since fallen silent — but the chatter of a dozen different languages. Polish, Lithuanian, Latvian, Romanian, Slovak. The sound of a new world being built on the ruins of the old. Back in 2004, when the European Union expanded eastwards, few in Whitehall predicted that the influx would be so dramatic. The official forecast was for around 13,000 new arrivals a year from the eight accession countries. Within two years, the actual figure was closer to half a million. And many of them ended up here, in this unassuming market town of around 10,000 souls, drawn by the promise of work at the Sports Direct warehouse on the outskirts. That warehouse is the reason Shirebrook changed. It wasn't a coordinated government policy or a grand migration scheme — it was a jobs marketplace. The company, founded by Mike Ashley, needed workers for its vast distribution centre, and the local labour pool had long since dried up. So the agency recruiters turned to Eastern Europe. And they came. Thousands of them. In the early days, the town wasn't ready. Landlords converted terraced houses into crowded multi-occupancy homes. The local school saw its intake of Polish-speaking children soar from zero to over 200 in just a few years. The pub on the corner, once the heart of the community, became a Polish grocery. The church started offering Mass in Polish. I remember talking to Harold, a retired miner, on my first visit. He sat on a bench opposite the war memorial, watching the new arrivals stream past. "They're not like us," he told me, with a sadness that wasn't anger but loss. "They work all hours, send money home, don't bother with anyone. It's like we've become strangers in our own town." Ten years on, I find Harold waiting on the same bench. He's frailer now, but his eyes still track the passers-by. Does he feel differently? He shrugs. "Some things have got better. The shops are busier. They've opened that Polish bakery — the bread's good, I'll give them that. But it's still not the same. The young people left. My grandson lives in Sheffield. There's nothing for him here." The young Eastern Europeans, however, are building lives. I meet Magda, who arrived from Warsaw ten years ago with nothing but a suitcase and a job offer. She now manages a team of 30 at the warehouse. She owns a house on the main street. She married a local man. Her children speak English with a Nottinghamshire accent. "People still ask me when I'm going back," she says, with a wry smile. "I tell them: I am back. This is my home." But the integration is not seamless. The warehouse operates in shifts around the clock, and many workers, even those who have been here a decade, live in a bubble of colleagues, compatriots, and the familiar comforts of home. The town's B&B — once a hotel for miners' families — is now a Lithuanian social club. The Friday night karaoke features Eastern European pop hits. The local MP, a blunt-spoken former journalist, tells me the story is one of economic necessity meeting demographic reality. "Brexit was not about immigration here — it was about sovereignty," he says, leaning over his desk. "But you can't ignore the fact that many of the people who voted Leave were the ones who felt left behind. They saw their wages stagnate, their housing market distorted, their cultural certainties eroded. Eastern Europeans didn't cause those problems, but they became the visible symbol of change." And change has been rapid. A 2021 census showed that in Shirebrook, the proportion of residents born outside the UK had risen to over 30 per cent, one of the highest in the East Midlands. At the local primary school, the headteacher shows me her enrolment figures. Over half her children now speak English as an additional language. "It's a challenge, but it's also a gift," she says. "We teach tolerance. We celebrate diversity. But I worry about the parents who feel disconnected because they can't communicate. The divide is invisible, but real." She points out that the school has had to adapt: bilingual teaching assistants, translated newsletters, extra English classes. The local library, too, has stocked up on Polish-language books. "Integration takes time," she says. "And you can't force it." The warehouse itself remains the economic engine. I stand outside its vast bulk, a grey behemoth against the flat East Midlands sky. Lorries line up, their cargo destined for every high street in Britain. Inside, the workforce is overwhelmingly Eastern European. The pay is minimum wage, the conditions demanding. Local workers, the manager admits, rarely apply. "The young people don't want this kind of work," he says. "It's repetitive, physical, unsociable. The Eastern Europeans are prepared to do it. That's why we recruit them." But the dependence on migrant labour has created a vulnerability. After the Brexit referendum, there was a surge in applications for settled status, but also a wave of departures. Some families decided they were no longer welcome. Others headed to Germany or the Netherlands, where conditions were better. The warehouse struggled to fill shifts. For a while, the local economy wobbled. Today, the balance has recovered, but the demographics have shifted again. More recent arrivals come from outside the EU, from Nepal, Nigeria, and Pakistan. The language landscape is gentrifying once more. I walk down the high street. The Polish butchers is closed — the owner has retired and his children moved to Warsaw. In its place, a vape shop. The Lithuanian club still thrives, but its regulars are older now. The young parents I see pushing prams are mostly British-born, the children of those first arrivals. They speak with accents that betray no hint of their parents' origins. "I'm English," one young father tells me, when I ask about his identity. "I was born here. I went to school here. I support Nottingham Forest. What else do I need?" Yet the question of belonging lingers. In the local pub — a formerly English establishment that now serves Polish beer — I meet a group of men repairing a tractor. They are from the countryside near Rzeszów, in southern Poland. They work in construction, dairy farming, logistics. They send money home. They spend little. They are polite but wary of my questions. "It's better here than there," one says, in careful English. "But it's not home. Home is where your history is." His friend nods. "We will go back one day. When Ukraine is rebuilt? Who knows." The Ukraine reference is not incidental. The war has reframed the migration debate. The same people who were once caricatured as 'Polish plumbers' or 'Latvian loan sharks' are now hailed as essential workers, their home countries threatened by Russian aggression. Shirebrook has taken in several Ukrainian families. The church has hosted suppers. The school has found places for children. "It's opened some eyes," the headteacher tells me. "People realise that these aren't just workers — they're people with stories, with fears, with hope." As dusk falls, I return to the war memorial. The names etched into the stone are of local men who died in two world wars. At the base, a fresh wreath of red poppies sits in a small metal stand. On the back of the bench, someone has scratched a few words: "All who come here, rest. All who leave, remember." It's in Polish. I ask a passer-by — a woman in her 60s, with a shopping trolley — if she knows who wrote it. She shrugs. "Someone who stayed, I suppose. Or someone who left. It's the same, isn't it? We all want to be remembered." Ten years ago, I asked Harold the miner whether he thought the town would ever feel whole again. He said no. Now I ask him again. He looks at the memorial, at the houses with their illuminated windows, at the distant glow of the warehouse. "It's not broken," he says slowly. "It's just different. And maybe that's all right. You can't stop the world from changing. You can only try to make sure the change isn't cruel." He gets up, holding his stick. "I'm old. I'll be under that stone soon enough. But the town will go on. With them, or without them. I think, in the end, they're part of it now." And perhaps that is the final verdict on Shirebrook, ten years on. A town that once defined itself by its industry and its insularity has been forced to redefine itself by its diversity and its dependence. The immigration has been transformative — economically necessary, culturally challenging, politically divisive, and ultimately, irreversible. The people who came looking for work have stayed, and their children have become as British as the beer and the football. But the scars of the transition remain: the boarded-up shops, the strained public services, the quiet resentment that sometimes still flares in a pub argument or a Facebook post. John Humphrys, for BBC News, in Shirebrook.

title: Aston Villa fans have paid tribute to the club's former striker Dalian Atkinson, who died after being shot with a Taser by police.
text_ai: Supporters held a minute's applause 10 minutes into the club's Championship game against Huddersfield Town. Fans at Villa Park also raised umbrellas around the ground in a tribute inspired by a famous celebration when Atkinson netted a memorable goal against Wimbledon. His death is being investigated. The tribute, orchestrated by the Villa Supporters' Trust and endorsed by the club, saw a sea of umbrellas raised across the Holte End and the Doug Ellis Stand, with many fans holding them aloft for the full duration of the 10th minute mark. The gesture was a direct homage to Atkinson's iconic goal against Wimbledon in October 1992, when he collected a through ball from Dean Saunders, danced past several defenders, and chipped the goalkeeper before celebrating by raising an umbrella that had been thrown onto the pitch by a fan. It remains one of the most celebrated moments in Villa's Premier League history. Atkinson, who was 48, died in the early hours of Monday in the Trench area of Telford, Shropshire, after being Tasered by police. The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has launched an investigation, and three officers from West Mercia Police have been suspended from frontline duties pending the outcome. The force said a 49-year-old man was also arrested on suspicion of assault and criminal damage in connection with the incident, but no further details have been released. The player's family issued a statement through the IOPC, describing him as a "loving father, brother, son and partner" and requesting privacy to grieve. They also thanked the club for "the incredible show of support" and noted that "Dalian would have been humbled by the outpouring of love from the fans he adored." Atkinson's former teammates have also paid tribute. Dean Saunders, who played alongside him in the early 1990s, told BBC Radio 5 Live that "Dalian was a gentle giant off the pitch, but a handful on it. He could score goals that left you speechless." Another former Villa striker, Gary Shaw, added: "He had that raw pace and power, but also the finesse. The Wimbledon goal summed him up – strength, skill, and a touch of showmanship." The circumstances of Atkinson's death remain under scrutiny. West Mercia Police said officers were called to reports of a person "threatening members of the public" but have not confirmed whether a Taser was used as a primary or secondary response. The IOPC is examining body-worn video footage, police logs, and witness accounts. A post-mortem examination is expected to take place later this week. Atkinson began his career at Ipswich Town before moving to Sheffield Wednesday and then Aston Villa in 1991 for a fee of £1.6m – then a club record. He scored 23 goals in 85 appearances for Villa, including a memorable hat-trick against Liverpool in 1993. He later played for Fenerbahçe, Manchester City, and several clubs in Spain and Japan before retiring. His death has reignited debate about the use of Tasers in the UK. The charity INQUEST, which monitors deaths in custody, said it was "deeply concerning" and called for a full public inquiry into "the use of force by police against black people." Atkinson was black, and the incident has drawn comparisons with the death of Mark Duggan in 2011, though there is no suggestion of a direct parallel. Villa manager Dean Smith, who was a youth-team coach at the club when Atkinson was a senior player, said before the match: "Dalian was part of the fabric of Aston Villa. His goal against Wimbledon is etched into the memory of every fan who saw it. The tribute is a fitting way for the Villa family to remember him." During the minute's applause, many fans could be seen wiping away tears. Chants of "There's only one Dalian Atkinson" echoed around the ground. The match itself finished 1-1, with Villa equalising late through a Tammy Abraham goal, but the result seemed secondary. For those inside Villa Park, the evening was about honouring a man who, for a fleeting period, lit up English football. The investigation continues. The IOPC has appealed for any witnesses to come forward, particularly anyone who may have filmed the incident on mobile phones. A final report is likely to take months, but for now, the tributes stand as a testament to the impact Dalian Atkinson had on those who watched him play.

title: MSPs have started to put themselves forward in the contest to become Holyrood's next presiding officer.
text_ai: Labour's Ken Macintosh and Johann Lamont have announced their candidacy for the non-party role, while colleague Elaine Smith is considering a run. The presiding officer is one of the most important roles in the Scottish Parliament, responsible for maintaining order during debates, interpreting standing orders, and representing the institution externally. The position is strictly non-partisan – once elected, the holder must resign their party membership for the duration of their tenure. "The presiding officer must be someone who commands respect across the chamber and who understands the weight of responsibility that comes with the office," she said. "I have never shied away from difficult decisions, and I will apply that same resolve to ensuring fair and effective proceedings." "Many colleagues have encouraged me to put my name forward, and I am giving it serious consideration," she said. However, she declined to reveal a timeline for her decision. "I have presided over some of the most contentious debates in recent years, including the independence referendum bill and the Scotland Act, and I have always done so without fear or favour," he said. He noted the need for a presiding officer who could "command the confidence of all parties" and stressed his own track record of working across the aisle on parliamentary reform. "The parliament has matured over 18 years, and the next presiding officer must reflect that maturity," he said. Other potential candidates are thought to be circling. The Liberal Democrats are expected to field a nominee, though none has yet publicly declared. The Scottish National Party, which holds the largest number of seats in the new parliament, will play a pivotal role in the ballot. Although the party does not officially endorse a candidate – the vote is by secret ballot – the preferences of SNP MSPs are likely to be decisive. Under the election rules, any MSP can stand. The winner must secure a simple majority of votes cast in the first round. If no candidate reaches that threshold, the lowest-placed candidate drops out and subsequent rounds are held until one person secures more than half the votes cast. The process, which usually takes less than an hour, will be overseen by the clerk of the parliament. The new presiding officer will inherit a chamber that has grown in stature and complexity. With the return of powers over income tax and social security to Holyrood, debates have become increasingly technical and, at times, partisan. The incoming holder must also manage the expansion of the parliamentary estate and oversee the introduction of new digital broadcasting systems. The salary for the role is £134,272, an increase of more than £50,000 on the standard MSP salary. The contest is being watched closely by political observers, who note that the presiding officer's neutrality can shape the tone of parliamentary debate. "A weak chair can allow proceedings to descend into rancour," said Dr. Louise Thompson, a politics lecturer at the University of Edinburgh. "A strong chair, by contrast, can keep the legislature focused on scrutiny and legislation." As the deadline for declarations approaches, the candidates are expected to conduct discreet lobbying among their peers. The election itself, which will follow the swearing-in of MSPs, is one of the first major acts of the new parliament. The winner will immediately be required to preside over the selection of a deputy presiding officer – a post for which several MSPs are already positioning themselves. For now, the field is still fluid. But with less than a week to go, the countdown has begun.

title: Little by little, plans are leaking out regarding the imminent battle to remove so-called Islamic State (IS) from Mosul, Iraq's second largest city.
text_ai: Michael Fallon, the UK defence secretary, said military co-operation agreements were finalised on 23 September, adding that "the encirclement operation will begin in the next few weeks" with Mosul being liberated "in the next few months". Michael Fallon, the UK defence secretary, said military co-operation agreements were finalised on 23 September, adding that "the encirclement operation will begin in the next few weeks" with Mosul being liberated "in the next few months". But neither the Iraqi government nor the US-led coalition, which has been bombing IS positions for more than two years, have confirmed any specific date. Officials in Baghdad have instead spoken of a campaign that will unfold in phases, with the initial aim of cutting off the city from its remaining supply routes and tightening the noose around the estimated 3,000 to 5,000 IS fighters believed to be inside. Those fighters, hardened by years of urban warfare and with nothing to lose, have had ample time to prepare. They have dug tunnels, planted booby traps, stockpiled ammunition and built a network of sniper positions, vehicle-borne improvised explosive devices (VBIEDs) and suicide belts. The question is not whether the battle for Mosul will be difficult, but how costly it will be for all sides. The city fell to IS in a lightning advance in June 2014, when a few hundred fighters overwhelmed a demoralised and poorly equipped Iraqi army division. The group's leader, Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, declared his caliphate from the Great Mosque of al-Nuri in Mosul's old city, where he gave a now-famous sermon calling on Muslims to obey him. Since then, the city has been the de facto Iraqi capital of the self-styled caliphate. To lose it would be a devastating symbolic and strategic blow. Iraqi forces have been preparing for this moment for more than a year. They have retaken the cities of Tikrit, Ramadi and Fallujah, each one a stepping stone towards Mosul. But the sheer scale of what lies ahead is daunting. Mosul is the size of a small country, with a pre-war population of around two million. Even after three years of war and a mass exodus, an estimated 1.2 million civilians still live under IS rule. They will be trapped between the militants and the advancing forces, used as human shields and subjected to brutal reprisals if they try to flee. The humanitarian implications are vast. The United Nations has warned that up to one million people could be displaced, triggering a crisis that Iraq's already strained resources are ill-equipped to handle. Camps are being built, supply lines are being laid, but the sheer speed and scale of the exodus could overwhelm the aid effort. The Iraqi government is racing to seal a deal with the autonomous Kurdish region to the north, where many civilians are expected to flee, but relations remain fraught. Politically, the battle is a minefield. The forces converging on Mosul are a loose coalition of convenience: the Iraqi army, the Kurdish Peshmerga, Sunni tribal fighters, Shia militias backed by Iran, and the US-led coalition providing air support and special forces. Each has its own agenda. The Shia paramilitaries, many of whom are accused of abuses against Sunni civilians, have been explicitly excluded from entering the city itself, but they will play a role in the surrounding desert. The involvement of Turkish troops, stationed at a base near Mosul, has infuriated Baghdad, which accuses Ankara of violating Iraqi sovereignty. Turkey insists it is there to protect its own interests, including the ethnic Turkmen population and its border security, but the row threatens to fracture the coalition before the main assault has even begun. Mr Erdogan's announcement of the start date may have been a deliberate attempt to pressure the Iraqi government into accepting Turkey's role, or a simple indiscretion. Either way, it has added to the confusion. Inside Mosul, IS is showing signs of desperation. The group has imposed a nightly curfew, executed suspected informers and banned the use of mobile phones. Reports suggest it is forcing families to hand over teenage sons for military training, and has ordered the execution of anyone found in possession of a SIM card. The group's propaganda machine, once prolific, has become patchy. But the fighters remain fanatical and well-entrenched. The battle plan is said to involve a multi-pronged advance. From the south, Iraqi army units will push up the Tigris valley, retaking towns like Qayyarah and Hammam al-Alil. From the east, Peshmerga forces will secure the Khazir river line and cut the main road to Erbil. From the north, a mix of federal police and army units will approach through the Nineveh plains, an area inhabited by Christians and other minorities who have suffered terribly under IS. From the west, the Syrian border crossings will be sealed to prevent fighters from escaping. The first major test will come in the coming weeks, as Iraqi forces attempt to retake the town of Sharqat, about 100 kilometres south of Mosul. If that falls quickly, momentum will build. But IS is expected to contest every inch, using suicide bombers and roadside bombs to slow the advance. The final phase, once the encirclement is complete, will be the street-by-street clearance of Mosul itself. This is where the most dangerous fighting will occur. US and UK special forces are likely to be embedded with Iraqi units, calling in air strikes and advising on tactics. The Iraqi counter-terrorism service (CTS), an elite unit trained by American and British forces, will lead the charge. CTS commander Lt Gen Abdul Wahab al-Saadi, a veteran of the Fallujah and Ramadi campaigns, has said his men are ready. But the cost will be high. In Ramadi, which fell in February 2016, the battle took months and left entire neighbourhoods in ruins. Fallujah, recaptured in June, was a ghost town. In Mosul, the destruction could be even greater. The city's ancient history, including the tomb of the prophet Jonah and the historic mosque where Baghdadi made his declaration, may not survive. There are also fears that the battle could trigger a wave of attacks in Baghdad and beyond, as IS cells try to divert attention. The group is already under pressure in Syria, where it has lost territory to Kurdish and Russian-backed forces, but it has shown an ability to adapt. For all the planning and preparation, the battle for Mosul remains a high-risk gamble. Victory is not guaranteed, and even if the city is recaptured, the underlying grievances that allowed IS to rise in the first place will remain. Iraq's political system is deeply fractured, its economy is battered and its society is traumatised. The Sunni population, which bore the brunt of IS's brutality but also provided some of its foot soldiers, will need to be reintegrated. The government in Baghdad has promised a post-IS reconciliation process, but trust is scarce. On the ground, the fighting is about to begin. Some 60,000 Iraqi forces, backed by American artillery, British engineers and French armoured vehicles, are poised to move. The US has deployed more than 5,000 troops in support roles, and has built a new air base at Qayyarah, south of Mosul, to provide close air support. UK Tornado jets and Reaper drones are already flying missions over the city. The clock is ticking. The offensive cannot afford to be delayed into winter, when rain and fog would ground aircraft and turn the surrounding plains into a muddy quagmire. October is the month of decision, whether or not Mr Erdogan gave it away. The world is watching. For IS, this will be its Stalingrad. For Iraq, it is a chance to reclaim its future. But the price of that reclamation will be counted not in days or weeks, but in the lives of soldiers and civilians caught in the crossfire. The first indications of how the battle will unfold are likely to come in the next few days, as the encirclement begins. The final outcome, however, will only be known after months of bitter fighting—and then, perhaps, the real work will begin.

title: Whether after four years or eight, all US presidents must eventually confront the question: What happens when I leave the Oval Office?
text_ai: For Barack Obama, the answer was a five-star Caribbean holiday - and a seemingly endless grin. The former commander in chief has been pictured beaming on a beach in a backwards cap, flanked by an equally cheery Michelle. The venue for this masterclass in chilling? a private estate on the Caribbean island of Nevis, owned by billionaire Sir Richard Branson. The Obamas, it seems, have entered the first phase of a transition every occupant of the White House must eventually navigate: the shift from the most powerful person on the planet to a private citizen, a former leader, a memoirist-in-waiting. For some, that transition is a crash course in anticlimax. For others, it is a carefully choreographed glide into a new life of lucrative speaking engagements, charitable foundations, and the occasional bout of public nostalgia. But the gap between the theoretical and the actual can be vast. The Obamas' immediate post-presidential itinerary — a holiday with celebrities, then a move to a new home in Washington DC while their daughter Sasha finishes high school — appears almost defiantly normal. Yet the grinning photos from Nevis also signal a deeper reality: the strenuous effort to reclaim a life that is no longer dictated by the daily threat of nuclear codes or the scrutiny of a 24-hour news cycle. The contrast with other recent exits is instructive. George W Bush famously returned to his Texas ranch to paint portraits of veterans and chop cedar trees, a self-imposed exile from political life that he has maintained with remarkable discipline. Bill Clinton, by contrast, has been a ubiquitous presence on the global lecture circuit and in the world of philanthropy, his foundation a sprawling empire of good works and occasional controversy. For Donald Trump, the question of what happens after the Oval Office remains unusually unresolved. He has refused to concede the 2020 election, promoted baseless claims of fraud, and maintained an iron grip on a large portion of the Republican party. His post-presidency, if it arrives, may be unlike any other — a potential mix of ongoing legal battles, media ventures, and a unique strain of political influence. But the underlying challenge is common to all: how to inhabit the role of "former president" without eclipsing the current one, and without succumbing to the irrelevance that has swallowed many of their predecessors. For much of the 20th century, ex-presidents often faded into a dignified obscurity, writing memoirs in quiet retirement. Herbert Hoover's post-presidential work on famine relief was a rare exception. Then came Jimmy Carter, who redefined the model with his obsessive dedication to international peace negotiations and building homes for the poor. Carter's 40-plus years in the role have set a standard of active citizenship that is both inspiring and daunting to his successors. For Barack Obama, the road ahead is both familiar and new. He and Michelle have signed multi-million dollar book deals with Penguin Random House, and together with Netflix they are producing an array of scripted and unscripted content. The Obama Foundation in Chicago is already planning the construction of his presidential library and a global leadership programme. The intention is clearly to remain a force in public life, but on his own terms — operating at a deliberate remove from the messy day-to-day of Washington politics. Yet the allure of power can be intoxicating, and the exit does not always last. Theodore Roosevelt could not resist returning to the stage in 1912, splitting the Republican vote. Richard Nixon, after his resignation, slowly rebuilt a reputation as an elder statesman of foreign policy. And as his former aides and allies now maneuver for position in a post-Trump era, the current White House occupant has made it unmistakably clear that his exit, if and when it happens, will be far from quiet. For now, the smiling figure on the beach seems to represent a more tranquil model of departure. The questions remain: how long will the holiday last? And when the plane flies back to Washington, what kind of influence will he seek to wield? The answer, as for all who have sat in the Oval, will help define not only his own legacy, but the contours of the office he once held. Because in America, the presidency never truly ends — it just changes shape.

title: More than 1,900 people have now died in West Africa's Ebola outbreak, the World Health Organization (WHO) says.
text_ai: There have been 3,500 confirmed or probable cases in Guinea, Sierra Leone and Liberia. "The outbreaks are racing ahead of the control efforts in these countries," WHO chief Margaret Chan said. The WHO is meeting on Thursday to examine the most promising treatments and to discuss how to fast-track testing and production. The meeting, which the WHO has described as "unprecedented", will bring together virologists, public health officials, and ethicists to weigh the use of experimental drugs that have not been tested in humans. Among the treatments under consideration is ZMapp, the unlicensed drug given to two US aid workers who later recovered. Other potential therapies include convalescent blood products, drawn from Ebola survivors, as well as antiviral drugs and immune-boosting compounds. Ethical questions loom large. "We must ask: under what circumstances is it ethical to use unregistered interventions for Ebola?" Dr Chan said earlier this week. "We must also ask: if we do not use such interventions now, when will we be ready to test them?" The WHO has stressed that any decision must balance the urgency of saving lives with the need to gather robust evidence of safety and efficacy. In a disease with a fatality rate of around 55%, according to the latest WHO figures, the calculus is stark. On the ground, the outbreak continues to spiral. In Liberia, the health system is overwhelmed, with many hospitals closed or functioning at minimal capacity. President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf has declared a state of emergency and imposed a 90-day curfew in some areas. In Sierra Leone, containment zones have been established in the worst-affected districts, but health workers face deep suspicion from communities who sometimes hide the sick or attack aid convoys. Guinea, where the outbreak began in March, has seen a second wave of cases after an initial lull. The WHO has warned that the number of cases could rise to more than 20,000 by November unless urgent action is taken. That projection, published in the New England Journal of Medicine, assumes that current control measures — tracing contacts, isolating patients, safe burials — are significantly scaled up. But those efforts are hampered by a shortage of protective gear, trained personnel, and reliable data. In some areas, only one doctor serves 100,000 people. International response has been slow but is now accelerating. The United States has pledged $12m in aid and sent a team of experts from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The UK has committed to building a 62-bed treatment centre in Sierra Leone and has offered military logistical support. The European Commission has allocated an additional €8m. But aid organisations say more is needed immediately — especially in rural areas where the virus is spreading undetected. The meeting on Thursday is expected to produce a framework for the ethical testing and deployment of experimental therapies. It will also consider the potential for accelerating clinical trials and manufacturing. "We cannot allow this outbreak to continue to spiral out of control," Dr Chan said. "The world must act now."

title: Millions of people in poverty live in UK households where at least one person works, the Living Wage Commission has said.
text_ai: The situation is a "national scandal" says commission chairman Dr John Sentamu, the Archbishop of York. The UK government should aim to cut the number of low paid workers by one million by 2020, the commission said. It recommended that the government should pay its own workers a "living wage". The commission, which is independently chaired by the Archbishop of York, defines the living wage as £7.65 an hour outside London and £8.80 in the capital – higher than the national minimum wage of £6.31 an hour for adults. It has argued that the current minimum wage fails to lift families out of poverty, leaving many working households reliant on tax credits and housing benefit to make ends meet. Dr Sentamu told the BBC’s Today programme that the scale of in-work poverty had reached "unprecedented levels". He said: "It is simply not acceptable that in the fifth richest economy on the planet, hard-working families are forced to choose between heating and eating. We have a moral duty to ensure work pays." More than five million workers earn less than the living wage, according to the commission's analysis of official data. Of these, around one in five is a public sector worker – including hospital cleaners, teaching assistants and administrative staff employed directly by the government or by contractors. The commission’s report, which was published on Monday, calls for a series of measures to be implemented over the next six years. These include: • Raising the minimum wage faster than inflation, with a clear target of reaching 60% of median earnings by 2020 – a level the commission says would effectively deliver a living wage for all. • Requiring all large employers – including the entire public sector – to pay the living wage as a condition of government contracts worth more than £500,000. • Creating a statutory code of practice to ensure that low-paid workers are not exploited through zero-hours contracts or bogus self-employment. • Expanding the role of the Low Pay Commission to monitor and enforce these measures. "The government has a golden opportunity to set a new standard," the report says. "If it pays its own workers a living wage, it will send a powerful signal to the private sector and to the millions of people who work for contractors delivering public services." The Living Wage Commission was established two years ago by a coalition of charities, trade unions and faith groups, including Citizens UK and the Joseph Rowntree Foundation. Its recommendations are not binding, but it has already won support from some large employers, including the bank Barclays, the accountancy firm KPMG, and the London Borough of Islington. However, the business lobby has expressed caution. The British Chambers of Commerce said that while the principle of fair pay was welcome, forcing firms to accelerate wage increases could backfire. "Many small businesses are already struggling with rising costs, and a government-imposed wage floor may lead to fewer jobs, not more," said a spokesman. The Confederation of British Industry (CBI) also urged the government to proceed "carefully", noting that the National Minimum Wage had already helped to lift pay rates for the lowest paid since its introduction in 1999. A Treasury spokesman said the government was "committed to making work pay" and pointed to recent increases in the personal tax allowance, which he said would take a million low earners out of income tax entirely. He added: "The National Minimum Wage has been increased each year by this government, and we have introduced a new system of tax-free childcare and free school meals to help hard-working families." But the commission said such measures were insufficient. "Tax credits and benefits are a sticking plaster," the report argues. "The real solution is to ensure that employment provides a genuine route out of poverty. That means a living wage – not just a minimum one." The think-tank the Resolution Foundation, which has long campaigned for a higher wage floor, welcomed the commission's report. "This is not about a sudden leap to a high-wage economy," said the foundation's chief economist, Matthew Whittaker. "It is about a steady, credible path over the next parliament that ensures no one working full-time is left in poverty." The report also highlights worrying regional disparities. In the South East and London, around one in five workers earns below the living wage. But in the North East and Yorkshire, the proportion rises to nearly one in three. "The geography of low pay reflects deep-rooted economic inequality," Dr Sentamu said. "We cannot allow parts of our country to be permanently left behind." The commission has called on all political parties to commit to the living wage target in their manifestos for the 2015 general election. "This is a test of our national conscience," the Archbishop said. "Will we continue to tolerate a situation where millions go to work every day and still cannot afford the basics of life? Or will we decide that enough is enough, and begin to build a fairer society?" The government is expected to respond formally to the commission's report within the next few weeks. Any decision to mandate a higher wage floor across the public sector would have significant budget implications, with the Treasury estimating the cost of paying a living wage to all directly-employed civil servants alone at around £1.5bn a year. But campaigners argue that the long-term savings from reduced welfare payments would offset much of that cost. "Every pound paid in a living wage is a pound less spent on tax credits," said a spokesman for Citizens UK. "It is not just morally right – it is economically sensible." The debate over the living wage is likely to intensify as the election campaign approaches. For millions of working families, the outcome could determine whether their relentless effort finally rewards them with a decent standard of living – or simply keeps their heads above water.

That is terrifying." Newcastle's hierarchy have so far publicly backed McClaren. Managing director Lee Charnley said last month the club would "give him all the support he needs". But with fans calling for change and the January transfer window approaching, pressure is mounting. Next up is a trip to Liverpool, followed by home games against Aston Villa and West Brom — fixtures that could define the season. Hall warned: "If they don't take something from those matches, it's over. They have to act now."

title: Ofcom is to investigate whether viewers were duped into voting for a stunt dog in the final of Britain's Got Talent.
text_ai: The broadcasting watchdog received 1,150 complaints after trainer Jules O'Dwyer used a second dog to perform a tightrope walk because her Border Collie, Matisse, was afraid of heights. Ofcom said it would examine whether the programme had breached rules on fairness and undue prominence. The controversy erupted after the final of Britain’s Got Talent on 31 May, when Jules O'Dwyer and her dog Matisse were announced winners. However, it emerged during the live broadcast that a second dog, Chase, had performed the vertiginous tightrope walk, while Matisse carried out the simpler parts of the routine. O'Dwyer had mentioned Chase's involvement off-screen during a pre-recorded interview, but viewers were not explicitly told that two animals had been used in the performance. Peter Fincham, director of television at ITV, told the BBC that the omission had been a "regrettable error". "We should have been clearer," he said. "It was an oversight, and we apologise to viewers who felt misled." He added that the production team had considered the matter "a minor detail" at the time. The controversy has raised wider questions about the integrity of voting in talent shows. Ofcom's guidelines state that audiences must not be deceived or unfairly influenced when casting votes. The watchdog has the power to impose fines or require ITV to broadcast an on-air apology if a breach is found. The BBC's media correspondent, David Sillito, said the case highlighted a growing tension between entertainment value and transparency. "In the age of social media, every editing choice is scrutinised," he said. "Producers need to anticipate how audiences will interpret what they see." ITV has already announced that it will review its procedures for future series. Meanwhile, Jules O'Dwyer has defended the use of two dogs, saying it was common to use stunt doubles for certain tricks. "Matisse is the star, but Chase is the specialist," she said. title: When Jose Mourinho walked out of his BBC interview after Wednesday's 0-0 draw with Hull, it was the latest example of a Premier League manager taking exception to a reporter's questions.
text_ai: So what is it like to be the person behind the microphone when an interview goes wrong? We asked reporters from Match of the Day, BBC Radio 5 live and BBC Scotland to share their most excruciating experiences. "We've all been there," says Alastair Bruce-Ball, a veteran sports correspondent for BBC Radio 5 live. "The moment when a manager's eyes narrow, his voice drops, and you know the next sentence is going to be a grenade." Bruce-Ball has conducted thousands of post-match interviews over two decades, but one stands out as the gold standard of awkwardness: a tense encounter with Manchester City's Roberto Mancini after a shock defeat to Sunderland in 2013. "I asked him if his players had let him down. He stared at me for what felt like a full minute. Then he said, 'You ask a question like a child. You don't understand football.' And he walked away. The producer in my ear was silent. The whole press room went quiet. I just stood there holding a microphone that was now broadcasting dead air. It was excruciating, but it's also part of the job. You learn to absorb it." Such moments have become a recurring feature of the Premier League landscape. Jose Mourinho's abrupt departure from his BBC interview after a goalless draw with Hull City on Wednesday was merely the latest entry in a long ledger of manager-reporter confrontations. The Portuguese coach took exception to a question about his team's lack of creativity, muttering "You have your notes, I have my notes" before removing his earpiece and leaving the room. It lasted barely 90 seconds. But what drives a manager to snap? And what is it like to be the reporter on the receiving end? To understand the delicate, often fraught dance between the dugout and the microphone, the BBC spoke to several of its most experienced sports journalists. Their stories paint a picture of a relationship that is part professional, part psychological warfare, and part theatre. **'You could feel the temperature rise'** For Match of the Day's Damian Johnson, the most memorable flashpoint came not in the Premier League but in the Scottish Premiership. In 2017, after Celtic's 2-0 win over Rangers, manager Brendan Rodgers reacted sharply to a line of questioning about his team's performance. "I asked him if he was satisfied with the manner of the victory, given that Rangers had created several chances," Johnson recalls. "He looked at me as if I'd insulted his mother. He said, 'You're always negative, you're always trying to find a problem.' Then he just turned and walked off. The thing is, I'd asked a perfectly reasonable question. But managers are under immense pressure. They've just been through 90 minutes of emotional intensity. Their defences are down." Johnson says the key is not to take it personally. "You're not the target. You're just the nearest available symbol of the media machine that they feel is always circling. But it still stings when it happens live on air." BBC Scotland's Kenny Macintyre has experienced similar treatment from managers across the Scottish game. One particularly vivid memory involves a post-match interview with Hearts manager Craig Levein in 2019. "He was irate about a refereeing decision. I asked him a follow-up question about his team's discipline. He pointed a finger at me and said, 'You're not listening. You're just trying to create a story.' Then he pushed past me. The camera caught it all. My phone rang immediately – the studio wanted to know if I was okay. I was fine, but you feel a bit exposed." **The power dynamic and the 'ever-present threat'** These incidents are not random. They are often calculated, according to sports media analyst Dr. Sarah Clarke of the University of Leicester. "Managers use post-match interviews as a tool to manage narratives, deflect criticism, and send messages to their players or board. Sometimes walking out is a performance – it can rally the fans behind them. But it also reflects a fundamental power imbalance. The manager controls the access, the timing, and the tone. The reporter is there at his or her pleasure." That imbalance can be stark. BBC Radio 5 live's Juliette Ferrington recalls a situation with a Premier League manager – she prefers not to name him – who refused to answer any questions that weren't about the scoreline. "He said, 'I'm only here because the contract says I have to be. Ask me the final result and we're done.' That's the ever-present threat: the interview is a contractual obligation, not a conversation. They can end it at any moment." For some, the pressure is especially acute when the manager is a charismatic figure with a loyal following. "Mourinho is a master of this," says Bruce-Ball. "He knows exactly how to frame the interview as a confrontation. He'll give you a long, theatrical stare, then answer a different question to the one you asked. It's a performance. And the audience loves it. But if you're the reporter, you're trying to do a professional job – to get information for the millions listening at home. You're not there to be part of a show." **'You feel the jaws of the press room tighten'** The walkout is the most dramatic form of rejection, but there are subtler versions. Journalists describe the "silent treatment" – a manager who looks through you as if you don't exist. Or the "monologue" – a manager who launches into a prepared speech and refuses to take a follow-up. BBC Scotland's Jane Lewis experienced a particularly cold shoulder from former Rangers manager Steven Gerrard after a defeat in 2020. "I asked about a tactical change he'd made. He just said, 'No comment.' Then he folded his arms. There was a long, painful silence. I tried another question. Same response. Eventually the press officer stepped in and ended the interview. You feel the whole room tighten. Other journalists are looking at their shoes. Your face is hot. But you have to smile and move on." These moments can be isolating. "It's a lonely place to be," says Ferrington. "You're out there alone, no script, no safety net. And you know that a clip of the exchange will be all over social media within minutes. People will judge your question, your tone, your body language. It's not just the manager you have to handle – it's the court of public opinion." **The backstage reality** Behind the scenes, reporters and broadcasters prepare meticulously for these encounters. They study the manager's recent moods, review past interviews, and rehearse potentially difficult lines of inquiry. They also rely on a largely invisible support network: producers, editors, and legal advisors watching from the gallery. "Before a big interview, I'll speak to the producer about the tone we want to strike," says Johnson. "We'll discuss whether the manager has been prickly lately, whether there's a sensitive issue around injuries or transfers. Our job is to hold them to account, but we also need to keep the channel open. If you ask a question that goes too far, you might lose access entirely." The relationship is a delicate ecosystem. Managers who feel respected are more likely to engage. Those who feel ambushed become defensive. "The best managers – like Pep Guardiola, for instance – are brilliant at giving thoughtful, expansive answers even when they're angry," says Bruce-Ball. "They understand the media's role. But others see it as an adversarial arena. That's when it gets tricky." **The aftermath of a walkout** When a manager walks out, the immediate fallout is logistical. The broadcasters must fill dead air, often by cutting to a pundit or back to the studio. Producers scramble to find alternative content. "We have contingency plans for everything," says Ferrington. "But a walkout still throws you. You've built a whole segment around that interview. Now you have a gaping hole." There are also ethical considerations. Should the network replay the walkout? Should it be discussed in commentary? "We try to be fair," says Johnson. "We'll show the exchange but we'll also explain the context. The audience is smart. They can see if a manager is being unreasonable. But we don't want to sensationalise it. Our job is to report, not to provoke." Sometimes the tension simmers for days. Managers have been known to ignore reporters at subsequent press conferences, or to make pointed remarks about "certain journalists". "You have to develop a thick skin," says Macintyre. "You can't carry a grudge. Next week you'll be standing in the same room asking another question. If you let it get to you, you're done." **The view from the other side** For balance, the BBC also approached several Premier League managers for comment. Most declined to speak on the record, but one – speaking on condition of anonymity – acknowledged the peculiar pressure of the post-match interview. "You've just come off the pitch. Your adrenaline is still pumping. Your mind is processing a result that could cost you your job. And then someone shoves a microphone in your face and asks why you lost. It's not a normal conversation. It's an interrogation. Sometimes you react badly. I've done it. I regret it later. But in the moment, it feels like survival." This perspective does not excuse the walkout, but it does contextualise it. "Managers are human," says Dr. Clarke. "They are often exhausted, emotional, and operating under extreme deadlines. The interview is a pressure valve. Some release that pressure through anger." **The personal toll** For reporters, each encounter leaves a residue. "You replay it in your head for days," says Lewis. "Did I phrase that badly? Could I have been more diplomatic? There's a constant fear of becoming the story yourself – of being known as 'the reporter that Mourinho walked out on'." Bruce-Ball agrees. "You start to second-guess yourself. You wonder if you're being too soft or too aggressive. It's a tightrope. And because the interviews are broadcast live, every word is permanent. You can't take it back." Yet most reporters insist they wouldn't trade the job. "The moment when a manager gives you a genuine, thoughtful answer – that makes up for the walkouts," says Ferrington. "When then you get a bit of insight that helps the audience understand the game better. That's the prize. The rest is just noise." **The broader trend** Is the frequency of manager walkouts increasing? Statistical evidence is anecdotal, but many observers believe the pressure of modern football – with its huge wages, instant scrutiny on social media, and job insecurity – has made managers more combustible. "A decade ago, a walkout was a rarity," says Johnson. "Now it feels like it happens every few months. The stakes are higher. The margins are thinner. And the media landscape is more unforgiving. Managers are constantly under a microscope. They feel every question is a trap." The BBC has repeatedly sought to improve the interview dynamic. Its guidelines encourage reporters to "maintain a professional but respectful tone", and producers are trained to de-escalate tense situations. But there are limits. "We can't control how a manager responds," says a BBC editorial executive. "What we can do is ensure our reporters are equipped to handle whatever comes. We also make sure that viewers understand the context – that this is a high-pressure environment where emotions run high." **What happens next?** For Jose Mourinho, there was no formal reprimand. The BBC declined to comment publicly, though sources suggest the matter was discussed internally. Mourinho himself later joked about the incident at a press conference, saying he had "just needed fresh air". The hullabaloo faded within 48 hours. But the underlying issue remains. The post-match interview is an essential part of football coverage – it is where analysis meets accountability. Yet it is also a zone of unpredictable risk. For reporters, every question carries a potential landmine. For managers, every answer is a potential headline. "It's a weird symbiosis," reflects Bruce-Ball. "They need us to get their message out. We need them to do our job. But sometimes it feels like we're dancing with a scorpion. The trick is to keep dancing without getting stung." As the final whistle blew on another Premier League weekend, the journalists packed up their microphones and headed for the next stadium. The managers retreated to their dressing rooms. And somewhere, in a future press conference, another interview was waiting to go wrong.
prefix: So what is it like to be the person behind the microphone when an interview goes wrong? We asked reporters from Match of the Day, BBC Radio 5 live and BBC Scotland to share their most excruciating experiences.

title: The Welsh medium stream at Brecon High School is to close, Powys council's cabinet has decided.
text_ai: It wants Welsh medium education to be centralised at Builth Wells High School instead but the plan has been strongly opposed by parents worried that pupils face a 40-mile (64km) round trip. The council said pupil numbers had decreased to such a low level that the Welsh medium stream was not viable. The decision, taken at a cabinet meeting on Tuesday, will see the Welsh language unit at Brecon High School phased out over the next two academic years. From September 2025, no new pupils will be admitted to the stream, and the final cohort of learners will complete their studies by summer 2027. Parents, who had campaigned vigorously against the closure, expressed anger and disappointment. "It's a devastating blow for Welsh-speaking families in this area," said Sian Morris, whose daughter is in Year 8. "A 40-mile round trip to Builth Wells every day is simply not feasible for many of us. Some parents are now considering moving their children to schools outside Powys, or even home-schooling." The local authority has defended its decision, arguing that maintaining a separate Welsh medium stream at Brecon High School had become unsustainable. Official figures show that only 32 pupils were enrolled in the stream during the last academic year, down from 58 five years ago. "We have a responsibility to ensure that all learners receive a high-quality education," said Cllr Pete Roberts, Powys County Council's cabinet member for education. "With such low numbers, we cannot justify the resources required to run the stream independently. Centralising provision at Builth Wells High School, where pupil numbers are higher and the Welsh medium curriculum can be delivered more efficiently, is the best option for the future of Welsh language education in the county." Critics, however, argue that the closure contradicts the Welsh Government's ambitious target of creating one million Welsh speakers by 2050. "This is a step backwards," said Dr. Alun Davies, a lecturer in education policy at Aberystwyth University. "Closing Welsh medium provision in a town like Brecon sends a signal that the language is not valued in rural areas. It will make it harder for parents who want their children educated through the medium of Welsh." The council has said it will provide free transport for eligible pupils to Builth Wells, but parents have expressed concerns about journey times, particularly in winter. "The school day starts at 8:45am," said James Jenkins, a father of two. "If the bus leaves at 7:30am from Brecon, that's a very long day for young teenagers. And what about after-school activities? They'll be impossible." Powys County Council acknowledged the strength of feeling but insisted the decision was based on educational and financial viability. "We understand the emotional attachment to the stream," said Cllr Roberts. "But we believe that by concentrating resources, we can offer a more robust Welsh medium curriculum at Builth Wells, with better progression opportunities for pupils." The impact on primary school provision in the area remains unclear. The Welsh medium stream at Brecon High School drew pupils from nearby primary schools, including Ysgol y Bannau in Brecon itself. Some parents have started a petition calling on the Welsh Government to intervene, arguing that the closure threatens the viability of Welsh medium education across the whole of south Powys. A spokesperson for the Welsh Government said it was "aware of the concerns" and would be "monitoring the situation closely". They added that the decision was a matter for the local authority, but stressed the importance of protecting Welsh language education in rural areas. As the school year draws to a close, the atmosphere at Brecon High School is sombre. For pupils like Llywelyn Jones, 14, the news has been unsettling. "I've been in this stream since Year 7," he said. "All my friends are here. I don't want to travel all the way to Builth Wells. I might just switch to English medium." The council has promised to work with affected families to ensure a smooth transition, but for many, the damage has already been done. The decision marks the end of an era for Welsh medium education in Brecon, and raises questions about the future of the language in the county's more rural communities.

title: The Met Police has been ordered to pay £400,000 in legal costs after it "unreasonably" used a Taser on a man.
text_ai: Daniel Sylvester, 53, was stopped three times in nine months by police. On the second time occasion, when Mr Sylvester was near his home in Edmonton Green, police used a Taser, sending him falling to the ground in agony. Judge Karen Rimmer, sitting at the Central London County Court, ruled that officers had used "disproportionate and unreasonable force" when they deployed the 50,000-volt weapon against Mr Sylvester in February 2021. She criticised the officers for failing to de-escalate the situation or consider less intrusive alternatives, despite Mr Sylvester posing no immediate threat. The court heard that Mr Sylvester, who has a diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia, was walking home from a local shop when officers stopped him under Section 60 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act, which allows police to search individuals in a defined area without reasonable suspicion. Body-worn camera footage showed Mr Sylvester complying with verbal commands but becoming confused and agitated as officers surrounded him. Within seconds of the stop, an officer fired the Taser, causing Mr Sylvester to collapse onto the pavement, striking his head. Mr Sylvester's lawyers argued that the use of force was "wholly unnecessary" and that officers had been aware of his mental health condition from previous interactions. In the first stop, just months earlier, police had detained him under the Mental Health Act but released him without charge. The third stop, in September 2021, also resulted in no further action. The Met Police initially denied liability, claiming officers believed Mr Sylvester was reaching for a weapon. However, Judge Rimmer found that the officers' account was "not credible" and that the Taser had been used as a "default option" rather than a last resort. Following the ruling, the Met confirmed it would pay the £400,000 in legal costs, which includes Mr Sylvester's own legal fees and disbursements. A spokesperson said the force "accepts the judgment" and has "apologised to Mr Sylvester for the distress caused". They added that officers are now undertaking mandatory training on de-escalation and mental health awareness. Mr Sylvester's solicitor, Sarah Walker of the law firm Hodge Jones & Allen, said the case highlighted "systemic failings" within the Met's use of Tasers. "Our client was a vulnerable man in a mental health crisis who needed care, not a 50,000-volt shock," she said. "This judgment sends a clear message that excessive force will not be tolerated." The case is the latest in a series of rulings against the Met for inappropriate Taser use. Last year, the force paid £300,000 in damages to a 14-year-old boy who was Tasered during a stop-and-search. Critics have repeatedly called for greater accountability, with the Independent Office for Police Conduct currently reviewing the Met's Taser policy. Mr Sylvester said he continues to suffer from flashbacks and anxiety. "I was just trying to get home," he said. "I don't feel safe in my own street anymore." The Met has agreed to review its deployments of Section 60 powers in Edmonton Green, where stop-and-search rates have risen sharply in recent years.

title: The company behind the proposed Wylfa Newydd nuclear power station on Anglesey has launched its second formal public consultation.
text_ai: People have until 25 October to respond to Horizon Nuclear Power's refined plans. The proposals will be on display at a series of exhibitions across north Wales. The company said the project will bring significant investment to the island. The company said the station would create up to 9,000 construction jobs and 850 permanent roles once operational, and generate enough low-carbon electricity to power around 1.5 million homes. The consultation, which runs until 25 October, will examine a range of revised proposals, including changes to the cooling water intake system, the layout of the main plant buildings, and the transport of materials during construction. Exhibitions are planned in Holyhead, Llangefni, Bangor, Caernarfon, and Wrexham, with virtual sessions also available online. Horizon said these events would allow residents to scrutinise detailed plans and ask questions directly to project engineers. "We want to hear from as many people as possible," the company's head of external affairs told BBC Wales. "The feedback we received in our first consultation has shaped these refined designs, and this is an opportunity for the community to have their say again." But opposition groups have voiced concerns. PAWB (People Against Wylfa B) said the new proposals were "insufficiently different" from earlier schemes, and accused Horizon of ignoring longstanding fears over nuclear waste and emergency planning. A spokesperson for the group said: "This is a multibillion-pound project on a vulnerable coastline – the risks are immense, and local people must not be railroaded into acceptance." The Welsh Government has not yet taken a formal position, but its energy spokesman said any new nuclear development must meet "the highest safety, environmental, and waste management standards." The UK Government, which has set a target for up to 24 gigawatts of nuclear capacity by 2050, has previously backed the Wylfa site as a priority location for new reactors. Horizon's plans remain subject to a development consent order from the Planning Inspectorate, following which a final investment decision would be made. Construction is not expected to begin before 2027, with first power generation possible in the mid-2030s if approvals are granted. The company has emphasised that the project would bring an estimated £4bn economic boost to Anglesey and the wider region over its lifetime. The consultation runs alongside a separate process for the proposed grid connection, which could involve new overhead lines and substations. Horizon says it will publish a final summary of consultation responses by the end of the year, with an updated application expected in 2025.

title: More than 30,000 non-EU students a year have had their visas curtailed by the Home Office in the past three years, figures obtained by BBC News show.
text_ai: And 410 educational establishments had their licences to sponsor international students revoked in the same period. The Home Office said it was cracking down on immigration abuse. But the National Union of Students said international students were being "scapegoated" in order to meet targets on net migration. The figures, obtained through a Freedom of Information request, reveal that between 2021 and 2024, a total of 92,507 non-EU student visas were curtailed – an average of more than 30,800 per year. A visa curtailment means a student's permission to stay in the UK is cut short, often because they have stopped studying, failed to attend classes, or breached the terms of their stay. The Home Office stressed that the vast majority of international students comply with the rules, but said enforcement action was essential to maintain the integrity of the immigration system. "We are taking decisive action to tackle those who seek to abuse the student visa route," a spokesperson said. "Curtailments are applied where individuals fail to meet the conditions of their visa, and revoking licences prevents rogue institutions from bringing in students under false pretences." The scale of the action has alarmed the higher education sector. Universities UK, which represents 141 institutions, said it was "concerned" by the number of curtailments, adding that many students may have been caught up in administrative errors or changes to course availability. "International students contribute £42bn to the UK economy each year," a spokesperson said. "It is vital that enforcement is proportionate and does not damage the UK's reputation as a welcoming destination for study." The number of sponsor licences revoked – 410 over three years – points to a major clampdown on so-called "bogus colleges". Many of these institutions, often operating from small premises, were found to have little or no genuine teaching activity. The Home Office said it had stepped up inspections and intelligence-led operations to identify such cases. In some instances, students at revoked colleges were given 60 days to find a new sponsor or leave the country. The National Union of Students (NUS) accused the government of using international students as a "political football". NUS president Martha McKenzie said: "These figures show a relentless focus on enforcement against students, rather than on the systemic failures that push them into vulnerability. International students are not the cause of our housing crisis or pressure on public services – they are being scapegoated to hit arbitrary net migration targets." The government has faced sustained political pressure to reduce overall net migration, which reached a record 745,000 in 2022. In January 2024, the then-Conservative government introduced a ban on most overseas students bringing dependants, a policy that the new Labour government has maintained. The Home Office has said the curtailment figures partly reflect this tougher stance, as students bringing family members were already subject to additional scrutiny. But critics argue the data reveals a system that is both punitive and confusing. Lawyers representing affected students report cases where curtailment notices were sent to wrong addresses, or where students were penalised for minor administrative delays. "Some students receive a curtailment letter months after they have already left the UK, unaware they have been flagged," said migration solicitor Ayesha Khan. "The process lacks transparency and can derail careers." The impact on individual students can be severe. Losing a visa can mean having to abandon courses, forfeiting tuition fees, and facing a re-entry ban. Many are from countries such as India, Nigeria and Pakistan, where studying abroad is seen as a major investment. One student from Nigeria, who did not wish to be named, told BBC News he had his visa curtailed after his university reported him for missing several lectures due to illness. He said he provided medical evidence but his appeal was rejected. The Home Office said all curtailment decisions were made on a case-by-case basis and that students had a right to request an administrative review. It added that the total number of sponsor licences revoked represented a small fraction of the more than 2,000 institutions approved to sponsor international students. The data has reignited debate over the purpose of the student visa system. While the government insists it is committed to attracting "the brightest and the best", the figures suggest enforcement has been prioritised. Labour has promised a "fair and humane" immigration system, but has declined to scrap the dependant ban or review the curtailment process. Universities warn that the continued crackdown could deter international applicants. Early data for 2024 shows a significant drop in visa applications from some key markets. The Home Office said it would continue to monitor the situation and adjust policy where necessary.

title: The UK government borrowed £25.6bn in the three months to the end of June, £2.3bn less than it did during the same period last year, and the lowest level since 2008.
text_ai: However the total amount owed continued to rise, reaching £1,621bn. That amounts to 84% of the value generated by the UK economy - otherwise known as gross domestic product (GDP). The measurement, which includes some forecasting, does not reflect the impact of the Brexit vote on 23 June. The better-than-expected figure was driven by a £1.5bn fall in central government spending, partly linked to lower debt interest payments. But economists cautioned that the data, published by the Office for National Statistics (ONS), was compiled before the full economic effects of the referendum could be measured. "While these numbers show a modest improvement, they reflect a period before the Brexit vote," said Samuel Tombs, chief UK economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics. "The real test will come in the coming months, when we see how business confidence and tax receipts respond to the uncertainty." The ONS noted that the deficit for the first quarter of the financial year – April to June – stood at £25.6bn, compared with £27.9bn in the same period last year. This represents the lowest borrowing for that quarter since 2008, when the financial crisis pushed the deficit sharply higher. However, the overall debt pile remains stubbornly large at £1,621bn, equivalent to 84% of GDP. That ratio is higher than in many comparable economies, and well above the 60% ceiling once considered prudent by international standards. The government's own fiscal watchdog, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), had forecast borrowing of £55.5bn for the full 2016-17 financial year. But that forecast was made before the referendum, and many analysts now expect it to be revised upward as the economic slowdown predicted by the Treasury begins to materialise. Chancellor Philip Hammond, in his first major economic statement since taking office last month, acknowledged that the UK faced "challenging times ahead". He insisted the government would continue to pursue fiscal discipline, but stopped short of repeating the previous administration's target of running a surplus by 2020. "The British people voted to leave the European Union, and we must respect that decision," Hammond said. "Our job now is to deliver the best possible deal for the UK and to ensure our economy remains resilient." Labour's shadow chancellor, John McDonnell, accused the government of "sleepwalking into a self-inflicted recession" and called for more investment to stimulate growth. "These figures show that the deficit is falling, but only because the economy was already slowing before the referendum," he said. "The Tories' austerity agenda is failing, and working people are paying the price." The ONS data also revealed that tax receipts rose by 2.8% in the first quarter, helped by a strong performance in income tax and corporation tax. But VAT receipts were flat, suggesting consumer spending may have softened ahead of the referendum. Separately, the UK's trade deficit widened in May, with exports to the EU falling by 9% compared with the same month last year. That has raised concerns that the uncertainty over Britain's future trading relationships is already damaging export performance. Looking ahead, the Bank of England is widely expected to cut interest rates from their current historic low of 0.5% when it announces its latest policy decision next week. title: Two men have been sentenced to three-and-a-half years for imprisoning a man who was found naked and battered in a taped-up wheelie bin in Ballymena.
text_ai: Teri Lau, 28, of Dunclug Park, and Roddy Patterson, 28, of Glendun Drive, Ballymena, had pleaded guilty to actual bodily harm and false imprisonment. They will serve half their sentences in custody and the rest on licence. Paula Wilson, 22, of Main Street, Cullybackey, was sentenced to two years, half to be spent on licence. The judge, Mr Justice Colton, described the attack on the 34-year-old victim as a “brutal and degrading ordeal” that had left him with lasting psychological scars. Speaking at Antrim Crown Court, the judge said the victim had been subjected to a “prolonged and cowardly assault” before being sealed inside the wheelie bin, where he was discovered by a passer-by in the early hours of 22 August last year. The court heard that the victim, who cannot be named for legal reasons, had been lured to a house in Ballymena under the pretence of a social gathering. Once inside, he was attacked by the three defendants, who punched and kicked him repeatedly, causing extensive bruising and a broken nose. They then forced him into the wheelie bin, taping the lid shut with industrial-strength tape, before abandoning the bin in a lane off Dunclug Park. Prosecution barrister David Russell told the court that the victim managed to escape only when a member of the public heard his cries for help and alerted the police. Officers arriving at the scene described the victim as “shocked and terrified”, with bin tape still wrapped around his ankles and wrists. He was taken to hospital for treatment and later discharged. The court was told the motivation for the attack stemmed from a long-standing feud between the victim and Lau, who had accused him of stealing from her. Defence barristers for all three defendants said their clients had expressed genuine remorse and had entered early guilty pleas, sparing the victim the ordeal of a trial. In his sentencing remarks, Mr Justice Colton said the offences crossed the threshold for immediate custody. “This was a deliberate and calculated act of violence, carried out with a callous disregard for the victim’s dignity and wellbeing,” he said. “The use of the wheelie bin to confine him added a particularly sinister element to an already appalling attack.” Detective Sergeant Peter Corscadden of the Police Service of Northern Ireland welcomed the sentences, saying the victim had shown “remarkable courage” throughout the investigation. He added: “This was a horrific incident that has had a profound impact on the victim and the wider community. We hope today’s outcome provides some measure of closure and serves as a deterrent to others.” None of the defendants made any visible reaction as the sentences were passed. Lau and Patterson were each handed three-and-a-half years, while Wilson received two years. All three will serve half their sentences in custody and the remainder on licence, meaning they could be released within months if granted parole. The victim, who was not present in court, has since moved out of the Ballymena area, police confirmed.
