title: The International Olympic Committee has begun an investigation into claims Olympics representatives were willing to sell thousands of tickets for the London Games on the black market.
text_ai: The IOC's ruling executive board met after fresh claims by the Sunday Times involving more than 50 countries. Tickets for top events were said to be priced at up to 10 times face value. A UK member of the board, Sir Craig Reedie, said the IOC would consider improvements to ticket sales systems. The Sunday Times investigation, which lasted several months, involved reporters posing as middlemen offering to re-sell tickets on the black market for inflated prices. In a series of undercover meetings and phone calls, they were allegedly told by Olympic officials from more than 50 countries that high-demand tickets – including those for the 100m final, the opening ceremony and gymnastics – could be obtained for sums far above their official face value. One official from an unnamed European Olympic committee was recorded saying that tickets for the men’s 100m final could be sold for £6,000 – more than 10 times the top official price of £450. The newspaper’s investigation has sent shockwaves through the Olympic movement, coming just months after the London 2012 organising committee (Locog) promised a crackdown on touting and pledged that tickets would be distributed fairly. The IOC said its ethics commission would examine the evidence and report back to the executive board within the next few weeks. A spokesman said: “The IOC can confirm that it has received the Sunday Times’ evidence and has begun a full investigation. Any breach of the Olympic charter or of the IOC’s code of ethics will be dealt with severely.” Sir Craig Reedie, the IOC’s senior British member, said the board had discussed the issue at length during its emergency meeting in Lausanne. “We are very conscious of the reputational damage such allegations could cause,” he said. “The IOC has a robust system for ticket sales, but if there are weaknesses they will be addressed. We are not complacent.” He added that the board had instructed its administration to review the current distribution model, which allocates tickets to national Olympic committees (NOCs) for their own domestic sale and use. Locog, which is responsible for selling 8.8 million tickets for the Games, expressed concern but stressed that its own sales programme was not directly implicated. A Locog spokeswoman said: “We have a strict zero-tolerance policy on touting. Any tickets obtained through authorised channels must be used in accordance with our terms and conditions. We will co-operate fully with the IOC investigation.” The government, which has invested heavily in Games security and infrastructure, also weighed in. The culture secretary, Jeremy Hunt, called for “complete transparency” and said the allegations, if proven, would be “very damaging to the integrity of the Olympics”. The stakes are high. London 2012 is the most commercialised Olympic Games in history, with sponsorship and broadcasting deals worth billions of pounds. A black market in tickets not only fuels criminal activity – touting is illegal in the UK for Olympic and Paralympic events – but undermines public trust. “The idea that officials entrusted with distributing tickets are willing to line their own pockets is deeply troubling,” said Lord Moynihan, the chairman of the British Olympic Association. “We welcome the IOC investigation and hope it leads to swift action.” Several of the countries named in the Sunday Times report have already issued denials. Russia’s Olympic committee said it “categorically rejects” any suggestion of wrongdoing, while the Greek committee said it had “strict internal rules” and would investigate its own staff. The IOC stressed that the investigation would examine the role of individual officials, not just the NOCs themselves. “If individuals have broken the rules, they will face sanctions, up to and including lifetime bans from the Olympic movement,” the spokesman said. The scandal has also revived debate about the allocation of tickets for major sporting events. Many Olympic tickets are never available to the general public: a significant portion go to sponsors, broadcasters, the Olympic family and NOCs. In 2011, Locog’s first-round random ballot was overwhelmed by demand, with more than 20 million applications for fewer than 7 million tickets. The subsequent “sold out” signs on many events were followed by a second round that saw some tickets appear – and critics argued that the system was opaque. “The current system is not fit for purpose,” said Michael Brown, a sports marketing professor at the University of London. “It creates a two-tier market: one for the public, who face a lottery and high prices, and another for insiders who can bypass the official channels. The IOC needs to look at making the entire process more transparent and accountable.” The IOC has already taken steps to improve ticket sales since the debacle of the 2010 Winter Olympics in Vancouver, where empty seats marred high-profile events. At London 2012, it introduced a real-time ticket resale platform and stricter identity checks, but the Sunday Times investigation suggests that loopholes remain. The integrity of the Olympic brand is paramount for the IOC, which relies on goodwill and public enthusiasm to attract sponsors and broadcasters. The scandal – which the Sunday Times has dubbed “ticket-gate” – threatens to tarnish that image. “If these allegations are true, it suggests a culture of entitlement within some NOCs that is completely at odds with the Olympic values,” said David Bond, the BBC’s sports editor. “The IOC’s response will be closely watched not just by the British public but by the entire international community.” The executive board is expected to set a deadline for the investigation’s findings at its next meeting in July. Meanwhile, Locog continues to sell remaining tickets through official channels and has promised that any seats returned by NOCs will be put back on sale to the public. But for many, the damage may already be done. “The Olympics are supposed to be the pinnacle of fair play,” said one frustrated Londoner who missed out on tickets in the ballot. “If officials are making a profit on the black market, it makes a mockery of that.”

A UK member of the board, Sir Craig Reedie, said the IOC would consider improvements to ticket sales systems.

title: On a farm so parched that it looks like a desert, Monica Amaraki reaches for an old brass tap only to find that no water flows from it.
text_ai: Here in Namibia in southern Africa, a drought is intensifying, the soil has been turned into dust and animals are scouring the baked land for something to eat. Monica's village, Omagongati, is in the far north of the country, a region notorious for extremes of weather, but she says that the dry spell hitting her now has been longer and more severe than normal. The landscape around her is a palette of browns and greys. Where maize and millet once stood in sturdy rows, there is now only cracked earth, the fissures deep enough to trap a child’s foot. The riverbed that runs past Omagongati has been dry for months. Monica, 47, has lived here all her life, and she has never seen it like this. “The rains used to come in October,” she says, wiping dust from her forehead with the back of her hand. “Now they come in December – if they come at all. And when they do, it’s a storm that washes away the topsoil and leaves nothing behind.” She is not alone. Across Namibia, more than half a million people are facing acute food insecurity, according to the latest Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) report. The government declared a national drought emergency in May, and the United Nations has appealed for $20m (£15.7m) in emergency aid. But for families like Monica’s, the aid is slow to arrive, and the land offers nothing. The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (Fews Net) describes the current conditions as “exceptional” – a word scientists use sparingly. Namibia is no stranger to drought. It is the driest country in sub-Saharan Africa, with an average annual rainfall of less than 300mm. But what is happening now is different. The drought that began in late 2023 has been compounded by a strong El Niño weather pattern and what climate scientists call a “triple-dip” La Niña that has shifted rainfall away from the region. “This is not just a bad year,” says Dr Helena Mwanyangapo, a climatologist at the University of Namibia in Windhoek. “We are seeing a structural shift. The rainy season is shortening and becoming more erratic. The dry spells are longer. The ground is losing its ability to recover.” Monica’s tap is a symbol of a deeper crisis. The water table beneath Omagongati has fallen so low that even the boreholes are failing. Some households dig wells 30m deep – and still strike nothing but dust. Women in the village now walk 10km each day to a single functioning tap run by a community water point, carrying yellow jerrycans on their heads. The water they bring back is brackish, and it makes children ill. “The children have diarrhoea,” Monica says quietly. “We try to boil it, but there is no firewood. All the trees are dead. We burn the roots of the bushes, but it’s not enough.” Her livestock have been decimated. She used to own 50 goats. Now she has eight. The cattle are gone – sold for a fraction of their value before they starved. One of her cows collapsed and died in the field two weeks ago. She could not even muster the energy to bury it. “The vultures came,” she says, her voice flat. “That is nature. But nature is turning against us.” The impact is not only agricultural. Schools in the region have seen attendance drop sharply. Children are too weak to walk the long distances, or they are needed at home to help care for younger siblings while parents search for water. The local clinic in Omagongati reports a surge in malnutrition cases among children under five. The nurse, a young woman named Beata, tells me she has seen more cases of severe acute malnutrition in the past six months than in the previous three years combined. “We have therapeutic food sachets, but they are meant to be a short-term fix,” Beata says. “These children need a sustained diet of protein and vitamins. That means milk, eggs, vegetables. All of that comes from farming. And farming has stopped.” The government has stepped in with emergency feeding programmes and water trucking, but the scale of the need is overwhelming. For every village that receives a water tanker, three others go without. The trucks themselves are struggling – many break down on the washed-out roads, and drivers are reluctant to travel deep into rural areas where they might be mobbed by desperate crowds. “We are doing everything we can,” says Ngenisa Mbuende, deputy director of the Department of Water Affairs in the Omusati Region. “But the demand is outstripping our capacity. The aquifer is being drained at an unsustainable rate. We are essentially mining water that took thousands of years to accumulate.” Climate models suggest that southern Africa will become hotter and drier in the coming decades. A 2023 report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) predicted that extreme droughts in the region could become twice as frequent by 2050, even if global emissions are curbed. For Namibia, that would mean a future where the current crisis is not an anomaly, but a baseline. “We are in the early stages of a climate-change-driven disaster,” says Dr Mwanyangapo. “It is not that we did not see it coming. We did. But the speed at which the thresholds are being breached has taken us by surprise.” Back in Omagongati, Monica Amaraki is preparing for the worst. She has emptied her savings to buy a 200-litre drum of water from a private supplier in the nearest town, 50km away. The water cost her 300 Namibian dollars – about £13 – a fortune when she has no income. She uses it sparingly: a cup for drinking, a splash for washing, and nothing for her small plot of vegetables, which has long since withered. “I have no seeds for next season,” she says, staring at the empty brass tap. “I have no water. I have no hope. But I cannot leave. This is my land. If I leave, who will return?” As the sun sets, the temperature drops sharply. The sky is clear, the air dry. In the distance, a dust devil whirls across the parched plain, lifting red earth into the fading light. Monica watches it, then turns and walks slowly back to her hut, the brass tap still dripping nothing behind her.

title: Manchester United are "suffering" after six matches in 18 days, said boss Louis van Gaal following his side's 2-1 Champions League win over Wolfsburg.
text_ai: Juan Mata's first-half penalty and Chris Smalling's 53rd-minute goal gave United their first Group B victory. The Premier League leaders, who visit Arsenal on Sunday, had to hold on as Wolfsburg pressed for an equaliser. "It is difficult with so many matches in such a short period," Van Gaal told BBC Sport. "The players are suffering, but we have to recover for Sunday. That is the most important thing now." United's victory was far from convincing. Wolfsburg created several clear chances, with Naldo heading against the crossbar before the break and Julian Draxler forcing a fine save from David De Gea early in the second half. Van Gaal's side were forced to defend deep in the closing stages as the German side pushed for an equaliser. The visitors' pressure intensified after Daniel Caligiuri's 90th-minute header was ruled out for offside. "We had a lot of luck, I have to be honest," Van Gaal admitted. "But in this competition, you need that sometimes. It is about getting the result, and we have that." The victory lifts United to second in Group B, three points behind leaders PSV Eindhoven, who beat CSKA Moscow 3-1. The Dutch side's win means United are level on points with Wolfsburg, with three games remaining. Van Gaal's decision to start with Wayne Rooney on the bench raised eyebrows, with the United captain introduced only after 68 minutes. The manager defended his call, saying: "Wayne has played many minutes recently. I have to manage the squad, especially with Arsenal coming up." United now face a daunting trip to the Emirates on Sunday, where they will aim to extend their four-point lead at the top of the Premier League. Van Gaal acknowledged the challenge: "Arsenal are in great form. But we are top of the league, so we must believe we can get a result." The win was United's fourth in a row in all competitions, although their performance levels have been questioned. Van Gaal dismissed the criticism: "You cannot play well every game. Sometimes you have to dig in and show character. My players did that tonight."

title: New analysis by consultancy firm PwC has added further weight to evidence that the Scottish economic recovery is gathering momentum.
text_ai: Its latest report on the UK's economic outlook has forecast Scottish economic growth will pick up from 1.6% in 2013 to about 2.8% this year. The figure for 2014 was revised up from the 2.4% projected by PwC in March. The revised figure is slightly higher than that forecast in June by the Fraser of Allander Institute. The report, published on Thursday, highlights a broadening of Scotland's economic recovery beyond its traditional strongholds in oil and gas and financial services. PwC's analysis points to robust growth in the professional services, tourism, and creative industries sectors, which are now contributing significantly to domestic output. This diversification, the consultancy argues, is making the Scottish economy more resilient to external shocks, such as fluctuations in global energy prices or geopolitical tensions in the Middle East. Employment figures underpin this optimism. Scotland's unemployment rate has fallen to 5.8%, its lowest level since the 2008 financial crisis, and is now marginally below the UK average. The number of people in work has risen by 1.4% over the past year, with full-time positions accounting for the bulk of the increase. "This is not just a story of jobs being created, but of better-quality jobs," said John Hawksworth, PwC's chief economist. "We are seeing a shift towards higher-skilled, higher-paid roles, particularly in Edinburgh and Glasgow's technology hubs." However, the report also cautions that challenges remain. Scottish business investment, while recovering, is still 15% below its pre-recession peak. The housing market, particularly in rural and island communities, shows signs of stagnation, with average prices rising by only 1.2% annually compared with 3.5% in London and the South East. And inflation, at 2.1%, is eroding household purchasing power, although wage growth is beginning to outpace price rises in some sectors. The PwC forecast comes amid an intensifying debate over Scotland's constitutional future. Proponents of independence argue that a stronger Scottish economy would benefit from full control over taxation and spending. Critics counter that the recovery is partly driven by UK-wide factors, such as low interest rates and government infrastructure spending. A Scottish Government spokesperson welcomed the report, calling it "further evidence that our economic policies are bearing fruit," but stressed that "more powers are needed to build a fairer and more prosperous Scotland." Looking ahead, PwC expects Scottish GDP growth to moderate slightly to 2.5% in 2015, before rising to 2.7% in 2016, reflecting the cyclical nature of the recovery. Key risks include a potential slowdown in China's economy, the ongoing eurozone debt crisis, and the unpredictable impact of a UK referendum on European Union membership. The report underscores that while Scotland is gaining momentum, the path ahead remains uncertain.

title: Martin Shkreli is facing a lawsuit claiming that his $2m (£1.38m) Wu-Tang Clan album includes work ripped off from a New York artist.
text_ai: Jason Koza said he did not allow his illustrations to be used in packaging for the album bought by Mr Shkreli. The former drug executive - who owns the only copy of the album - has not issued any comment. Mr Koza, a digital artist from New York, claims he created a series of illustrations in 2015 that were later incorporated into the album's packaging without his consent. The images, which he says were part of a project called "The Garden of Eden", appear on the inner sleeve and booklet of the one-of-a-kind Wu-Tang Clan record *Once Upon a Time in Shaolin*. The album, recorded over six years in secret, was sold by the group to Mr Shkreli in 2015 for $2m - a deal that made headlines as the most expensive album ever sold. The former pharmaceutical executive, who earned notoriety for raising the price of a life-saving drug by 5,000%, became the sole owner of the only physical copy. He has since been known to play the album for friends and even threatened to destroy it if not purchased at a higher price. In court documents filed in a New York federal court, Mr Koza stated: "I never authorised the use of my artwork for any commercial purpose, let alone for a multimillion-dollar album that has been the subject of global publicity." He is seeking unspecified damages and an injunction to prevent further use of the illustrations. The lawsuit adds another layer of legal trouble for Mr Shkreli, who is currently serving a seven-year prison sentence for securities fraud. He was convicted in 2017 of defrauding investors in two hedge funds he ran, and of conspiring to manipulate the stock of a pharmaceutical company he controlled. He has maintained his innocence and is appealing the conviction. Wu-Tang Clan have not commented on the lawsuit. The group's members have expressed mixed feelings about the sale of the album to Mr Shkreli, with some describing it as a "work of art" and others lamenting that it ended up in the hands of a figure widely reviled by the public. Legal experts say the case could hinge on whether Mr Koza can prove that his work was used without permission and that it constitutes a significant part of the album's packaging. If successful, he could be entitled to a share of the profits from the sale of the album, or damages for copyright infringement. Mr Shkreli's defence team has not yet responded to requests for comment. The album remains in the possession of the US government, which seized it as part of Mr Shkreli's assets after his conviction. It has not been publicly released, though excerpts have been played in limited settings. The case is expected to proceed in the coming months, with both sides likely to present expert testimony on the originality and use of the artwork.

title: The biggest shake-up of school funding in England for decades will see less money for big cities such as London, Manchester, Liverpool and Birmingham and bigger budgets for schools in the suburbs and shires.
text_ai: Education Secretary Justine Greening has announced a new national funding formula for schools from 2018-19, saying it would resolve "unfair" and "inconsistent" funding levels. But it will not increase the overall budget - and the National Audit Office says schools face cuts of Â£3bn. Schools across inner London will see their funding cut. The new formula, which will be phased in over two years, aims to redistribute money based on a "fairer" set of criteria, including the number of pupils from disadvantaged backgrounds, the cost of living in different areas, and the number of pupils with special educational needs. But, as the Education Secretary acknowledged, it will not increase the overall schools budget in real terms. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) has calculated that, in cash terms, per-pupil funding will remain flat until 2022, meaning a real-terms cut of around 8% over the decade. Ministers say the changes will "level up" funding for those schools that have historically been underfunded, particularly in rural and coastal areas. Under the proposals, the average per-pupil funding in the shire counties of Northamptonshire, Suffolk and Warwickshire is set to rise by more than 7% by 2021-22. But for schools in inner London – which currently receive the highest per-pupil funding, largely because of the additional costs of living and higher staff salaries – the picture is stark. The new formula means a significant reduction in their budgets. The Borough of Hackney, for example, could see its per-pupil funding fall by more than £700 – a cut of around 8%. Head teachers in the capital reacted with dismay. Kevin Gilmartin, a former head teacher now representing the Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL), said the changes were "a hammer blow" for London schools, many of which have seen recent improvements in results. “They have been the engine room of rising standards,” he said. “To take money away now, when they are already struggling with rising costs, is completely the wrong priority.” The prospect of cuts comes at a time when schools across England are already under severe financial pressure. The National Audit Office (NAO) has warned that the overall schools budget is being stretched by rising costs, including higher employer pension contributions and national insurance, and the need to recruit and retain specialist staff. In a report published last month, the NAO said that by 2019-20 schools will have been forced to absorb £3bn in real-terms cuts since 2015. Many schools have already cut teaching assistants, increased class sizes and made non-teaching staff redundant. The new funding formula does not reverse this trend. It simply re-allocates the existing pot of money – around £41bn – in a different way. For every school that gains, another must lose. The Department for Education (DfE) admits that around 10,000 schools – about half the total – will see their budgets fall. For secondary schools in Liverpool, Manchester and Birmingham, the effect is particularly acute. These cities have historically received higher-than-average funding due to deprivation and high costs. Under the new formula, funding per pupil in such areas is set to fall by between 3% and 5% over the next five years. The Education Secretary defended the changes, insisting that the current system – which is based on historical allocation and local authority decisions – is "not fair". In a written ministerial statement, Justine Greening said: "This is about ensuring that a child's education is not determined by where they live. For too long, schools in some parts of the country have been funded far more generously than others, with no justification." But critics argue that the new formula fails to recognise that London schools face unique pressures: higher staff costs, higher rent and rates, and cheaper housing elsewhere meaning teachers can be more difficult to retain. The Mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, said the cuts were "unfair" and would "undermine the good work of London's schools". The Opposition Labour Party accused the government of presiding over a "school funding crisis". Shadow Education Secretary Angela Rayner said: "These plans will see children lose out in our greatest cities. The government is cutting the budgets of schools that are already under immense pressure." Meanwhile, the National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) warned that the new formula, despite its aim of fairness, could still leave many schools with unsustainable finances. General Secretary Paul Whiteman said: "The maths simply does not add up. Even if some schools get a small increase in cash terms, the real-terms value is declining. We are seeing the slow erosion of education funding." The DfE has also announced a transitional arrangement: no school will lose more than 3% of its budget in any single year, and the full effect of the cuts will be felt gradually over five years. But head teachers say this does little to reassure them, as they must plan budgets now for the years ahead. There is also concern among schools in the shires that the promised "levelling up" may not be enough. The National Foundation for Educational Research (NFER) has calculated that, even with the formula changes, schools in the most disadvantaged areas – many of which are in the north of England and coastal towns – will still lag behind. The new formula will be in place for the 2018-19 academic year, with full implementation from 2021-22. But given the mounting criticism, the Education Secretary faces an uphill battle to convince schools, parents and politicians that this is genuinely a fairer settlement – rather than a politically driven redistribution of a shrinking fund.

title: The Rolling Stones have confirmed they're working on a new, blues-inspired album for release this year.
text_ai: "We're actually in the studio in the moment cutting new stuff," Keith Richards told BBC 6 Music. Guitarist Ronnie Wood added that the band recently "cut 11 songs in two days. The new material marks a significant departure from the band's recent output, which has largely focused on re-releases, live albums and occasional standalone singles. The last studio album of original material, *Blue & Lonesome* (2016), was entirely composed of blues covers. The new project, by contrast, is described by insiders as a collection of original blues-inflected songs, recorded with the kind of raw spontaneity the band has not captured since the 1970s. Sources close to the group say the sessions were held at a private studio in London earlier this year, with producer Andrew Watt – known for his work with Pearl Jam, Ozzy Osbourne and Iggy Pop – at the helm. Watt has reportedly encouraged the band to embrace a stripped-down, live-in-the-room sound, minimising overdubs and digital editing. "It's very much a 'what you hear is what you get' approach," one source told the BBC. "They wanted to capture the energy of a band playing together, not a studio-constructed album." The project is said to include contributions from longtime keyboardist Chuck Leavell, bassist Darryl Jones and backing vocalists, though no guest artists have been confirmed. Richards, 79, described the sessions as "a kind of reset" in a recent interview, noting that the pandemic-induced touring break had given the group time to rediscover their instinctive chemistry. Fans will note that the Stones have not released an entirely original studio album since *A Bigger Bang* in 2005 – a 19-year gap that, if the new record arrives on schedule, will be the longest between collections of new material in the band's history. Jagger, 78, has previously expressed caution about rushing into the studio, but the swiftness of these sessions suggests a decisive shift in momentum. A release date has not been announced, but industry insiders expect a late 2024 or early 2025 launch, potentially accompanied by a tour. The band's management declined to comment on specifics, but a statement is expected within weeks. For now, the prospect of a new Rolling Stones album – their first original work in nearly two decades – has already generated considerable excitement among music historians and casual listeners alike. The blues has always been the bedrock of their sound, and this project may well reaffirm why, after 60 years, they remain one of rock's most formidable creative forces.

title: Much is written about the Herculean effort to move one family out of the White House and a new family in within the space of just a few hours.
text_ai: But in our modern age, the digital moving trucks must also roar into action, as prime presidential online real estate gets a makeover, and eight years of President Obama's social media chat is confined to the national archives. Behind the scenes, a small team of digital strategists, web developers, and social media managers have been working for months on what is, in effect, a virtual handover of the highest order. The transition of the @POTUS Twitter account, for instance, is not simply a matter of changing a password. title: The US and Russian military will hold talks "as soon as possible" to avoid clashing in Syria, the countries' top diplomats say.

title: The Independent State of Samoa, known as Western Samoa until 1997, is made up of nine volcanic islands, two of which - Savai'i and Upolu - make up more than 99% of the land.

A Sophos engineer showed us a perfectly ordinary-looking email – a routine invoice from a supplier. But then, with a few keystrokes, he revealed what was lurking beneath. The email had been generated entirely by an artificial intelligence tool, trained on months of the company's internal correspondence. The language, the phrasing, the layout – all were indistinguishable from a genuine message. The malicious payload, a piece of ransomware, had been hidden inside a seemingly benign PDF attachment. "What we're seeing now," said John Shier, Sophos's field chief technology officer, "is a level of social engineering we've never encountered before. The AI doesn't just mimic language; it mimics *personality*. It learns your boss's tics, your colleague's turn of phrase, the way your finance team signs off. It's not a spam campaign – it's a bespoke, personalised attack aimed at a single individual in a single organisation." The implications are chilling. For years, cybersecurity experts have told us to look for red flags: bad grammar, suspicious links, an urgent tone. But the AI can now remove those flags. It can craft a message that is grammatically perfect, contextually appropriate, and utterly persuasive. Shier warned that the technology is already in the hands of criminal groups, and that the number of such attacks is doubling every few months. "We are in a new arms race," he said. "And at the moment, the attackers are winning." From the corporate battlefield, we turned to the political one. Our second story this week focuses on the use of automated bots in the final weeks of the US election campaign. Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have published a new analysis showing that bot-driven accounts are now responsible for a significant proportion of political discourse on X – the platform formerly known as Twitter – and on TikTok. The bots are not just posting; they are engaging in long, seemingly natural threads, arguing, retweeting, and even responding to critics. "We're seeing a sophistication that goes beyond simple amplification," said Dr. Amelia Briggs, the lead author of the study. "These bots are designed to create the illusion of grassroots support – or opposition. They engage in what we call 'astroturfing' – fake groundswell. And they adapt their arguments based on the responses they receive, using simple language models to keep the conversation going." The detection tools, Dr. Briggs noted, are lagging behind. Platforms are trying to remove bots, but the bot operators are constantly evolving their methods, using generative AI to create unique profiles with realistic photos and biographies. The result is a digital environment where it is increasingly difficult to know who is real – and who is a machine programmed to manipulate your opinion. Which brings us to our final story – the broader, more existential anxiety about artificial intelligence itself. This week, a group of leading AI researchers released an open letter calling for a moratorium on the development of "frontier" AI systems – the most powerful models – until proper safety protocols are in place. The letter, signed by figures from Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and academic institutions, warns that the technology is moving faster than our ability to understand or control it. "We are not Luddites," said Prof. Eleanor Shaw, one of the signatories. "But we are scientists who have seen what these systems can do. They can manipulate, deceive, and generate content that is indistinguishable from truth. They can also, in theory, be used to discover new knowledge – but the risks of releasing them without adequate safeguards are catastrophic." The debate is familiar, but the tone has shifted. A year ago, such warnings were often dismissed as science fiction. Today, with generative AI already reshaping industries – from journalism to law to medicine – the calls for regulation are growing louder. Governments are scrambling to draft rules, but the technology is moving at a pace that regulators cannot match. As we left the Sophos office, Jat and I discussed the threads that connect these three stories. Each reflects a deepening anxiety: not about whether technology will work, but about what it will do to us. The hackers who can impersonate your colleague. The bots that can sway an election. The AI that can create realities we cannot distinguish from fact. Our digital world is becoming a hall of mirrors – and we are only just beginning to peer into the dark.

title: On the surface, their lives appeared to be very different - radio DJ, civil servant and retired police officer, bus driver, cabaret singer and publican and businessman.

They groomed them with kindness and then destroyed them with cruelty. The psychological scars are still visible today." She told them: "You exploited positions of trust, you used your outward respectability as a shield, and you showed no remorse. You are a danger to children still." The cabaret singer and publican, 76, got 19 years. The businessman, 78, received 21 years. Outside court, the mother of one victim said: "These men stole my son's childhood. He has never married, never had a family. He still has nightmares. But today, justice has been done." Many victims say their experiences were never properly investigated until now. Detective Inspector Hughes acknowledged that the police had been "too slow" to act in the past. "In the 1970s and 80s, society did not understand grooming. Children were not believed. Today, we know better. We urge any other victims to come forward. You will be heard." Its founder, a woman who was not herself a victim but whose brother was abused, said: "The men looked like ordinary members of the community. That is the horror. One victim's lawyer, Gareth Morgan, said: "These men were clever. They chose children who were isolated, who were not believed. And they had a network. They protected each other. It was only when one victim had the courage to speak that the whole house of cards came tumbling down." title: Nick Clegg has outlined his proposals to curb benefits to European Union migrants, during a meeting with his German counterpart in Berlin.
text_ai: The deputy PM insists the UK could find allies in Europe to support efforts to tackle "benefits tourism" - without challenging free movement in the EU. He discussed the issue with Germany's Sigmar Gabriel. UK PM David Cameron is due to set out his own plans to restrict EU migration later on Friday. The deputy PM insists the UK could find allies in Europe to support efforts to tackle "benefits tourism" - without challenging free movement in the EU. He discussed the issue with Germany's Sigmar Gabriel. UK PM David Cameron is due to set out his own plans to restrict EU migration later on Friday. Speaking alongside Mr Gabriel at the German economics ministry, Mr Clegg said the UK was not seeking to "pull up the drawbridge" but wanted to ensure that the principle of free movement was not abused. He argued that changes to the way benefits are accessed could be framed as a matter of social fairness rather than a direct attack on the EU's founding principles. "This is not about renegotiating the fundamental architecture of the European Union," Mr Clegg told reporters. "It is about making sure that the rules on freedom of movement are properly enforced, and that people do not come to the United Kingdom simply to claim benefits they have not contributed to." The Liberal Democrat leader, who is also the UK's deputy prime minister, stressed that any changes would have to be agreed with other member states and should not undermine the economic benefits of migration. He pointed to Germany's own recent efforts to tighten welfare rules for EU migrants, including a law introduced last year that restricts access to certain benefits for those who have not worked in the country. Mr Gabriel, the German vice-chancellor and economy minister, appeared to offer cautious backing for the British position, saying that any "abuses" of the system should be addressed. However, he warned against any measures that would "stigmatise" EU citizens or create a "two-tier" Europe. "There is a shared interest in making sure that the principle of free movement is accepted by our citizens," Mr Gabriel said through an interpreter. "But we must also ensure that it does not lead to a race to the bottom in social standards. Germany is also looking at how we can better prevent abuses without harming the integrity of the single market." The meeting came at a crucial juncture for the UK's EU renegotiation campaign. Mr Cameron has promised to secure changes to the terms of Britain's membership before holding an in/out referendum by the end of 2017. One of his key demands is the ability to limit the number of EU migrants coming to the UK, particularly those who have not found work within a certain period. Downing Street has indicated that the prime minister's speech later today will focus on how to restrict access to in-work benefits for EU nationals - a proposal that has divided opinion within the Conservative Party and among Britain's EU partners. Some member states, particularly in Central and Eastern Europe, have expressed strong opposition, arguing that it would discriminate against their citizens. But Mr Clegg's overture to Germany suggested the UK was seeking to build a coalition of like-minded northern European countries that share concerns about welfare tourism. Officials in Berlin have previously indicated that they are open to technical changes to the coordination of social security systems, but have ruled out any treaty change or permanent emergency brakes. The issue is highly sensitive across the EU, where free movement of workers is one of the four fundamental freedoms of the single market. Recent Eurobarometer polls show that while a majority of EU citizens support free movement, concerns about its impact on welfare systems have risen sharply in several countries, including the UK, Germany, and the Netherlands. Mr Clegg acknowledged that the UK needed to win over sceptical member states, but insisted that a compromise was possible. "No one wants to tear up the rulebook," he said. "What we are talking about is a sensible, targeted reform that would allow countries to apply a waiting period before new arrivals from elsewhere in the EU can access benefits. This is already done in some form in several member states." The deputy PM also used the visit to push back against suggestions that Britain's stance was damaging its influence in Europe. He pointed to recent EU agreements on financial regulation and energy security where the UK had played a leading role. "I think the idea that Britain is somehow isolated or on the margins of Europe is a myth," he said. "We are at the heart of the debate on reform, and we are finding partners who share our concerns." Despite the cautious optimism from Berlin, serious hurdles remain. The European Commission has repeatedly warned that any restrictions on benefits that are not based on objective criteria could be challenged in the European Court of Justice. Some legal experts argue that the so-called "emergency brake" on benefits, which Mr Cameron is reportedly considering, would require a treaty change - a prospect that many EU leaders are keen to avoid so close to a British referendum. Moreover, the political dynamics in Germany are complex. While Mrs Merkel's Christian Democrats are open to some reform measures on migration, their coalition partners, the Social Democrats - of which Mr Gabriel is a leading figure - have traditionally been more cautious. Any German support for UK proposals would therefore need to be carefully balanced against domestic pressures. Mr Gabriel sought to manage expectations, telling reporters that the EU's focus should remain on creating jobs and growth rather than restrictive policies. "The best way to tackle concerns about migration is to have a strong economy that provides opportunities for everyone," he said. Nevertheless, the meeting in Berlin signalled a shift in tactics for the UK government. Rather than issuing ultimatums, Mr Clegg's approach appeared designed to build consensus gradually, using bilateral diplomacy to soften the ground before wider EU discussions. The prime minister's speech later today is expected to flesh out the details of his proposed reforms, including the introduction of a four-year ban on welfare payments for new EU migrants, as well as tighter rules on housing benefit and child benefit for children living abroad. Mr Cameron will also call for longer "re-entry" bans for those who have been deported for begging or rough sleeping. But with only 18 months until the planned referendum, time is running short. EU leaders are due to discuss the UK's demands at a summit in Brussels in December, but disagreements remain over what can be achieved without reopening the EU treaties. Mr Clegg acknowledged that the clock was ticking. "This is not something that will be resolved overnight," he said. "But I believe we have laid important foundations today. The conversation in Europe is starting to change."

title: Two of the bloodiest battles of World War One, Verdun and the Somme, are being marked 100 years on, but in Switzerland, centenary commemorations are taking place for a far less known wartime event.
text_ai: The first contingent of wounded British soldiers arrived on 30 May 1916 for internment in the tiny village of Chateau d'Oex. Between 1916 and 1918, Switzerland accepted 68,000 sick and injured soldiers: French and German as well as British. The first contingent of wounded British soldiers arrived on 30 May 1916 for internment in the tiny village of Chateau d'Oex. Between 1916 and 1918, Switzerland accepted 68,000 sick and injured soldiers: French and German as well as British. They came not as prisoners of war, but as guests of a neutral nation — a humanitarian experiment that remains one of the Great War's most remarkable and overlooked chapters. For the men who trudged down from mountain trains into Alpine villages, Switzerland offered not just sanctuary but a strange kind of freedom. The war was still audible, a distant rumble of artillery across the Jura Mountains, but here, in the crisp air of the Bernese Oberland, they could walk unguarded, sleep without fear of shellfire, and, for the first time in months, look at a clock without wondering how many seconds remained until the next bombardment. The arrangement, brokered by the International Committee of the Red Cross and the Swiss government, was born of desperation. By early 1916, the warring powers faced a crisis: thousands of wounded men were occupying hospital beds that could be used for fresh troops, and many were deemed "incurable" — suffering from tuberculosis, severe neurological damage, or amputations that would never heal. Rather than exchange these men outright, the belligerents agreed to send them to Switzerland on condition they remain interned for the war's duration. They would be guests, not prisoners, but they could not return home until the armistice. Chateau d'Oex, a village of 1,500 souls nestled in the valley of the Saane River, became a microcosm of this extraordinary experiment. The first British arrivals were met by villagers who had never seen a soldier from outside their own cantonal militia. There was no enemy here — only men in pyjamas and blue hospital coats, many on crutches or in wheelchairs. Local women organised knitting circles to produce socks and scarves. Farmers donated milk and cheese. Children, fascinated by the accents and uniforms, became informal translators, learning English from soldiers who taught them to play cricket on the village green. But the internment was not an idyll. The men were still soldiers, and the war was never far from their minds. Many suffered what was then called "shell shock" — now recognised as post-traumatic stress disorder. They woke screaming, haunted by the mud of the Somme and the forests of Verdun. The Swiss authorities, unprepared for the scale of the psychological crisis, improvised. In a chalet above the village, a former sanatorium was converted into a psychiatric ward. Orderlies were trained in the new field of occupational therapy. Men were encouraged to work: painting, woodcarving, gardening, even composing music. The Alpine landscape itself became a therapy. "The mountains have a way of swallowing noise," one British officer wrote in his diary. "Even the shells in your head grow quieter." By the end of 1916, nearly 12,000 British soldiers were interned in Switzerland, spread across 30 sites. The largest colony was in Mürren, where the entire village became a hospital. Others were housed in hotels commandeered by the Swiss army — grand Belle Époque establishments that had once hosted Russian aristocrats and British climbers, now filled with men whose lungs had been poisoned by gas or whose spines had been shattered by shrapnel. The transformation was jarring. Waiters became nurses. Ballrooms became wards. The spa baths, once the preserve of wealthy invalids, were used to treat trench foot. The impact on the Swiss host communities was profound. The war had isolated Switzerland, surrounded by belligerent powers and dependent on imports for food and coal. The arrival of thousands of wounded soldiers brought not only humanitarian purpose but economic relief. The British government paid a daily rate for each man — enough to keep local hotels and farms afloat during the lean years. But there was also a cultural exchange that left a lasting mark. The villagers of Chateau d'Oex still speak of the "English years." A local bakery still sells a type of biscuit inspired by the soldiers' request for "something like a digestive." The church contains a stained-glass window donated by the survivors. The French and German internees lived in separate enclaves, but the Swiss authorities insisted they be treated equally. In the town of Lucerne, a German hospital and a French hospital stood on opposite sides of a lake. Men from the two armies could see each other across the water but were forbidden to fraternise. Yet in the evenings, when the wind carried the sound of a German choir singing "Die Wacht am Rhein," the French would answer with "La Marseillaise." The songs never changed, but the tone, those who heard it said, grew less defiant over time. By 1917, the two sides were exchanging cigarettes across the lake, thrown in weighted pouches. The Swiss guards looked the other way. Perhaps the most extraordinary aspect of the internment was the role of the Red Cross. The ICRC, based in Geneva, used the Swiss internment as a test case for its broader humanitarian mission. Delegates visited every colony regularly, documenting conditions and reporting to the belligerent governments. Their reports, now preserved in the ICRC archives, are remarkable for their clinical detail and moral clarity. "The men are well fed but listless," one report reads. "Their bodies heal, but their minds wander home. We recommend more exercise, better lighting, and, above all, news from the front." The news from the front, when it came, was devastating. The internees learned of the Somme's early losses in July 1916 through Swiss newspapers, which were smuggled into the wards. Some men wept. Others demanded to be returned to their units. The Swiss authorities, fearing a breakdown of order, imposed a strict bulletin system: only official communiqués from the Red Cross could be posted on notice boards. The men formed their own news networks, befriending Swiss guards who read them letters from home. One guard, a farmer from the Valais, recalled a British sergeant begging him for news of his brother, missing since the first day of the Somme. The guard could only shake his head. The centenary commemorations in Switzerland this year are modest compared to the grand ceremonies at Verdun and the Thiepval Memorial. In Chateau d'Oex, a small memorial stone will be unveiled in the village square. Veteran's descendants have been invited. A Swiss military band will play the "Last Post" and "Ich hatt' einen Kameraden" — the German equivalent. The two songs will be played back to back, a gesture of reconciliation that would have been unthinkable a century ago. But perhaps the most significant commemoration will be silent. Many of the buildings that housed the internees still stand — hotels in Mürren, sanatoriums in Leysin, and the chalets of Chateau d'Oex. They now host skiers and hikers, tourists who pay little attention to the faded brass plaques near their doorways. The village children, when asked, know that wounded soldiers once stayed here, but the details are hazy. "They were English," one 12-year-old told a reporter. "They played football in the snow." The football in the snow — that is what many veterans remembered best. In the final years of the war, the internees organised a league, complete with referees and league tables. Teams bore names like "The Lame Ducks" and "The Alpine Amblers." The Swiss villagers, who had never seen the game played properly, became passionate supporters. Matches drew crowds of hundreds. The Red Cross donated a trophy, still housed in the Chateau d'Oex museum. When the armistice was signed on 11 November 1918, the internees did not immediately return home. The Swiss authorities, worried about the spread of Spanish flu, kept them in isolation until the spring of 1919. The last of the British left Switzerland in June. Many were reluctant to go. They had families now, of a sort — not wives and children, but a community that had nursed them and accepted them as they were. One officer, a captain from Yorkshire, wrote to the Swiss police: "I have no home to return to. My house was bombed. Must I leave? I would rather stay here and work the land." He was allowed to stay. He married a local woman and became a farmer. His descendants still live in the valley. The story of the 68,000 is not one of glory. There are no Victoria Crosses, no celebrated charges. But it is a story of survival — and of a small, neutral nation that dared to open its doors when the rest of the world was at war. In Switzerland, the war never came, but the war never left. The men in the blue hospital coats are gone now, their names recorded in ledgers at the Red Cross museum in Geneva. But the mountains remain, and so does the quiet memory of a time when, in one corner of Europe, humanity found a way to pause the slaughter.

title: The UK has not seen a bomb attack like the Manchester outrage since 2005 for three simple reasons:
text_ai: For more than a decade, the BBC Home Affairs Unit has monitored every single terrorist incident, attempted or failed, that has made it into the public domain. For more than a decade, the BBC Home Affairs Unit has monitored every single terrorist incident, attempted or failed, that has made it into the public domain. Quite simply, most of the people we have seen dragged through the courts are not capable of this kind of incident. Their plots are often amateurish, their bombs faulty, their ambitions limited to knives or vehicles. The Manchester Arena bombing in 2017 was a brutal exception – a sophisticated, high-casualty device detonated in a crowded space. To understand why such an attack had not occurred in the UK since the 7/7 London bombings in 2005, we must look beyond capability to three structural factors: the erosion of bomb-making expertise, the tightening of security services’ net, and the strategic shift in jihadist targeting. The first reason, incompetence, is well illustrated by case after case. MI5 and counter-terror police have disrupted dozens of plots since 2005, but most involved crude pipe bombs, homemade explosives that failed to detonate, or attackers armed only with knives. In 2017, a plot to attack Parliament with a bomb made from drain cleaner and nails was foiled after the would-be attacker’s device was deemed unlikely to work. Another man, planning a suicide vest, was arrested before he could even acquire the chemicals. The Manchester bomber, Salman Abedi, was different: he travelled to Libya, received training from a bomb-maker linked to the Islamic State group, and returned with the knowledge to construct a viable shrapnel-filled device. That transfer of expertise – direct, foreign-based instruction – is the missing ingredient that most UK-based plotters have lacked. The collapse of the Islamic State’s caliphate in 2019 reduced such opportunities, but for the decade before, only a handful of individuals managed to gain the necessary skills. The second reason is the relentless pressure applied by the security services. Since 2005, the UK’s counter-terrorism architecture has been reshaped. The number of police officers dedicated to counter-terror has more than doubled, to over 4,000. The security service’s budget has risen by over 50% in real terms. Intelligence-sharing with foreign partners – particularly the US, France, and Germany – has improved, and the introduction of the Prevent strategy has seen thousands of potential extremists referred for support. This means that the “needle” of a capable plotters is hidden in a much larger “haystack” of chatter, but the haystack is constantly being searched. Between 2006 and 2016, MI5 and police disrupted an average of one serious plot every six months – most of them at an early stage. The Manchester bomber, however, slipped through. He was known to MI5 as a “subject of interest” but was assessed as low-risk; his travel to Libya was not followed up. That case exposed gaps, but it remains an anomaly. The overall system is designed to catch the incompetent majority and to intercept the rare capable individual before they act. The third reason is the changing nature of jihadist targeting. After the 7/7 bombings, which killed 52 people on public transport, al-Qaeda and later Islamic State strategists concluded that large-scale bomb attacks in the UK were too hard to pull off – the security response was too effective. They shifted encouragement toward simpler, “low-tech” attacks: stabbings, vehicle rammings, hostage-taking. The 2020 Fishmongers’ Hall attack, the 2019 London Bridge stabbing, the 2017 Westminster Bridge vehicle attack – all were carried out with blades or cars. These required no bomb-making skill, no explosives, no travel for training. They were harder to detect because the attackers often acted alone, with minimal communication. The result is that the UK has suffered a series of deadly but smaller-scale attacks, none approaching the magnitude of Manchester. The Islamic State’s official propaganda magazine, *Rumiyah*, explicitly urged followers: “Use knives, rocks, cars, or fire – anything that can cause harm.” Bomb-making was reserved for the few who could access expertise. Yet Manchester was a horrific return to the 2005 model – a nail bomb in a backpack, detonated by a suicide bomber, killing 22 children and adults at an Ariana Grande concert. Why did it happen? The answer lies in a convergence of factors that temporarily pierced the UK’s defences. Abedi had the skills, the intent, and the support network. He returned from Libya undetected, bought the components locally, and assembled the device in a rented flat. The security services were focused on other threats – the volume of intelligence was immense, and Abedi’s travel had not triggered a full investigation. The attack was a shock, but it did not signal a new trend. After Manchester, the UK’s terrorism threat level was raised to “critical” – the highest – for just four days. No subsequent plot has matched its sophistication. What does this mean for the future? The threat from lone-actor attacks with knives and vehicles remains high, and the murder of Sir David Amess in 2021 shows that even a single assailant can cause devastating harm. However, the return of large-scale bomb attacks requires a combination of factors that are now rarer than ever: access to bomb-making training, the ability to travel to conflict zones, and the capacity to operate under the radar of a vastly improved intelligence machine. The Islamic State’s successor groups, such as the group known as Islamic State Khorasan, have shifted focus to Afghanistan and Europe, but their ability to inspire or direct a Manchester-style attack in the UK is diminished. The UK’s security services, for all their flaws, have made that kind of attack the exception, not the rule. The three reasons – incompetence, intense surveillance, and tactical shift – remain the pillars of a grim but effective defence. The question is not whether another Manchester-style attack will happen, but whether the UK can sustain the investment and vigilance that has kept it at bay for most of the past two decades.

Three others – all women – were later bailed pending further inquiries. Community leaders have condemned the assault. Imam Mohammed Osman of the Croydon Islamic Centre said: “This is not who we are as a city. We stand with Reker and his family. There is no place for such hatred in our society.” The seven charged include two brothers aged 17 and 19, and a sister and brother aged 16 and 20. A fifth defendant is also a 20-year-old man, and the remaining two are a 46-year-old man and a 43-year-old woman. The Metropolitan Police has increased patrols in the area and is urging anyone with footage or information to come forward. The case has reignited concerns about the treatment of asylum seekers in the UK. Refugee charities have called for stronger protections and for hate crimes to be met with the full force of the law. A vigil is being planned for Friday evening outside Croydon Town Hall.

title: The Scottish secretary has insisted it will be "perfectly possible" for the Conservative government to operate despite losing its majority.
text_ai: But David Mundell said it was inevitable that the government would need to "cut and change its proposals" to win enough support in the Commons. It could not come as a greater contrast to the era of single-party rule the Conservatives enjoyed for the past two years, albeit with a slender majority. Now, with no party commanding the 326 seats needed for an outright Commons majority, the arithmetic of power has shifted decisively. "There is no doubt we will need to listen to other parties, to take their views on board, and to be prepared to compromise where necessary," he said. "That is the reality of a hung parliament. He pointed specifically to the Brexit negotiations, due to begin in earnest on Monday, as an area where cross-party co-operation was not only desirable but essential. "On Brexit, there is a clear mandate from the British people to leave the European Union," he said. "That is something I believe we can find common ground with other parties, even if there are disagreements about the precise shape of our future relationship." Mr Mundell defended the arrangement, saying it was a "pragmatic" way to ensure the government could function on key votes, including the Budget and the Queen's Speech. He insisted that it did not represent a shift in Westminster's approach to Scotland or the rest of the UK. But the DUP's influence has already been felt: the party's demand for no new checks on goods crossing the Irish Sea after Brexit is at odds with the EU's negotiating position and could complicate the prime minister's already difficult task. On the question of a second Scottish independence referendum, Mr Mundell was unequivocal. He repeated the prime minister's view that now was "not the time" for another vote, arguing that the 2014 referendum had been a "once in a generation" event. "The SNP needs to get back to the day job of running Scotland's schools and hospitals, not obsessing about another referendum," he said. "The people of Scotland have made their view clear – they do not want a second independence referendum any time soon." "The Scottish secretary is in an unenviable position," said Professor John Curtice of Strathclyde University. "He must try to project an image of stability and authority at a time when the government is, in reality, extremely vulnerable. The Queen's Speech, expected to be presented later this month, will set out the government's legislative agenda for the next two years. title: Of all the frustrations that a broken ankle brings, it is missing life at Firhill that is paining David Beattie most.
text_ai: The Partick Thistle chairman is stuck in Spain as he recovers, but his mind is never far from events in the west end of Glasgow. "It's absurd, really," Beattie admits, speaking via video call from his temporary Spanish base, a crutch visible in the corner of the frame. Beattie, a chartered accountant by trade, took over as Thistle chairman in 2017, stepping into a club that had long teetered on a financial knife-edge. His predecessor, the late David Mackinnon, had steadied the ship but left a legacy of careful housekeeping rather than grand ambition. Beattie’s own style was clinical, almost detached: he spoke of "sustainable growth", "risk mitigation", and "fan-owned governance" — phrases that warmed the hearts of auditors but did little to stir the terraces. His father, a lifelong Jags supporter who had taken young David to Firhill in the 1980s — the era of Johnny Lambie and the famous 3-1 win over Celtic in the Scottish Cup — had wanted his son to feel the same visceral pull. But Beattie confesses he never quite caught the bug. "I loved the club, but I didn't love going to games. The noise, the anxiety, the chaos — it wasn't for me. I preferred the calm of the boardroom, the clarity of a spreadsheet." That changed, gradually, after he accepted the chairmanship. The first hint came during the 2018-19 season, when Thistle narrowly avoided relegation from the Championship. My heart was pounding. I thought, 'This is what my father felt. This is what they all feel.'" Yet he still maintained his distance. "I didn't want to become one of those chairmen who interfere, who sit in the dugout giving the manager advice. That's not my job. My job is to make sure the club exists next season, not to pick the team." Now, as he stares at the plaster cast on his ankle — the result of a misjudged step on a marble floor in his holiday apartment — that hands-off approach is being tested. The injury occurred just before the start of the 2024-25 season, forcing him to postpone his planned return to Glasgow. Instead, he manages the club from a portable desk, surrounded by bottles of sun cream and half-read financial reports. "It’s frustrating because I can't be there for the small things," Beattie says, his voice betraying a hint of weariness. "I can't walk the corridors of Firhill, have a coffee with the groundsman, check the state of the pitch after a storm. Those informal conversations — they matter. They tell you things no email ever will." The club, meanwhile, faces the familiar challenges of Scottish football’s second tier: a tight budget, a squad rebuilt each summer, and the constant threat of financial insolvency. Recent fan unease over ticket pricing and a perceived lack of ambition has bubbled up on social media, with some supporters questioning whether Beattie’s cautious stewardship is holding the club back. "I understand the frustration," he says, leaning forward. "Fans want to see progress on the pitch. They want signings that excite them. But the reality is that Thistle must survive before it can thrive. The number of Scottish clubs that have gone into administration in the last decade is frightening. I will not be the chairman who lets that happen on my watch." He pauses, looking off-camera. "I’m a fan — I care deeply about this club. But I’m not a supporter in the way that my father was. He would be in that stand every Saturday, rain or shine, happy or miserable. I can’t be that man. But I can be the man who makes sure that stand is still there for the next generation." The broken ankle, he jokes, has given him an unexpected gift: time. Time to think about the club’s long-term strategy, to read the historical archives he’s been meaning to explore, to understand why the Jags — "the only senior club in Scotland named after a cartoon" — inspire such fierce loyalty. "I’ve been watching old videos of the 1971 League Cup final. We won it, you know. I’d forgotten how that felt," he says, with a smile that flickers like a distant memory. "My father was there. He never stopped talking about it." As the Spanish sun begins to set behind him, Beattie concedes that his enforced exile may be changing him. "I miss Firhill. I miss the old creaking stands. I even miss the rain. That’s something I never thought I’d say." He plans to return to Glasgow in November, crutch and all, just in time for the run-up to Christmas — the most financially critical period for the club. But for now, he remains in Marbella, refreshing his screen, watching the Jags from afar, and learning, slowly, what it means to be both fan and supporter. "I’m not there yet," he says, "but the ankle is healing. And maybe so is something else."

title: The NHS has come under intense pressure this winter, with record numbers of patients facing long waits in accident and emergency units among other challenges.
text_ai: We asked some of those who have fallen ill, and the families of others, to share their experiences of winter 2016-17. "She had been there since 7am. No one had offered her anything to eat. Her water jug was empty. The call bell was out of reach. My mother is a proud woman – she had been a nurse herself. She was in tears. I felt helpless." Irene was eventually moved to a ward after 18 hours in A&E. But the care on the ward was patchy, Paula said. Drugs were not given on time. A catheter became infected. Irene was finally discharged on Christmas Eve, but at home she was too weak to manage. She was readmitted on Boxing Day with a urinary tract infection. "Every winter I worry," Paula said. "But this year was different. It felt like the system had just collapsed." The government has said extra funding has been provided for the NHS, including £100m for social care this winter. But many health leaders argue that the cuts to local authority budgets since 2010 have left social care unable to cope with rising demand. The King's Fund think tank warned in December that the NHS was "stumbling" into a winter crisis that had been "entirely foreseeable". Meanwhile, the number of people aged 85 and over in England is projected to double by 2040. Emergency admissions among the over-75s have risen by a third in the past five years. Many of these admissions are for conditions that could have been managed in the community if enough GPs and district nurses were available. But GP practices are also under pressure. In January 2017, a survey of GPs by Pulse magazine found that one in six practices said they were considering handing back their contract because they could not cope with demand. The British Medical Association said the average GP now sees 40 to 50 patients a day – up from 30 a decade ago – and that many are burning out. For families like Sue's, the long-term consequences of this winter will be lived with for years. Her father is now in a care home 20 miles from her home. She visits twice a week. "He knows who I am most of the time, but he gets agitated. He asks me when he can go home. I have to lie. I say 'Soon, Dad, soon.' It breaks my heart." Sue says she does not blame the individual doctors and nurses, who she says worked "impossible shifts" and "cared deeply". But she believes the system failed her father. "He was a healthy, independent man. He should not have ended up like this. The NHS is a wonderful institution, but it is being broken – by underfunding, by short-sighted decisions, by a lack of political will." As the winter of 2016-17 draws to a close, the questions remain. Will the lessons be learned? Will next winter be different? Dr Harris, the geriatrician, is pessimistic. "We are firefighting. We are not fixing the roof. Until we invest properly in social care, in community nursing, in public health, in mental health support – until we stop treating the NHS as a crisis service and start treating it as a comprehensive healthcare system – we will keep having these winters. And they will only get harder." For now, families like Sue's, Margaret's and Paula's are left to pick up the pieces. Their stories are not just statistics. They are a human testimony to a winter in which the NHS, for many, simply could not deliver the care it promised.

title: The Home Office has "insufficient information" on how much further it can cut police funding in England and Wales without "degrading services", the National Audit Office (NAO) has said.

title: A mass burial for about 300 people killed by a mudslide and flooding has taken place on the outskirts of the capital Freetown.

Wrapped in white shrouds, the victims were laid to rest in long trenches, with imams, priests and traditional leaders offering prayers in turn. Many of the coffins were marked only with numbers – the bodies were too badly decomposed or disfigured to be identified by relatives. “We have run out of space in the mortuaries, and the bodies are decomposing quickly,” said Victor Williams, the deputy head of the National Disaster Management Agency. “This is the only dignified option we have left. "We've seen examples in France where salmon is smoked and packaged with tartan designs and images of Scottish landscapes, yet the fish has never been within 500 miles of Scotland," said Paul Wightman, managing director of Associated Seafoods. Since leaving the European Union, the UK has established its own geographical indication (GI) schemes, mirroring the EU system that protects products such as Champagne, Parma ham and Stilton cheese. Scottish beef, lamb and the Arbroath smokie – a smoked haddock delicacy – already hold GI status. If approved, the new status would apply across the whole of the UK, and the company hopes that it would eventually be recognised by trading partners through future trade deals. "Scotland's coastal waters are some of the finest in the world for salmon farming," added Mr Wightman. "The fish are reared in clean, cold currents, and our smoking traditions go back generations. The name 'Scottish smoked salmon' is not just a description – it is a statement of quality. And quality deserves protection."

title: The world's best swimmers will face up to seven anti-doping tests in the run up to August's Rio Olympics.
