title: The trust that ran the scandal-hit Stafford Hospital should be dissolved, administrators have recommended.
text_ai: The Mid Staffordshire NHS Trust went into administration on 16 April after a report concluded it was not "clinically or financially sustainable". Critical care, maternity and paediatric services should also be cut, the proposals unveiled by Trust Special Administrators (TSA) say. The trust's two hospitals would come under two other trusts. In a document published on Tuesday, the TSA – a team led by Alan Bloom, a partner at Ernst & Young – said the trust's two hospitals, Stafford Hospital and the County Hospital in Cannock, should be split. Stafford would be taken over by the University Hospital of North Staffordshire NHS Trust, while Cannock would come under the Royal Wolverhampton Hospitals NHS Trust. The controversial proposals, which will now be subject to a 45-day public consultation, also recommend that Stafford Hospital's accident and emergency department be downgraded to a 24-hour urgent care centre. The hospital would lose its consultant-led maternity unit, with deliveries transferred to the University Hospital of North Staffordshire in Stoke-on-Trent. Paediatric inpatient beds would also be moved, leaving only a midwife-led unit and a children's assessment unit at Stafford. "These are difficult but necessary changes," Mr Bloom said. "The current model of care is not sustainable. The trust has a legacy of poor clinical outcomes, financial deficits and low staff morale. We believe these proposals will create a safer, more resilient NHS for patients in mid Staffordshire." The trust collapsed in the wake of a public inquiry chaired by Sir Robert Francis QC, which found that between 2005 and 2009, an estimated 400 to 1,200 more people died at Stafford Hospital than would have been expected. The inquiry uncovered a "dysfunctional" culture focused on targets and cost-cutting rather than patient care. Nurses and doctors were found to have ignored patients' cries for help, while managers failed to act on warnings. In November 2012, the government ordered the trust to be put into administration, a move that effectively stripped its board of power. The TSA was appointed in April this year, and its recommendations are the first major step towards the complete dissolution of the body that ran the hospital. The proposals have already drawn fierce criticism from local campaign groups, who argue that downgrading services will leave patients in a largely rural area without adequate emergency care. Stafford lies within a triangle of major hospitals – Stoke-on-Trent, Wolverhampton and Stoke-on-Trent again – but journey times can be lengthy, particularly in winter. "There is no way we are going to accept these cuts," said Julie Bailey, founder of Cure the NHS, a campaign group formed by former patients and relatives. "The people of Stafford have already suffered enough. We will fight this tooth and nail. The government cannot be allowed to dismantle our hospital in the name of efficiency." The local Labour MP for Stafford, Andrew Griffiths, also condemned the proposals. "This is a betrayal of patients and staff who have worked so hard to turn the hospital around," he said. "The TSA has ignored the views of local people and instead put financial savings ahead of clinical safety. I will be demanding the Secretary of State for Health, Jeremy Hunt, rejects these plans." But Mr Hunt defended the process. Speaking in the House of Commons, he said the administration was designed to ensure that patients in mid Staffordshire received "honest answers and better care". He added: "We cannot allow the mistakes of the past to continue. The trust is no longer viable, and it is right that the TSA has put forward a plan that addresses the fundamental weaknesses of the system." The TSA's report acknowledges that its recommendations would have a "significant impact" on local access to services. It says that under the proposed changes, some patients would have to travel up to 30 minutes longer to reach an A&E department. But it argues that the overall standard of emergency care would improve because the services at Stoke-on-Trent and Wolverhampton are better equipped and staffed. The report also highlights the financial state of the trust, which ran up a deficit of £11.2m last year. It says that without the changes, the annual deficit would grow to £24m by 2015-16. The TSA claims its plan would reduce the deficit to £6.1m by the following year. However, the proposals do not go as far as some had feared. The TSA recommended against closing Stafford Hospital entirely, citing the need to maintain an inpatient unit for elderly and stroke patients, as well as a diagnostic centre and outpatient services. The hospital would also retain its day-case surgery unit and a CT scanner. But the loss of acute services will be deeply felt. Stafford has already seen its maternity unit downgraded in recent years, and the town has a high proportion of elderly residents who rely on local care. The private ambulance service has warned that the longer journey times could put pressure on its vehicles. The 45-day consultation period, which begins on 10 June, will include public meetings in Stafford, Cannock and nearby towns. The TSA will then submit its final report to the Secretary of State, who will decide whether to accept, reject or modify the plan. A final decision is expected by the autumn. The fate of the trust's remaining staff is also a major concern. The trust employs about 4,000 people, and the TSA says the plan would lead to a reduction of about 500 posts, though it hopes to avoid compulsory redundancies. Staff have already endured years of job uncertainty and low morale. Unison, the public services union, said the proposals were "a blueprint for breaking up the NHS". Its head of health, Christina McAnea, said: "Patients in Stafford and Cannock are being punished for the failures of management. The right thing to do is to bring those responsible to justice, not to close services that people rely on." The TSA's report also contains detailed clinical evidence to support its case. It notes that the number of births at Stafford Hospital has fallen by 40% over the past decade, with many expectant mothers already opting to travel to Stoke-on-Trent. It says the maternity unit is underused and unsafe for emergency cases. Similarly, the TSA says that the paediatric unit sees fewer than 1,000 admissions a year, well below the threshold for a safe service. The report argues that it is impossible to maintain the necessary specialist skills among staff with such low patient numbers. But the local acute trust, University Hospital of North Staffordshire, has warned that it would need significant investment to absorb the extra workload. Its chief executive, Mark Hackett, said: "We are committed to making this work, but the Secretary of State must ensure that the necessary funds are made available." The future of Cannock Hospital is also uncertain. Under the TSA's plan, it would lose its maternity unit entirely and become a centre for community health services, run by the Royal Wolverhampton Trust. Some local residents have welcomed the idea, saying it would boost services in a town that has long felt neglected. But others fear that the fragmentation of the trust will lead to a postcode lottery for healthcare in the area. The county council has said it will scrutinise the plan to ensure the needs of the most vulnerable are met. The administration process itself has been controversial. The TSA was appointed under a new legal framework designed to fast-track the restructuring of failing trusts. Critics say the process is too secretive and does not give enough weight to local opinion. The Francis inquiry made a series of recommendations aimed at preventing a repeat of the Stafford scandal, including greater transparency, stronger professional regulation, and a new legal duty of candour. However, campaigners argue that the government has been slow to implement them. The Trust Special Administrator's report runs to more than 200 pages and includes detailed appendices on financial modelling, clinical modelling and workforce planning. It is available for public inspection at local libraries and online. As the consultation begins, both sides are gearing up for a long battle. The campaign group Save Stafford Hospital has already started a petition, while the TSA has promised to hold a series of "listening events" to hear people's concerns. "I hope we can reach a consensus, but if not, we will do what is best for patients," Mr Bloom said. "The decisions we have taken are not taken lightly. We understand the strong emotions involved. But we have to be honest: the current situation is harming patients, and it must change." The final decision rests with Jeremy Hunt. He has said he will "carefully consider" the proposals, but he has also made clear that he will not allow a failing trust to limp on indefinitely. The coming months will determine the future of healthcare in mid Staffordshire – and test the government's commitment to learning the lessons of the past.

title: A man who was forced to live in his car after a relationship breakdown has talked of continuing to work full-time.
text_ai: Isaac Brobbey used an Asda car park in Greater Manchester as a base for a month and a McDonald's to wash in. The father-of-two, who managed to hold down his job at a truck rental firm, said his kind of experience shows how homelessness is often misunderstood. “People see someone sleeping rough and they think they know that person's story,” Mr Brobbey told BBC News. “But I was in a suit and tie every day, driving to work, doing my job. No one at my office had any idea I was sleeping in my car at night.” The 42-year-old, originally from Ghana, had been living with his partner and their two children in a rented flat in Salford. When the relationship ended abruptly, he found himself locked out of the property with nowhere to go. His savings were minimal, and with rent prices in the city soaring, he could not afford a deposit on a new place. “I thought, I have a car, I can survive for a bit,” he said. “I didn't want my children to see me on the streets. I didn't want my employer to think I was unreliable. So I just kept going.” For a month, his daily routine was a carefully choreographed act of survival. He would park his silver Ford Focus at the far end of the Asda car park in Eccles, arriving late to avoid drawing attention. Each morning, he drove to a nearby McDonald's, where he used the toilet to wash and change into his work clothes. He bought a cheap coffee to justify his presence. “I’d brush my teeth, put on my shirt, and walk out looking like any other customer,” he said. “But I was living in a metal box.” Mr Brobbey’s experience reflects a growing but often invisible phenomenon: people who are in work but have no home. According to the charity Crisis, one in four people experiencing homelessness in England is in employment. The term “hidden homelessness” covers those sofa-surfing, living in cars, or staying in hostels while holding down a job. “I was exhausted,” Mr Brobbey recalled. “The car seat is not a bed. My back ached. I was worried about security. I’d wake up in the middle of the night if someone walked too close.” His employer, a truck rental firm in Trafford Park, was unaware of his situation. He never missed a shift. “I felt a sense of shame, even though I knew I hadn't done anything wrong. I thought if they knew, they might treat me differently.” The turning point came when a colleague noticed him washing in the office bathroom more often than usual and asked if everything was okay. Reluctantly, Mr Brobbey opened up. The colleague put him in touch with a local housing charity, which helped him secure a room in a shared house within a week. Now living in stable accommodation, Mr Brobbey says the experience has changed his outlook. “Homelessness is not just a person with a sleeping bag. It’s the man in the suit who smiles at you. The person next to you in the queue.” He wants to see better support for those in work but without a home. “Employers need to know that asking for help is not a weakness. And the public needs to understand: you never know what someone is going through.” He still parks his car in the same Asda car park sometimes. “Just to remind myself how far I’ve come.”

title: A mental health patient found dead in a garden a month after going missing was failed by police, a report has said.
text_ai: Valon Pitts, 36, was reported missing by his family on 31 July 2012 and was found dead on 22 August in Devon. The Independent Police Complaints Commission (IPCC) said police call handlers "completely missed the signs" that Mr Pitts was in danger. Devon and Cornwall Police admitted the response was "below the standard expected". The IPCC investigation found that when Mr Pitts' family first contacted police to report him missing, the call handler failed to record that he suffered from paranoid schizophrenia and had stopped taking his medication. The handler also did not log details of a previous incident in which Mr Pitts had gone missing and was later found in a distressed state, according to the report. "Critical opportunities to identify him as a high-risk missing person were missed," the IPCC said. "The call handler completely missed the signs that Mr Pitts was a vulnerable person who required an urgent response." It took more than 24 hours for officers to begin searching for him, by which time he had travelled more than 200 miles from his home in London to Devon. His body was discovered in the garden of a property in the village of Chagford, near Dartmoor, on 22 August 2012. A post-mortem examination gave the cause of death as unascertained, though no suspicious circumstances were found. Devon and Cornwall Police said in a statement: "We accept the findings of this report and apologise unreservedly to Mr Pitts' family for the failings identified. The response he received fell below the standard expected." The force said it had since implemented new procedures for handling missing person reports, including mandatory training for call handlers on identifying vulnerability and risk. Mr Pitts' family described him as a "loving and gentle soul" who had struggled with his mental health. In a statement, they said: "We trusted the police to help us find him. They let us down. We hope no other family has to endure what we have been through." The IPCC also recommended that the College of Policing revise its guidance on missing persons to ensure mental health issues are flagged at the earliest opportunity.

title: Two-time Wimbledon champion Petra Kvitova will be out of tennis for at least six months as she recovers from a knife attack - but should be able to resume her career.
text_ai: The Czech, 26, underwent surgery to tendons and nerves on her playing hand following the attack by an intruder at her home in Prostejov on Tuesday. The rehabilitation process will then be slow and gradual, starting with gentle movements to prevent stiffness before progressing to strength training. Dr Tomas Krejci, a sports medicine specialist who has worked with Czech tennis players, said the timeline was realistic. "The tendons in the hand are very delicate," he explained. "Even after they heal surgically, there is a risk of adhesions and reduced flexibility. A six-month minimum is appropriate for a return to high-level sport, and it could easily be longer." Kvitova's absence will be a significant blow to the women's tour. The left-hander has won 20 WTA titles, including Wimbledon in 2011 and 2014, and reached the US Open quarter-finals earlier this year. She is known for her fearless, attacking style and devastating forehand - a shot that will require particular care to rebuild. Messages of support have flooded in from the tennis world. Martina Navratilova, a fellow Czech and 18-time Grand Slam champion, said she was "shocked and heartbroken" by the news. "Petra is a fighter on and off the court," Navratilova wrote on Twitter. "I have no doubt she will come back stronger." The WTA Tour also issued a statement, calling the attack "deeply troubling" and offering full support for Kvitova's recovery. "Our thoughts are with Petra during this difficult time," the statement read. "We look forward to seeing her back on court when she is ready." Kvitova's team has not yet confirmed when she will be able to start practising, but early indications suggest she could miss the French Open in May and June. Wimbledon, where she has her fondest memories, remains a long shot for 2017. The tournament begins on 3 July. For now, the priority is simply healing. "The most important thing is that Petra is safe and that her hand will recover," Vondracek said. "Tennis will wait."

title: What will Peter Capaldi bring to the role of the 12th Doctor, and what does his casting mean for the show as it reaches its 50th anniversary?
text_ai: If you had kept an eye on the betting odds last week it was no great surprise when actor Peter Capaldi, the bookies' favourite, was revealed to be the new star of Doctor Who in a live TV special on Sunday. The announcement had been the worst-kept secret in television, but the manner of its unveiling—a live BBC One broadcast hosted by Zoë Ball, complete with a countdown and a slickly produced montage of previous Doctors—ensured the moment still carried weight. For the legions of fans who had watched the speculation unfold, the choice of Capaldi represented a deliberate shift in tone for a series approaching its half-century. Capaldi, 55 at the time of his casting, became the oldest actor to take on the role since William Hartnell, the First Doctor, who was 55 when the show first aired in 1963. That fact alone sent a clear signal: the show was not seeking a youthful heartthrob in the mould of his immediate predecessor, Matt Smith, or even David Tennant before him. Instead, the BBC was investing in gravitas, in a performer whose CV was thick with political thrillers and dark comedies—most famously his role as the sweary spin doctor Malcolm Tucker in *The Thick of It*, a character light-years away from the eccentric, grandfatherly alien he was about to inhabit. Speaking to the press immediately after the announcement, Capaldi addressed the obvious comparison. "Malcolm had a certain way with words, but he was a man of anger. The Doctor is a man of compassion, of curiosity, of joy. I think people will be surprised," he said. "I've been a fan of the show since I was a child. I used to hide behind the sofa. To be standing here, holding the sonic screwdriver—it's a dream." That fandom is genuine. Capaldi had previously appeared in the series—as Caecilius in the 2008 episode "The Fires of Pompeii," a role that required him to be rescued by the Tenth Doctor (David Tennant). It was a running joke among fans that his character's face would later be used by the Twelfth Doctor in a future regeneration, but the coincidence was merely that—a production team reuse of a mask, not a plot point. "I'm not going to play my own ancestor," Capaldi quipped, "but I suppose it's a nice bit of continuity." His casting also answered a question that had lingered since Tennant's departure in 2010: would the show ever choose an older actor again? Smith, at 26, was the youngest ever Doctor. His tenure was defined by youthful energy and a kind of alien eccentricity that played well with younger audiences. But as the 50th anniversary approached, showrunner Steven Moffat suggested the time was right for a "new dimension." "Peter brings a weight, a sense of history," Moffat said in the broadcast. "He's not just playing the Doctor—he's playing a man who has lived a thousand years. That age, that weariness, is in his eyes. And yet he also has a twinkle, a dark wit. I think fans will be thrilled." The reaction online was split, as it always is with such decisions. Some welcomed the return to a more seasoned Doctor, recalling the patriarchal warmth of Hartnell or the eccentric wisdom of Patrick Troughton's Second Doctor. Others wondered whether the show risked alienating the younger demographic it had so successfully courted under Smith and Tennant. But the BBC's controller of drama, Ben Stephenson, was emphatic: "Peter is one of Britain's finest actors. This is a statement of intent for the next chapter." The timing of the announcement—mere months before the 50th anniversary special, "The Day of the Doctor"—meant that Capaldi would not appear on screen until the 2013 Christmas special. Instead, viewers would first see his Doctor in a brief regeneration sequence following Matt Smith's final episode, "The Time of the Doctor." That arrangement allowed the production team to give Smith a fitting farewell while building anticipation for the new era. For Capaldi, the role represented a kind of apotheosis. Born in Glasgow, he had started his career in the 1980s as a punk musician (fronting the band Dreamboys) before moving into acting. His breakout TV role came in the 1990s sitcom *The Comic Strip Presents*, but it was his turn as a foul-mouthed government spin doctor in *The Thick of It* that made him a household name. He also directed the 2014 film *The Devil's Due*—though he set aside such ambitions for his stint in the TARDIS. "There's no one else I'd rather be spending my next few years with," he told the *Radio Times*. "The Doctor is the most thrilling, terrifying, wonderful character in television. And I get to be him." As the 50th anniversary approached, the announcement of Capaldi as the Twelfth Doctor did more than just fill a casting gap. It reaffirmed the show's central premise: that the Doctor is infinite, capable of renewal in any form. The 12th Doctor would be older, fiercer, with a touch of the Scottish brogue that had been missing since the Second Doctor (Patrick Troughton, who was also Scottish—though he suppressed his accent on screen). Capaldi promised a Doctor who would be "less approachable, more mercurial. He's had enough of being nice. He's a warrior, a traveller, a man of science—but he's also a man who has seen too much." In the months that followed, fans would catch glimpses of that promise: a whisper of the TARDIS doors, a silhouette in the regeneration glow. The 50th anniversary special itself featured three Doctors—Tennant, Smith, and John Hurt as the War Doctor—but no Capaldi. That was deliberate. The show wanted to honour its past while looking forward. And for millions of viewers, that forward-looking figure was a middle-aged Scot with a wild head of hair and eyes that had seen the stars. The question of what he would bring was still unanswered. But the betting odds, as they so often had, turned out to be right.

title: Two years ago the Philippines was entrenched in the bitterest of disputes with regional giant China, bringing a David v Goliath-style case against it over the South China Sea islands.
text_ai: Fast forward to present day: now, the Philippines wants Chinese cash. What happened? Well in part there is a genuine dilemma here for the Philippines. It's a small island country, stuck on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific, surrounded by much larger, powerful nations. Now, that same government is rolling out the red carpet for Chinese investment, infrastructure loans, and even security cooperation. The shift is stark—and for many observers, bewildering. The answer lies in a combination of economic necessity, geopolitical pragmatism, and a changing of the guard in Manila. When President Ferdinand Marcos Jr took office in 2022, he inherited an economy battered by the pandemic, with debt levels at record highs and a pressing need for foreign capital to fund everything from railways to ports. China, with its deep pockets and willingness to finance large-scale projects under its Belt and Road Initiative, was an obvious partner. But the turnaround is not simply about money. It is also about the Philippines’ enduring strategic dilemma: how to balance its security alliance with the United States—which remains its most important defence partner—against its growing economic dependence on its giant neighbour. For decades, Washington was the dominant external power in the region, but China’s rise has reshaped the playing field. The Philippines now finds itself in the unenviable position of needing both. In private, Philippine officials admit the calculus is brutal. “We cannot afford to antagonise China on every front,” one senior diplomat told the BBC on condition of anonymity. “We need their investments, their tourists, their market for our exports. But we also need America’s security umbrella. The art is in not being forced to choose.” This balancing act has produced a foreign policy that sometimes appears contradictory. In public, Marcos has been careful not to repeat the kind of fiery rhetoric against Beijing that marked the tenure of his predecessor, Rodrigo Duterte, who in 2016 won a landmark legal ruling from the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague ruling that China’s expansive claims in the South China Sea had no legal basis. That ruling was celebrated by Philippine nationalists, but Beijing has ignored it entirely, and the new administration has quietly downplayed it. Instead, Marcos has sought to open dialogue. In January 2023, he became the first Philippine president to visit China in six years, securing pledges of investment worth more than $22bn. The deals covered everything from solar farms to agricultural exports, and were accompanied by warm photo opportunities with President Xi Jinping. On the surface, it looked like a decisive pivot towards Beijing. Yet the reality is more nuanced. Even as Manila courts Chinese capital, it has also deepened its military ties with Washington. In 2023, the two allies announced an expansion of the Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement (EDCA), granting US forces access to four additional military bases in the Philippines—including sites in the northern provinces facing Taiwan. The move was widely seen as a hedge against any Chinese aggression, and it drew an angry response from Beijing, which accused the Philippines of “betraying the trust” built during Marcos’s visit. The tension between these two policy tracks is now acute. Some analysts argue that Marcos is attempting a classic “hedging” strategy—keeping both great powers close enough to benefit, but not so close that he alienates either. “It is a high-risk game,” says Dr Maria Tolentino, a Southeast Asian affairs expert at the University of the Philippines. “The Philippines is a very small player. It cannot afford to make a miscalculation. If it leans too far towards China, it loses its security guarantee from the US. If it leans too far towards the US, it risks provoking Chinese economic retaliation.” Economic retaliation is a real fear. China is the Philippines’ top trading partner and a major source of foreign direct investment. In recent years, Beijing has shown a willingness to use economic leverage to punish countries that challenge its interests—witness the temporary ban on Philippine bananas in 2020, widely seen as a response to Manila’s questioning of Chinese fishing rights in the South China Sea. A similar dynamic is playing out now with the Philippines’ neighbour Vietnam, which has also tried to balance Chinese investment with territorial disputes. Domestically, the shift has not been without critics. Nationalist lawmakers and civil society groups accuse Marcos of “selling out” the country’s sovereignty. The ruling from The Hague remains a powerful symbol in Philippine public opinion, and many feel the current administration has been too quick to set it aside for short-term financial gain. “We fought for that ruling. It was a historic victory for a small country against a giant,” said Senator Risa Hontiveros in a recent speech. “Now we are acting as if it never happened.” Yet Marcos’s supporters argue that the world has changed. The old certainties of the Cold War, when the US was the undisputed guardian of the liberal order, have given way to a multipolar reality. “We cannot afford the luxury of idealism,” said economic adviser Michael Ricafort. “The reality is that China is here to stay. We have to find a way to coexist.” That coexistence may already be taking shape beneath the surface. Behind closed doors, Philippine and Chinese officials are holding regular talks on maritime cooperation—fisheries, marine conservation, even joint resource exploration. These discussions remain confidential, but they hint at a more pragmatic approach than the public confrontation of earlier years. The question now is whether that pragmatism can survive the next flashpoint. In the Scarborough Shoal—a disputed reef inside the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone—Chinese vessels have been increasingly active, sparking low-level confrontations with Philippine coast guard ships. So far, both sides have avoided any serious escalation, but the potential for a spark is ever-present. For the Philippines, the path forward is narrow. It needs Chinese investment, but it also needs to protect its maritime claims. It wants American security, but without becoming a pawn in a larger US-China rivalry. And it must keep its own domestic politics from boiling over. “It is like walking a tightrope in a typhoon,” says Tolentino. “And no one knows how long the rope will hold.” In the end, the Philippines’ dilemma is also the region’s dilemma. As Asia’s smaller states watch Manila’s delicate manoeuvring, they are asking themselves the same question: in a world of giants, how does a David survive? The answer, it seems, is to keep talking—to everyone—and hope the rope does not snap.

"It shows Beijing's growing influence over the group's internal decision-making." The final session is scheduled for Friday, with ministers expected to hold bilateral meetings on the margins. No further joint declarations are anticipated.
prefix: The Asean summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, also involves counterparts from the US and China. US officials said China had lobbied members for the issue to be left out of the traditional closing statement. But China said "certain other countries" had interfered.

title: US rapper Kanye West has been taken to hospital following an emergency services call, media reports say.
text_ai: A police spokesperson told the BBC they had received a "disturbance call" on Monday afternoon, but did not name the singer. Police sources later confirmed to US media that the individual involved was the 47-year-old rapper, who has faced intense scrutiny in recent months over a series of erratic public statements and social media posts. In February, he faced widespread backlash after posting a series of antisemitic comments on social media, leading to the suspension of his X (formerly Twitter) account and the termination of several business partnerships, including with Adidas and Gap. Last October, West sparked international outrage when he praised Adolf Hitler during an interview on the right-wing conspiracy channel InfoWars and said he saw "good things" about the Nazi leader. The rapper has also been open about his struggles with bipolar disorder, a condition he first disclosed in 2018. In a series of tweets at the time, he wrote: "I have bipolar disorder. Monday's incident comes just weeks after West returned to the public eye with a surprise album release, "Vultures", which debuted at number one on the Billboard 200 chart. However, his promotional appearances were marked by rambling monologues and confrontational remarks, including an attack on Jewish people during a listening party in Miami. Fans and industry insiders have expressed concern about his wellbeing, with several calling on him to seek professional help. "Kanye is a genius but he's also a human being," said music journalist Karen Civil in an interview with the BBC. "He needs support, not more pressure." Police said no arrests were made and that the investigation into the original disturbance call had been closed. West's wife, Bianca Censori, was reportedly with him at the time of the incident, but did not accompany him to hospital. The couple were married in a private ceremony in January 2023. As of late Monday evening, no further updates had been released on West's condition or when he might be discharged. The BBC has approached representatives of the rapper for further comment. In 2016, he was admitted to the UCLA Medical Center for psychiatric evaluation after cancelling the remaining dates of his Saint Pablo tour. Some peers have offered public support, while others have criticised West's behaviour as harmful and dangerous. Rapper Diddy, who has known West for decades, wrote on Instagram: "Praying for my brother Ye. We need you healthy." Kanye West – an icon, a provocateur, a man in crisis – remains in hospital, his next steps uncertain.

title: A series of high street retailers' ethical audits failed to spot one of their suppliers was employing "a slave workforce", a jury has been told.
text_ai: Staff at Kozee Sleep, which supplied retailers including John Lewis and Next, were paid as little as Â£10 a day. Company owner Mohammed Rafiq and employees Mohammed Patel and Mohammed Dadhiwala are accused of conspiracy to traffic individuals within the UK. All three men deny any wrongdoing in their trial at Leeds Crown Court. The prosecution alleges that between 2017 and 2019, Kozee Sleep operated a "modern-day slavery" operation, luring vulnerable workers from India and Pakistan with promises of well-paid jobs and accommodation. Instead, jurors were told, they were forced to work up to 18-hour shifts in cramped conditions, sleeping on mattresses in overcrowded houses, and were subjected to threats and intimidation. Prosecutor David Gordon KC told the court: "These men were not employees; they were commodities, bought and sold for the profit of the defendants." One alleged victim said he was "terrified" to leave the factory, believing he would be arrested without documents. The ethical audits conducted by the retailers – which included high-street names such as John Lewis and Next – were described as "superficial" and "easily bypassed". The court heard that Kozee Sleep would present a "show workforce" on the days of inspections, made up of workers paid a normal wage and given proper living conditions, while the exploited employees were hidden elsewhere. John Lewis and Next have both issued statements expressing shock and regret. A John Lewis spokesperson said: "We have rigorous ethical trading standards and are deeply distressed by these allegations. We have suspended all orders with Kozee Sleep and are cooperating fully with the investigation." Next similarly stated it had "zero tolerance" for such practices and had terminated its contract. The trial, expected to last up to eight weeks, continues.

title: Ulster ran in six tries as they moved to within five points of fourth-placed Scarlets in the Pro12 by securing a bonus-point win over Zebre in Parma.
text_ai: Chris Henry and Ruan Pienaar crossed for Ulster but Guglielmo Palazzani touched down for a resurgent Zebre, who went in trailing 14-10 at the interval. Stuart Olding, Jacob Stockdale, Robbie Diack and David Busby ran in second-half tries, Mattia Bellini for Zebre. Ulster have now earned bonus-point wins from their last three Pro12 matches. The victory extended Ulster’s winning run in the league to four matches and lifted them to within five points of the Scarlets, who occupy the final play-off berth. With seven rounds remaining, Les Kiss’s side have reignited their challenge for a top-four finish after a mid-season slump that saw them win just three of eight fixtures between October and December. Ulster’s dominance was not reflected in the scoreboard at half-time. They had enjoyed the better of the early exchanges, with Henry burrowing over from close range after a relentless spell of pressure inside the Zebre 22. Pienaar added the conversion and then dropped a clever cross-field kick that nearly resulted in a second try for Stockdale. But the Italian side, coached by former Ulster assistant Michael Bradley, refused to buckle. Palazzani’s try, finished off after a neat loop play with Carlo Canna, kept them in touch and exposed some frailties in Ulster’s defensive alignment. The visitors’ scrum, which had come under scrutiny in recent weeks, held firm in the first half, but their lineout malfunctioned on several occasions, allowing Zebre to clear their lines. The Irish province also struggled to contain the physicality of the home pack, with lock George Biagi and flanker Maxime Mbanda making significant inroads. After the interval, Ulster ratcheted up the tempo. Olding, playing at inside centre, showcased his footwork and vision to slice through a gap and score under the posts. Pienaar converted, and then Stockdale, the 20-year-old winger who has been a revelation this season, finished a sweeping move from 40 metres out, stepping inside the covering defender to touch down. Diack, the veteran back-row forward, added the bonus-point try when he drove over from a maul, and Busby, a late replacement for the injured Andrew Trimble, crossed in the final moments after a slick handling sequence. Zebre’s solitary second-half score came from Bellini, who gathered a clever kick from Canna and sprinted clear. The Italian side also had a try from winger Kayle van Zyl disallowed for a forward pass, while Ulster replacement John Andrew was sin-binned in the closing stages for a dangerous tackle. Ulster’s head coach Kiss praised his side’s resilience but acknowledged there were areas to improve. “We knew Zebre would put up a fight – they always do at home,” he told BBC Sport. “We showed good character to come out after half-time and get the bonus point. But we need to be more clinical. We left a few tries out there. The lineout was a bit off, and we gave away too many penalties. Against the better sides, that will cost you.” The result leaves Ulster fifth in the standings with 47 points, five behind the Scarlets (52) and seven adrift of third-placed Leinster (54). Glasgow Warriors lead the table with 60 points, while defending champions Connacht are sixth on 45. The race for the play-offs is intensifying, and Ulster’s run-in includes a trip to Leinster and a home fixture against the Scarlets – matches that will likely decide their fate. Zebre, meanwhile, remain bottom of the table with just three wins all season. Yet there were positives for head coach Bradley. “Our first half was as good as we’ve played this year,” he said. “We matched Ulster physically and created chances. But we made too many individual errors in the second half. Against a team of Ulster’s quality, you cannot afford to do that.” Ulster’s director of rugby, Les Kiss, also highlighted the importance of building momentum. “We’ve had some tough weeks, but the boys are starting to play with confidence again,” he said. “We have a big block of games coming up. If we can keep winning, we’ll give ourselves a chance.” The victory was Ulster’s third successive bonus-point haul, following wins over Treviso and the Dragons. They have scored 19 tries in that period, a statistic that underlines their attacking potency. The return of key players from injury, including centre Stuart McCloskey and lock Franco van der Merwe, has added depth to the squad. Next up for Ulster is a home fixture against Edinburgh, a team just two points behind them in the table. A win would further strengthen their play-off credentials. Zebre travel to Cardiff Blues, looking to end a run of five consecutive defeats. In Parma, the Stadio Sergio Lanfranchi crowd witnessed an entertaining contest that ebbed and flowed. Ulster’s first-half struggles were a reminder that no fixture in the Pro12 can be taken for granted, but their second-half surge demonstrated the quality that has made them perennial contenders. With the Scarlets within striking distance, the Northern Irish province have every reason to believe a top-four finish is still within reach.

title: A lover of fast cars, vintage wine, trout fishing and game farming, South Africa's Deputy President Cyril Ramaphosa is one of the country's wealthiest politicians with a net worth of about $450m (£340m).
text_ai: Once a leading trade unionist, he became the symbol of black capitalism in South Africa after the African National Congress (ANC) came to power at the end of white minority rule in 1994. But business was never his passion. His first love was politics and he harboured ambitions to become the deputy of Nelson Mandela, South Africa's first black president. That ambition, however, would take more than two decades to be fully realised. For much of the period between the end of apartheid and his eventual ascension to the presidency in 2018, Mr Ramaphosa was a figure of immense influence but always seen as something of a perennial bridesmaid — a consummate dealmaker and negotiator, but never quite the man at the top of the ticket. The roots of his political career lie deep in the anti-apartheid struggle. Born in 1952 in Soweto, a sprawling township on the edge of Johannesburg, he studied law at the University of the North (now University of Limpopo) before joining the Black People's Convention, a black consciousness movement. His early activism saw him detained without trial in 1974 for organising pro-Frelimo rallies in support of Mozambique's independence. But it was his leadership of the National Union of Mineworkers (NUM), which he founded in 1982, that first brought him to national prominence. Under his guidance, the NUM grew into the largest and most militant trade union in South Africa, with more than 300,000 members. He led a massive strike in 1987 — the longest in South African history — that shook the mining industry and the apartheid state to its core. The strike ultimately failed to achieve all its demands, but it cemented his reputation as a formidable negotiator and a strategist of extraordinary patience. It was a quality that would define his later career in both business and politics. When the ANC was unbanned in 1990, Mr Ramaphosa was a natural choice to serve as its secretary-general. In this role, he played a pivotal part in the negotiations that ended apartheid, forging a close working relationship with the government's chief negotiator, Roelf Meyer. Together they crafted the interim constitution that paved the way for the country's first democratic elections in 1994. Many expected Mr Ramaphosa to be named deputy president under Nelson Mandela. But Mandela chose Thabo Mbeki instead, a decision that blindsided Ramaphosa and sent him into what became known as his "wilderness years". It was a bitter blow. Rather than languish in political obscurity, however, Mr Ramaphosa turned to the corporate world with characteristic pragmatism. He secured a seat on the board of the New African Investments Limited (Nail), one of the first black-owned companies listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange, and quickly built a formidable business empire. His holdings came to span everything from McDonald's franchises in South Africa to a platinum mining firm, a stake in the country's largest mobile phone operator, and a sprawling game reserve called Ntaba Nyoni. As his wealth grew, so did his influence. He was appointed chairman of the board at the South African diamond giant De Beers, and later served as a director of the London-listed mining company Lonmin — a position that would later come under intense scrutiny. His personal fortune, estimated at more than $450 million, made him not just the richest ANC politician but one of the wealthiest individuals in the country. He cultivated an image of rugged luxury — often photographed in safari gear at his game farm, or inspecting his prize-winning cattle. He had become, in the words of one biographer, the "capitalist of the struggle". Yet he never abandoned his political ambitions entirely. While critics accused him of becoming too close to white corporate power, he remained a powerful behind-the-scenes figure in the ANC, using his business network to fund party activities and maintain alliances. When the global financial crisis of 2008 struck, and then the scandal-ridden presidency of Jacob Zuma damaged the ANC's reputation, calls for Mr Ramaphosa's return grew louder. He was elected ANC deputy president in 2012, a position that made him the country's deputy president under Zuma. But the tragedy that would define his return to frontline politics occurred just months after his election, in the countryside near his game farm. At the Marikana platinum mine, 34 striking miners were shot dead by police — the worst single use of force by South African security forces since the end of apartheid. Mr Ramaphosa, who had been a director of Lonmin at the time, faced intense scrutiny over his role. Emails emerged in which he had described the strikers as "dastardly criminals" and called for "concomitant action" against them. He denied any responsibility for the police response, but the Marikana bloodshed haunted his political rise. Despite this, he successfully positioned himself as the clean pair of hands needed to rescue the ANC from the corruption and stagnation of the Zuma era. In December 2017, he narrowly defeated Nkosazana Dlamini-Zuma, the former president's ex-wife, in a bitterly contested election for ANC president. A few months later, in February 2018, Zuma was forced to resign, and Mr Ramaphosa became President of South Africa. His presidency has been a study in cautious reform. He promised to root out corruption — a pledge that earned him the nickname "Cyril the Savior" among supporters — but he has faced enormous resistance from factional allies of Zuma within the ANC. His economic agenda, centred on attracting foreign investment and kick-starting stalled growth, has been hampered by a struggling state power utility, Eskom, and the structural damage wrought by years of state capture. On the international stage, he has been a steady if unflashy presence, steering a foreign policy that maintains South Africa's traditional non-aligned stance. He has sought to balance ties with China and the West, while defending the country's interest in multilateral forums. Domestically, he has continued to enjoy a reputation for personal probity, but the taint of Marikana has never fully receded. In 2022, his own party criticised his response to a scandal involving the alleged looting of his farm — known as the "Phala Phala affair" — when hundreds of thousands of dollars in foreign currency were reported stolen from his property. He has denied any wrongdoing. Now 71, Mr Ramaphosa remains a figure of contrasts: the trade unionist who became a billionaire, the negotiator who never gave up on his political dream, and the reformer who inherited a broken party. His legacy is still being written. But few doubt that his journey from Soweto to the Union Buildings in Pretoria, via the boardrooms of Johannesburg and the mines of the Vaal, has been one of the most remarkable in modern African politics.

title: Ulster moved to the top of the Pro12 table as a late Paddy Jackson penalty secured victory over the Dragons.
text_ai: Jackson's 78th-minute kick put Ulster ahead for the first time in the game. An Adam Hughes try helped the lively Dragons lead 10-0 before Sean Reidy's score cut the margin to 10-7 by half-time at Kingspan Stadium. The Dragons emerged from the interval with renewed purpose, and it was the visitors who struck first in the second period. A scrum penalty on the Ulster 22 allowed fly-half Angus O'Brien to slot a straightforward kick between the posts, extending the Dragons' lead to 13-7. The Kingspan Stadium crowd, which had been buoyant after Reidy's try before the break, fell quiet as the Welsh side began to control territory. Ulster's response was immediate but lacked the finishing touch. A series of phases on the Dragons' line were repelled by a dogged defence, with lock Cory Hill making a crucial turnover. However, the home side's pressure eventually told. On the hour mark, a clever loop move between centres Stuart McCloskey and Luke Marshall created space out wide. Full-back Louis Ludik, on as a substitute, burst through a gap to score near the posts. But fly-half Jackson's conversion attempt drifted wide, leaving the score at 13-12 to the Dragons. The miss seemed to galvanise the visitors, who re-established their territorial advantage. O'Brien had a chance to stretch the lead further when Ulster were penalised for offside, but his long-range effort from 45 metres drifted just left of the posts. The let-off gave Ulster new life, and they began to press again. As the clock ticked into the final 10 minutes, the tension inside the stadium was palpable. Ulster earned a scrum on the Dragons' 10-metre line, and after a powerful shove, scrum-half John Cooney whipped the ball to Jackson. The fly-half probed the line, but the Dragons' defence held firm. Then, with just two minutes remaining, the crucial moment arrived. Substitute forward Rodney Ah You went off his feet at a ruck, and referee George Clancy penalised the Dragons. Jackson, calm under pressure, stepped up from 35 metres and slotted the kick smoothly through the posts to put Ulster ahead for the first time in the game. The home crowd erupted, and although the Dragons had one final chance from the restart, Ulster secured the restart and kicked the ball dead to seal a hard-fought victory. Speaking to BBC Sport NI after the match, Ulster head coach Dan McFarland praised his side's resilience. "We were not at our best for long periods, but the character the players showed to stay in the fight was outstanding," he said. "Paddy's kick was ice-cold, and that's why he's one of the best in the business." Dragons director of rugby Dean Ryan was left to rue missed opportunities. "We dominated the first half and had chances after the break to put the game away," he told BBC Sport Wales. "But we let them back into it, and you can't afford to give a side like Ulster that kind of time and space. We are disappointed with the result but the performance showed good signs." The win moves Ulster to the top of the Pro14 table, above Munster on points difference, with both sides having played nine games. The result also extended Ulster's unbeaten run at Kingspan Stadium to six matches in all competitions. Meanwhile, the Dragons remain in ninth place, but with a gritty performance that will give them hope for the remainder of the campaign. For Ulster, attention now turns to a crucial interprovincial derby against Leinster next weekend – a fixture that will test their title credentials. If they can show the same fighting spirit they displayed against the Dragons, they will be a formidable opponent for any side in the league.

title: A report has found it has become "more difficult" for Scots students to get a place at a university in Scotland.
text_ai: Public spending watchdog Audit Scotland has carried out its first major review of higher education. It detailed "significant challenges" facing the sector. The report highlighted a 6% real terms cut in the amount of cash universities receive from the Scottish Funding Council (SFC). The findings come as Scottish universities grapple with a perfect storm of rising costs, growing student demand, and a funding model that has remained largely unchanged for years. The report warns that the real-terms cut in SFC funding – which fell from £1.17bn in 2019-20 to £1.1bn in 2023-24 when adjusted for inflation – is now beginning to bite in ways that directly affect access for home students. “This is not simply a question of belt-tightening,” said Audit Scotland’s lead investigator for higher education, Dr. Fiona MacLeod. “The reduced purchasing power of SFC grants is forcing institutions to make difficult choices about where to allocate finite resources. And increasingly, those choices are narrowing the path for Scottish-domiciled applicants.” The squeeze is particularly acute given that the number of school-leavers in Scotland is projected to rise by 8% over the next decade, according to the latest Scottish Government population figures. Yet the number of funded places for Scottish students has not kept pace. Universities Scotland, the representative body for the sector, estimates that for every 10 qualified applicants from Scotland, only about eight are offered a place at a Scottish institution – a gap that has widened from roughly one in 10 a decade ago. “The competition for places has intensified markedly,” said Professor Alastair Sim, director of Universities Scotland. “We are seeing students with outstanding Highers – including multiple A grades – being turned away from their first-choice universities because there simply aren’t enough funded places to accommodate them. This is deeply concerning for a nation that prides itself on educational opportunity.” The report highlights that the 6% real-terms cut in SFC funding is compounded by the freeze on home tuition fees, which remain at £1,820 per year for Scottish-domiciled students studying in Scotland – a rate set in 2008. Since then, inflation has eroded the real value of that fee by more than 40%. Universities are forbidden from increasing it without government permission, meaning they must absorb the shortfall from other income sources, including international student fees and research grants. However, the report notes that international recruitment – which has provided a vital revenue stream for many universities – is itself facing new headwinds. The UK government’s tightening of visa rules and the removal of the right for most international students to bring dependants have already begun to slow application numbers from key markets such as Nigeria and India. “This creates a double risk,” the report warns. “Reduced international income makes universities more reliant on SFC grants, but those grants are shrinking in real terms.” The implications for students are stark. Audit Scotland found that the proportion of Scottish-domiciled students entering higher education within one year of leaving school has fallen slightly, from 41.2% in 2019 to 40.6% in 2023. While that decline is modest, it represents a reversal of a long-term upward trend and masks wider disparities. Students from the most deprived backgrounds are disproportionately affected: their participation rate stands at just 27%, compared to 51% for those from the most affluent areas. “The ambition to widen access is colliding with the reality of reduced funding,” said Dr. MacLeod. “Universities are being asked to do more with less. They are expected to maintain high-quality teaching and research, keep class sizes manageable, and expand outreach programmes for disadvantaged students – all while facing a cut in their core grants. Something has to give.” The report identifies several coping strategies universities have adopted. Some have increased the number of students admitted through clearing or late-entry routes without additional SFC funding, effectively operating over their allocated intake. Others have expanded partnership arrangements with colleges, allowing students to start degrees at further education institutions before transferring to university. A growing number have also cut academic posts or merged departments to save money. But these measures come with risks. The report notes that students entering via unconventional pathways may not receive the same level of support or face higher dropout rates. It also warns that the growing use of over-recruitment could strain resources and damage institutional finances if the Scottish Government later penalises universities for exceeding their intake targets. The Scottish Government’s response has been cautious. A spokesperson said: “We recognise the financial pressures on the higher education sector and remain committed to providing the best possible opportunities for students. Our funding settlement for universities in 2024-25 includes an additional £15m for widening access and mental health support. However, we must also take a balanced approach to public finances, which are under severe strain across the board.” Critics argue that the government’s position is inconsistent. The recent budget announced a £100m increase for the Scottish Funding Council, but much of that is earmarked for further education and skills training, not universities. Moreover, when adjusted for inflation, the total SFC budget for higher education is still 4% lower than it was in 2019-20. Labour’s shadow education secretary, Michael Marra, described the report as “a damning indictment of the SNP government’s management of higher education”. He said: “For years, the government has boasted about free tuition, but that boast rings hollow when students cannot get a place at all. Free tuition only means something if there is a seat in the lecture hall.” The Scottish Liberal Democrats called for an immediate review of university funding, with leader Alex Cole-Hamilton saying: “We cannot continue to squeeze our universities until they break. This report shows that the current model is unsustainable. The government must either increase funding or allow universities to adjust fees in a controlled way.” However, the report also acknowledges the political sensitivity of the tuition fee issue. The SNP’s policy of free tuition for Scottish students has long been a flagship commitment, and any move to raise fees would be intensely controversial. But the report hints that something may have to give if the funding gap is not closed. “The status quo is not an option,” said Dr. MacLeod. “Without additional investment from the Scottish Government, or a relaxation of the fee cap, universities will be forced to make even more difficult choices. That could mean fewer places for Scottish students, larger class sizes, fewer course options, or a greater reliance on international students – all of which carry their own risks.” The report also examines the impact on student experience. Staff-to-student ratios have worsened across the sector, with the average now standing at one academic per 18.5 students, up from one per 16.8 in 2015. This has been linked to declining student satisfaction scores in national surveys, particularly around teaching quality and feedback. Meanwhile, the cost-of-living crisis is adding to the pressure. Students are struggling with higher rent, energy bills, and food costs. The report notes that the student support system – including bursaries and loans – has not kept pace with inflation, leaving many reliant on part-time work or parental support. “The whole system is being stretched,” said Professor Sarah Davidson, principal of the University of the Highlands and Islands. “We are seeing more students arriving with complex needs, both academic and pastoral. We are doing our best, but without adequate funding, something has to give. No university can do everything.” The report concludes with a series of recommendations. It calls on the Scottish Government to set out a clear, long-term funding plan for higher education; on the SFC to develop more transparent criteria for allocating places; and on universities to improve forecasting and financial planning. It also urges a national debate about the purpose and funding of higher education. “This is not just about money,” said Dr. MacLeod. “It is about the kind of society Scotland wants to be. Higher education is a gateway to opportunity, to innovation, to prosperity. If that gateway is narrowing, we will all feel the consequences.”

title: A review of the New York police's recent chokehold cases has found discipline recommended by a complaints board was very often not followed.
text_ai: In seven out of 10 cases studied, a prosecutor or the police commissioner imposed lesser punishments on officers who used chokeholds, which are banned The report is in response to the death of Eric Garner, who died after being placed in a chokehold by police. and the Civilian Complaint Review Board (CCRB) had recommended harsher measures. The review, released on Tuesday, examined more than 200 cases between 2010 and 2016, a period that included Garner's death in July 2014. The findings have reignited debate over police accountability in New York, where the use of chokeholds has been prohibited since 1993. The report noted that in 70% of instances where the CCRB found officers had used unauthorised neck restraints, its recommendations for discipline — ranging from dismissal to suspension — were rejected or significantly reduced by the police department or the district attorney's office. In many cases, officers faced no internal punishment at all. The review also found that the process for investigating and adjudicating such complaints was often opaque, with delays of months or even years. "Too often, the system that is supposed to hold police accountable has failed," said the report's lead author, Susan Lerner, executive director of Common Cause New York, a government watchdog group. The death of Eric Garner, an unarmed black man who died after being placed in a chokehold by Officer Daniel Pantaleo, sparked widespread protests and calls for reform. A grand jury declined to indict Pantaleo in 2014, and the officer was not fired until 2019 — more than five years after the incident. The new review suggests this pattern of leniency was not an isolated case. Civil liberties groups have seized on the findings. "This confirms what we have long known: that the system is rigged to protect officers, not the public," said Donna Lieberman, executive director of the New York Civil Liberties Union. She called for more robust civilian oversight and legislative changes to ensure that discipline recommended by independent boards is binding. The New York Police Department (NYPD) defended its record, arguing that each case is assessed individually. "The NYPD takes allegations of misconduct seriously," a spokesperson said in a statement. "Decisions on discipline are made based on the totality of evidence, not solely on a board recommendation." title: Up to 60 million people in Pakistan are at risk from the deadly chemical arsenic, according to a new analysis of water supplies.

Replacement scrum-half Dan Robson darted over from close range after a quickly-taken penalty, and Josh Bassett added a fifth try in the corner as the visitors ran in 24 unanswered points to seal a commanding 58-15 victory. It was a scoreline that flattered the visitors, but one that underlined their clinical edge when faced with a depleted opposition. Leicester, however, will point to a harsh decision from referee Matthew Carley, who deemed Ford's challenge as reckless rather than a genuine attempt to intercept. Director of rugby Geordan Murphy said afterwards: "It's a tough one to take. I thought George was trying to compete for the ball, and the contact was minimal. But we have to accept the decision and move on. The game is what it is." Wasps counterpart Dai Young praised his side's composure. "We executed our game plan superbly," he said. "To come here to Welford Road and win by that margin, especially given the history, is a massive statement from the group." The victory lifts Wasps to fifth in the Premiership table, while Leicester remain rooted in the bottom half after a fifth defeat in seven league matches. For the visitors, it was a first win at the home of the Tigers in 11 years, ending a run of 10 consecutive home defeats in the fixture. The result will also bolster Wasps' confidence as they prepare for a European Challenge Cup clash next weekend. Leicester, meanwhile, face an anxious wait over Ford's potential suspension, with the club likely to appeal the red card.

title: The strikes that forced Nigeria's government to restore some of the withdrawn fuel subsidy have been described as "Nigeria's Harmattan".
text_ai: They did not last as long as the Arab Spring - but Africa's most populous country and biggest oil producer will never be the same again. Nigerians have long decried their leadership but now young, well-educated groups have organised themselves on social networking sites such as Twitter - using #OccupyNigeria - to force President Goodluck Jonathan to back down. The concessions came after 10 days of nationwide strikes and protests that paralysed Africa’s largest economy, shutting banks, shops, and petrol stations, and bringing cities like Lagos, Abuja, and Port Harcourt to a standstill. But while Mr Jonathan’s U-turn on Monday – restoring a partial subsidy on petrol and diesel, and slashing the price from about 150 naira ($0.95; £0.60) to 97 naira per litre – was hailed as a victory by the #OccupyNigeria movement, analysts say the underlying crisis remains dangerously unresolved. “This is not a revolution, but a warning shot – a Harmattan that has cleared the air but not changed the season,” said Dr. Adebayo Olukoshi, a political economist at the Nigerian Institute of International Affairs in Lagos. “The government blinked, but the fundamental challenge of how to subsidise a population of 160 million when oil revenues are volatile and corruption is endemic has not been addressed.” The Harmattan metaphor is apt. Just as the dry, dusty harmattan winds sweep across West Africa each year, obscuring visibility and disrupting daily life, the protests stripped away the veneer of stability that had long masked Nigeria’s deep-seated grievances: a ruling class that spends billions on itself while ordinary people struggle to afford transport, food, and medicine; a president widely seen as weak and indecisive; and an economy that remains dangerously dependent on crude oil – which accounts for about 80% of government revenues but employs less than 1% of the workforce. For many young Nigerians, the fuel subsidy was not just an economic issue but a symbol of the state’s failure to deliver on its basic promises. The government had argued that removing the subsidy – which cost an estimated $8bn (£5bn) a year – would free up funds for infrastructure, education, and healthcare. But critics pointed to a litany of corruption scandals, including the disappearance of $6bn in fuel subsidy payments between 2009 and 2011, and said the savings would simply be stolen. “They told us the subsidy was unsustainable, but they continue to pay themselves huge salaries, fly in private jets, and build luxury homes for senators,” said Oby Ezekwesili, a former education minister who resigned in 2007 over the government’s failure to tackle graft. “The young people who took to the streets are not just angry about petrol prices – they are angry about a system that has betrayed them.” The protests were also notable for their demographic composition. Unlike previous labour-led strikes, which were often dominated by union activists and the urban poor, the #OccupyNigeria movement was propelled by university graduates, professionals, and the so-called “alphabet generation” – Nigerians who have grown up with mobile phones, social media, and a globalised sense of entitlement. Many of them had voted for Mr Jonathan in the 2011 elections, expecting him to bring change, but had become disillusioned by his administration’s lack of vision. “We are not just agitators – we are the future of this country,” said Chika Nwosu, a 28-year-old architect who helped organise protests in Lagos. “We don’t want handouts; we want accountability. We want a government that respects its own laws. And we now know that if we come together on Twitter, we can make them listen.” The government’s response was initially heavy-handed. Police used tear gas, water cannons, and in several instances, live ammunition to disperse crowds. At least 10 people were reported killed, according to human rights groups, and hundreds more were arrested. But as the strikes dragged on, and as international pressure mounted – with the United States and the United Nations urging restraint – Mr Jonathan appeared to lose his nerve. His decision to partially restore the subsidy, announced in a late-night televised address, was seen by many as a tactical retreat. But it also exposed the deep divisions within his own administration. Vice-President Namadi Sambo was reportedly among those who argued for a climb-down, fearing the unrest could spiral into a broader anti-government movement that would destabilise the country ahead of the 2015 elections. “The president is in a very difficult position,” said Dr. Olukoshi. “He cannot keep the subsidy forever – the arithmetic doesn’t add up. But every time he tries to remove it, he faces the wrath of a population that has no social safety net. This is not just a Nigerian problem; it is a challenge faced by many oil-dependent states in Africa and beyond. But Nigeria’s sheer size and the sophistication of its civil society means the stakes are higher.” For now, the immediate crisis has passed. Petrol queues have shortened, and the streets of Lagos are once again clogged with the usual traffic. But the #OccupyNigeria movement has not disbanded – its leaders say they will continue to campaign for better governance, anti-corruption measures, and an end to the “predatory” politics that have defined the country since independence. “This is just the beginning,” said Nwosu. “The Harmattan has swept through, but it will return. And next time, we may not be so willing to accept a partial victory.” What remains to be seen is whether President Jonathan – or his successor – will learn the lesson of the past two weeks: that in the age of social media and mass mobilisation, ignoring the voices of the young is no longer an option. Nigeria’s Harmattan may have passed, but its winds have changed the political landscape forever.

title: A man who admitted raping a 12-year-old girl has walked free from court.
text_ai: Daniel Cieslak, 21, had believed the girl - who he met in a taxi queue in Edinburgh in July 2015 - was 16. He burst into tears when police later revealed her true age. The judge, Lady Scott, said she was taking the "wholly exceptional decision" not to sentence Cieslak. She told him: "You are a young man of good character who has shown genuine remorse. This was an isolated incident, and I accept you genuinely believed the girl was 16." The judge added that a custodial sentence would "ruin" Cieslak's life and that the "public interest" would not be served by sending him to prison. Instead, he was ordered to carry out 225 hours of unpaid work and placed on the sex offenders register for three years. Cieslak, a Polish national who had been living in Edinburgh, had pleaded guilty to rape at an earlier hearing. The court heard he met the young girl while waiting for a taxi in the early hours of 18 July 2015. They began chatting, and he said she told him she was 16. She was in fact 12. The pair later went to a flat, where the rape took place. The case has sparked fresh debate over the law on underage sex and the defence of mistaken belief about a child's age. Under Scottish law, the age of consent is 16. However, the law also recognises that a person may genuinely believe a child is older, and that can be a mitigating factor in sentencing. But the Crown Office, which prosecutes cases in Scotland, said it was "considering the sentence carefully" and that it "noted the judge's remarks". Victim support groups have condemned the decision. Sandy Brindley, national co-ordinator of Rape Crisis Scotland, said: "This sends out a deeply troubling message that if you rape a child, you can walk free. "The focus should be on the victim, not on the offender. A 12-year-old girl was raped. That is the starting point. That should be the focus of the court's attention. "We are very concerned that the judge appears to have placed significant weight on the fact that the offender believed the girl was 16. But the law is clear: the age of consent is 16. And a child cannot consent to sex. The fact that she was 12, not 16, is the issue." The girl's family have also expressed their dismay. In a statement released through police, they said they were "sickened" by the sentence, adding: "Our daughter's life has been changed forever, and the person who did this to her is walking free. "We feel let down by the justice system." Cieslak's defence lawyer, Ian Duguid QC, argued that his client had been "naive" and that the incident had left him "deeply traumatised". Mr Duguid said: "He has no previous convictions. He is a young man who came to Scotland to work and build a life. He has shown genuine remorse from the moment he discovered the true age of the girl. "This is not a case of a predatory older man targeting a child. He believed she was 16. That belief was not unreasonable given the circumstances." The court heard that when police arrested Cieslak, he broke down and repeatedly said: "I thought she was 16. I did not know. I am sorry." The judge also noted that the girl had been "sexually active" and had told Cieslak she was 16. The court was told she had previously been the subject of a child protection investigation. Lady Scott said: "This is a wholly exceptional case. I have to balance the need to protect the public with the need to treat you fairly. "You were 20 at the time, she told you she was 16. You have no previous convictions, no history of sexual offending, and you have shown genuine remorse. "A custodial sentence would be disproportionate. It would ruin your life, and I do not believe it would serve any useful purpose." The case has also prompted questions about the law on mistaken belief. Professor James Chalmers, a legal expert at the University of Glasgow, said: "The defence of reasonable mistake as to age is not available in the same way as it might be in some other jurisdictions. "But it can be a factor in sentencing. The judge has to decide whether the offender's belief was genuinely held and reasonable in the circumstances. "In this case, the judge clearly felt it was. But many will argue that the fact the girl was 12 should outweigh any such consideration." The Scottish Government said it was "aware of the case and the concerns it has raised" but that it "would be inappropriate to comment on individual sentencing decisions". However, a spokesperson added: "The law on sexual offences is clear. Anyone who has sex with a child under 16 commits a serious offence. Sentencing is a matter for the independent judiciary." Cieslak left the court without speaking to reporters, his face hidden behind a coat. He is now subject to supervision by social workers and must comply with the terms of the community payback order. If he fails to complete the unpaid work, he could be recalled to court and resentenced. The case has reignited a wider debate about how the legal system handles cases where the victim is a child but the offender claims they did not know. Rape Crisis Scotland has called for a review of the law, saying it places too much emphasis on the offender's perception and not enough on the realities of child sexual abuse. Ms Brindley said: "The message from this case is that if you rape a child and you can make a plausible case that you thought they were older, you may escape a prison sentence. "That is not acceptable. The age of consent exists to protect children. It should be enforced."

title: A policy group run by the Department of Education (DE) has criticised the impact of academic selection.
text_ai: The department's strategic planning and policy development forum also criticised a number of the department's policies for promoting inclusion. Academic selection concentrated "lower-achieving pupils, often from socially deprived areas, into a small group of 11-16 schools", the report said. It added that NI's formal school leaving age should rise from 16 to 19. The report, which was drawn up by the Department of Education's (DE) internal strategic planning and policy development forum, warns that the current system is entrenching inequality and failing to equip young people with the skills needed for a modern economy. It proposes that the compulsory school leaving age should be increased from 16 to 19, with pupils required to remain in education or training until they have attained a Level 2 qualification—equivalent to five good GCSEs—or reached 19, whichever comes first. "A significant minority of young people leave school at 16 without the essential skills to thrive in employment or further learning," the document states. "Raising the participation age would ensure that every young person has the opportunity to build a strong foundation for their future, reducing the number of NEETs (not in education, employment or training) and addressing long-term social and economic costs." The forum's analysis points to stark disparities in outcomes between grammar and secondary schools. It notes that the current transfer test system, used by most grammar schools, "disproportionately benefits pupils from more affluent backgrounds" and "consigns a large cohort of lower-achieving pupils, often from socially deprived areas, into a small group of 11-16 schools that struggle to attract high-quality teachers and adequate resources." The criticism extends beyond academic selection to several of the department's own policies. The report argues that initiatives intended to promote inclusion—such as the Common Funding Formula and the Entitlement Framework—have been "insufficiently robust" in counteracting market-driven pressures on schools. "Rather than fostering collaboration, existing funding mechanisms incentivise competition between schools for the highest-achieving pupils," it says. "This undermines the principle of equality of opportunity and perpetuates a two-tier system." The forum also takes aim at the DE's own Special Educational Needs (SEN) framework, describing it as "fragmented" and "under-resourced". It urges a fundamental review of how SEN funding is allocated, warning that the current patchwork of statutory assessments and school-based support leaves many children "effectively excluded from meaningful learning". Political reaction has been mixed. The SDLP's education spokesperson described the report as "a damning indictment of decades of educational inertia", while the Alliance Party said it "validates what many have been saying for years". However, the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) cautioned against "knee-jerk reforms", arguing that academic selection remains popular with many parents and that grammar schools deliver "excellent outcomes" for pupils. The Ulster Unionist Party echoed concerns about the feasibility of raising the school leaving age, pointing to the need for substantial investment in vocational education and apprenticeships. The report acknowledges the political sensitivity of its proposals. "Any move to raise the participation age must be accompanied by a comprehensive expansion of vocational pathways and a renewed focus on early intervention," it says. "Without those, increasing compulsion risks simply extending the period of disengagement for some young people." The DE has declined to comment formally on the forum's findings, saying only that they "form part of ongoing internal deliberation". But sources within the department suggest that the paper represents a growing consensus among civil servants that the current system is unsustainable. The debate now looks set to intensify, with the report adding fresh impetus to long-running calls for a single, unified post-primary system. For now, however, the future of academic selection and the school leaving age remain firmly in the political arena.
