title: We assume that in our hyper-connected world, we can always access the information we need and track down the people we want to find.
text_ai: But the tragedy at Grenfell Tower has thrown up a further horrible reality - two weeks on, the exact number of people who died is still unknown. On Wednesday, Detective Superintendent Fiona McCormack announced that the number of dead and missing had risen to 80. The figure, she stressed, was provisional. The true number may never be known with certainty. The search of the tower, floor by floor, has been painstaking, often halted by structural instability. Each recovered body must be formally identified — a process complicated by the intensity of the fire, which reached temperatures of over 1,000C. In some cases, only DNA fragments remain. For the families waiting, the uncertainty is a second tragedy. Several have publicly criticised the authorities, saying they have been left in limbo, unable to confirm whether their loved ones are among the dead or among the missing. The Metropolitan Police has set up a dedicated family assistance centre, but the logistical and emotional toll is immense. The challenge of establishing a precise death toll highlights a deeper problem in modern disaster response. In an age of smartphones, social media and near-instantaneous communication, one might assume that locating individuals should be straightforward. Yet the Grenfell fire has exposed critical gaps. Many residents were not on official electoral registers. Some were undocumented migrants, fearful of coming forward. Others were elderly, with no digital footprint. The building’s management, the Kensington and Chelsea Tenant Management Organisation, had incomplete records of who lived there. The census data was outdated. In the immediate aftermath, families turned to Facebook and Twitter, posting photos and pleas for information. These posts were shared thousands of times, creating a chaotic, self-organising search effort. But authorities struggled to reconcile online reports with official records. The police have warned that some names circulating online are erroneous, and that information should only be provided through official channels. The fire also raises questions about the role of technology in emergency preparedness. Many residents reported that the building’s fire alarms were not working on the night of 14 June. The absence of a functioning alarm system meant that residents had to rely on word of mouth and phone calls. In some cases, neighbours knocked on doors to alert others. For those on higher floors, the fire spread so fast that escape was impossible. In a digital era, one might expect a sophisticated emergency response system. Instead, the tower had a single staircase. The building’s cladding — later found to be highly flammable — was installed despite warnings from fire safety experts. The official inquiry, which has now begun, will examine not only the immediate causes but also the wider failures in building regulation, local governance and emergency planning. For the community, the trauma is compounded by a sense that they were not heard. Many had complained about safety issues for years. Their concerns were dismissed. In the aftermath, the government promised that all similar cladding would be removed from other towers across the country. But for the families of the 80 — and perhaps more — that promise is cold comfort. The police investigation continues. Detectives are working with forensic anthropologists and odontologists to identify remains. They are also cross-referencing phone records, bank transactions and NHS data. But many residents had no bank account, no GP registration. Their lives were invisible to the state. Now, their deaths are almost as hard to count. The tragedy at Grenfell Tower is a stark reminder that the hyper-connected world is not equally connected. It reveals the disparities in who is counted, who is missed, and who is forgotten. As the search goes on, the nation watches, waiting for a final number that may never come. And for the families, each day without news is a day of hope and dread — a cruel limbo in a disaster that should never have happened.

title: A prosecutor has urged a jury to convict a couple of the "sustained and brutal" murder of a Montrose mother-of-three.
text_ai: Steven Jackson and Michelle Higgins deny killing and dismembering Kimberley MacKenzie in October last year. Ashley Edwards QC told a jury in her closing speech that the couple had committed an act of "depravity". Defence QC Donald Findlay, representing Mr Jackson, said the Crown had not proved the charge against his client. She told the jury at the High Court in Edinburgh that the pair had acted together to kill the 33-year-old mother and then cut up her body in an attempt to conceal their crime. "These two individuals acted in concert to inflict a sustained and brutal attack on Kimberley MacKenzie," Ms Edwards said. "They then went to considerable lengths to dispose of her remains." The court has heard that parts of Miss MacKenzie's body were found in a number of locations around Montrose and the surrounding area in the days following her disappearance last October. Her torso was discovered in a wheelie bin, while other remains were recovered from a nearby river and a wooded area. Ms Edwards said the couple had shown "no remorse" and had instead tried to blame each other for the killing. She described the evidence against them as "overwhelming". But Mr Findlay told the jury that the Crown had failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that his client, Mr Jackson, was responsible for the murder. He said there was no direct evidence linking him to the killing, and that the case relied on "circumstantial" material. "Steven Jackson is not a saint, and he is not being tried for being a saint," Mr Findlay said. "He is being tried for murder, and the Crown has not proved that case." The defence lawyer also questioned the reliability of key prosecution witnesses, including a man who claimed Mr Jackson had confessed to him while they were both in prison. Representing Michelle Higgins, defence QC Brian McConnachie said his client had been "manipulated" by Mr Jackson and had played no part in the killing. He described her as a "vulnerable" woman who had been in a "toxic" relationship. Miss MacKenzie, a care worker and mother of three children aged between eight and 13, was last seen alive on the evening of 22 October last year. She had been to a pub in Montrose before visiting the couple's flat. The trial, now in its fourth week, has heard harrowing evidence from forensic experts and pathologists. The jury was shown photographs of the crime scene and heard details of the injuries sustained by Miss MacKenzie. Ms Edwards, in her closing speech, urged the jury to set aside any sympathy for the accused and focus on the facts. "This was a brutal, callous and depraved act," she said. "The only just verdict is guilty." The judge, Lord Pentland, is expected to deliver his summing-up on Monday before the jury retires to consider its verdict. The case has shocked the close-knit community of Montrose, where Miss MacKenzie was well known and liked. Friends and family have paid tribute to her, describing her as a "devoted mother" who was "full of life".

title: A mother who was talking to her daughter on her mobile phone heard her being attacked and mugged in Edinburgh.
text_ai: Brian Auchterlonie, 27, has been jailed for 40 months for attacking Casey Thomson, 32, between Rutland Square and Festival Square on Tuesday 12 July. Auchterlonie had pleaded guilty previously to assault and robbery. Ms Thomson's mother could hear her calling out: "Mum, mum, I'm being mugged". The court heard how Ms Thomson, a marketing executive, had been walking home after a night out when Auchterlonie approached her from behind and demanded her phone and handbag. Prosecutor Fiona McIntosh told the High Court in Edinburgh that Ms Thomson’s mother, who has not been named, was on the line at the time. “She heard her daughter shouting ‘Mum, mum, I’m being mugged’. There was then the sound of a scuffle and the line went dead,” she said. The mother immediately called police, who traced Ms Thomson’s phone signal to Festival Square, where they found her shaken and bleeding from a cut to her head. Auchterlonie had fled but was arrested nearby shortly afterwards, still in possession of the stolen items. In a victim impact statement read to the court, Ms Thomson said she now suffers from anxiety and panic attacks. “I no longer feel safe walking alone, even in daylight. That one moment has changed how I view the world,” she said. Defence advocate Neil Wilson said Auchterlonie, who has a history of drug abuse, had been “deeply ashamed” of his actions. He said the attack had been opportunistic and that his client had “no excuse”. Sentencing, Judge Lady Scott said: “This was a terrifying ordeal for Ms Thomson, made all the more harrowing by the fact that her mother was forced to listen helplessly. You preyed on a woman walking home alone. The public must be protected from such behaviour.” Auchterlonie, from the Muirhouse area of Edinburgh, was placed on the sex offenders register for seven years due to the violent nature of the offence. He was also made subject to a non-harassment order banning him from contacting Ms Thomson. Detective Inspector Mark Lumsden of Police Scotland said: “This was a despicable attack on a lone woman. title: UK interest rates have been held at 0.5% again by the Bank of England.
text_ai: The Bank also kept the size of its bond-buying stimulus programme unchanged at Â£375bn. The decision by the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) comes more than six years after the record low was introduced. The half-dozen years of ultra-low interest rates have cut savings' returns, while mortgage borrowers have benefited from lower repayments. The decision, widely anticipated by economists, reflects the Bank's ongoing caution over the pace of the UK's economic recovery. While inflation has ticked up slightly in recent months, it remains well below the MPC's 2% target, giving policymakers little impetus to raise borrowing costs. "There is still significant slack in the economy," said Ruth Miller, UK economist at Capital Economics. "Wage growth remains subdued, and global uncertainties, particularly around Brexit and trade tensions, continue to weigh on business investment." The MPC noted that household spending had held up better than expected, supported by solid employment and low inflation for goods. However, it warned that the outlook for exports remained weak, and that the manufacturing sector was still contracting. "The housing market has shown some signs of stabilisation, but activity remains low compared to historical norms," the Bank said in its minutes. For savers, the prolonged period of low returns shows no sign of ending. Experts say the near-zero base rate has cost UK savers tens of billions in lost interest since 2009. "Anyone relying on savings income is still struggling," said Sarah Coles, a personal finance analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown. "The best easy-access accounts now pay around 1.3%, but inflation at 1.5% means real returns are still negative." Mortgage holders, by contrast, continue to benefit. The average two-year fixed-rate deal now stands at around 2.1%, close to record lows. However, first-time buyers face rising property prices and tight lending criteria. "Those already on the housing ladder are fine, but getting on it is increasingly tough," added Coles. Looking ahead, most economists expect the Bank to keep rates on hold for the foreseeable future, until there is clearer evidence of sustainable wage growth or a Brexit deal that removes business uncertainty. "We do not see a rate rise until at least mid-2020, and even then it will be only gradual," said Miller. The MPC's next meeting is scheduled for early November, when it will also update its quarterly economic forecasts.

title: A miners' union has said it is confident about its future despite moving to sell off its Nottinghamshire headquarters due to falling membership.
text_ai: The Union of Democratic Mineworkers (UDM) once had more than 25,000 members but this has fallen to about 1,000. It has now submitted plans to Mansfield District Council for its building on Berry Hill Lane to be sold for housing. Despite this, officials said they believed mining would continue locally for at least a decade. The building, which has served as the union's administrative base since the 1990s, could be redeveloped into up to 12 homes under the plans submitted to the local authority. A decision is expected within the next few months. The UDM was formed in 1985 during the bitter miners' strike, breaking away from the National Union of Mineworkers (NUM) over the decision to end the walkout without a deal. At its peak, it represented thousands of miners across Nottinghamshire, Derbyshire and the Midlands coalfields. But the decline of the British coal industry has been relentless. The last deep coal mine in Nottinghamshire, Thoresby Colliery, closed in 2015, and the UK's final deep mine, Kellingley in Yorkshire, shut later that year. Today, only a handful of opencast sites remain in operation. General secretary Paul Stanley said the decision to sell the headquarters had been difficult but necessary. "We've had to adapt to a very different landscape. Our membership is now concentrated among a small number of active opencast sites and former miners who still want representation," he told the BBC. He insisted, however, that mining was not finished in the region. "There are still reserves that could be extracted economically, and we are working with companies on future projects. We believe there is at least a decade of mining activity left in Nottinghamshire and the wider area." The union's finances have been under pressure for years. Its annual accounts show a steady decline in income from subscriptions, prompting it to rent out parts of the Berry Hill Lane building to other organisations in recent years. Local historian and former miner John Broughton said the sale marked the end of an era. "The UDM was a symbol of the Nottinghamshire mining community's independence. Many former members still feel a strong attachment to it." The union will relocate to smaller rented offices in Mansfield if the sale is approved. It said its core functions – representing members on health, safety and pensions issues – would continue uninterrupted. Mr Stanley added that the UDM was also exploring new ways to engage younger members of mining families. "We need to make sure the traditions and expertise of our industry are not lost, even as the numbers dwindle."

title: We met in the cavernous interior of the foreign affairs ministry where the old regime once plotted its campaigns against international sanctions and isolation.
text_ai: On the walls are the portraits of past Burmese leaders, beginning with her father General Aung San, assassinated on the eve of independence in 1947, and continuing into the era of thuggish military rule, face after forgotten face for whom nobody had ever voted in a democratic election. We walk past these forgotten faces, their eyes staring out from beneath peaked caps and elaborate hairstyles, into a modern conference room where a different kind of power is now wielded. Here, the foreign minister, a senior figure from the National League for Democracy, receives us. He wears a simple longyi and a checked scarf, the civilian dress of a movement that spent decades in opposition. There is no bravado about him, no sense of victory. Instead, there is a quiet, almost weary, determination. “We are learning how to run a government while the country is still at war with itself,” he says, his voice low but clear. He does not name the army directly, but we understand. The ceasefire deals that exist are fragile, broken daily by skirmishes in remote jungles in Kachin and Shan states. The peace process, once the central promise of the transition, has stalled. And yet, he argues, diplomatic isolation is no longer the tool of the regime; it is now a weapon used by the military to undermine the democratically elected government. “We have two foreign policies,” he explains, drawing a simple diagram on a notepad. “One is the official diplomacy of the ministry. The other is the shadow diplomacy of the generals, who still maintain their own contacts in Beijing, Moscow, and in the capitals of Southeast Asia. They tell foreign governments that we are weak, that we cannot control the country. They offer themselves as the only stable partner.” This is the paradox of modern Myanmar. The civilian government, led by Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, has been in power for over three years, yet real authority over security, the economy, and the constitution remains with the commander-in-chief and his cadre of senior officers. The 2008 charter, written by the junta, guarantees a quarter of parliamentary seats to the military and gives the army control over key ministries — Home Affairs, Border Affairs, Defence. No amendment can pass without the approval of the military bloc. It is a democracy locked inside a dictatorship. The minister gestures towards the window. Outside, the city of Naypyidaw sprawls in a bizarre, orderly grid of empty highways and oversized government buildings. This purpose-built capital was created by the generals to escape the chaos of Yangon, to consolidate their power in a place where dissent was impossible to organise. Now, the same city houses the parliament and the civilian ministries. But the layout itself suggests a perpetual state of siege. Every building is separated from the next by wide, grassy buffers. There are no cafes, no markets, no gathering places. The population consists almost entirely of bureaucrats and soldiers. “The military still believes they built this country,” the minister says. “They do not see themselves as occupiers. They see themselves as guardians. And that is the most difficult thing to change — a mindset.” We ask about the next election, due in November 2020. The NLD has promised a free and fair vote, but there are already worrying signs. The Union Election Commission, still dominated by military appointees, has refused to accept new voter registration systems. The army-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) is preparing its campaign, funded by business interests that flourished during the sanctions era. And then there is the question of the Rohingya. No conversation about Myanmar’s foreign policy can avoid this subject. The minister shifts uncomfortably. He knows that the genocide case at the International Court of Justice, brought by The Gambia and supported by dozens of Muslim nations, has tarnished the reputation of the country beyond repair. He knows that Daw Aung San Suu Kyi’s personal appearance at The Hague, defending the army against charges of ethnic cleansing, was a strategic disaster for the civilian government. But he also knows that he cannot criticise the army openly. “We are trying to address the root causes,” he says carefully. “We have a plan for the repatriation of displaced persons. We have a commission of inquiry. But the international community wants immediate justice, and we cannot deliver that. We are not a country that has a functioning judiciary. We are a country where the army can still arrest a judge.” He pauses. The portraits on the wall in the corridor outside seem to watch us. The old regime plotted here against sanctions and isolation, but they also created a system so entrenched that even an election landslide cannot dislodge it. The civilians are now learning to govern, but they are also learning to survive. In the end, the minister offers a sobering conclusion. “We have a saying,” he says. “In Myanmar, you can change the face in the portrait, but the wall remains the same.”

title: UK troops posted to Kenya are returning home after diplomatic wrangling over British army training in the country was resolved.
text_ai: The 900 troops were waiting to return home after completing their training because of delays over clearance for the officers who will replace them. The first flights carrying the returning personnel are expected to depart from Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport later this week. A Ministry of Defence spokesperson said: "We welcome the swift resolution of this administrative issue. UK troops have long trained in Kenya, and this partnership remains vital for both our nations' security." The BATUK facility, based in Nanyuki on the slopes of Mount Kenya, hosts around 10,000 British personnel each year for exercises that simulate arid and semi-arid conditions similar to those in Afghanistan and other operational theatres. The training is considered a cornerstone of the UK's ability to deploy forces rapidly. Analysts noted that while the delay was relatively short, it underscored the fragility of even the most established defence arrangements when diplomatic tensions arise. Relations between the UK and Kenya remain broadly strong, underpinned by a defence co-operation agreement signed in 2021. The Foreign Office has not revised its advisory, but a senior Kenyan official indicated that "the matter is now behind us".

title: UK prisoners could challenge the blanket ban on them voting in European elections after a European Court of Justice ruling on a case in France.
text_ai: Convicted murderer Thierry Delvigne claimed a ban on him voting in European Parliament elections violated his civil and political rights. But the court ruled the ban was "proportionate" to the offence. The decision means some UK prisoners could make a challenge if a ban would not be proportionate in their case. The ruling by the European Court of Justice (ECJ) in Luxembourg does not automatically overturn the UK's blanket ban on prisoner voting in European Parliament elections, but it opens a narrow legal pathway for individual challenges. Legal experts said the decision hinged on the principle of proportionality — a core concept in EU law — meaning that prisoners serving sentences for less serious offences could argue that a total ban was disproportionate to their crime. The UK has since introduced limited reforms — allowing prisoners on temporary release or those released on licence to register — but the blanket ban remains in place for all sentenced inmates. The ECJ's ruling in the Delvigne case, however, applies only to elections to the European Parliament, not to national or local elections. It emerged from a reference by the French Constitutional Council, which asked whether a lifetime ban on a convicted murderer was lawful under EU law. The ECJ said that while the ban was proportionate for Delvigne's grave offence, each case must be judged individually. This means French authorities — and by extension any EU member state, including the UK — must assess whether a disenfranchisement is proportionate to the severity of the crime and the length of sentence. For UK prisoners, the ruling could be significant. Although the UK is no longer a member of the EU, the European Parliament elections in May 2019 — the last in which British citizens participated — were still governed by EU law. Any challenge by a British prisoner who was disenfranchised at that time could now be brought before a UK court, citing the ECJ's interpretation of proportionality. "This is a potentially important development," said Dr. Alice Donald, a human rights law expert at Middlesex University. "It provides a clear legal basis for a prisoner to argue that their individual ban was not proportionate, even if the blanket ban itself is not directly overturned." The UK government has consistently resisted any move to give prisoners the vote, despite repeated rulings from Strasbourg. In 2017, then-Justice Secretary Liz Truss announced that the government would not implement the ECHR's judgment, saying it was a matter for Parliament. The current government has maintained that position. A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "We have no plans to change our longstanding position that prisoners should not have the right to vote." However, the ECJ ruling could force a rethink, at least for European Parliament elections. The practical impact in the UK may be limited because the next European Parliament elections are not scheduled until 2029, and the UK's participation is uncertain given Brexit. But the ruling could still be used in legal challenges for the 2019 elections. "Any prisoner who was denied a vote in those elections could now seek damages or a declaration that their rights were violated," said barrister David Prescott, who specialises in electoral law. "The threshold for disproportionality is likely to be low — for example, someone serving a short sentence for a non-violent offence might have a strong case." Human rights campaigners have welcomed the ruling as a step towards ending what they call a "Victorian-era policy". The charity Prison Reform Trust said the blanket ban was "outdated and unjust", noting that the UK is one of the few European countries that denies all convicted prisoners the vote. "This ruling reinforces the principle that disenfranchisement should be reserved for the most serious offences, not applied indiscriminately," said a spokesperson. The case also highlights the ongoing tension between UK domestic law and European legal standards, even after Brexit. The ECJ's decision is binding for EU members, but the UK's relationship with the court has changed. However, the judgment could still be cited in UK courts as persuasive authority, particularly on the point of proportionality. "It doesn't create a direct legal obligation, but it provides a strong argument that a blanket ban is disproportionate," Dr. Donald added. In France, the Delvigne ruling has already prompted debate about the country's own voting restrictions. The French government had argued that a lifetime ban on murderers was justified, but the ECJ insisted on a case-by-case assessment. The French Constitutional Council will now have to apply that standard to future cases. For UK prisoners, the immediate effect may be limited, but the legal door is now ajar. As one legal commentator put it: "The blanket ban is still there, but it has a hole in it — and that hole is the principle of proportionality. Prisoners with lighter sentences or shorter terms now have a clear argument that they should have been allowed to vote." Whether they will succeed remains to be seen, but the ECJ has given them a powerful new weapon in a long-running legal fight.

title: A recent drought shut down the Amazon Basin's carbon sink by killing trees and slowing trees' growth rates, a study has shown.
text_ai: The term carbon sink refers to the ability of a natural zone to absorb CO2 from the atmosphere. In the first basin-wide study of the impacts of the 2010 drought, data showed trees' mortality rate went up while growth rates declined. The findings have been published by the Global Biogeochemical Cycles journal. The research, led by scientists from the University of Leeds and the University of Oxford, analysed data from 189 forest plots spanning the entire Amazon basin. It found that during the 2010 drought, the region's trees absorbed 1.1 billion fewer tonnes of carbon than in a normal year — effectively turning the world's largest rainforest from a carbon sink into a carbon source for that period. "This was a shocking result," said lead author Dr Luiz Aragão, a remote sensing specialist at Brazil's National Institute for Space Research (INPE) and the University of Exeter. "The Amazon has long been considered a buffer against climate change, absorbing about a quarter of the carbon dioxide that humans release into the atmosphere each year. But this drought showed that buffer can be severely weakened, even temporarily reversed." The 2010 drought was one of the most intense on record, with rainfall deficits of up to 75% across large swathes of the basin. It followed a similar but less severe drought in 2005. The study's findings, published in the journal *Global Biogeochemical Cycles*, are the first to quantify the combined effect of increased tree mortality and reduced growth on the Amazon's carbon balance. Trees in drought-stressed areas died at rates 1.5 times higher than normal, while surviving trees grew 30% slower. The result was a net release of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. The researchers calculated that the 2010 drought caused the Amazon to emit roughly 1.1 billion tonnes of carbon — more than the annual emissions of Japan. "This is a significant blow to the idea of the Amazon as a reliable carbon sink," said co-author Dr Erika Berenguer, a senior research associate at the University of Oxford. "If droughts become more frequent and intense under climate change, as many models predict, the Amazon could shift from being a sink to a regular source of carbon, accelerating global warming." The study highlights the vulnerability of even the most robust ecosystems to climate extremes. The Amazon rainforest has evolved over millions of years to cope with seasonal dry periods, but the severity and frequency of recent droughts appear to be pushing these limits. "The trees are adapted to a certain amount of dryness, but the 2010 drought was beyond what many could withstand," said Dr Aragão. "We saw mortality spike across all species, not just the most drought-sensitive ones. That suggests the entire forest system is under stress." The findings have major implications for climate policy. The Amazon's ability to absorb carbon has been factored into global emissions targets and carbon offset schemes. If that ability is compromised, the world may need to reduce emissions even faster to meet the goals of the Paris Agreement. "This is a wake-up call," said Dr Berenguer. "We cannot rely on the Amazon to mop up our carbon pollution indefinitely. The forest itself is threatened by the very climate change it helps mitigate. Protecting the Amazon means more than just halting deforestation — it means stabilising the global climate." The research team plans to continue monitoring the plots to see how the forest recovers. Preliminary data suggests that in some areas, the carbon sink has partially recovered, but the long-term trend remains uncertain. "What we learn from the 2010 drought gives us a glimpse of what a warmer, drier Amazon might look like," Dr Aragão added. "It is not a pretty picture. If we want to keep the Amazon as a carbon sink, we need to keep the climate from reaching those extremes."

title: UKIP Leader Nigel Farage has defended comments made in the TV leaders' debate about migrants using the NHS for HIV treatment costing £25,000 per year.
text_ai: Plaid Cymru's Leanne Wood responded by calling the comment "scaremongering" and saying he should be "ashamed". And HIV charity the Terrence Higgins Trust said "HIV doesn't discriminate and politicians shouldn't either". However, on Friday, Mr Farage repeated his view that "we shouldn't spend on health tourism". Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s *Today* programme, Mr Farage insisted he had raised a legitimate point about the cost of treating foreign nationals with HIV, which he claimed ran to £25,000 per year per patient. He argued that while the NHS should provide emergency care to anyone in need, non-urgent treatments should not be available free of charge to people who have not contributed to the UK tax system. “We have a health service that is under enormous strain,” Mr Farage said. “It is not xenophobic to ask whether we can afford to offer expensive, lifelong treatments to people who come here specifically to access them. We need to be honest about the pressures on public services.” The UKIP leader’s remarks have reignited a fierce debate about health tourism and the boundaries of NHS provision. Critics, however, have accused him of playing on fears about immigration and stigmatising people living with HIV. Dr Michael Brady, medical director at the Terrence Higgins Trust, said the idea that people travel to the UK for HIV treatment was “a myth” perpetuated by a small number of politicians. “The evidence shows that people coming to the UK from abroad are generally healthier than the British-born population,” Dr Brady said. “There is no data to suggest significant numbers are coming here specifically for HIV care. What Mr Farage is doing is dangerous and feeds prejudice.” Labour’s shadow health secretary, Jonathan Ashworth, described the comments as “divisive and irresponsible”, while Liberal Democrat leader Tim Farron accused Mr Farage of using the NHS as a “political football”. The SNP’s health spokeswoman, Dr Philippa Whitford, said the remarks risked undermining public confidence in the health service. Mr Farage’s defence came as new polling suggested the issue could resonate with voters. A YouGov survey conducted after the debate found that 44% of respondents supported the idea that non-UK citizens should be charged for non-emergency NHS treatment, though only 12% saw health tourism as a major problem facing the country. NHS England figures show that the cost of treating HIV is indeed high—antiretroviral drugs can cost around £10,000 to £15,000 per patient per year—but officials stress that the vast majority of care is provided to UK residents. The Department of Health estimates that the total cost of health tourism across all conditions is between £100 million and £300 million annually, a fraction of the NHS budget of more than £120bn. Mr Farage nonetheless pressed his argument, saying the principle mattered more than the precise figures. “We are a generous country, but we cannot be a soft touch,” he said. “The debate we need to have is about who pays and who benefits.” Leanne Wood, the Plaid Cymru leader who confronted Mr Farage during the debate, reiterated her view that his comments were “designed to divide communities”. She added: “We must not let the politics of fear dictate how we treat people who are already vulnerable.” The controversy is likely to feature prominently in the final days of the referendum campaign, with both sides using the episode to rally their supporters. For Mr Farage, the incident has reinforced his image as a straight-talking outsider; for his opponents, it has provided further evidence of what they call his divisive approach to public debate.

title: A man who used Facebook to groom a 15-year-old girl who was later raped and murdered has been found guilty of false imprisonment.
text_ai: Luke Harlow, 28, of Ibstock, Leicestershire, admitted grooming and sexually touching Kayleigh Haywood but had denied taking her captive. Stephen Beadman, 29, who admitted raping and murdering Kayleigh, was found guilty of imprisonment on Monday. Both men are due to be sentenced at Nottingham Crown Court on Friday. The court heard how Harlow, who had been in contact with Kayleigh through Facebook, groomed her over a period of weeks, sending her messages and encouraging her to meet him. On the night of 13 November 2015, she was driven to his home in Ibstock, where he sexually assaulted her. Later, Beadman, a friend of Harlow's, arrived and raped and murdered the teenager. Her body was found in a woodland near Measham, Leicestershire, two days later. Prosecutor Michael Evans QC told the jury that Harlow had "created a situation" in which Kayleigh was "vulnerable and isolated" after he had groomed her. "He knew she was only 15, he knew she was a child," Mr Evans said. "He used social media to target her, to win her trust, and then to lure her to his home." The prosecution argued that Harlow's actions amounted to false imprisonment because he prevented Kayleigh from leaving his house, even after the sexual assault, by using a combination of physical restraint and psychological pressure. Harlow claimed she had stayed voluntarily and that he had not stopped her from leaving. But the jury of six men and six women took just over three hours to convict him, rejecting his defence. Judge Nicholas Dean QC, the Recorder of Leicester, thanked them for their "meticulous and careful" consideration of the evidence. Outside court, Detective Superintendent Tim Lindley, of Leicestershire Police, said the case was "one of the most harrowing" he had ever encountered. "Kayleigh was a vulnerable young girl who was targeted by these two men for their own sexual gratification," he said. "Harlow used Facebook to groom her, building a relationship of trust which he then exploited in the most appalling way. Beadman then subjected her to a horrific and violent attack that ended her life." Kayleigh's mother, Stephanie Jackson, said in a victim impact statement read to the court that her daughter's death had "destroyed" the family. "She was a beautiful, intelligent, loving girl with her whole life ahead of her, and it has been taken away in the most brutal and senseless manner," she said. "We will never recover from this loss. The pain is constant." The court also heard that Beadman had a history of sexual offending against children and had been subject to a sexual harm prevention order at the time of the murder. He had previously been convicted of indecent assault on a girl under 16. During his trial, Beadman claimed he had not killed Kayleigh but had woken to find her dead in Harlow's house, then panicked and moved her body to the woodland. The jury rejected that account, finding him guilty of murder and rape as well as false imprisonment. Judge Dean said the case was "exceptional in its cruelty" and that the pair had shown "a complete disregard for the life of a child". He adjourned sentencing until Friday, warning both men they faced "very substantial" custodial sentences. Det Supt Lindley said the police investigation had been "complex and painstaking", involving extensive forensic work and the recovery of thousands of electronic communications. "We were able to trace the grooming messages Harlow sent to Kayleigh, and the movements of both men on that night," he said. "This case should serve as a stark warning to parents and to young people about the dangers of online grooming. Predators use social media to befriend children, gain their trust, and then exploit them in the most horrific ways." He added that support services had been offered to Kayleigh's family and that the force was working with schools and youth groups to raise awareness of the risks. The conviction of Harlow for false imprisonment is relatively unusual in cases of grooming and murder, but prosecutors argued that his actions in preventing Kayleigh from leaving his home amounted to a separate and serious offence. "He did not simply persuade her to stay – he physically and psychologically prevented her from going anywhere else," Mr Evans said. In his defence, Harlow's barrister, John Butterfield QC, said his client had been "manipulative and deceitful" but had not intended to imprison the girl. "He accepts he did terrible things, but false imprisonment is not one of them," Mr Butterfield said. "Kayleigh could have left at any time, and he did not force her to remain." The jury disagreed, and the verdict has been welcomed by campaign groups working to protect children from online abuse. Mary Sharpe, chief executive of the Safeguarding Children Coalition, said the outcome sent "a powerful message" that perpetrators of grooming would "face the full force of the law". She said: "The use of false imprisonment charges in this case is important because it recognises the coercive control that groomers exert over their victims. Children are not simply persuaded – they are trapped." Kayleigh's family have said they will attend Friday's sentencing, expecting to see both men jailed for life. "We want them to know the pain they have caused, and we want the law to reflect the severity of their crimes," a family spokesman said. The case has also raised questions about the effectiveness of online safety measures. Harlow was able to contact Kayleigh through Facebook despite her being under the age of 18. The social media company said it had "strict policies against the grooming of minors" and that it worked closely with law enforcement, but campaigners argue more must be done to prevent adults from contacting children on the platform. A Facebook spokesperson said: "Our thoughts are with Kayleigh's family and friends. We have no higher priority than the safety of young people on our platforms, and we have a dedicated team that works around the clock to help prevent grooming and other forms of exploitation. We will continue to invest in technology and human moderation to keep children safe." Det Supt Lindley said the case should prompt a wider debate about the responsibilities of tech companies. "Social media platforms are being used by predators to find and groom children," he said. "We need to ask whether the current safeguards are strong enough, and whether companies are doing enough to protect the most vulnerable users." The court was told that Harlow had sent more than 200 Facebook messages to Kayleigh in the weeks leading up to her death, many of which were sexual in nature. Beadman had also contacted her, though to a lesser extent. Neighbours in Ibstock said they had seen Kayleigh being led into Harlow's house on the night of her death, but did not realise she was in danger. One resident, who asked not to be named, said: "It's horrifying to think what happened just a few doors away. You think you know your neighbours, and then something like this happens. It makes you realise how easily a child can be led astray." The trial lasted four weeks, during which forensic experts gave detailed evidence about the cause of Kayleigh's death. The pathologist confirmed she had been strangled and had suffered multiple injuries consistent with a violent struggle. Both men will be sentenced on Friday at Nottingham Crown Court. Beadman is expected to receive a life sentence with a minimum term, while Harlow faces a significant custodial sentence for false imprisonment and sexual offences. The judge has indicated he will also consider whether to impose a sexual harm prevention order on Harlow, given his history of offending. Kayleigh's mother said she would be at court to see justice done. "There is nothing that can bring my daughter back," she said. "But knowing these men will spend many years in prison is the only comfort we can have." The case has once again highlighted the dangers of online grooming and the vulnerability of young people to manipulation through social media. Police have urged parents to monitor their children's online activity and to report any concerns immediately. "If something feels wrong, it probably is," Det Supt Lindley said. "Don't ignore the signs. Report it."

title: A small boy almost fell from a moving train carriage on to the track below because the toilet floor was missing.

title: US President Donald Trump says transgender people cannot serve in "any capacity" in the military.
text_ai: He tweeted that he had consulted with military experts and cited "tremendous medical costs and disruption". "The men and women who serve in uniform should be judged solely on their ability to fight and win," he said. title: In the Disney Pixar animation The Incredibles, the daughter in the family of superheroes, Violet, has a particular superpower.

title: How do you make rum in Venezuela when your factory is surrounded by a brutal gang war?
text_ai: "You make the thugs play rugby," says Alberto Vollmer, the CEO of Santa Teresa, Venezuela's most prestigious rum company. "Rugby is a contact and a team sport that allows you to efficiently teach values like respect, discipline and teamwork," he tells the BBC. "We first invited them to play in 2003," Vollmer explains, leaning forward in his office at the Hacienda Santa Teresa, a sprawling colonial estate that has produced rum since the 19th Century. "The gangs were extorting our workers, stealing from the fields, and recruiting our young people. We had two choices: arm ourselves or find another way." Santa Teresa chose the latter. The result is the 'Proyecto Alcatraz' – named after a solitary confinement cell on the estate – which uses rugby to rehabilitate former gang members and integrate them into the workforce. More than 15,000 young Venezuelans have passed through the programme since its inception. Many now work in the distillery, bottling the very rum that their former associates once tried to steal. The logic is brutally simple. On the rugby pitch, gang hierarchies collapse. A teenage sicario learns to pass the ball to a rival from a neighbouring barrio. A former extortionist discovers that his survival depends on defending a teammate he once would have shot. The scrum becomes a metaphor for controlled aggression – and the post-match beer a ritual of truce. "We have former gang leaders working on the production line next to men they tried to kill," says Vollmer, his voice matter-of-fact. "They don't have to be friends. But they must respect the ruck, the tackle, the lineout. It's the only common language we found." The challenges, however, are immense. Santa Teresa sits in the state of Aragua, a region that has become the stronghold of the feared Tren de Aragua gang. The group's tentacles reach into every corner of local life – from illegal mining to extortion and contract killings. In 2022, the gang intensified its operations, forcing many businesses to close. Santa Teresa's trucks have been ambushed. Workers have been threatened. The distillery now operates under a permanent state of high alert, with armoured vehicles escorting its most valuable cargo. "When we started, we could just negotiate with the local gangs," Vollmer recalls. "Now we are dealing with a transnational criminal organisation. They don't want a cut of the rum. They want the entire business – the land, the brand, the distribution network." The company's response has been characteristically unorthodox. Beyond rugby, Santa Teresa has turned its hacienda into a self-contained fortress. Solar panels keep the lights on during frequent blackouts. A private water treatment plant ensures production continues even when the municipal supply fails. And a network of former gang members now work as security guards – their tattoos and street knowledge making them uniquely effective at spotting trouble before it arrives. "We pay them more than the gangs do," says Vollmer, with a wry smile. "Loyalty is a matter of opportunity. We provide the better opportunity." The rum itself has become a symbol of defiance. Santa Teresa's premium blends – aged in ex-bourbon and sherry casks for up to 18 years – sell for hundreds of dollars in London, Paris and New York. On the company's website, the product descriptions make no mention of the armed guards, the bullet-shattered windscreens, the funerals of former players. But the paradox is not lost on Vollmer. "People buy luxury rum to forget their problems," he says. "But every bottle from Santa Teresa is a testament to people who refused to be victims." The wider context is stark. Venezuela's economy has collapsed, with hyperinflation and US sanctions crippling both imports and exports. The agricultural sector has been particularly hard hit, with many sugar cane plantations abandoned. Santa Teresa has survived – even thrived – by diversifying into other products like artisan chocolate and coffee, and by maintaining a direct relationship with its workers in a country where the minimum wage buys barely a loaf of bread. "We are not philanthropists," Vollmer insists. "We are realists. If the factory stops, the community dies. And if the community dies, the factory becomes just another looted building." As dusk falls over the hacienda, the sounds of training drift from a floodlit pitch. Teenagers in mud-splattered shirts sprint, pass and tackle under the watchful eye of a coach who once ran a gang in the nearby town of Maracay. The scrum forms. The whistle blows. For a few hours at least, the war outside can wait. "We don't claim to have solved the problem," says Vollmer, rising to shake hands. "But we have shown that when the state fails, the private sector can improvise. And sometimes, the only way to make rum is to make men."

title: It has been a tradition since the days of Winston Churchill that the prime minister's address at the annual Lord Mayor's Banquet in London is devoted to foreign policy.

And Mr Cameron, in 2011, used it to announce a "golden age" of trade with the Commonwealth. This year, the tone was markedly more sober. One of the most striking sections of the speech was his admission that the "hard headed" focus on economic self-interest had sometimes blinded the government to the values that underpin Britain's international standing. "We cannot be a country that speaks only of pounds and pence," he said. "We must also speak of principle." It was a subtle but significant shift in emphasis — a recognition that the moral authority of British diplomacy, built on decades of support for human rights and the rule of law, cannot be replaced by a balance sheet. Critics, however, were quick to point out that this was the same government that had cut aid to Libya, that had been accused of turning a blind eye to Saudi Arabia's human rights record, and that had been slow to condemn Russia's actions in Ukraine. The speech also touched on the Middle East — a region where British foreign policy had been repeatedly tested. The collapse of the Libyan state, the chaos in Syria, the rise of Islamic State, the grinding conflict between Israel and the Palestinians — all were mentioned, but none were given the detailed attention that the occasion might have warranted. Instead, Mr Cameron focused on the need for a "comprehensive approach" that combined military action with diplomacy, development and counter-terrorism. It was a safe, consensual position, but one that offered little new direction. Perhaps the most revealing moment came when he turned to the Commonwealth — a subject close to his heart. He spoke of the trade links with India, the shared values of democracy and the rule of law, and the potential of a "modern Commonwealth" to act as a force for good in the world. But again, the reality was more complex. The Commonwealth is a diverse and often divided organisation, and Britain's influence within it is not what it once was. The EU referendum, which could pull Britain out of its most important trading bloc, has made many Commonwealth leaders nervous: they see a post-Brexit Britain as a weaker, not a stronger, partner. As the speech drew to a close, Mr Cameron returned to the theme of resilience — a word he used repeatedly. "We have been tested by economic crisis, by conflict, by the threats of terrorism and extremism," he said. "And we have not bowed. We have not broken. We have adapted, and we have prevailed." It was a message designed to reassure, but it also felt defensive. The world was changing faster than any prime minister could keep up with, and the Lord Mayor's Banquet, for all its grandeur, was a reminder that foreign policy is never as simple as a speech. Outside the Guildhall, the rain was falling on the old city. The carriages had gone, replaced by black limousines with darkened windows. And the journalists, huddled under umbrellas, were already writing their analyses. The Prime Minister had made his case. But whether it would be enough to convince a sceptical public, a restive party, and a world that was increasingly unpredictable, remained to be seen. For the first time in many years, the foreign policy speech at the Lord Mayor's Banquet had left more questions than answers.

title: Hungary has sealed the last gaps in its new border fence to migrants, and the authorities will decide later on whether to declare a state of emergency along the border with Serbia.
text_ai: Extra police, army, and now judges have been drafted into the region. Pressed by Hungarian TV2 on whether he would declare an emergency, Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban replied: "If you want to place a bet on it, I would say go ahead." The comments from Mr Orban came as the final section of the 175km (109-mile) barrier of razor wire and fencing was completed near the town of Roszke. Hungarian authorities have been working around the clock to seal the border since the beginning of the summer, when the number of migrants crossing from Serbia into Hungary surged. More than 160,000 people have entered Hungary illegally so far this year, according to official figures, most of them fleeing conflict in Syria, Iraq and Afghanistan. The fence – which runs along the entire Hungarian-Serbian border – has been criticised by human rights groups and the United Nations. They argue it is a blunt instrument that does nothing to address the root causes of migration. “This is not a solution, it is a wall of shame,” said a spokesperson for Amnesty International. “It forces people to take more dangerous routes and leaves them at the mercy of smugglers.” But Mr Orban, who has made opposition to migration a central plank of his government’s agenda, defended the measure. “We have to protect our borders and our way of life,” he said in a radio interview on Friday. “If we do not, Europe will be overwhelmed.” A state of emergency – if declared – would allow the government to deploy the military more effectively and impose stricter measures along the border. It would also enable the use of so-called “transit zones” where asylum seekers could be held while their claims are processed. Budapest has already brought in new laws that make it a criminal offence to damage the fence or to enter Hungary illegally. Those caught face up to three years in prison. The situation has strained relations with Serbia. Belgrade has said it will not accept any migrants who are forcibly returned from Hungary. “Serbia is a transit country, not a destination,” said Serbian Prime Minister Aleksandar Vucic. “We cannot be turned into a buffer zone for Europe.” The European Union has urged Hungary to stick to its legal obligations under EU asylum rules. The European Commission said it was closely monitoring the situation. “Member states have the right to protect their borders, but they must do so in accordance with EU law,” a spokesperson said. “The right to seek asylum must be respected.” Meanwhile, the migrants themselves have been forced to find alternative routes. Many are now heading towards Croatia, which shares a border with Serbia to the west. But Croatia has also begun to tighten its own controls. On Friday, Croatian authorities reported a sharp increase in the number of people crossing from Serbia, raising fears of a new humanitarian crisis in the Balkans. The Hungarian government has said it will announce its decision on the state of emergency in the coming days. Mr Orban’s confident tone suggests that an emergency declaration is likely. “If you want to place a bet on it, I would say go ahead,” he told TV2. For the thousands of migrants still stranded in Serbia, the prospect of a sealed Hungarian border – backed by judges, police and soldiers – leaves few options. International aid agencies have warned that the winter months will make the situation even more desperate. With temperatures already dropping, many migrants are living in makeshift camps with little shelter. “People are freezing, they are hungry, and they have nowhere to go,” said a representative of the UN’s refugee agency. “A political solution is urgently needed – not more walls.” The EU has pledged additional funding to help Serbia and other countries along the Balkan route manage the influx. But so far, no comprehensive deal has been reached. As Hungary prepares to tighten its grip, the broader question remains: how can Europe respond to the biggest migration crisis since the Second World War – without tearing apart the very principles of solidarity and free movement that define the union?

title: Introducing the first official hustings of UKIP's leadership contest, chairman Paul Oakden reflected that it had been a "challenging few weeks" for his party.
text_ai: In the past month, it has lost its new leader after 18 days and seen an MEP resign after a much-publicised fracas in Strasbourg. This came after months of infighting and tussles between rival factions within the party. In a community centre in a market town in the East Midlands, around 200 party members had gathered to hear from the three remaining candidates. The atmosphere was subdued. The days of buoyant rallies, fuelled by the euphoria of the 2016 Brexit vote, felt like a distant memory. Now, the party that once commanded nearly four million votes was struggling to define its purpose in a post-referendum landscape, and struggling even harder to project an image of competence. The first candidate to speak was Gerard Batten, a long-serving MEP and the party’s former Brexit spokesman. He struck a combative tone, insisting that UKIP must return to its core message of “radical, unapologetic Euroscepticism”. “We are not a Conservative tribute act,” he told the room, his voice rising above the hum of an ageing air-conditioning unit. “And we are certainly not a vehicle for the personal ambitions of a few remaining councillors.” He warned that the party risked being “hollowed out” by internal bickering, and called for a “complete reset” of its internal structures. Next came a far less familiar figure: John Rees-Evans, a former Army officer and political novice. His pitch was one of renewal and professionalism. “We have to stop looking backwards. We have to stop fighting each other,” he said, pausing to let the words land. “If we cannot govern ourselves, how can we expect to govern the country?” He proposed a rigorous new code of conduct for party officials, and suggested that the next leader should serve only a two-year term, to prevent the kind of “personality cults” that had damaged previous administrations. The final contender was Neil Hamilton, the former Conservative MP turned Ukip veteran. He drew on his decades of political experience, but also acknowledged the scale of the crisis. “The party is not dead,” he said. “But it is in a coma. And it needs a leader who knows the geography of the battlefield.” He defended the party’s record, pointing to its role in forcing the Brexit referendum, but conceded that recent events had “severely tested the patience of our loyal supporters”. Questions from the floor were pointed. One member, a retired engineer from Grimsby, asked bluntly: “Why should anyone take us seriously now?” Another, a woman who said she had been a member since 2014, demanded to know how the new leader would prevent further defections to the Conservatives or the Brexit Party. Oakden, seated at the side of the stage, took notes but did not intervene. The hustings lasted two hours. Afterwards, as tea was served in plastic cups, the mood was one of cautious hope mixed with deep anxiety. Many members expressed a desire for unity, but few could articulate how it might be achieved. One local branch secretary summed it up: “We’ve got the policies. We’ve got the people. We just need someone to hold it all together.” Whether any of the three candidates can do that remains to be seen. The result of the ballot is due in two weeks. For UKIP, it might be the last chance to avoid sliding into irrelevance.

title: In the 73rd minute at the Amsterdam ArenA on Thursday, Ajax had a free-kick inside the Celtic half, too far from Craig Gordon's goal to think about a shot, but in decent enough position to think about dropping something into the goalkeeper's air space in the hope of causing some consternation.
text_ai: For the umpteenth time, the delivery was poor. It was low, harmless and easily cleared. In that moment, Arkadiusz Milik, Ajax's impressive young striker who bizarrely started the match on the bench, threw his hands in the air in frustration at the botched set piece. Davy Klaassen, the captain, shouted his anger. For the umpteenth time, the delivery was poor. It was low, harmless and easily cleared. In that moment, Arkadiusz Milik, Ajax's impressive young striker who bizarrely started the match on the bench, threw his hands in the air in frustration at the botched set piece. Davy Klaassen, the captain, shouted his anger. It was a scene that summed up Ajax's night in Amsterdam – a night of control without incision, of possession without purpose, of frustration that mounted with every misplaced pass and every wasted dead-ball opportunity. The free kick in the 73rd minute was, perhaps, the most glaring example. But it was far from the only one. The home side had dominated the ball for long spells. Their midfield, orchestrated by the busy Lassana Schöne and the dynamic Klaassen, had strung together sequences of 15, 20, even 25 passes. They had forced Celtic deep into their own half, pinned the Scottish champions to the edge of their own penalty area. They had made goalkeeper Craig Gordon work – a sharp low save from Anwar El Ghazi in the first half, a fingertip stop from a curling Schöne effort early in the second. Yet the scoreboard remained level. 0-0. The goal that would break Celtic's resistance never arrived. Celtic, for their part, were disciplined, organised, and occasionally dangerous. Their game plan was clear: soak up pressure, hit on the counter. Leigh Griffiths, operating as a lone striker, was a constant outlet, his pace a threat whenever Ajax lost possession in midfield. When the visitors did break, they did so with purpose. A quick ball from Scott Brown sent Griffiths clear in the 35th minute – his shot, however, was sliced wide. Another break, midway through the second half, saw James Forrest cut inside and curl a left-footed effort that flew just over Jasper Cillessen's crossbar. For all of Ajax's dominance, it was Celtic who created the clearer openings. The frustration among the home fans was palpable. A low grumble had settled over the Amsterdam ArenA by the hour mark. This was a side that, on its day, could dismantle opponents with slick, one-touch football. But Thursday night was not that day. Milik, introduced from the bench just after the hour mark, was meant to be the catalyst. His movement was sharp, his hold-up play strong. But service to him was erratic. When he did get a sight of goal – a header from a cross by right-back Kenny Tete in the 79th minute – he directed it straight at Gordon. Celtic's resistance was not purely defensive. They were selective in their pressing, well-drilled in their shape. The central pairing of Dedryck Boyata and Virgil van Dijk – the latter a former Ajax youth product, now plying his trade in Glasgow – was commanding. Van Dijk, in particular, read the game superbly, stepping out to intercept passes, winning headers, and even sparking counters with crisp distribution. It was a performance that reminded those in the stands just what Ajax had let go when they sold him to Celtic in 2013. As the clock ticked into the final ten minutes, Ajax threw caution aside. Left-back Nicolai Boilesen pushed high, almost playing as a winger. Klaassen drove into the box, demanding the ball. But each time, Celtic cleared their lines. A last-ditch block from Emilio Izaguirre denied a goal-bound effort from substitute Amin Younes in the 87th minute. In stoppage time, a scramble in the six-yard box saw the ball pinball off several players before eventually being hacked clear by Brown. The final whistle brought a mixed reaction. Celtic's players embraced, their manager Ronny Deila punched the air on the touchline. A point away from home in European competition – against a side with Ajax's pedigree – was a result to cherish. For Ajax, it was two points dropped. The sense of an opportunity missed hung heavily in the damp Amsterdam air. After the match, Ajax's coach, Frank de Boer, was measured but clearly frustrated. "We had control, we had the possession," he said. "But we lacked the final pass, the final cross, the final finish. In the Europa League, these details decide the result. We have to be sharper." He was right. This was a performance that, for all its slickness in the middle third, was blunt in the decisive areas. The dead-ball delivery – epitomised by that ineffective free kick in the 73rd minute – was symptomatic. Celtic's Deila, meanwhile, praised his side's character. "Everyone worked so hard," he said. "To come here and get a clean sheet, to limit a team like Ajax to so few clear chances – that is a fantastic effort. We showed we can compete at this level." For Ajax, the result leaves them with work to do in the group. They had aspired to top the section, but now face an uphill battle. Celtic, meanwhile, earned a valuable point that keeps their hopes alive. European football at the Amsterdam ArenA had promised drama, flair, and goals. On this night, it delivered frustration instead – a lesson in the fine margins that separate promise from reward.

title: It was a case that shattered confidence in the British legal system, sparked an Oscar-winning film and eventually an apology from a prime minister.
text_ai: Some thought when Tony Blair apologised to Gerry Conlon, Paddy Armstrong, Paul Hill and Carole Richardson, it drew a line under one of the most scarring episodes of the Troubles in Northern Ireland. But supporters of the group, known as the Guildford Four, believe the fight for justice continues. Now, decades later, a new generation of campaigners is demanding a full public inquiry into what they describe as a "catastrophic failure" of the criminal justice system. They argue that the Guildford Four case was not an isolated miscarriage – but part of a pattern of behaviour in which the police and prosecuting authorities were willing to bend or break the law to secure convictions against Irish republicans. The convictions of Gerry Conlon, Paul Hill, Paddy Armstrong and Carole Richardson for the 1974 Guildford pub bombings – which killed five people and injured scores more – were quashed by the Court of Appeal in October 1989. The judges concluded that the confessions upon which the case was built were unreliable and that key evidence had been withheld. It was a watershed moment, exposing the extent to which the anti-terrorist squad had fabricated interviews and suppressed alibis. Yet for all the public apologies and the enduring cultural impact of the film *In the Name of the Father*, which starred Daniel Day-Lewis as Conlon, many feel the full truth has never come out. The core question – why did senior officers conspire to frame innocent people? – remains unanswered. "What happened to the Guildford Four was a stain on British justice," said Dr. Emma O'Connell, a legal historian at Queen's University Belfast who has studied the case. "But if you look at the aftermath, there was no systematic reckoning. The police officers involved were never properly held to account. There was no public inquiry that examined the institutional culture that allowed it to happen." The families of the four have long called for a statutory inquiry with the power to call witnesses under oath. They point to other major miscarriages, such as the Stephen Lawrence case, which led to the Macpherson Report, or the Post Office Horizon scandal, which has prompted ongoing public hearings. They ask: why not the Guildford Four? The answer, some believe, lies in the delicate political calculus of the Northern Ireland peace process. Tony Blair's apology in 2000 – given after the Queens University Belfast gave the four honorary degrees – was widely seen as a gesture of reconciliation. At the time, the Good Friday Agreement was bedding down, and the British government was keen to avoid reopening old wounds that might antagonise the security establishment. "The apology was welcome," said Paul Hill, speaking to the BBC from his home in London. "But it was never meant to be the end of the story. The prime minister said sorry for what the state did to us. He didn't say sorry for the fact that the people who did it got away with it." Now, a new development has given fresh momentum to the campaign. In December 2023, the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) announced it was examining previously undisclosed documents relating to the case. The documents, uncovered by a team of investigative journalists, appear to show that senior officers in the Metropolitan Police's anti-terrorist branch coordinated a cover-up that went far beyond the four suspects. According to the files, a detective chief superintendent who led the investigation wrote a secret memo in 1975 acknowledging that the confessions were "entirely unsupported" by forensic evidence. The memo was never disclosed to the original defence team. If it had been, the trial judge might have been forced to stop the case. "The existence of that memo is devastating," said Gareth Peirce, the solicitor who represented the Guildford Four and who has spent a lifetime fighting miscarriages of justice. "It shows that the senior investigating officer knew, at the time, that there was no case. And yet he pressed on. The question is: who else knew?" Peirce has long argued that the Guildford Four case was not just a product of individual rogue officers, but of a system that incentivised convictions over truth. The anti-terrorist squad in the 1970s was under immense pressure to produce results after a wave of IRA bombings. In that environment, she says, the rights of suspects became secondary. "The police were effectively given a licence to cut corners," she said. "And when the corners were cut, and the wrong people were convicted, the instinct was to protect the institution, not to correct the error." Supporters of a new inquiry also point to the case of the Maguire Seven – relatives of the Guildford Four who were convicted of handling explosives, largely on the basis of flawed forensic evidence. Their convictions were also quashed, but not before they had served long sentences. The Conlon family, in particular, was devastated: Gerry Conlon's father, Giuseppe, died in prison. "The tragedy of the Guildford Four is that it was a family tragedy," said Joe McVeigh, a retired priest and long-time campaigner for justice. "You had an innocent man, Gerry Conlon, convicted for something he didn't do. You had his father, Guiseppe, a pillar of the community, sent to prison and dying there. You had the entire Maguire family destroyed by a false positive in a test that was later discredited. The state never properly apologised to them." The campaign for a public inquiry has also drawn support from across the political spectrum. In 2022, a cross-party group of MPs wrote to the then Home Secretary, Priti Patel, urging her to establish a statutory inquiry. The letter cited "overwhelming evidence" of a miscarriage and argued that only an inquiry could restore public confidence. The Home Office declined, saying that the quashing of the convictions and the subsequent apologies had been sufficient. But campaigners say that position is untenable. They note that in 2021, the Director of Public Prosecutions, Max Hill, issued a rare apology for the role of the Crown Prosecution Service's predecessor in the case. Still, no individual officer has ever been charged with perjury or perverting the course of justice. One of the main detectives, John Donaldson, died in 2019 without ever facing scrutiny. Another, Thomas Buck, retired with a full pension. "There is a real sense that the system can do great harm and then simply close ranks," said Professor Michael Mansfield QC, who represented some of the Guildford Four in their appeal. "The only way to break that cycle is a full, judge-led inquiry with compulsion. Anything less is a whitewash." The case also continues to resonate far beyond the UK. In Ireland, the story of the Guildford Four is taught in schools as a cautionary tale about the dangers of state overreach. The film *In the Name of the Father* remains a staple of Irish cinema, and Gerry Conlon, who died in 2014, is remembered as a symbol of resilience. In recent interviews, Carole Richardson – the youngest of the four, who was just 17 when arrested – has spoken of her enduring anger. "They took my youth," she said. "I was a child. I was terrified. And they just used me to get a conviction. I want the truth. I want to know why they did it." The campaign now faces a crucial test. The CCRC review could lead to a referral back to the Court of Appeal, which might issue new findings about police misconduct. But even that, campaigners warn, would not be enough. "The Court of Appeal can only look at whether the convictions were safe," said Dr O'Connell. "It cannot investigate the wider question of how the system allowed this to happen. That requires a public inquiry." Meanwhile, the passage of time is taking its toll. Paddy Armstrong, who has spoken openly about his struggles with mental health since his release, said in a recent documentary that he fears the full story will never be told. "I'm 68 now," he said. "I don't have forever. And neither does the truth." As the debate continues, one thing is clear: the original opening line of this story – "a case that shattered confidence in the British legal system" – has not lost its potency. The shards of that shattered confidence still lie scattered across the landscape of British justice, waiting for someone to put them back together. Those who live with the legacy of the Guildford Four are determined that the next chapter will not simply be an epilogue, but a reckoning.
