title: Indian leaders must sometimes have felt a little overwhelmed when they arrived in Brussels.
text_ai: India has always been the poor relation in economic terms and more often than not the question has been how Europe - that great union of some of the richest and most powerful countries in the modern world - can help India. This time is very different. Indian leaders must sometimes have felt a little overwhelmed when they arrived in Brussels. India has always been the poor relation in economic terms and more often than not the question has been how Europe - that great union of some of the richest and most powerful countries in the modern world - can help India. This time is very different. The tables have turned with a rapidity that has caught many in European capitals off guard. When Prime Minister Narendra Modi touched down in Brussels for the latest EU-India summit, he was not there to ask for aid or concessional loans. He was there to negotiate as an equal, or, as some diplomats now privately concede, as a partner with whom Europe must urgently do business. India's economy, now the world's fifth largest and poised to become third within this decade, has transformed its international standing. The International Monetary Fund projects growth of over 6% this year, while much of Europe stagnates below 1%. That arithmetic alone has rewritten the script of a relationship long defined by donor-recipient dynamics. "The days of European development assistance to India are essentially over," said Dr. Anuradha Katyal, a visiting scholar at the European Institute for Asian Studies in Brussels. "What we are witnessing is a recalibration of the relationship around trade, technology and strategic autonomy. India no longer needs Europe's charity; it needs Europe's market access, and Europe needs India's supply chains and geopolitical heft." The summit's agenda reflected this shift. Trade liberalisation topped the talks, with both sides keen to revive negotiations for a Free Trade Agreement that have been stalled since 2013. But the tone was markedly different. Indian officials arrived armed with data showing that tariffs on European goods have already been reduced from 13% to under 7% in recent years - and they demanded reciprocity on services and skilled labour mobility. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen acknowledged the change, describing India as "an indispensable partner" for Europe's future prosperity and security. Behind the diplomatic language, the message was clear: Europe can no longer afford to treat India as a junior partner. The geopolitical context adds urgency. Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine jolted European leaders into recognising the danger of over-reliance on any single supplier - particularly China. India, with its large workforce, rapidly improving infrastructure and robust legal system, emerges as a natural alternative for European companies seeking to diversify their supply chains. "Brussels is finally waking up to the fact that India is not just a market of 1.4 billion consumers, but a potential production hub and a vital buffer against Chinese dominance," said Dr. Alexandra Schmidt, a trade policy analyst at the Centre for European Reform. "The calculus has shifted from 'how can we help India develop' to 'how can we integrate India into our economic architecture before it's too late'." But this new confidence also breeds friction. Indian leaders in Brussels have been demanding greater access for Indian professionals to European labour markets - a sensitive issue in EU member states where immigration is politically charged. They have also pushed back against European carbon border adjustment measures, arguing they amount to "green protectionism" that penalises developing economies. "India is not going to be lectured on climate or labour standards," warned Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal in a recent interview with the Financial Times. "We have our own sustainability goals, our own social models. The relationship must be one of mutual respect." European officials, for their part, have expressed frustration at India's reluctance to condemn Russia in the UN, its continued purchase of Russian oil, and its protectionist stance on agriculture. The trade talks remain complex, with Europe insisting on strong intellectual property protections and India resisting what it sees as constraints on its generic pharmaceutical industry. Yet both sides are acutely aware of the stakes. The EU is India's largest trading partner, with bilateral trade exceeding €100 billion annually. India is the EU's ninth-largest trading partner, but its share is growing fast. A free trade agreement could more than double trade volumes within a decade, according to European Commission estimates. There are also strategic agreements being signed on the sidelines. A €10 billion infrastructure connectivity partnership, modelled on the EU's Global Gateway, aims to link India's digital and transport networks with Southeast Asia, Africa and Europe - challenging China's Belt and Road Initiative. Joint exercises between the Indian Navy and European navies in the Indian Ocean are becoming routine. The EU has also backed India's call for reform of the United Nations Security Council, including a permanent seat for New Delhi. Perhaps the most telling sign of the shift is the language used. European officials now speak of "de-risking" from China, not "decoupling" - and they see India as the key hedge. The European Union's new Indo-Pacific strategy, published last year, explicitly names India as a "natural partner" for navigating the region's strategic challenges. "The relationship is no longer a one-way street," observed a senior EU diplomat who spoke on condition of anonymity. "India knows its value. It knows Europe needs it more than it needs Europe. The challenge for us is to prove we are a reliable partner - and that is a very different conversation from what we were having a decade ago." As the summit concluded with a joint statement pledging to "deepen the strategic partnership", both sides acknowledged that tough negotiations lie ahead. But the tone, the posture and the underlying economic realities have all been transformed. Indian leaders may still feel overwhelmed in Brussels - but it is no longer the overwhelming weight of European condescension. It is the overwhelming weight of expectation, the sheer scale of the opportunity, and the complexity of a relationship that is no longer about aid, but about power. And that, for a country long cast as the poor relation, feels very different indeed.

"The net migration figure of over 600,000 last year," he says, "includes a huge number of international students who come here, pay fees, contribute to our economy, and often go home. That is not the same as permanent settlement." Yet the political climate has rarely been less favourable to such distinctions. Rishi Sunak's "stop the boats" pledge and Labour's promise to reduce net migration by tying it to skills training reflect a consensus that the numbers must fall. That is not a sensible policy for a country that wants to grow." His view is not universally popular. Migration experts point out that the system is already heavily tilted towards the skilled, and that the backlash is as much about culture and identity as economics. A YouGov poll this month found 64% of Britons want immigration reduced, with the highest concern among older voters in Conservative-held seats. Bilimoria acknowledges the strains, but says the solution is investment, not closing the door. "We need to build more homes, train more people, and invest in infrastructure. That is the answer – not turning our back on the world." As the election campaign gears up, immigration is set to dominate again. Bilimoria's voice is a counterpoint to the prevailing wind – but in a storm, it may struggle to be heard. The net migration figures, when they land, will tell only part of the story. The politics will tell the rest.
prefix: And this week's net migration figures will only add fuel to the argument. Suddenly it's difficult to find anyone who has anything good to say about it at all. But the recently installed Chancellor of the University of Birmingham Lord Karan Bilimoria says there is such a thing as "good immigration".

title: Islamist militant al-Shabab fighters have launched an attack on a Kenyan military base in southern Somalia.
text_ai: The al-Qaeda-linked group says it has killed more than 50 soldiers and seized military vehicles and weapons. But a Kenyan military spokesman said the dawn attack was repelled, the base was not overrun and scores of insurgents were killed in the fighting. The attack occurred at the El-Ade base, near the border between Somalia and Kenya, which has been used by Kenyan troops as part of the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (Atmis). Kenyan forces have been stationed there for years, helping to push al-Shabab out of key strongholds. The militants often use such raids to seize weapons and vehicles to replenish their arsenal. In a statement, al-Shabab claimed its fighters had killed 59 Kenyan soldiers and captured several armoured vehicles and heavy weaponry. The group released graphic footage showing burnt-out military trucks and what it said were the bodies of soldiers, though the authenticity of these images could not be independently verified. Analysts say the insurgents frequently exaggerate battlefield successes for propaganda purposes. Kenya Defence Forces (KDF) spokesperson Col Zipporah Kiio confirmed that an attack took place at around 05:00 local time, but insisted that it had been repelled. "Our troops responded swiftly and effectively. The base remains firmly under our control," she said. "Several al-Shabab fighters were killed, and others fled with injuries. We are assessing the situation and will provide more details later." The assault comes as al-Shabab continues to wage a deadly insurgency across much of southern and central Somalia. The group wants to overthrow the internationally recognised government and impose its own harsh interpretation of Islamic law. Despite losing swathes of territory in recent years, it retains the ability to stage complex attacks on military and civilian targets. Kenya has been a key contributor to the African Union force, and its soldiers have often been in the crosshairs of al-Shabab. In 2016, the group overran the same El-Ade base, killing dozens of Kenyan troops. That incident prompted a major review of security procedures. Witnesses in the nearby town of Dhobley reported hearing heavy gunfire and explosions for several hours. Some said they saw bodies of militants being removed from the area by the Kenyan forces. The exact number of casualties remains unclear, but the incident underscores the persistent threat that al-Shabab poses to regional security. The United Nations and African Union have called for restraint and for a full investigation into the fighting. For now, the base remains operational, but the rival narratives from both sides make it difficult to determine the true outcome of the dawn raid.

title: How successful robots have been in providing care and assistance to patients is expected to be revealed within the next two months.
text_ai: NHS Western Isles and NHS Shetland have been trialling the use of a robot called Giraff in patients' homes. Giraff stands 1.5m (4ft 11in) tall, has wheels and a screen instead of a head. A relative or carer - potentially miles away - can drive the machine around the house to check that everything is all right. The robots have been deployed in homes of elderly and vulnerable patients, allowing remote check-ins without the need for a physical visit. In the trial, relatives or carers log in via a web interface to drive the Giraff around, speak through its screen, and observe the patient's environment. But while the technology promises to reduce isolation and ease pressure on healthcare staff, questions remain about its effectiveness compared to human interaction. Dr. Fiona MacGregor, a consultant in elderly care at NHS Western Isles, said the trial had been "carefully monitored" to ensure patient safety. "We're looking at whether Giraff can help people stay in their own homes for longer," she said. "Early feedback suggests patients feel less lonely when they can see a familiar face, even through a screen. But we need robust data on whether this reduces hospital admissions or improves wellbeing." The robot's design is intentionally simple. It moves at a slow, steady pace and can be controlled from a laptop or smartphone. It cannot lift objects, administer medication, or respond to emergencies on its own – it is purely a communication tool. Yet proponents argue that even this limited capability can be transformative for housebound individuals who may go days without seeing another person. Critics, however, point to the risk of over-reliance on technology. "There's a real danger that robots become a substitute for proper human care," said Prof. James Henderson, a social care expert at the University of Glasgow. "We must ensure they supplement, not replace, face-to-face visits. The most vulnerable patients need touch, empathy, and human judgement – things a machine cannot provide." The trial also tested the robot in different settings: some patients had it for two months, others for six. Researchers collected data on how often it was used, whether families found it helpful, and whether it led to fewer emergency calls. One surprise finding was that some patients treated Giraff as a companion, naming it and talking to it even when no one was logged in. Results from both health boards are expected to be published by the end of March. If successful, the technology could be rolled out more widely, particularly in remote rural areas where district nurses face long travel times. But officials caution that cost is a factor: each Giraff unit costs around £4,000, though bulk purchasing could reduce that. In the meantime, patients like 82-year-old Murdo MacLeod from Stornoway have already become converts. "It's like having a window to the world," he said. "My daughter in Glasgow can pop in every evening. It's not the same as a hug, but it's better than being alone."

title: In our series of letters from African journalists, Yousra Elbagir of Sudan's Elephant Media group explains what it is like to live in a country subject to US sanctions.
text_ai: 2017 at first felt like new era for Sudan - a country often regarded as a pariah state. Subject to US sanctions for two decades for "sponsoring terrorism" - and with a president wanted for war crimes over the conflict in Darfur - life has not been easy for many Sudanese. Then, in October 2017, the United States lifted most of its trade embargo, a move that sparked cautious optimism. For the first time in 20 years, Sudanese could hope to reconnect with the global economy, to travel freely, and to see their currency stabilise. But that hope was short-lived. By 2018, the economy was in freefall. Inflation soared past 60%. The Sudanese pound lost more than half its value. And the political landscape, which had seemed to be shifting, hardened once more. The sanctions were originally imposed in 1997, after Sudan was accused of harbouring militants, including Osama bin Laden. They were tightened in 2006, over the government's role in the Darfur conflict. For ordinary Sudanese, the consequences have been profound. You cannot buy a new iPhone, because Apple won't ship to Sudan. You cannot use PayPal or international credit cards. You cannot rent a car abroad, or book a hotel room online, because your ID is not recognised by global booking systems. Even something as simple as updating a smartphone app can be a struggle, because the US-based Google Play Store refuses to accept Sudanese IP addresses. When the sanctions were partially lifted in 2017, many hoped that the worst was over. But the relief was conditional. The US kept Sudan on its list of state sponsors of terrorism, a designation that carries its own crushing restrictions. Banks around the world are terrified of doing business with anyone from a country on that list, for fear of US Treasury penalties. So even after the trade embargo was lifted, international wire transfers remained nearly impossible. Sudanese businessmen tell me they have to carry suitcases of cash to Dubai to pay for imports. The cost of doing business is astronomical. And then, in April 2019, the long-time leader Omar al-Bashir was ousted after months of protests. The civilian-led transitional government that followed desperately needed international support. It negotiated with the US to finally be removed from the terrorism list. In December 2020, that removal came. It felt like a second dawn. But the economic benefits have been slow to materialise, and the political situation remains fragile. A military coup in October 2021 derailed the transition. Today, Sudan is once again in turmoil, and the sanctions - though formally lifted - cast a long shadow. To live under sanctions is to live with a kind of invisible barrier. You are constantly reminded that your country is considered a threat. When I try to open a bank account in London, the manager looks at my Sudanese passport and asks for three additional forms of proof of address, a credit check from my home country, and a letter from my employer confirming my salary. I have all these things, but the process takes weeks. For a Syrian or an Iranian, it is even worse. The stigma is real. There is also the psychological toll. You grow up knowing that your country is on a list, that you are not welcome in many places. When I travel, I have to apply for a visa months in advance, even for short visits. My British friends can book a weekend in Morocco with a few clicks. I cannot. And the moment I land at an airport, I am pulled aside for "random" security checks. It happens every single time. The officers see my passport, see the word Sudan, and their tone changes. I have learned to be patient, to smile, to answer the same questions about my family, my job, my reasons for travelling. I have nothing to hide, but I feel like I am always on trial. Yet, despite everything, there is a resilience here that is hard to explain. Sudanese people are among the most resourceful I have ever met. When the internet goes down - which it does, frequently - people still find ways to communicate. When petrol shortages leave cars idle, people walk or use donkey carts. When the bread queues stretch for hours, families share what they have. There is a deep sense of community, a refusal to be broken. But the sanctions are not just an economic burden. They are also a political tool. They have been used to pressure governments, but they have rarely achieved their stated goals. In Sudan, they did not bring about democracy or human rights. They made life harder for ordinary people, while the ruling elite found ways to bypass them. The same is true in many other sanctioned countries. In 2017, I allowed myself to believe that a new era had truly begun. I have since learned to be more cautious. The sanctions may have been lifted, but the scars they left are deep. Sudan is still struggling to find its place in the world, and the memory of those two decades of isolation will not fade quickly. For now, we continue to live with the consequences, hoping that one day, the barriers will truly fall.

title: Human rights groups have condemned a Singapore court's decision that a law banning gay sex is constitutional.
text_ai: The Court of Appeal on Wednesday rejected two legal challenges arguing that the law, Section 377A, infringes on gay citizens' rights. Under Section 377A, men who engage in "gross indecency" privately or publicly can be jailed for up to two years. Singapore, which largely remains conservative, has seen intense debate in recent years over gay rights. Human rights groups expressed deep disappointment, calling the verdict a "setback for equality and human dignity in Singapore." The decision effectively upholds a colonial-era statute that has long been a focal point for activists. "This is not just about a law that is rarely enforced," said a spokesperson for the local group Pink Dot. "It is about the message it sends: that gay men are second-class citizens whose private lives are a matter for the state." But the government has consistently defended Section 377A, arguing that it reflects the moral values of the majority. Attorney-General Lucien Wong told the court that the law was not discriminatory because it applied equally to all men and that its existence did not prevent the state from offering other protections to the LGBT community. "Society's views are evolving, but the law should not be used as a tool for social engineering ahead of that evolution," he said. Singapore remains one of several former British colonies in Asia that retain such laws, though enforcement has been rare in recent decades. The case was brought by three men — including a retired doctor and a DJ — who argued that the law violated their constitutional rights to equality and privacy. The Court of Appeal, however, ruled that the ban was "not irrational" and fell within Parliament's authority to legislate on public morality. The ruling comes amid a wider debate over gay rights in the city-state. While public attitudes have gradually liberalised, especially among younger Singaporeans, the conservative establishment has held firm. Last year, Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong said the government would not repeal the law, but would also not actively enforce it. Activists say such a position leaves the LGBT community in a legal limbo. Human rights groups now warn that the decision could embolden other governments in the region to resist reform. "Singapore is often seen as a model of rule of law and economic progress," said Phil Robertson, deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch. "This verdict undermines that image and sends a troubling signal that discrimination is acceptable." The case may now be taken up by Singapore's Parliament, but observers say a repeal remains politically unlikely in the near term.

title: Hundreds of people have attended two rallies calling for Wales to become an independent country within the EU.
text_ai: Campaign group A Free Wales in Europe/Cymru Rydd yn Ewrop gathered on the Maes in Caernarfon, Gwynedd, and Cardiff on Saturday. It follows the referendum decision, which saw 52.5% of voters in Wales vote leave. Pro-Brexit campaigner David Jones MP said what the campaign group called for was "profoundly undemocratic". The rallies, which organisers said drew several hundred participants, took place amid ongoing debate over Wales's constitutional future. In Caernarfon, speakers addressed the crowd in both Welsh and English, emphasising what they described as the "democratic anomaly" of Wales having voted to remain in the EU yet being taken out of the bloc. "Wales is a nation with its own distinct identity and history," said Gwenllian Lansdown, a spokesperson for the group. "The 2016 referendum did not give a mandate to take us out of Europe permanently. We deserve a proper say on our future relationship." The Cardiff event, held in the city's Cathays Park, featured similar calls for a future independence referendum. Supporters waved Welsh and EU flags, with some carrying placards reading "Wales for Europe" and "Independence in Europe". Among those attending was retired teacher Angharad Thomas, 68, from Pontypridd, who said she felt "disenfranchised" by Brexit. "I voted Remain, like the majority of Welsh voters. Now we are locked out of the single market and freedom of movement," she told the BBC. "An independent Wales in the EU is the only way to restore our voice." However, the pro-Brexit campaigner and former Welsh secretary David Jones described the group's position as "nonsensical". Speaking to the BBC, he said: "The people of Wales voted decisively in 2016 to leave the European Union. To overturn that result through independence would be profoundly undemocratic. The Welsh electorate have repeatedly shown they do not support separation from the UK." The rallies come as support for Welsh independence has fluctuated in opinion polls, typically garnering between 20% and 30% backing in recent years. The Welsh Government, led by Labour, has ruled out holding an independence referendum in the current term. A spokesperson said the government's focus was on "delivering for Wales within the Union". Organisers of Saturday's events said they planned further actions, including a rally in Llangollen next month. They insisted the campaign was about democratic renewal, not division. "We are not anti-English," said Ms Lansdown. "We are pro-Welsh and pro-European — and that is a positive, forward-looking message." The police reported no incidents at either gathering. Both rallies concluded peacefully by late afternoon.

title: It was the discovery of a lifetime, an audacious Indiana Jones-style story of daring diving that uncovered a 400-year-old long-lost haul of Spanish treasure.
text_ai: When Belgian Robert Sténuit discovered pieces of eight in the murky, freezing seabed off Northern Ireland's north coast 50 years ago he knew he'd finally found it. Gold and artefacts deposited at the resting place of one of the most important ships in the Spanish Armada - the Girona. The first glint of gold in his torchlight was unmistakable. Sténuit, a 31-year-old former Belgian army officer turned professional diver, had spent years chasing legends. Now, 400 years after the Girona's final, violent plunge, he was staring at a hoard that would rewrite naval history. The Girona was no ordinary galleon. Part of the Spanish Armada, the great fleet dispatched by King Philip II to invade England in 1588, she was a 645-tonne warship armed with 50 guns and carrying some 1,500 men. After the Armada's disastrous defeat by English fireships and storms, the surviving ships tried to limp home around Scotland and Ireland. The Girona, badly damaged, sought refuge in the neutral port of Killybegs on the Irish coast. There, she was repaired and took on survivors from two other wrecked Armada ships, the Duquesa Santa Ana and the Santa María de la Rosa. Her complement swelled to nearly 1,300 men. ## A desperate escape On 28 October 1588, against the advice of local pilots, the Girona set sail for Scotland. A fierce gale blew up. The ship was driven onto the rocks at Lacada Point, near the Giant's Causeway in what is now County Antrim. She broke up within minutes. Only nine men survived – a miracle of sorts, but hollow given the scale of loss. The wreck settled in 12 to 15 metres of water, hidden by shifting sands and treacherous currents. For four centuries, the Girona became a ghost story. Fishermen spoke of catching coins in their nets. In the 1960s, amateur divers found a few cannonballs. But the precise location remained a puzzle – until Sténuit and his team from the Belgian Historical and Archaeological Diving Club took up the challenge. Sténuit had already made a name for himself. In 1966, he had been part of a team that located the wreck of the Dutch East Indiaman *Hollandia* off the Isles of Scilly. But the Girona was different. It was not just a wreck; it was a time capsule. ## The dive On the morning of 2 July 1967, Sténuit descended into the grey, churning water. Visibility was poor. He could barely see his hand in front of his face. He followed a reef line, feeling his way along the rocky bottom. Then, his fingers brushed against something solid and round. He brought it to his mask: a silver piece of eight, stamped with the arms of Bourbon and Spain. He knew instantly. "This is it," he later recalled thinking. "I have found the Girona." Over the following weeks, Sténuit and his team recovered a staggering haul: 12,000 gold and silver coins, solid-gold jewellery, intricately engraved silver plates, and religious artefacts. Among the most spectacular finds were a gold salamander pendant studded with rubies, a mother-of-pearl necklace, and a golden dolphin brooch. The treasure's estimated value at the time was nearly £7 million – and its historical worth was incalculable. But the Girona's story is not just about gold. The coins told of the reach of the Spanish Empire: pieces from Mexico, Peru, and Potosí. The medallions, crucifixes, and rosaries spoke of faith amid catastrophe. And the personal items – a gold ring with the initials of an unknown sailor, a set of surgeon's instruments – brought the human cost into sharp focus. ## Ownership and controversy The discovery sparked immediate legal battles. Under British law, the wreck was technically Crown property. The Irish government also laid claim, arguing the waters fell within its jurisdiction. Sténuit and his team had to navigate a complex web of international maritime law, salvage rights, and heritage protection. In the end, a compromise was reached. The collection – now considered one of the finest examples of Armada treasure ever recovered – was bought by the Ulster Museum in Belfast for £1.8 million. It remains on display there, a permanent reminder of the Armada's fateful voyage. Sténuit himself became a reluctant celebrity. He gave interviews, wrote a book, and helped inspire a generation of underwater archaeologists. But he never profited hugely. "The real treasure," he once said, "is the knowledge we gained." ## Legacy Half a century on, the Girona excavation is still studied as a model of careful underwater recovery. Sténuit's meticulous documentation – every object photographed and catalogued in situ – was pioneering. It was a far cry from the treasure-hunting free-for-alls that had marked earlier salvage attempts. The wreck also deepened understanding of the Spanish Armada. For years, the story had been told from an English perspective – the heroic defeat of a Catholic invasion. The Girona's artefacts, particularly the religious items, revealed the deeply pious nature of the Spanish crew. They went into battle clutching crucifixes, praying for victory, and perhaps for salvation. Today, the site off Lacada Point is protected under the Northern Ireland Monuments and Archaeological Objects Order. Divers are banned from disturbing it. The memory of the Girona rests, as it should, in the cold, dark water, its secrets safely sealed. As for Robert Sténuit, he died in 2023 at the age of 87. But his name is forever linked to that moment when a beam of torchlight caught the gleam of silver, and a lost chapter of history was brought back to the surface.

title: Iran is ready to show more transparency on its nuclear programme, says President-elect Hassan Rouhani.
text_ai: In his first news conference since Friday's election, Mr Rouhani described as "unfair" sanctions imposed on his country. He also said Tehran would not suspend uranium enrichment activities. The West suspects Iran of trying to develop nuclear weapons. Iran says its programme is entirely peaceful. In his first news conference since Friday's election, Mr Rouhani described as "unfair" sanctions imposed on his country. He also said Tehran would not suspend uranium enrichment activities. The West suspects Iran of trying to develop nuclear weapons. Iran says its programme is entirely peaceful. But the president-elect struck a noticeably more conciliatory tone than his predecessor, Mahmoud Ahmadinejad, who often used his own press conferences to rail against the West and question the Holocaust. "We will be more transparent and we will show that the Islamic Republic of Iran is not acting against international regulations," Mr Rouhani said, speaking in fluent Arabic and occasionally switching to Persian. He added: "The world should know that the era of intimidation has passed. There is a new atmosphere in the country." Mr Rouhani, a former nuclear negotiator, was elected in a landslide victory on Friday, securing more than 50% of the vote in the first round. His campaign focused on a pledge to "re-engage" with the international community and seek a lifting of the crippling economic sanctions that have isolated Iran and sent its inflation rate soaring above 30%. Analysts say his remarks on Tuesday were a calculated attempt to reassure both domestic hardliners and foreign powers that Iran's nuclear programme – which the West fears is a cover for weapons development – would not be abandoned, but would be conducted with greater openness. "The idea is to signal that Iran is willing to negotiate seriously while not giving up its right to enrich uranium under the Non-Proliferation Treaty," said Dr Mahsa Rouhi, a Middle East analyst at the Institute for Strategic Studies in Tehran. Mr Rouhani served as Iran's chief nuclear negotiator from 2003 to 2005, a period when Tehran voluntarily suspended enrichment and reached a deal with Britain, France and Germany – only to see the talks collapse after the election of Mr Ahmadinejad. That experience appears to have shaped his current approach. He explicitly stated that Iran would not stop enriching, but suggested that the country could accept more intrusive inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) to verify that its programme remains peaceful. "We are ready to show greater transparency and to build trust," he said. "But we will never bow to pressure." The West's response was cautious. The White House said it welcomed "more responsible rhetoric" from Iran but stressed that "words must be matched by actions". The European Union's foreign policy chief, Catherine Ashton, said she was ready to work with Mr Rouhani "if he is serious about engaging". The United Nations Security Council has imposed four rounds of sanctions on Iran since 2006, and the US and EU have added their own targeted measures aimed at Iran's energy and banking sectors. These have hit the economy hard, pushing oil exports down by more than a third and driving up unemployment. Mr Rouhani said these sanctions were "unfair" and "illogical", and argued that they were harming ordinary Iranians, not the government. He vowed to pursue a policy of "constructive interaction" with the world, though he did not specify how quickly he would seek to reopen talks with the so-called P5+1 group – the US, UK, France, Russia, China and Germany. "Dialogue is the only way to solve the issue," he said. Domestically, Mr Rouhani's comments were seen as a delicate balancing act. Hardliners in Iran's political and military establishment have long insisted that enrichment is a "red line" that cannot be crossed, and the president-elect was careful not to appear weak. "The supreme leader has the final say on the nuclear issue, and Mr Rouhani knows he cannot deviate from that," said Dr Saeed Khorshidi, a political scientist at the University of Tehran. Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iran's supreme leader, has repeatedly stated that he is not opposed to nuclear talks but has expressed deep distrust of the United States. However, he has also signalled that he may be open to a more pragmatic approach under the new president. The nuclear standoff has been a central issue in Iranian politics for over a decade, and Mr Rouhani's election has raised hopes in the West that a diplomatic breakthrough might be possible. But analysts warn that the positions of both sides remain deeply entrenched, and that significant progress will be slow. "The scale of mistrust is enormous," said Dr Simon Henderson, director of the Gulf and Energy Programme at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. "It took years to get to this point, and it will take years to get out of it." Mr Rouhani is due to take office in early August. In the meantime, he said he would form a new negotiating team and begin internal preparations for a fresh round of talks. "Those who think that the era of Iran's passivity has ended are correct," he said. "The era of interaction has begun."

title: In a video filmed in June, 14-year-old Khorshid tips her skateboard off the high edge of a quarter-pipe, at Kabul's indoor skatepark.
text_ai: She appears fearless - and she was, say her friends, until she was killed by a Taliban suicide bomber last weekend. A bright pink blur, she launches at speed over the ramps and berms at the skateboard park, called Skateistan. Khorshid, whose full name is being withheld for security reasons, was among dozens of victims of a devastating blast that tore through a crowded market in the Dasht-e-Barchi district of western Kabul last Saturday. The predominantly Shia Hazara area has been a repeated target of the Islamic State Khorasan Province (ISKP), a rival of the Taliban, which claimed responsibility for the attack. But for Khorshid's friends at Skateistan, the distinction between the perpetrators matters little. What matters is that a vibrant, laughing presence has been extinguished. "She was the heart of our group," says 16-year-old Laila, cradling a skateboard decorated with stickers of flowers and a faded Afghan flag. "She was always the first to try a new trick, even if it meant falling. She said falling was just part of learning to fly." Laila pauses, wiping her eyes with the sleeve of her sweatshirt. "On Saturday, she was just buying bread for her mother. She wasn't doing anything dangerous." Skateistan, a non-profit organisation that runs educational and skating programmes across Afghanistan, opened its Kabul indoor facility in 2012. It was a radical concept in a deeply conservative country where girls' sports were, under the previous Taliban regime from 1996 to 2001, effectively banned. Even after the Taliban's return to power in August 2021, Skateistan has continued to operate, albeit under strict new rules. Girls can still skate, but only in gender-segregated sessions and with their faces covered. Khorshid, according to her instructors, always wore a pink hijab and a loose-fitting tunic, skating with an intensity that defied the limitations. The programme's founder, Oliver Percovich, said from Berlin that the team was "devastated" by the loss. "Khorshid represented everything that Skateistan stands for: courage, determination and joy in the face of adversity," he said in a statement. "She was a leader among her peers, always helping younger children strap on pads or encouraging those who were scared. She will be deeply missed." In the video from June, which has been viewed thousands of times on social media, Khorshid appears utterly concentrated. Her body leans into a carving turn, her arms outstretched for balance. She doesn't smile — this is serious business — but her eyes are alight. The quarter-pipe she tips her board off is the tallest in the park, a steep curve of polished wood that many older skaters avoid. "She just went for it," says another friend, 15-year-old Ahmad, shaking his head. "She wasn't afraid. But now we are all afraid." The suicide bombing in Dasht-e-Barchi killed at least 68 people and wounded more than 120, according to hospital sources. Many were women and children shopping ahead of the Eid al-Adha holiday. Khorshid's mother, a widow who had lost two sons to previous attacks, is said to be in a state of profound shock. Neighbours have been bringing food, but she has not left her home. For the remaining skateboarders, the park has become a place of mourning. Boards lean against walls, unridden. A small shrine of flowers and candles has appeared near the entrance, with a handwritten note: "Khorshid, you taught us to fly. Now you are an angel." The Taliban's Ministry of Interior has condemned the attack but offered little detail on security improvements. Many in the Hazara community feel abandoned. "We are not safe in our own city," says a shopkeeper who knew Khorshid's family. "Skateistan gave these girls hope. But hope does not stop a bomb." Khorshid's death is the second recent tragedy to strike the skateboarding community in Kabul. In March, a 12-year-old boy was killed in a separate blast while walking home from a session. Skateistan has launched a fund to support Khorshid's family and to reinforce mental health services at the park. "Skateboarding teaches you resilience," says Laila, picking up her board. "But some things are too big to just get back up from. Khorshid is not coming back. But her spirit is here. We will skate for her." She turns the board over, fingers tracing the grip tape. The video of Khorshid is still playing on a loop on a phone nearby. A bright pink blur, mid-air, suspended for a moment against the grey walls of Kabul. Then the clip ends.

title: Israel's parliament has passed a law that would allow it to impeach an MP who incites racism or supports armed struggle against the state.
text_ai: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the measure ended an "absurd situation" whereby someone who "supports terror" was allowed to serve in the Knesset. But critics said it was anti-democratic and aimed mainly at Israeli Arab MPs. The law would require three-quarters of the Knesset's 120 members to vote in favour of any impeachment motion. The threshold, at 90 votes, is deliberately high, meaning the measure would require cross-party support. Yet critics argue that the very existence of such a law could chill dissent and be used selectively against Arab lawmakers, who make up about a fifth of the Knesset. “This is not about fighting extremism — it’s about silencing political opposition,” said Ayman Odeh, leader of the Joint List, a predominantly Arab alliance. “They want to criminalise our legitimate struggle for equality and peace.” Odeh’s party has been a frequent target of right-wing ire, with previous attempts to ban individual members failing due to legal obstacles. The new legislation amends the Basic Law on the Knesset, giving the full chamber the power to remove an MP who “incites racism” or “supports armed struggle against the state of Israel”. Supporters insist it closes a loophole: under the old rules, a parliamentary committee could recommend a suspension, but the process was lengthy and often blocked by political manoeuvring. “An MP who backs terror cannot be a lawmaker,” Mr Netanyahu told reporters after the vote. “Now there is a clear mechanism to remove them.” His coalition government, a patchwork of right-wing, religious and centrist parties, pushed the bill through despite opposition boycotts and procedural complaints. But legal experts warned the law could be abused. The definition of “inciting racism” is broad, they note, and could encompass legitimate criticism of state policy. “This gives the majority the power to interpret what is racist in a deeply politicised environment,” said Dr. Amnon Rubinstein, a former justice minister. “It risks turning the Knesset into a place where only one viewpoint is safe.” The vote comes amid heightened tensions between Israel’s Jewish majority and its Arab minority, which makes up about 20% of the population. Arab leaders have long complained of discrimination and of being treated as second-class citizens. Rights groups say the law is the latest in a series of measures — including the 2018 Nation-State law, which declared Israel the nation-state of the Jewish people — that erode democratic space. Internationally, the move drew swift condemnation. The European Union said it was “deeply concerned about any legislation that could restrict the democratic rights of elected representatives”. The United States State Department urged Israel to “uphold the democratic values that have always been the bedrock of its society”. Despite the high impeachment threshold, opposition MPs say the law will have a chilling effect. “This is a dangerous political weapon,” said Merav Michaeli of the Labour Party. “They have created a sword that can hang over any MP who dares to criticise the government.” The law’s supporters counter that it is no different from similar provisions in other democracies — including the United Kingdom, where MPs can be expelled for “conduct which is so serious as to warrant disqualification”. They point out that any impeachment would require the consent of a three-quarters majority, making it a safeguard against partisan abuse. But with the next election due by 2023 at the latest, and with Mr Netanyahu facing a corruption trial, the timing of the law has raised eyebrows. “This is not about principles,” said Odeh. “It’s about trying to distract the public and crush anyone who stands in the way.” The law now awaits a final reading before taking effect — a process that could be completed within days.

title: International talks in Bonn have made progress towards a new global deal on climate change, says the UN, amid calls from NGOs for a faster pace.
text_ai: Countries are working towards options to limit greenhouse gas emissions from 2020 in time for a crunch Paris summit. The UN said progress had been made towards streamlining the text of a new agreement at talks in Bonn. Environmental groups said ''difficult issues'' such as finance and emissions cuts had yet to be addressed. The two-week negotiating session in the German city, which ended on Friday, was intended to condense a sprawling 86-page draft negotiating text into a more manageable document ahead of December's UN climate conference in Paris. Delegates said they had reduced the number of bracketed passages — indicating areas of disagreement — from over 1,000 to roughly 900. While modest, UN climate chief Christiana Figueres described the progress as "significant" given the complexity of the task. "We have seen a real willingness to engage constructively and to find common ground," she told reporters. "The pace is picking up, but we need to accelerate further." However, environmental groups expressed frustration that key political decisions were being deferred. "Negotiators have done important technical work, but they have barely scratched the surface of the hardest questions," said Samantha Smith of WWF International. "Finance, long-term emissions goals, and how to share the effort fairly between rich and poor nations remain unresolved." The talks come as countries are required to submit their national pledges for cutting or curbing emissions by the first quarter of 2015. So far, major emitters including the US, EU, and China have submitted their plans, but several large developing nations such as India and Brazil have yet to do so. The Bonn session also saw renewed tensions over the issue of "loss and damage" — compensation for poor countries already suffering from climate impacts. Wealthy nations resisted calls for a formal mechanism, arguing it could open the door to unlimited liability. "We cannot have a Paris agreement that ignores the reality of loss and damage for the most vulnerable," said Nawaj Sharif, lead negotiator for the least developed countries. A key sticking point remains the long-term goal. The EU and many developing nations want a commitment to decarbonise the global economy by 2050, but fossil fuel-dependent countries, including Saudi Arabia and other OPEC members, have pushed back. The US has also been cautious, preferring to leave the goal open-ended. Observers say the Paris deal will need to bridge these competing visions if it is to be both ambitious and universally accepted. With only two more formal negotiating sessions scheduled before Paris — in June in Bonn and a final meeting in October — the clock is ticking. "We are making headway, but the real crunch is yet to come," said Alden Meyer of the Union of Concerned Scientists. "The political decisions cannot be postponed much longer." The UN says it remains confident that a robust, legally binding agreement can be reached in December, but success will depend on trust and compromise between developed and developing nations.

title: International trade secretary Liam Fox gave a speech on Thursday about the benefits of free trade.
text_ai: The claim: The European Union would lose out more than the UK from the introduction of tariffs. Reality Check verdict: The EU would risk more in cash terms. The UK would risk a higher proportion of its exports. "Don't just look at it from a UK perspective," he said. Mr Fox went on to argue that the UK's departure from the EU would allow it to strike new trade agreements with fast-growing economies, such as India and China, and that these would more than compensate for any loss of access to European markets. "The opportunities are immense," he told an audience of business leaders in London. "We are not just leaving the EU; we are rejoining the world." But his optimism was not universally shared. Critics pointed out that the EU is still the UK's largest trading partner, accounting for 44% of all British exports in 2019. Dr Anna Jerzewska, a trade policy analyst, said: "The idea that we can easily replace that with new deals elsewhere ignores the reality of supply chains and the time it takes to negotiate comprehensive agreements." The speech came as the government published its updated tariff regime, due to take effect from January 2021. Under the new UK Global Tariff, tariffs on many goods will be scrapped or reduced, but some agricultural products and cars will still face charges. Mr Fox insisted this would lower prices for consumers and boost competition. However, the EU has warned that any divergence from existing standards could lead to costly non-tariff barriers. A European Commission spokesperson said: "We will not sacrifice the integrity of the single market. The UK will have to accept that access comes with rules." The debate over tariffs is central to the ongoing trade negotiations, which are deadlocked over fishing rights and level playing field commitments. With just months until the transition period ends, both sides have warned they are prepared to walk away without a deal. Mr Fox's speech was seen by many as an attempt to rally domestic support for a no-deal outcome, portraying it not as a failure but as a "liberation". Yet for businesses already struggling with the impact of coronavirus, the prospect of new customs checks and tariffs in January is unsettling. One exporter of Scottish salmon told the BBC that a no-deal Brexit would be "catastrophic", adding: "We cannot simply pivot overnight to selling to China." Mr Fox acknowledged the short-term disruption but insisted the long-term prize was worth it. "No great nation ever achieved greatness by hiding behind barriers," he concluded.

title: India's restive Jammu and Kashmir state is again facing crisis following the death of chief minister Mufti Mohammad Sayeed on 7 January.
text_ai: His daughter and heir apparent Mehbooba Mufti has so far declined to take oath as his successor, pushing the state under federal rule. Mr Sayeed was heading a tricky coalition with India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) - one he stitched together following intense back-door and open negotiations. His daughter and heir apparent Mehbooba Mufti has so far declined to take oath as his successor, pushing the state under federal rule. Mr Sayeed was heading a tricky coalition with India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) - one he stitched together following intense back-door and open negotiations. The decision to keep the state under governor's rule - effectively central government control - was announced late on Thursday by a spokesman for the federal Home Ministry. It came after days of frantic political consultations in Srinagar and New Delhi, with no clear breakthrough in sight. The Bharatiya Janata Party, which holds 25 seats in the 87-member state assembly, had made it clear it would not support any government headed by Mehbooba Mufti unless she formally confirmed the alliance first. But she has insisted she needs time to consult party workers and the people of Kashmir before taking that step. The political paralysis has deep roots. Mr Sayeed's Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) won 28 seats in the 2014 assembly elections - the most of any single party, but far short of a majority. The BJP, with its 25 seats, emerged as the second-largest party. An alliance between the two seemed almost unthinkable at first: the BJP is a Hindu-nationalist party that advocates for the full integration of Muslim-majority Jammu and Kashmir into India, while the PDP has traditionally championed greater autonomy and a resolution of the long-running insurgency through dialogue with separatist groups. Yet after five months of tortuous negotiations, including a secret meeting between Mr Sayeed and Prime Minister Narendra Modi in New Delhi, the unlikely pact was sealed in March 2015. The agreement was built on a fragile set of compromises: the BJP agreed to soften its stance on controversial issues like the revocation of Article 370, which grants special status to the state; the PDP, in turn, agreed to a "zero tolerance" policy towards militants from across the border. Many analysts described it as a "marriage of convenience" that satisfied neither party's core base. Mr Sayeed, a seasoned politician who had served as chief minister before and also as union minister, was seen as the glue that held the coalition together. His death at the age of 79, following complications from pneumonia, has exposed the fragility of that arrangement. "He was the only one who could manage the BJP's scepticism about the PDP and also sell the alliance to a deeply divided electorate," said political commentator Riyaz Bhat in Srinagar. "Without him, the coalition risks unravelling completely." Mehbooba Mufti, 56, is herself a political veteran, having served as a member of parliament and as a state minister. She is widely viewed as a charismatic leader with a strong base in the Pir Panjal region, her father's traditional stronghold. But she has also faced criticism for being erratic and for lacking the strategic patience her father possessed. Her refusal to take the oath has been interpreted by some as a tactical move to extract better terms from the BJP - or perhaps to force early elections that could boost her party's standing. The BJP, for its part, appears unwilling to make further concessions. Party leaders have privately expressed frustration that the PDP is not honouring the terms of the 2015 alliance, particularly on issues of security and the establishment of a boards for the development of the state's most backward regions. "We entered this alliance with the PDP in good faith, but it seems some in their party still want to have a foot in both camps - one with us, and one with the separatists," a senior BJP leader told the BBC on condition of anonymity. Governor's rule has been imposed in Jammu and Kashmir before, most recently in 2014 for several months before the elections. It means that the state will be administered by the governor, acting on the advice of the central government. The governor can issue ordinances and exercise powers normally reserved for the council of ministers. For the people of the state, it often signals a return to a more direct form of federal control, which many resent. The imposition of governor's rule also raises the stakes for both the PDP and the BJP. If no stable government can be formed within six months, fresh elections will be called. That could be risky for both parties: the BJP's growth in the Kashmir Valley has largely stalled, while the PDP has seen defections of its legislators to rival camps. Separatist leaders, meanwhile, have called for a political resolution to the conflict rather than a return to the ballot box. On the streets of Srinagar, reactions were mixed. "Why should we be forced to accept a government that doesn't represent our aspirations?" asked Bilal Ahmad, a shopkeeper in the old city. Others expressed a desire for stability. "We need someone who can govern, not just endless talks and confusion," said a woman who gave her name as Fatima. The coming weeks will test whether a new coalition can be resurrected. Meetings between PDP leaders and BJP interlocutors are expected to resume after the period of mourning ends. But with the state now under federal rule, time is short, and the political temperature is rising. For Mehbooba Mufti, the dilemma is acute: take the oath and risk alienating her base, or hold out and see the state slip into another period of uncertainty. The legacy of her father, and the future of his party, hang in the balance.

title: In the not-too-distant future, our fields could be tilled, sown, tended and harvested entirely by fleets of co-operating autonomous machines by land and air.
text_ai: And they'll be working both day and night. Driverless tractors that can follow pre-programmed routes are already being deployed at large farms around the world. Drones are buzzing over fields assessing crop health and soil conditions. Ground sensors are monitoring the amount of water and nutrients in the soil, triggering irrigation and fertiliser applications. But these are just the opening moves in a revolution that could fundamentally reshape not only agriculture, but the rural economies and landscapes that have defined human civilisation for millennia. The fully autonomous farm of the future is no longer a speculative concept. Researchers at institutions like Harper Adams University in Shropshire and the University of Lincoln have already demonstrated prototype systems where a single operator oversees a fleet of machines from a control room miles away. These "swarms" of smaller, lighter robots can work together, communicating with each other and with satellites to perform tasks with a precision that no human driver could match. "We're moving from the age of the big tractor to the age of the intelligent swarm," says Prof Simon Blackmore, head of agricultural robotics at Harper Adams. "A large tractor weighing 20 tonnes compacts the soil, wastes energy, and treats every part of the field the same. A swarm of small robots can treat each plant individually. They can apply a drop of pesticide precisely where it's needed, not a blanket spray across the whole field. This is not just about replacing the driver – it's about rethinking the entire system." That rethinking is already underway in the fields of the East of England, where the Hands Free Hectare project demonstrated the world's first crop grown entirely by robots. The project used a small autonomous tractor and a drone to sow, tend and harvest a crop of spring barley. While the yield was lower than conventional farming – about 4.5 tonnes per hectare compared with a typical 7 tonnes – the project proved the principle. Since then, the technology has advanced rapidly. Start-ups in the UK and abroad are now producing commercial swarms. Small, solar-powered robots weighing just a few kilograms can weed fields using artificial intelligence to distinguish crops from weeds, then either zap them with a targeted laser or remove them with a mechanical arm. Others can plant seeds at precise depths, apply fertiliser only where soil sensors indicate a deficiency, and monitor for pests using spectral cameras. The potential benefits are enormous. By eliminating the need for heavy machinery, soil compaction – a major cause of reduced yields and increased run-off – can be dramatically reduced. By applying inputs only where needed, farmers could use dramatically less water, fertiliser and pesticide. The UK’s Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board (AHDB) estimates that precision farming techniques could reduce fertiliser use by up to 30% and pesticide use by up to 90%. "Precision is the key to sustainability," says Dr Helen Metcalfe, an agricultural economist at the University of Reading. "We are facing a future where the global population will approach 10 billion by 2050, and agricultural production must increase by 60% to feed everyone. At the same time, we need to reduce the environmental footprint of farming. Automation offers a path to square that circle." But the road to the fully autonomous farm is not without its obstacles. The most immediate is cost. While the price of sensors and computing power has fallen, the upfront investment for a fleet of robots and the necessary connectivity infrastructure remains high. For the many small family farms that still dominate the landscape of the UK and Europe, these costs can be prohibitive. "We can't just have a two-tier system where large agribusinesses have all the benefits and small farmers are left behind," warns Dr Metcalfe. "That would exacerbate the existing trend of consolidation and rural depopulation. There will need to be co-operative models – sharing of equipment, or 'robotics as a service' – to make the technology accessible." Then there is the issue of connectivity. Autonomous machines rely on robust, low-latency data links, both to communicate with each other and to access cloud-based AI models for decision-making. In rural areas, where mobile and broadband coverage is often patchy, this is a significant challenge. The UK government has pledged to extend 5G coverage to rural areas, but progress has been slow. Regulation is another hurdle. Current UK law requires that an agricultural vehicle be operated by a person with a licence, and that it be insured in the conventional way. The Department for Transport is consulting on changes to allow for remote supervision of autonomous vehicles, but the timeline for legislative change is uncertain. There are also questions of liability: if a robot fails and causes damage or injury, who is responsible – the manufacturer, the software developer, or the farmer who deployed it? These are not insurmountable problems, but they will require a concerted effort from industry, government and academia. The UK – with its world-leading agricultural research, its strong robotics sector, and its highly productive farming industry – is well placed to lead the way. The government's Farming Innovation Programme has already awarded millions of pounds to projects developing robotics and automation. "The next 10 years will be transformative," says Prof Blackmore. "We will see the first commercial farms running entirely autonomously, probably in controlled environments like glasshouses or polytunnels. Then, as costs come down and reliability improves, we will see it spread to open fields. By 2040, it's likely that a significant proportion of arable farming in the UK will be done by machines that never need a coffee break." The implications for the workforce are profound. Agriculture is one of the largest employers in the world, and in the UK it provides jobs for around 470,000 people. Many of those jobs are physically demanding, seasonal and low-paid. Automation could eliminate some of the most arduous tasks – such as fruit picking or weeding – but it will also create new roles in machine supervision, data analysis and system maintenance. "There may well be fewer people working directly on the land," says Dr Metcalfe. "But those people will need new skills. We will need agronomists who can interpret data, engineers who can maintain the robots, and technicians who can program the swarms. The key will be to ensure a just transition – retraining workers and supporting rural communities through the change." The environmental case for the autonomous farm is powerful, but it is not without its critics. Some argue that a high-tech, data-driven approach risks deepening the industrialisation of agriculture, moving further away from nature-friendly farming practices that prioritise biodiversity and soil health. Yet proponents counter that the very precision of robotics makes it possible to reconcile productivity with ecology. "Imagine a field where the robot avoids the skylark's nest, applies fertiliser only where the crop needs it, and leaves strips of wildflowers for pollinators," says Prof Blackmore. "That is what autonomous farming can deliver – a level of care and precision that is simply impossible at the scale of the modern tractor." As dusk falls on the rolling fields of Shropshire, the first generation of these agricultural robots is already at work. They are small, quiet and unobtrusive, their progress marked only by a faint hum and a blinking LED. They do not replace the farmer's eye for the land, but they augment it with a thousand sensors and a tireless attention to detail. The fields of the future may not be empty, but they will be different – and the change, once begun, will be as irreversible as the plough.
